payload_json: {"assumptions":["the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph","a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster","a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure","typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993751+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5e3fa35e1a6d931ebdc3e155642b0dc3bd61f17553d02dc415ed8ee523ff71e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps scales as n^{1/(2+theta)} for some theta>0 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate showing R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) grows faster than linearly, of order r^{1+theta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. Combining volume growth and resistance growth via the Nash/heat-kernel machinery, or a direct expected-exit-time computation, gives the subdiffusive exponent. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-07T05:37:56.275926+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2509.26030, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_b5e9402766bd4ba38427f09638ab674f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5.3 of arXiv:2509.26030, 'Muon Outperforms Adam in Tail-End Associative Memory Learning'] If Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 hold, with fixed $\\alpha,\\beta$ such that $\\alpha\\neq\\beta$, and $K$ goes to infinity, we obtain the following results for one-step gd, Muon, and Adam. • For gd, for any $\\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\\displaystyle\\varrho_{\\text{GD}}^{\\epsilon}=O(\\epsilon^{-r(\\alpha,\\beta)}K^{r(\\alpha,\\beta)-1}),\\text{ where }r(\\alpha,\\beta)=\\min\\bigg\\{\\frac{\\alpha(1-\\beta)}{\\beta(1-\\alpha)},\\frac{\\beta(1-\\alpha)}{\\alpha(1-\\beta)}\\bigg\\}<1.$ • For Muon, for any $\\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\\displaystyle\\varrho_{\\text{Muon}}^{\\epsilon}\\geq 1-\\epsilon\\bigg(1+O\\bigg(\\frac{\\log K}{K}\\bigg)\\bigg),\\text{ and }G_{\\text{Muon}}(W_{0})=-\\widetilde{E}E^{\\top}+O\\bigg(\\frac{1}{K}\\widetilde{E}J_{K,K}E^{\\top}\\bigg),$ where $J_{K,K}\\in\\mathbb{R}^{K\\times K}$ is the matrix with all elements equal to $1$. The big- $O$ notation for matrices means that for $A=O(B)$, each entry satisfies $A_{ij}=O(B_{ij})$ for all $i,j$. • For Adam, there exist $\\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\\varrho_{\\text{SignGD}}^{\\epsilon}\\geq 1-\\epsilon.$ There also exist $\\widetilde{E}^{\\prime}$ and $E^{\\prime}$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\\displaystyle\\varrho_{\\text{SignGD}}^{\\epsilon}=O(\\epsilon^{-0.7}K^{-0.3}),\\text{ and }\\frac{\\sigma_{\\min}\\big(G_{\\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\\big)}{\\sigma_{\\max}\\big(G_{\\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\\big)}\\leq 25\\%,$ where $\\sigma_{\\max}$ and $\\sigma_{\\min}$ are the largest and smallest singular values, respectively.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:25:55.403379+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5eaa74e6e1ee099015d33ae293f118aad892623a0682b4c56cc8f394f3daeae","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[De 1 of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] (1) Fix a filtered probability space carrying an $\mathbb{R}^m$-valued Brownian motion $B$ and an $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable random variable $X_0$. An adapted continuous $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued process $X$ is called a \emph{strong solution} of (\ref{2.1}) if
\[
\mathbb{E} \int_{0}^{t}\bigg\{\big\|b(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})\big\|_{\mathbb{R}^d}+\big\|\sigma(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})\big\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}}\bigg\}ds<\infty,\,\, t\geq0,
\]
and if, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely,
\[
X(t)=X_0+\int_{0}^{t}b(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})ds+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})dB(s),\,\, t\geq0,
\]
where $\mathcal L_{X(t)}\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ for every $t\geq0$. \emph{Pathwise uniqueness} holds if any two such strong solutions defined with respect to the same $B$ and the same $X_0$ coincide almost surely.
		
(2) A pair $(\tilde{X}(t),\tilde{B}(t))_{t\geq0}$ is called a \emph{weak solution} of $(\ref{2.1})$ if it solves the equation on some stochastic basis $(\tilde{\Omega},\tilde{\mathcal{F}},\{\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_t\}_{t\geq0},\tilde{\mathbb{P}})$ and $\tilde B$ is an $\mathbb R^m$-valued Brownian motion on that basis.","status":"unverified"}

 \begin{itemize}

 \item[(P6)] The random $3K$-tuple $(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}^\circ, \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}^\circ, \boldsymbol{N}^\circ)$ is a deterministic affine function of the random $K$-tuple $\boldsymbol{Q}^\circ$. Furthermore, for any $k \in[K]$, the difference $N^{\circ}_k-\N \mu([\hat a^{\circ\,\prime}_k, \hat b^{\circ\,\prime}_k])$ is a deterministic affine function of $(Q_1^\circ,\ldots,Q_k^\circ)$ and the linear coefficient of $Q_k^\circ$ takes values in $\big\{1,-\frac{1}{\theta_{1,1}},\ldots,-\frac{1}{\theta_{H,H}}\big\}$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.601656+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5f194bb56f96226a6d429567b61e6f594cbf75024f50d4c52beef93d277870b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:inradius of arXiv:2606.11248, 'Persistent Homology of the Planar Wiener Sausage: Brownian Scaling and a Logarithmic Expec'] Define
\[
N_{\mathrm{in}}(\eta)=\operatorname{card}\{i\ge1:\rho_{K_{1}}(A_{i})>\eta\},
\]
which is exactly the unit-time cavity count in the notation of Section~(sec:cavity of the paper), i.e.
\[
N_{\mathrm{in}}(\eta)=N_{K_{1}}(\eta)=N_{1}(\eta).
\]
Then there exists an absolute constant $c_{-}>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
\liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta^{2}(\log(1/\eta))^{2}\,\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{in}}(\eta)]\ge c_{-}.
\end{equation}
In particular, after decreasing $c_{-}$ if necessary, there exists $\eta_{0}>0$ such that, for every $0<\eta<\eta_{0}$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{in}}(\eta)]\ge\frac{c_{-}}{\eta^{2}(\log(1/\eta))^{2}}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:52:51.758558+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5f728cb20575617f1ae92999f55e411c79a6cf913b967ba90122ac18ea6586d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:mixed-perturbative-excursion of arXiv:2604.24389, '``True" self-avoiding walks on general trees'] There exists $K_0\in\mathbb N$ such that for every $K\ge K_0$ and every $u\in W_K$, there exists a function

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:51:44.838101+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5f76443341dad768ec0f4dc7b31e4886cd44dcbb30fde7486912f86f61b3e7e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 54 of arXiv:2608.26823, 'Evolutes, involutes and parallels of Legendre curves in hyperbolic and de Sitter 2-spaces '] Let $(\bgamma_T,\bgamma_T^d):I\rightarrow\Delta_5$ be a timelike Legendre curve  with curvature $(m_T,n_T)$. Suppose that there exists   $\widetilde{f}:I\rightarrow\R  $ such that $m_T(t)+\widetilde{f}(t)n_T(t)=0$ for all $t\in I$.  For any $t_0\in I$, the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate} 
\item[$(1)$]  $\widetilde{\mathcal{DE}}^\pm(\bgamma_T,\bgamma_T^d) $ is singular at $t_0$ if and only if  $  2\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)n_T(t_0)=0 $.
\item[$(2)$]  $\widetilde{\mathcal{DE}}^\pm(\bgamma_T,\bgamma_T^d) $ has a $(2,3)$-cusp at $t_0$ if and only if  $n_T(t_0)\neq0$,  $  2\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)n_T(t_0)=0 $ and $ 2\ddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\pm 2\widetilde{f}(t_0)\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)n_T(t_0)\pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)\dot{n}_T(t_0)\neq0$.
\item[$(3)$] $\widetilde{\mathcal{DE}}^\pm(\bgamma_T,\bgamma_T^d) $ has a  $(3,4)$-cusp at $t_0$ if and only if  $n_T(t_0)\neq0$, $2\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)n_T(t_0)=2\ddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\pm2\widetilde{f}(t_0)\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)n_T(t_0)\pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)\dot{n}_T(t_0)=0$     and  $ \pm2\dot{\widetilde{f}^2}(t_0)n_T(t_0)\pm 2\widetilde{f}(t_0)\ddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)n_T(t_0)\pm 4\widetilde{f}(t_0)\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\dot{n}_T(t_0) \pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)\ddot{n}_T(t_0)+2\dddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\neq0$.

\item[$(4)$] $\widetilde{\mathcal{DE}}^\pm(\bgamma_T,\bgamma_T^d) $ has a  $(2,5)$-cusp at $t_0$ if and only if  $n_T(t_0)=0$, $\dot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)=0$, $  2\ddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\pm \widetilde{f}^2(t_0)\dot{n}_T(t_0)\neq0 $ and $ -\ddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\ddot{n}_T(t_0)+\dddot{\widetilde{f}}(t_0)\dot{n}_T(t_0)\neq0 $.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:49.842588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b5fc02baf6d1bb7cf3ba2526a16bbfb200bd121668bc0313032a700ba3529abe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 10 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {Multi-dimensional Itô Integral}{}
 let $(W_t)_{t \geq 0}$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. Furthermore, let $f(t, \omega): [0, T] \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ be a matrix of $\mathcal{F}_t$-adapted processes such that each entry $f_{ij}(t, \omega)$ belongs to the space $L^2([0, T] \times \Omega)$, i.e.,
 \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T \| f(t) \|_F^2 \, \mathrm{d}t \right] < \infty,
\]
where $\| f(t) \|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm of the matrix $f(t)$. Then the \textbf{multi-dimensional Itô integral} is defined as:
\[
\int_0^T f(t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t = 
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum\limits_{j=1}^d \int\limits_0^T f_{1j}(t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t^j, \dots, 
\sum\limits_{j=1}^d \int\limits_0^T f_{nj}(t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t^j
\end{pmatrix}^\top,
\]
where each term is a sum of scalar Itô integrals.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6037c8c8459122d7c3759452aab6b463cb95829c2fce94e8bb116ffceef2ba7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 255 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\chi'(1) \le L^2$.

\begin{proof}
Throughout this proof we abbreviate $\bg\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$.  Consider small positive $\delta$, and define
    \[\begin{aligned}
    \bx&=\cA( (1-\delta)^{1/2}\bg+\delta^{1/2}\bg')\,,\\
    \by &= \E(\bx\,|\, \bg)\,,\\
    \bz &= \bx-\by\,.
    \end{aligned}\]
By iterated expectations, we have
    \[
    \frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\by)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta)\,, 
    \]
as well as $\E(\by,\bz)=0$. It follows that
    \beq
    \chi(1)
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\bx)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}+\frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta) + \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}\,.\eeq
Let us treat $\bz$ as a function of $\bg'$ for fixed $\bg$. Note that $\E(\bz\,|\,\bg)=0$. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, we see that $\bz$ is $(L\delta^{1/2})$-Lipschitz as a function of $\bg'$. It follows (using e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
    \[
    \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N} \le O(L^2\delta)\,.
    \]
Recalling \eqref{eq:bz}, we see that $\chi(1-\delta) \ge \chi(1)-O(L^2\delta)$, which implies $\chi'(1) \le L^2$ as claimed. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:49.842828+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b61605865fc4fb12f849c3892139984bb0137acc0b2f2670fd98e6c359d68d58","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {Itô's Integration by Parts}{}
Let \(\{X_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) and \(\{Y_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) be two Itô processes defined by
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = \mu_X(t, X_t) \, \mathrm{d}t + \sigma_X(t, X_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t, \quad
\mathrm{d}Y_t = \mu_Y(t, Y_t) \, \mathrm{d}t + \sigma_Y(t, Y_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t,
\]
where \(W_t\) is a Brownian motion. Then, the product \(Z_t = X_t Y_t\) satisfies
\[
\mathrm{d}(X_t Y_t) = X_t \, \mathrm{d}Y_t + Y_t \, \mathrm{d}X_t + \mathrm{d}\langle X, Y \rangle_t,
\]
where \(\mathrm{d}\langle X, Y \rangle_t\) is the differential of the quadratic covariation process of \(X_t\) and \(Y_t\), given by
\[
\mathrm{d}\langle X, Y \rangle_t = \sigma_X(t, X_t) \sigma_Y(t, Y_t)^\top \, \mathrm{d}t.
\]
Therefore, expanding the terms explicitly gives
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{d}(X_t Y_t) 
&= \big( X_t \mu_Y(t, Y_t) + Y_t \mu_X(t, X_t) 
+ \sigma_X(t, X_t) \sigma_Y(t, Y_t)^\top \big) \, \mathrm{d}t \\
&\quad + X_t \sigma_Y(t, Y_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t 
+ Y_t \sigma_X(t, X_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.096304+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b619662167f1d705824aec518ea871ba76c4eb8c3ab8057e009a8540a570f01f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 33 of arXiv:2604.26026, 'Stochastic Ordering of Dependent Systems under Transformation Models and Archimedean Copul'] Let $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n),\,\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
    \begin{enumerate}

     The vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is said to be majorized by another vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, denoted by $\boldsymbol{\alpha} \overset{m}{\preceq}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, if for each $\ell=1, \ldots, n-1$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \alpha_{i:n} \geq \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \beta_{i:n}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i:n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_{i:n}$, where $\alpha_{i:n}$ and $\beta_{i:n}$ represent the coordinates of $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, respectively, ordered increasingly.
    \item (\cite{marshall2011}, Definition~3.A.1)
	A function $h:A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is said to be Schur-convex (Schur-concave) on $A$ if
	$$
	\boldsymbol{\alpha} \overset{m}\succeq \boldsymbol{\beta} \Rightarrow h(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) \geq(\leq)\; h(\boldsymbol{\beta}),
    \quad \text { for all } \boldsymbol{\alpha},\, \boldsymbol{\beta} \in A.
	$$
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:01:15.329883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b61e048f046c0793ed53f034843febd8b7079965d002730ea65fcb0af41cf4ab","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 4 (Second-order origin of the empirical ranking) of arXiv:2608.30374, 'Compact and Infinite-Order Error Analysis\\ for Null-Space SVD Estimation'] Let
\(\lambda_{(0)}(\sigma)\leq\cdots\leq
  \lambda_{(m-1)}(\sigma)\)
be the increasingly ordered eigenvalues of \(A(\sigma)\), and let
\(P_{(i)}(\sigma)\) be rank-one eigenprojectors from an ordered
orthonormal eigenbasis.  When an eigenvalue is simple its projector is unique;
the associated unit eigenvector is unique up to sign.  For \(0\leq i<q_0\),
define
\begin{equation}
 R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
   =\frac1\tau\operatorname{tr}\!\left(
      A(\sigma)P_{(i)}(\sigma)\right),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma)
   =\mathbb E_{\mathrm{tr}}
      [R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)].
 
\end{equation}
Then, exactly for every realization,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
       =\frac{\lambda_{(i)}(\sigma)}{\tau}},
 \qquad
 R_{\mathrm{emp},0}^{\mathrm{ord}}\leq\cdots\leq
 R_{\mathrm{emp},q_0-1}^{\mathrm{ord}}.
 
\end{equation}
For every \(1\leq q\leq q_0\), these branch risks decompose the aggregate
risk, both before and after expectation:
\begin{equation}
 R_{\mathrm{emp},q}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
   =\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},q}(\sigma)
   =\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma).
 
\end{equation}
If \(\mu_0\leq\cdots\leq\mu_{q_0-1}\) are the ordered eigenvalues of
the effective matrix \(W\) in \eqref{eq:effective-splitting}, then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
   =\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau}\mu_i+O_{\mathcal T}(\sigma^3),
   \qquad \sigma\downarrow0.}
 
\end{equation}
Thus \(W\), rather than an arbitrary clean null-space basis, governs the
first nonzero small-noise separations.  If \(W\) is simple, its locally
analytic labelled sheets coincide with \(\lambda_{(i)}\) for all sufficiently
small \(\sigma>0\).  At larger noise, an eigenvalue crossing may exchange
sheet labels; the parenthesized index always denotes instantaneous SVD order.

Under the Gaussian assumptions of \Cref{sec:equal-ranked-equal}, suppose
also that \(\tau\geq m\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 W\sim\operatorname{Wishart}_{q_0}(\tau-n,I_{q_0}),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma)
   =\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau}\,\overline\mu_i+o(\sigma^2),
 \quad \overline\mu_i=\mathbb E[\mu_i],
 
\end{equation}
and
\(\overline\mu_0<\cdots<\overline\mu_{q_0-1}\).
Let \(\overline{\V{\mu}}=(\overline\mu_0,\ldots,
\overline\mu_{q_0-1})^T\).  Consequently, if
\(\V{e}_{\mathrm{emp}}\) collects the expected ordered empirical risks, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma)}
      {\|\V{e}_{\mathrm{emp}}(\sigma)\|_2}
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{\overline\mu_i}{\|\overline{\V{\mu}}\|_2}
 \quad(\sigma\downarrow0),
 
\end{equation}
which, when \(q_0>1\), is strictly ranked rather than uniform.  Moreover, for every
\(\sigma>0\) the Gaussian sample covariance has simple spectrum almost
surely, so the expected inequalities in \eqref{eq:exact-empirical-order}
are strict.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:21:56.740528+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6228d2a805c6c154d1255a5409ec31daa09a016b65c3048af96e212db9d85e3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition definition-RWREdiscrete of arXiv:2507.19222, 'Convergence of the KMP model to the KPZ equation'] On a probability space $(\Omega^{(\epsilon)}, \mathcal{F}^{(\epsilon)}, \mathbb{P}^{(\epsilon)})$, we define the following random variables: for each bond $(x,x+1)$, let  $\left(\mathcal{I}_{x,x+1}^{(n)}\right)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}}$ be a Bernoulli process with parameter $\epsilon\in [0,1]$,  independent for each bond. 
	
	
	For each bond $(x,x+1)$ and each $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}$,  let  $B_{x,x+1}^{(n)}$ be an independent random variable distributed as  Beta$(\alpha,\alpha)$. 
	We denote a realization of the  environment by $(\text{Bin}, \omega)\in \Omega^{(\epsilon)}$, where  $\text{Bin}$ is a realization of the Bernoulli processes and $\omega$ is a realization of the Beta variables.
	
	
	Given $(\text{Bin}, \omega)\in \Omega^{(\epsilon)}$, we define a random walk $(X^{\epsilon}(n))_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}}$ as follows. If at discrete-time $n$, $X^{\epsilon}(n)=x$,  the update rule is as follows:
	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=12pt]
		\item If $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = \mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x,x+1} = 1$ or if $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = \mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x,x+1} = 0$ the particle does not move. These events happen with probability $\epsilon^{2}$ and $1-2\epsilon(1-\epsilon)$ respectively. 
		\item If $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = 1$ and $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x,x+1} = 0$: the walker moves to $x+1$ with probability $1 - B^{(n)}_{x,x+1}$, or remains at $x$ with probability $B^{(n)}_{x,x+1}$. This event happens with probability $\epsilon(1-\epsilon)$.
		\item If $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = 0$ and $\mathcal{I}^{n}_{x,x+1} = 1$: the walker moves to $x-1$ with probability $B^{(n)}_{x-1,x}$, or remains at  $x$ with probability $1 - B^{(n)}_{x-1,x}$. This event happens with probability $\epsilon(1-\epsilon)$.
	\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:17:33.997008+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6453c40d44a0d196e4c9c4897c99e9dcee39c5230d07e285e06304c3f27a5da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2609.03403, 'Hyperpositive functions, sector bounded functions and a trace formula'] Let $(H_+ , H_-)$ be a pair of of selfadjoint operators defined on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, and with the following two properties:\\

{"assumptions":["the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2","the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:18:07.915757+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_b65e4f03214b2aa782f369b54d75f83a80e5af182457d205fd6bc537075ff3c0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (23 and 18 members; 285 and 40 outputs; 932 and 800 calibration rows; the per-sample relative metric; 70 cells, paired). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\\lambda_{\\max}/\\lambda_{\\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\\,\\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result, paired gains against the $0.05$-floor RIE: the raw covariance, the eta-RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie at full calibration (median paired gain 0.00 on both corpora; means +0.05, +0.04, +0.09, -0.86 on 40 EMIT cells, the last from one cell at -16; +0.16, +0.01, +0.15, +0.09 on 30 OCO-2 cells), while at $n = 60$ the eta-RIE itself is the worst of them: on OCO-2 raw +6.4, LW2020 +6.0, NERCOME +4.9 percent over it on 30 of 30 cells (on EMIT +0.6, +1.3, +1.0 with 20-28 of 40 wins), and at $n = 240$ on OCO-2 +1.1, +1.0, +0.8 on 30 of 30 at full calibration and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose 1.2 and 6.5 percent on EMIT at full calibration (0.2 and 1.1 on OCO-2), 4.5 percent for the heavy floor at $n = 60$ on EMIT; linear shrinkage loses 6.3 percent on EMIT at full calibration and 15 percent at $n = 60$ (a wash on OCO-2, where the members are fewer and the shrinkage target closer); and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose 2 to 7 percent at full calibration on EMIT and 13 to 105 percent at $n = 60$; on OCO-2 the raw sum-to-one form is off by factors of 30 to 3,000 (an 18-member rank-deficient covariance inverted). Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\\times10^{2}$-$3\\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$); the floors and the linear shrinkage keep MORE members active (EMIT: raw 7.2, RIE 7.6, RIE with the 0.05 floor 8.3, floor 0.2 9.4, floor 1.0 12.2, linear shrinkage 13.9, LW2020 7.3, NERCOME 9.6 of 23; OCO-2: 6.9, 7.5, 8.0, 9.1, 11.3, 8.9, 7.1, 7.2 of 18), which is how they lose - a lifted small eigenvalue makes a duplicate look independent. By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; by the entrywise risk bound all of them obey the same $O(\\sqrt{\\log M/n})$ excess-risk guarantee while a floor is a bias that does not vanish with $n$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.986447+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b65ecc20e0f2ffa816c678bcbf24993c3ad47e4dc34fd97f6462fd461f6ab701","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:FinalLBTwoStream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1/2)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.818468+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b660eac045fab5bece417ad477af4c706728de855fd8f9968aae03e4c462c646","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem intro:1-d continuum T>0:RS of arXiv:2605.05631, 'Wandering Exponents and the Free Energy of the High-Dimensional Elastic Polymer'] The model is RS if and only if

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.340592+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6703bad009d889652cc64f04abead235202be056bb91938fe6e010ea70e1bed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Pointwise macroscopic-loop bounds for integer loop weights) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\).

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
    \item \textbf{Random regular graphs.}
    Let \(d\ge 3\), let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices, and let \(p_{d,n}\) denote its law. Assume
    \[
    d>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(d)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    p_{d,n}\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs.}
    Let \(\lambda>0\), and let \(G_n\sim G(n,\lambda/n)\). Assume
    \[
    \lambda>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
    \]
    Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\lambda)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Simple bounded-degree configuration model.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\), that is, the pairing model conditioned on simplicity. Assume that
    \[
    1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
    \qquad\text{for all }i,n,
    \]
    and
    \[
    \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho.
    \]
    If
    \[
    \rho>2c_{\theta,u}
    =
    2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr),
    \]
    then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
    \[
    t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\rho)+\delta,
    \]
    one has
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The symmetric part of the operator must dominate: for genuinely non-self-adjoint problems backward uniqueness can fail.","The estimate is an interpolation between the endpoints and is NOT a bound of the solution at time 0 by the solution at time T alone - the backward problem remains ill posed, only uniqueness is recovered, and quantitative continuous dependence requires a prior bound."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.870954+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, parabolic equations","id":"claim_b67257027da5be281d79a2ea52bbc955fdea182929264200a1d02ca9174d08e3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a Hilbert space, A a self-adjoint (or more generally accretive with a symmetric part dominating the antisymmetric one) operator, and let u solve the differential inequality || u'(t) + A u(t) || <= C ( ||u(t)|| + ||A u(t)||^{1/2} ||u(t)||^{1/2} ) on [0,T]. Then the function t -> log ||u(t)||^2 is CONVEX up to a correction linear in t; consequently ||u(t)|| <= C ||u(0)||^{1 - theta(t)} ||u(T)||^{theta(t)} for an exponent theta(t) in (0,1). The consequence used in practice is BACKWARD UNIQUENESS: if u(T) = 0 then u vanishes identically on [0,T]. {"assumptions":["Real separable Hilbert space and one isonormal Gaussian process.","Symmetric Hilbert tensor kernels; homogeneous chaos degrees are finite.","Multiple integrals use factorial Wiener-Ito normalization."],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:16:42.368311+00:00","domain":"Gaussian chaos; Wick products; symmetric tensors","id":"claim_b687cec7bb61a2abc0e15b180b10ee69a882b996dd8aedb3d3b2e51eee89d2fc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"CLASSICAL LITERATURE COROLLARY, no novelty claimed. Let H be a real separable Hilbert space, W an isonormal centered Gaussian process on H, and I_k its multiple Wiener-Ito integral normalized by E[I_k(f)^2]=k! ||f||^2 for symmetric f in H^{odot k}. Let p,q be positive integers, f in H^{odot p}, g in H^{odot q}, F=I_p(f), and G=I_q(g). Define the Wick product F diamond G=I_{p+q}(Sym(f tensor g)). It is the orthogonal projection of the ordinary product FG onto chaos p+q. Then ||F diamond G||_2^2 <= binom(p+q,p) ||F||_2^2 ||G||_2^2. More generally, for finitely many homogeneous factors F_j=I_{p_j}(f_j) with positive degrees and K=sum_j p_j, their iterated Wick product has squared L2 norm at most K!/(product_j p_j!) times product_j ||F_j||_2^2. Constants and zero kernels extend the formula by I_0(c)=c. No independence between the factors is required: they are functionals of the same W. The binomial constant is sharp, attained by nonzero rank-one kernels f=a h^{tensor p}, g=b h^{tensor q}, ||h||=1. These bounds concern Wick/highest-chaos products, not ordinary products, arbitrary mixed-chaos multiplication, or joint posterior projections after a noisy observation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.763059+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6a71a162c105d8a6febcacfb7ce2231a6554619f66b3d159e5747dd1d2c52f1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:chaining-square-no-sqrtlog of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Fix $0<\beta<\tfrac12$ and $\gamma>0$.

{"assumptions":["1 ≤ p < ∞","Ω = R^n, or Ω bounded open with Lipschitz boundary (an extension domain); for W^{1,p}_0 any open Ω","compactness statements require Ω bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492521+00:00","domain":"Sobolev spaces, embedding theorems, compactness","id":"claim_b6b2ca78bf6d58de47692329336d31951c68502f00143a7631b268179675e75b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n ≥ 1, 1 ≤ p < ∞, and let Ω ⊂ R^n be either all of R^n or a bounded open set with Lipschitz boundary (more generally a bounded W^{1,p}-extension domain). For p < n write p* = np/(n − p) (Sobolev conjugate, 1/p* = 1/p − 1/n).

(i) Subcritical case p < n (Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) continuously. On R^n one has the scale-invariant form ||u||_{L^{p*}(R^n)} ≤ C(n,p) ||∇u||_{L^p(R^n)} for every u ∈ W^{1,p}(R^n). For bounded Ω, W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every 1 ≤ q ≤ p*, and the embedding is COMPACT for every q < p* (Rellich–Kondrachov), but not for q = p*.

(ii) Critical case p = n ≥ 2. W^{1,n}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) for every q ∈ [1, ∞), compactly when Ω is bounded, but W^{1,n}(Ω) is NOT contained in L^∞(Ω): in the unit disc of R^2, u(x) = log log(1 + 1/|x|) belongs to W^{1,2} and is unbounded. (For n = 1, W^{1,1} on an interval consists of absolutely continuous functions and does embed into the continuous functions.)

(iii) Supercritical case p > n (Morrey). W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{0,γ}(Ω̄) with γ = 1 − n/p: every u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω) has a representative that is Hölder continuous with exponent γ, and ||u||_{C^{0,γ}(Ω̄)} ≤ C ||u||_{W^{1,p}(Ω)}. For bounded Ω the embedding into C^{0,β}(Ω̄) is compact for every β < γ, in particular into C(Ω̄).

(iv) Higher order, Ω bounded Lipschitz, k ≥ 1. If kp < n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ L^q(Ω) with 1/q = 1/p − k/n, compactly into L^r for r < q. If kp > n then W^{k,p}(Ω) ↪ C^{k − ⌊n/p⌋ − 1, γ}(Ω̄), where γ = ⌊n/p⌋ + 1 − n/p when n/p is not an integer, and γ is any number in (0,1) when n/p is an integer.

(v) Zero boundary values. Every statement holds for W^{1,p}_0(Ω) (resp. W^{k,p}_0) on an ARBITRARY open set Ω, bounded for the compactness claims, with no regularity of ∂Ω, because such functions extend by zero to W^{1,p}(R^n).

Where it fails. Without an extension property (Lipschitz or comparable boundary) the embedding W^{1,p}(Ω) ↪ L^{p*}(Ω) can fail for bounded Ω: there are bounded domains with a sufficiently sharp outward cusp on which it is false. Compactness fails at the critical exponent q = p* (the rescaled bubbles u_λ(x) = λ^{(n−p)/p} u(λx) keep constant L^{p*} norm and W^{1,p} seminorm but converge weakly to 0) and fails on unbounded domains such as R^n (translates of one bump). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.765296+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6cdc6ff50b7ac34c05e0dff7d40e513235272b708d660b11cbab411c570ee19","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 12 ({\cite[Lemma~5.9) of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] {amy-cle-resampling}}]

Suppose that $\Gamma$ is a nested \clekp{} in a simply connected domain $D$. For each $a\in(0,1)$, $b>0$ there exist $p > 0$ and $c>0$ such that the following holds.

Let $z\in D$ and $j_0\in\Z$ be such that $B(z,2^{-j_0})\subseteq D$. There exists a resampling $\Gamma^\resampled_{z,j}$ of $\Gamma$ within $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$ for each $j>j_0$ with the following property. Let $F_{z,j}$ be the event that
\begin{itemize}
 \item no loop in $\Gamma^\resampled_{z,j}$ crosses the annulus $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$,
 \item denoting $\CC$ the loops in $\Gamma$ that cross $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$, the collection of loops of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^\resampled_{z,j}$ remain the same in each connected component of $\C \setminus \bigcup\CC$ that is not surrounded by a loop in $\CC$ and intersects $B(z,2^{-j})$, and the gasket of $\Gamma$ in these components is contained in the gasket of $\Gamma^\resampled_{z,j}$.
\end{itemize}
For $k\in\N$, let $\wt G_{z,j_0,k}$ be the event that the number of $j=j_0+1,\ldots,j_0+k$ so that
\[ \p[ F_{z,j} \mid \Gamma ] \geq p\]
is at least $(1-a)k$.  Then
\[ \p[(\wt G_{z,j_0,k})^c] \le c e^{-b k} . \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\(\Sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}_r^{++}(\R)\), and

\[
 F_{\Sigma,\boldsymbol\tau}(\boldsymbol x)

 (\Sigma^{-1})_{ab}\langle x_a,x_b\rangle
 +
 i\sum_{a=1}^r\tau_aP(x_a),
\]
the oriented real contour

\[
 \Re F_{\Sigma,\boldsymbol\tau}(\boldsymbol x)

On every admissible chamber, the integral row of the real Gaussian contour is

\begin{equation}
 C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Betti}}
 =
 \#_{\mathrm{or}}
 \bigl(\R^{rd}\pitchfork\check\Gamma_\alpha\bigr).
 
\end{equation}
At a block-diagonal base point, with product orientations,
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^{(r)}
 =
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^{(1)}
 \otimes\cdots\otimes
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^{(1)}.

Let $X,Y\in \mathrm{St}(n,k)$ satisfy $\|X-Y\|\leq 1$, and let

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.202067+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b6fb3780a597ac88fdb2d567e655163bfc44db277c717ca5da83d3ba219559b6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Geometric characteristic number of a THP) of arXiv:2608.03575, '2608.03575'] Let $P$ be a trivalent hyperbolic polyhedron in $\mathbb{H}^{3}$ and let $v$ be one of its vertices. Denote the three faces incident to $v$ by $f_{1}, f_{2}, f_{3}$, and write
\[
e_{ij}=f_{i}\cap f_{j}, \quad 1\le i<j\le 3.
\]
Let $\Theta_{ij}$ be the dihedral angle of $P$ along $e_{ij}$. For $\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}$, define
\[
\theta_{v}^{f_{i}}=\arccos\left(\frac{1+\cos\Theta_{ij}+\cos\Theta_{ik}-\cos\Theta_{jk}}{2\sqrt{1+\cos\Theta_{ij}}\sqrt{1+\cos\Theta_{ik}}}\right)
\]
Equivalently, $\theta_{v}^{f_{i}}$ is the angle at the vertex corresponding to $f_{i}$ in the auxiliary Euclidean triangle whose side lengths are $\ell_{ij}=\sqrt{2+2\cos\Theta_{ij}}$ for $1\le i<j\le 3$.

For a face $f$ of $P$, its geometric characteristic number is defined by
\[
L_{f}(P)=2\pi-\sum_{v\in f}\theta_{v}^{f}.
\]
The geometric characteristic number of $P$ is the collection $L(P)=(L_{f}(P): f\in F(P))$, where $F(P)$ denotes the set of faces of $P$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent (product) probability measure on the input coordinates","f is a bounded, typically boolean, function of finitely many coordinates","existence of a randomized decision tree computing f exactly, with well-defined per-coordinate revealments","revealments computed under the same measure used for Var(f) and Inf_i(f)"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.972746+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b71abce6cf84475d6e6984b0c6a4d7ee2a29f331d669301354889ab502d006c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1} be evaluated exactly by a randomized decision-tree algorithm T that, over its internal randomness, queries coordinate i with probability delta_i(T) (its revealment), and let Var(f) denote the variance of f under a product probability measure on the input. The OSSS inequality states Var(f) <= sum_{i=1}^n delta_i(T) Inf_i(f), where Inf_i(f) is the influence of coordinate i under the same measure. Consequently, exhibiting an algorithm with small maximal revealment forces the sum of influences to be large, giving lower bounds on total influence and noise sensitivity via algorithmic constructions; for critical planar percolation, an exploration-path algorithm gives revealments comparable to arm-event probabilities, and combined with quasi-multiplicativity this yields sharp bounds on noise sensitivity and, via the Duminil-Copin-Raoufi-Tassion route, on sharpness of the phase transition in all dimensions without reflection positivity or duality. The inequality does not directly compute Inf_i itself, does not apply to non-product (dependent-coordinate) measures without a separate generalization, and it is an inequality rather than an identity, so it can be loose or even vacuous if the algorithm chosen is not well matched to f's structure. Typical failure: Plugging in a naive, non-adaptive algorithm (e.g. querying coordinates in a fixed deterministic order) and expecting a sharp bound; the inequality is only informative when the algorithm is cleverly matched to the function's geometric structure, such as an exploration process for a crossing event, and a poorly chosen algorithm produces a valid but essentially vacuous bound that is easy to mistake for a genuine obstruction to sharper influence or sensitivity estimates. Canonical reference: O'Donnell, Saks, Schramm and Servedio, 2005, Proceedings of the 46th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science; Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion, 2019, Annals of Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

Suppose that Assumption (asshol of the paper) holds and that there exists a positive real number $\alpha$ such that $r_D(A(-\alpha)) = -\log(1-p_{1})$. Then $\alpha$ is unique, and the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
\item  There exist constants $0<C_1\le C_2<\infty$ such that
\begin{align} 
\widetilde{M}C_1 \le y^\alpha \mathbb{P}(P_T>y) \le \widetilde{M}C_2
\end{align}
for all sufficiently large $y$; that is, $P_T$ has a Pareto-type tail.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

\[

\]
\end{enumerate}
In (propmaina of the paper) and (propmainb of the paper), $\widetilde{M}$ is positive and given by
\[
\widetilde{M} = \left(\frac{q_{1}p_{1}}{1-p_{1}}\right) \frac{(w_0' x_{p})(y_{p}'1_N)}{-\,y_{p}' B^{(1)}(-\alpha)x_{p}},

where $B(s) = e^{\log(1-p_{1})I+A(s)}$, $B^{(1)}(s) = \frac{d}{ds}B(s)$, and $x_p$, $y_p$ are right and left eigenvectors of $B(-\alpha)$ associated with the unit eigenvalue.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.584221+00:00","domain":"combinatorics","id":"claim_b77b87e08d73f761ed5ff25ec04b1c15efb7d1bd8d686854a4b8fb7376cb33b6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider finite rooted trees with vertices labeled from a fixed well-quasi-ordered set. One tree topologically embeds in another if there is an injective, ancestor-order-preserving map of vertices to vertices sending labels to weakly larger labels and sending each edge to a path, these paths being internally vertex-disjoint. Kruskal's tree theorem states that finite labeled trees, ordered by topological embeddability, form a well-quasi-order: in any infinite sequence of such trees, some tree embeds into a later one. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:43:16.152996+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b77f7def15b8beed58d0a2a6f104076a097150a5d2a84ba2160773e9755c1f2f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Arizmendi and Perales {\cite[Proposition 3.3) of arXiv:2604.13819, 'Convolution, cumulants and infinitesimal generators in the formal power series ring'] {arizmendi2018cumulants-joctsa}}]
Given $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$, the finite free cumulants $\kappa_{1}^{(d)}, \dots, \kappa_{d}^{(d)}$ are unique maps satisfying the following conditions. 
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (i)]
\item $\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f)$ is a polynomial in $p_{1}(f), \dots, p_{i}(f)$ with leading term $\frac{d^{i-1}}{(d)_{\underline{i}}} p_{i}(f)$. 
That is, there exists a polynomial $F_{i}$ in $i-1$ variables such that 
$$
\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f) = \frac{d^{i-1}}{(d)_{\underline{i}}}p_{i}(f) + F_{i}(p_{1}(f), \dots, p_{i-1}(f)).
$$ 
\item Homogeneity: $\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(D_{r}f) = r^{i}\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f)$ for any $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and $i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$.
\item Additivity: $\kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f \boxplus_{d} g) = \kappa_{i}^{(d)}(f) + \kappa_{i}^{(d)}(g)$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:22:46.463555+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b78e8a7e6ec3aca84432af2daf603cbcd6fa8788ae86890f9006ceca98c49048","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 32 (Metric duality and musical notation) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] If $V$ is a spacetime vectorfield, then $V_{\flat}$ denotes the one-form that is

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent (arbitrary measurable state spaces, not necessarily identically distributed)","E[Z^2] < infinity","X_i' an independent copy of X_i"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T04:29:00.269210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b7911cc88f0c4e9cbcd38f7c8f3a5c04","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables taking values in arbitrary measurable spaces - they need NOT be identically distributed and need not be real-valued - and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with E[Z^2] < infinity. Let X_i' be an independent copy of X_i, independent of everything else, and put Z^{(i)} = f(X_1, ..., X_{i-1}, X_i', X_{i+1}, ..., X_n). Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z^{(i)})^2 ] = sum_{i=1}^n E[ ((Z - Z^{(i)})_+)^2 ]. Equivalently, and often more convenient, Var(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ (Z - Z_i)^2 ] for ANY random variables Z_i that are measurable functions of the n-1 variables other than X_i; taking Z_i = inf over the i-th coordinate of f gives the version used for suprema and for first-passage times. Equality in the replace-one bound (in either form) holds if and only if f is a sum of functions of the individual coordinates; equality in the bound with arbitrary Z_i holds if and only if, in addition, Z_i = E[Z | X_j, j != i] almost surely for every i. Independence is the only structural hypothesis and it is essential; the inequality is FALSE for dependent coordinates. Applied with a bounded-difference function it recovers the variance half of McDiarmid's inequality; applied to first-passage percolation with the geodesic length as the influence bound it produces the linear variance upper bound. [Efron and Stein (1981), Steele (1986); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Nonzero feasible rank-at-most-r target; full-row-rank design and noiseless labels","B0=0; nondegenerate Gaussian A0","Step schedule fixed conditional on design independently of A0","Isotropic population prediction risk"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:54:30.733548+00:00","domain":"LoRA gradient dynamics and excess risk","id":"claim_b794a3607b41a0b1d035b802d142402b820e6cfccddde42c0fd0b798721070a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; T419-C006 v1, proof (unaudited), no novelty claim. Let Delta be any nonzero m-by-p matrix of rank at most r and X a fixed full-row-rank p-by-n design. For noiseless Y=Delta X, the global rank-r empirical least-squares estimate equals Delta, so its isotropic population parameter risk is zero. Simultaneous factor GD from B0=0 and nondegenerate Gaussian A0, with any step schedule fixed conditional on X independently of A0, almost surely has B_t A_t != Delta at every finite t. Each finite-iterate entry is a polynomial in A0; at A0=0 both factors remain zero, so a residual entry corresponding to nonzero Delta_ij has a nonzero constant term. Its zero set is Lebesgue-null, and a countable union over t remains null. This also excludes exact recovery at an almost-surely finite integer stopping time selecting these iterates. Consequently a finite-time constant-factor comparison to the noiseless zero-risk benchmark needs a limit, an additive optimization tolerance or other qualification. This does not cover arbitrary initialization-dependent adaptive step rules and does not refute the intended infinite-time or noise-dependent-stopping target.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:41:54.341806+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b7e9ae5d7f8dc9a0e31d70cdf304972c9704a43153c4e3ed8f7ba3e1bbbc9b99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:KPS of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] We say that $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge0}$ is \emph{weak$^\ast$-mean
ergodic} if there exists a Borel probability measure $\mu_\ast$ on ${\mathcal B}(H)$, such that
\begin{equation}\text{w-}\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T P_t^\ast\mu\,\mathrm{d} t=\mu_\ast\quad\text{for every }\quad
\mu\in{\mathcal M}_1(H,{\mathcal B}(H)),
\end{equation}
where the limit is in the sense of weak convergence of probability measures.

We say that the \emph{weak law of large numbers} holds for $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge0}$, for a function $F\in\operatorname{Lip}_{b}(H)$ and for a probability measure $\mu$ on ${\mathcal B}(H)$ if
\[\mathbb{P}_\mu\text{-}\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T F(X_t^\mu)\,\mathrm{d} t=\int_H F\,\mathrm{d}\mu_\ast,\]
where $\mu_\ast$ denotes the invariant probability measure of $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge 0}$ and $\{X_t^\mu\}_{t\ge 0}$ denotes the Markov process related to $\{P_{t}\}_{t\ge 0}$ whose initial distribution is $\mu$ and whose path measure is $\mathbb{P}_\mu$, and where the convergence takes place in $\mathbb{P}_\mu$-probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on Z^2 with F(0) = 0","mu is the axial time constant; the comparison is with the expectation of the minimum of four independent weights","the refutation is Ahlberg's (2019/2020); this is a rederivation with an explicit instance"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869107+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_b80639d38026a14989da0a86aa6755d6ea3593aa2551d349ffb00e6d55126985","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: literature_counterexample_rederived - the primary two-page proof was read and the arithmetic author-checked; the result is Ahlberg's, not ours, and novelty is not claimed] For i.i.d. nonnegative edge weights on Z^2 with F(0) = 0, Auffinger, Damron and Hanson (50 years of first-passage percolation, Question 12) ask whether the axial time constant mu is at least the expected minimum of four independent edge weights. CLAIM: NO, and the question was already settled in the literature by Ahlberg (2019/2020), whose bound mu <= 2 t_{2/3} - twice the 2/3-quantile - refutes it. EXPLICIT INSTANCE: take tau = eta + epsilon U with P(eta = 0) = 3/4 and U uniform on [0,1]. For epsilon > 0 this law is atomless and bounded with F(0) = 0. Solving (3/4) t / epsilon = 2/3 gives t_{2/3} = 8 epsilon / 9, hence mu <= 16 epsilon / 9. The expected four-edge minimum is at least 1/256, the probability of the event that all four edges are expensive. At epsilon = 1/1024, mu <= 16/(9 x 1024) = 1/576 < 1/256, so the proposed inequality is reversed. All sufficiently small epsilon do the same. THIS IS NOT AN OPEN PROBLEM and the store's earlier node for P0096 records only a bounded-search exclusion; this node records what the counterexample actually is.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:52:17.579759+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b80a10c3b56c8cb2551d53a2e1cd1fb73910ee05bdecfec729d485fd19663807","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:CoincidenceDomains of arXiv:2411.14936, 'Massive Particle Systems,\\Wasserstein Brownian Motions,\\ and the Dean--Kawasaki Equation'] Assume~$\big({\mssE,\msD(\mssE)}\big)$ satisfies~(equation eq:QPP of the paper), and let~$\big({\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi)}\big)$ be the Dir\-ichlet form defined in Proposition~(p:StandardCyl of the paper). Then,~$\hCylP{}{0}\subset\msD(\mcE_\pi)$.

\begin{proof}
In light of the diffusion property~(equation eq:l:DiffusionP:0.1 of the paper), it suffices to show that~$\hat f^\star\in\msD(\mcE_\pi)$ for every~$\hat f=\varphi\otimes f$ with~$\varphi\in\msR_0$ and~$f\in\msA$.

Let~$\left(g_\epsilon\right)_{\epsilon}$ be the family of functions constructed in Lemma~(l:DiagonalEqPot of the paper), and choose representatives~$\tilde{g_\epsilon}$ with~$\tilde{g_\epsilon}^\diag= 1$ everywhere on~$M$ and~$\tilde{g_\epsilon}\geq 0$ everywhere on~$M^{\scriptscriptstyle\times 2}$.

Now, consider the family of functions~$\seq{u_{f,\tilde{g_\epsilon},\varphi}}_\epsilon$  in~(equation eq:l:CapacityConnector:0 of the paper).
It suffices to show that~$\epsilon\mapsto \mcE_\pi(u_{f,\tilde{g_\epsilon},\varphi})$ is uniformly bounded and that~$u_{f,\tilde{g_\epsilon},\varphi}$ converges to~$\hat f^\star$ in~$L^2(\mcQ_\pi)$, in which case the conclusion follows from~[MaRoe92].

The first bound follows from~(equation eq:l:CapacityConnector:1 of the paper) and Lemma~(l:DiagonalEqPot of the paper)(i:l:DiagonalEqPot:3 of the paper).

As for the $L^2(\mcQ_\pi)$ convergence, respectively by: Jensen's inequality and boundedness of~$f\in\msA\subset\mcC_0(\tau)$, by smoothness of~$\varphi$, and again by Jensen's inequality,
\begin{align*}
\int& \abs{\int\braket{\varphi(\mu_x) - \varphi\paren{\int \tilde{g}_\epsilon(x,y) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y)}f(x)}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x)}^2\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mcQ_\pi(\mu)
\\
&\leq \left\lVertf\right\rVert_0^2\int \abs{\varphi(\mu_x)-\varphi\paren{\int \int \tilde{g_\epsilon}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y)}}^2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mcQ_\pi(\mu)
\\
&\leq \left\lVertf\right\rVert_0^2 \left\lVert\varphi'\right\rVert_0^2 \int \int\abs{\mu_x-\int \tilde{g_\epsilon}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(y)}^2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu(x) \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mcQ_\pi(\mu)
 \\
&=\left\lVertf\right\rVert_0^2 \left\lVert\varphi'\right\rVert_0^2 \int\!\!\!\!\!\int \sum_i^N s_i \abs{s_i-\sum_j^N s_j\, \tilde{g_\epsilon}(x_i,x_j)}^2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\nu(\mbfx)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi(\mbfs)
\\
&=\left\lVertf\right\rVert_0^2 \left\lVert\varphi'\right\rVert_0^2 \int\!\!\!\!\!\int \sum_i^N s_i \abs{\sum_{j:j\neq i}^N s_j\, \tilde{g_\epsilon}(x_i,x_j)}^2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\nu(\mbfx)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi(\mbfs)
\\
&\leq \left\lVertf\right\rVert_0^2 \left\lVert\varphi'\right\rVert_0^2 \int \sum_i^N s_i(1-s_i) \sum_{j:j\neq i}^N s_j\, \int\abs{\tilde{g_\epsilon}(x_i,x_j)}^2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\nu(\mbfx)
\\
&\leq \left\lVertf\right\rVert_0^2 \left\lVert\varphi'\right\rVert_0^2 \norm{\tilde{g_\epsilon}}_{L^2(\nu^{\scriptscriptstyle\otimes 2})}^2 \,\mathrm{.}
\end{align*}
Since the latter term vanishes as~$\epsilon\to 0$ by Lemma~(l:DiagonalEqPot of the paper)(i:l:DiagonalEqPot:3 of the paper), we have~$L^2(\mcQ_\pi)$-$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow 0} u_{f,\tilde{g_\epsilon},\varphi}=\hat f^\star$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.735503+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b80ea27e23a611f0a4114404b317d491952ee4d6242e4c6648d917fa0934209f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 13 of arXiv:2506.10213, 'Coupling of forward-backward stochastic differential equations on the Wiener space, and ap'] Let Assumption~\ref{coefficient:assume:general}, Assumption~\ref{fbsde:basic:assume:p:general},

    $\Tz := (X,Y,Z)$ on $[t,T]$ if $T - t \leq \dz$.
    Moreover, if $T - t \leq \dz$,
    considering the coupling operator $\cC_{\vz}$ with respect to the measurable function $\vz: [0,T] \to [0,1]$,
    the following estimation holds
    \begin{align}
        CV_p([t,T])
        &\leq c_{\eqref{equ:small:decoupling}} \left\{\E\left[|\xi - \xi^{\vz}|^p + \left|g(X_T) - g^{\vz}(X_T)\right|^p\right] \right.\notag\\
        &\quad \qquad \left. + \E\left[U_p([t,T])\right] + S_p([t,T])\right\},

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space","T is linear and defined on all of H","T is symmetric on all of H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770915+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_b83724a836de510cead5d5abdc582741b93bc84255e7612eaa8cc08da2cc76f3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a Hilbert space and let T: H → H be a linear operator defined on all of H satisfying ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ for all x, y ∈ H. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.367957+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b83995558f11a0cf86aa4ede2b48fa7923510b738bae15c52401b224e24fc69b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 117 (Predictable differentiation of causal trace-class paths) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $q:\Omega_H\to C([0,T];\mathcal S_2(H)_{\rm sa})$ be total Borel and raw
causal, and let $G$ be a Borel stopping-stable set on which every $q(x)$ takes
values in $\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa}$ and is Bochner absolutely continuous in
trace norm.  Put $\Delta_n=T2^{-n}$ and $t_k^n=k\Delta_n$, and define lagged
dyadic averages
\[
 (\mathscr D_nq)_t
 :=\begin{cases}
 0,&0\le t\le\Delta_n,\\[1mm]
 \Delta_n^{-1}\bigl(q_{t_k^n}-q_{t_{k-1}^n}\bigr),
 &t_k^n<t\le t_{k+1}^n,
 \end{cases}
\]
as an $\mathcal S_2(H)_{\rm sa}$-valued process.  Let
$\iota_1:\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa}\hookrightarrow
\mathcal S_2(H)_{\rm sa}$ denote the continuous inclusion and set
\[
 L_1(q):=\bigl\{(t,x):(\mathscr D_nq)_t(x)\in
 \iota_1(\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa})\ \text{for every }n\bigr\}.
\]
Define the totalized trace-class derivative by
\begin{equation}
 (\mathscr Dq)_t(x):=
 \begin{cases}
 \operatorname{Lim}_{\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa}}
 \bigl((\iota_1^{-1}(\mathscr D_nq)_t(x))_{n\ge1}\bigr),
 &(t,x)\in L_1(q),\\
 0,&(t,x)\notin L_1(q),
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where the Borel selector of \Cref{lem:causal-Borel-limit} returns zero when
the displayed sequence does not converge.  Then $\mathscr Dq$ is a total
Borel predictable
$\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa}$-valued process and, for every $x\in G$,
\begin{equation}
 q_t(x)=\int_0^t(\mathscr Dq)_r(x)\,\dd r,
 \qquad
 \mathscr Dq(x)=\dot q(x)\quad\text{a.e.}
\end{equation}
If the path field $q$ obeys exact stopping, shift, or concatenation identities,
then, on the corresponding loci where the transformed paths also belong to
$G$, the derivative classes obey the restriction, time-shift, and
concatenation identities almost everywhere.  The same conclusion holds for
substitution of a bounded raw stopping time whenever the stopped path remains
in $G$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:22:21.902848+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b83b198ef9953ff7287ae50f4bdff9d98eb19ead2dd6ae8a0010e2fbe2991af1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:improved_asymptotic_poincaré_under_PL of arXiv:2411.11415, 'The ballistic limit of the log-Sobolev constant equals the Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz constant'] Suppose that $f \in C^2(\R^d)$, has a unique minimizer $x_\star$,

Let $\alpha, r_0 > 0$ be such that $\nabla^2 f(x) \succeq \alpha I$ for all $x \in B(x_\star, r_0)$.
Define $\delta  \deq  r_0^2/(2C_{\msf{PL}})$,
take any
$k \geqslant 1$, and put
$$
t_0  \deq  \frac{2\delta}{C_{\msf{PL}} L_0 + 2\delta L_1 + 2k-2}\,.
$$
Then for all $t < t_0$,

\begin{equation}
C_{\msf{P}}(\mu_t) 
\leqslant \frac{C_{\msf{PL}} t/ k}{1 - L_1 t - (k - 1)t/\delta - C_{\msf{PL}} L_0 t/(2\delta)}
+

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0257-law-of-large-numbers-and-constants-for-nuv-lengths","No independent review"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T09:27:45.507393+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b840dbb568d20ad9e5b1edc1d1b2857f52ee52ecedc785865e7147f767cd8824","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Law of large numbers and constants for NUV lengths structural calculation Result: An elementary geometric lower bound comes from nearest-neighbor distances d_v: the ordered discovery walk has a departure from every vertex except its final one, and every such segment is at least d_v. Hence L_NUV>=sum_v d_v-max_v d_v. For unit-intensity planar Poisson points, Palm P(d_v>r)=exp(-pi*r^2), so E d_v=1/2. In the growing-square binomial version, the bulk expectation tends to1/2 and E max d_v=O(sqrt(log n)), yielding liminf E L_NUV/n>=1/2. In the complete graph with independent mean-n exponential edge lengths, the analogous bound gives liminf E L_NUV/n>=1. Check: The mean-field minimum at each vertex has mean n/(n-1), and a union bound gives expected maximum O(log n); independence between vertices is unnecessary for these expectation bounds. The Euclidean boundary affects only a vanishing bulk fraction for the lower bound, and the maximum estimate follows from empty-ball bounds. Obstruction: These are lower constants only and may be weaker than established optimized-tour bounds. No subadditivity or stabilization argument proves convergence of the greedy length, and the source finite-size simulation constants are not theorem values.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.717324+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b86443b327e4de4c0085b4913492700e12e974b45855b12d40400447aaebe503","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2605.00997, 'Asymptotic probability of a fixed edge being on the boundary of the convex hull of a rando'] Let $k,m$ be two positive integers, at least one of them nonzero. $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, $S_0:=\boldsymbol{0}$, where the one-dimensional jumps $X_i$ are independent, identically distributed according to the law:
\[
\mathbb{P}(X_i = k) = \mathbb{P}(X_i = -k) = \mathbb{P}(X_i = m) = \mathbb{P}(X_i = -m) = \frac14.
\]
Let $N_n$ denote the number of positive partial sums among $S_1,\dots,S_n$, and set $p_n = \mathbb{P}(N_n = n)$, $p_0 = 1$. Then the asymptotic equality holds
\[
p_n \sim \frac{C_{k,m}}{\sqrt{\pi n}},\quad n\to\infty,
\]
where
\[
C_{k,m} = \exp\left(\frac1{4\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\ln\bigl(1 - \tfrac12(\cos k\theta + \cos m\theta)\bigr)\,d\theta\right).
\]","status":"unverified"}

Result: On K_n^d every vertex has degree d(n-1); at p = lambda/(d(n-1)) the exploration is close to a branching process; the first correction to the branching ratio comes from triangles: each vertex lies in d (n-1)(n-2)/2 triangles (all in one coordinate line), so the effective number of NEW vertices reached in two steps is reduced by a relative amount of order 1/d... normalising, the triangle correction is of relative order (n-2)/(d(n-1)) ~ 1/d, not 1/n, so it shifts p_c at relative order 1/d which is absorbed into a_1(d)?? The source states a_1(d) = 1/d exactly and the corrections are in powers of 1/n, so the d-dependence at fixed order is packaged into a_i(d). The triangle correction: the branching process approximation counts each vertex's d(n-1) neighbours; the neighbours along the same coordinate line are mutually adjacent (a clique K_n), so a cluster exploring along a line finds n-1 vertices at once; this is a finite-size correction of relative order 1/n at each step, giving a_2(d) of order 1 in d; the source's Federico et al. result identifies it. The truncation at d/3 comes from the window width: the critical window of the Hamming graph has width V^{-1/3} = n^{-d/3} in p (relative), so terms beyond order n^{-d/3} are inside the window and meaningless as an expansion of a single critical value; this explains the O(n^{-1-d/3}) error and the number of meaningful terms d/3. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236593+00:00","domain":"numerical analysis","id":"claim_b8a68d2eccee5860bfb70fd0f24e13b2b7626e3471541b131b79447a4472e0ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a floating-point number system, the machine epsilon eps is the smallest positive representable number such that 1 + eps, computed with that system's rounding rule, is strictly greater than 1; equivalently, eps is the gap between 1 and the next larger representable floating-point number. For IEEE 754 binary double precision (53-bit significand, including one implicit leading bit), eps = 2^(-52). The associated unit roundoff u = eps/2 = 2^(-53) bounds the relative error of rounding a real number x, within the representable range, to the nearest floating-point number fl(x): |fl(x) - x| / |x| <= u. More generally, each basic arithmetic operation (+, -, *, /) computed in IEEE arithmetic satisfies fl(a op b) = (a op b) * (1 + delta) for some |delta| <= u.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:48:00.296081+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b8ab82999fefb43edeb515d77eaed8b7f3878d6c086bd96a599f64c1e7989fea","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem random_apprx_noisless of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a compact metric space, let $\mu\in\mathcal{P}(X)$, and let
$X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be i.i.d.\ with law $\mu$.  Fix $\varepsilon>0$, set
$M_\varepsilon\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} N_{\varepsilon/4}(X,\rho)$, and let
$x_1^\star,\ldots,x_{M_\varepsilon}^\star\in X$ be such that
$X=\bigcup_{m=1}^{M_\varepsilon}B_\rho(x_m^\star,\varepsilon/4)$.
Assume that
$
    p_\varepsilon
    \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
    \min_{m\in[M_\varepsilon]_+}
    \mu\big(B_\rho(x_m^\star,\varepsilon/4)\big)
    >
    0.
$
Then, for every $f\in \operatorname{Lip}((X,\rho);1)$ and every $\delta\in(0,1)$, if
\begin{equation}

    N
    \ge
    \frac{1}{p_\varepsilon}
    \log\left(\frac{M_\varepsilon}{\delta}\right)
,
\end{equation}
then the noiseless estimator
$\mathcal{E}(f|((X_n,0))_{n=1}^N)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \sup_{x\in X}\,
        \big|
            f(x)
            -
            \mathcal{E}(f|((X_n,0))_{n=1}^N)(x)
        \big|
        <
        \varepsilon
    \right)
    \ge
    1-\delta
.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.967682+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b8af826c0cd9366894fae1ba5a6454ce9f31cafe8f46b48911fc599e3dcb8bba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2607.22416, 'A multi-player optimal stopping game based on a spider Brownian bridge'] Fix $d>0$.
    Recall the definition of $\Gamma_d$ in \eqref{ExpressionGammap0.5} and define $\Upsilon = \Upsilon_d = \Upsilon_{\alpha,\theta,d}:[0,\infty) \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ by $\Upsilon(z) = \Gamma_d(z) - h_\alpha(z)$.
 Then $\tilde{z}$ is a turning point of $\Gamma_d$ if and only if $\tilde{z}$ is a root of $\Upsilon$.
  
The function $\Gamma_{d}$ admits a maximizer, denoted $z^{*}=z^{*}(\alpha,\theta,d)$. 
Furthermore, there exists $\hat{\Theta}:(0,\infty) \times (0,\infty)$ with $\Theta_*(\alpha,d) \leq \hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d)\leq \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\theta < \Theta_*(\alpha,d)$ then
$\Upsilon$ has a unique root $z_1 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$, and that root is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\theta = \Theta_*(\alpha,d)$ then 
$\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_1=0$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$, and $z_2$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\Theta_*(\alpha,d) < \theta < \hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_1 \in (0, \frac{\alpha}{2})$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$ and  $z_2$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\theta= \hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_{1}\in (0,\frac{\alpha}{2})$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$. Both $0$ and $z_{2}$ are maximisers of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\hat{\Theta}(\alpha,d) < \theta < \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$ has two roots $z_{1}\in (0,\frac{\alpha}{2})$ and $z_2 \in (\frac{\alpha}{2}, \bar{z}(\alpha))$. 0 is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$.

\item If $\theta = \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ then $\frac{\alpha}{2}$ is the unique root of $\Upsilon$ and $0$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$. 

    
\item If $\theta > \Theta^*(\alpha,d)$ then $\Upsilon$  has no roots and $0$ is the maximiser of $\Gamma_d$. 
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.936368+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b8be77236b9f2840d028ddb7d4ca0d0143afa7501eb6ba9a01ef02776414bf10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Main meeting-time bounds) of arXiv:2607.13183, '2607.13183'] There are absolute constants $0<c<C<\infty$ such that the first two assertions

\[
        c n

        \le C n .
\]

\[
        c n

        \le t_{\rm meet}(\mathcal C_1)

\]

\item Fix $A_0\ge0$ and suppose that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:44:12.645435+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b8cb276b9f61563954f345c8ccc5baad97296424c146601a48fc833ea8ad8d65","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Multipliers \(\mathcal O_M(\R^d)\) and slow growth of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] A function \(a\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is called \emph{slowly increasing at infinity} if for every multi–index
\(\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n\) there exists \(N_\alpha\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(C_\alpha>0\) such that
\[
  \left|\partial^\alpha a(x)\right| \le C_\alpha\,(1+\left|x\right|)^{\,N_\alpha}\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^d .
\]
We write
\[
  \mathcal O_M(\mathbb{R}^d)
  := \bigl\{ a\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d): \text{each } \partial^\alpha a \text{ has at most polynomial growth}\bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(\mathcal O_M(\mathbb{R}^d)\) is the space of \emph{multipliers} of \(\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)\): those
\(a\) for which \(a\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)\) for all \(\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^d)\), and the map
\(\varphi\mapsto a\varphi\) is continuous \(\mathcal S\to\mathcal S\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.750964+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b8ddcfebe7b6b76baaf17d5f38740303af576b97f5b1dea16705e2d5a3786c75","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:trace-to-replica of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Let $G$ be the Gibbs measure, $P=\mathrm{Cov}(G)$ and $T=\diag(P)$.

\[

\qquad
f:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i,
\qquad
\widehat\sigma_i^\ell:=\frac{\sigma_i^\ell-m_i}{\sqrt{1-m_i^2}},
\qquad
\widehat f:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (\widehat\sigma_i^1-\widehat\sigma_i^2)(\widehat\sigma_i^3-\widehat\sigma_i^4).

\mathsf{Tr}[PDP] &= \frac{n^2}{4}\,\langle f\widehat f\rangle, \\
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \langle a_i^2\rangle &= \frac{4}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ii}^2.  \\

\mathsf{Tr}[TP^2] &= \frac{n^2}{4}\,\langle f\,f^{\mathrm{diag}}\rangle, \\

It provides sufficient conditions for a set-valued function defined on a convex, compact subset of a Euclidean space to have a fixed point, i.e. a point which is mapped to a set containing it. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.475586+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b927d4bfca0e0ed183d4a2cbb709c014fb7b926ca197c2f13b9ef4edad23f4c2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $G$ be compact with left Haar measure $\mu$ and let $G^{\op}$ denote the opposite group of $G$. 
Take the right Haar measure on $G^{\op}$ to be $\mu$. 
Then, 
\[ \Sym_L^G(f) = \Sym_R^{G^{\op}}(f) , \]
where $f$ is any probability density on $G$. 

\begin{proof}
Denote the group operation on $G$ by $\cdot$ and on $G^{\op}$ by $\cdot^{\op}$. 
Note that for any $\mu$-measurable $A \subseteq G^{op}$ and $x \in G^{op}$, 
\[ \mu(A\cdot^{\op} x) 
= \mu(\{ a \cdot^{\op} x \mid a \in A \})
= \mu(\{ xa \mid a \in A \})
= \mu(x\cdot A) 
= \mu(A)
\]
So indeed $\mu$ is a right Haar measure on $G^{\op}$. 

Now take $f,g$ to be probability densities with respect to $\mu$ in $G$. 
Since $G$ and $G^{\op}$ have the same topology, $f,g$ are also probability densities on $G^{\op}$. 
Thus, 
\begin{align*}
\Sym_R^{G^{\op}}(f)
&= \{ g \mid \forall y \quad (f *^{\op} g)(y) 
                           = (f *^{\op} g)(y^{-1})  \} \\
&= \left\{ g \mid \forall y \quad \int_{G^{\op}} f(w) g(w^{-1}y) \,d\mu(w) 
                           = \int_{G^{\op}} f(w) g(w^{-1}y^{-1}) \,d\mu(w) \right\} \\

&= \left\{ g \mid \forall y \quad \int_{G} g(s) f(ys^{-1}) \,d\mu(s) 
                           = \int_{G} g(s) f(y^{-1}s^{-1}) \,d\mu(s) \right\} \\
&= \{ g \mid \forall y \quad (g * f)(y) 
                           = (g * f)(y^{-1})  \} \\
&= \Sym_L^{G}(f) .\qedhere
\end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.496908+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b931729135640d03b6c4fe1eb338bc5aaefb0c83d4cce9e6a788cde552029029","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm commutation_relation_u0 of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] In the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, consider $n$ radial SLEs starting at $e^{i\theta_1}, e^{i\theta_2}, \ldots, e^{i\theta_n} \in \partial \mathbb{D}$, with a marked interior point \( u=0 \).
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] Let the infinitesimal diffusion generators be
    \begin{equation}
     
    \mathcal{M}_i = \frac{\kappa}{2} \partial_{ii} + b_i(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n) \partial_i + \sum_{j \neq i} \cot\left(\frac{\theta_j - \theta_i}{2}\right) \partial_j,
     \end{equation}
    where \( \partial_i = \partial_{\theta_i} \). If the $n$ SLEs locally commute, the associated infinitesimal generators satisfy:
    \[
    [\mathcal{M}_i, \mathcal{M}_j] = \frac{1}{\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta_j - \theta_i}{2}\right)} (\mathcal{M}_j - \mathcal{M}_i).
    \]

    There exists a positive function $\psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, defined on $\mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, such that the drift term satisfies
    \[
    b_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \kappa \partial_i \log \psi,
    \]
    and $\psi$ satisfies the null vector equations:
    \begin{equation}
    \frac{\kappa}{2} \partial_{ii} \psi + \sum_{j \neq i} \cot\left(\frac{\theta_j - \theta_i}{2}\right) \partial_i \psi + \left(1 - \frac{6}{\kappa}\right) \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{1}{4 \sin^2\left(\frac{\theta_j - \theta_i}{2}\right)} \psi - h_j(\theta_j) \psi = 0,
    \end{equation}
    for \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, n \), with undetermined functions $h_j(\theta_j)$.

    \item[(ii)] By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of two adjacent growth points \( \theta_i \) and \( \theta_{i+1} \) (with no marked points between them), we further deduce that \( h_i(\theta) = h_{i+1}(\theta) \). Consequently, if all growth points are consecutive with no marked points between them, there exists a common function $h(\theta)$ such that
    \[
    h(\theta) = h_1(\theta) = \cdots = h_n(\theta).
    \]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined electrical network with nonnegative conductances, on a finite graph or an infinite graph with appropriate limiting or boundary conditions","the comparison is between two networks differing only in conductance values on a common edge set, or related by a clean edge addition, deletion, or vertex identification","finite total energy for the relevant flows or potentials, so the variational characterization is well posed","for random-walk conclusions, the standard correspondence between the electrical network and a reversible Markov chain"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993128+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_b9387245512e1cdb33d492e04652cfd536ce550cebd97a2fc52f4dd9dc6c0a91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an electrical network on a graph with nonnegative edge conductances c_e, the effective resistance R_eff(a,b) between vertices a, b is defined variationally, via Thomson's principle, as the minimum of sum_e (1/c_e) i_e^2 over unit flows i from a to b obeying Kirchhoff's node law, or equivalently via Dirichlet's principle over voltage functions. Rayleigh's monotonicity law states that R_eff(a,b) is monotone nonincreasing as a function of each conductance: increasing any conductance, adding an edge, or short-circuiting (identifying) any pair of vertices can only decrease or preserve R_eff(a,b), while decreasing a conductance, or deleting an edge, can only increase or preserve it. This purely variational fact underlies comparisons between random walks on different graphs via the resistance-recurrence correspondence, that a network is recurrent for its associated random walk if and only if R_eff(a,infinity)=infinity, comparisons of hitting and commute times, and resistance-based bounds on percolation-type crossing quantities. It gives only monotone comparisons, no quantitative rates, and using it for random-walk conclusions requires the standard electrical network-reversible Markov chain correspondence, with conductances proportional to transition rates, to be correctly set up first. Typical failure: Applying Rayleigh monotonicity to compare effective resistances between two networks that differ in more than conductance values on a shared edge set, such as networks on genuinely different vertex sets or after a modification that is not literally a conductance increase/decrease, edge addition/deletion, or vertex identification; the monotonicity is a coupling statement about the same underlying network with modified weights, and applying it across structurally different networks without an explicit embedding produces an unjustified comparison. Canonical reference: Rayleigh, 1871, Philosophical Magazine; Doyle and Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks, 1984, Mathematical Association of America; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}
