{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.594873+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c11c93a31630fef9ceceed0d5860dd7b8408b9f813e6ced1defab956704fd454","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398, '\\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] Recent work has shown that sub-Gaussian random variables are dominated in convex order by a sharp multiple of a Gaussian. We study the analogous question for the sub-Gamma class underlying Bernstein's inequality, with the Laplace law as the majorant. Here the moment generating function is controlled by a Bernstein-type bound over a finite range of frequencies, rather than by a purely quadratic bound. We derive a variational formula for the optimal multiple, show that it is strictly larger than the natural scale $σ\\vee α$, and prove that this value is sharp, being attained by an asymmetric two-point distribution. We then turn to the sub-exponential class, which has a quadratic bound as in the sub-Gaussian case, but only over a bounded range as in the sub-Gamma case. Interestingly, the sub-exponential class displays a different behavior: the optimal multiple is exactly $σ\\vee α$, but is attained only when $α\\leq σ$; when $α> σ$, the constant remains sharp, but equality cannot hold for any non-affine convex function. Both results rely on a sharp finite-range variant of the Kearns-Saul inequality, which is of independent interest. (abstract text taken from the arXiv listing metadata; the TeX carried no abstract environment)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:30.016157+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c12bf9d3c3a8abb63308ee247eecf7accaa4b1b45fcd8237561c328d3a969ba9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \begin{enumerate}
\item A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Kato class measure} if it satisfies \( \lim_{\alpha \to \infty}\|U_\alpha \mu\|_{\infty, q} =0.\) Denote by \(\mathcal{K}\) the set of all Kato class measures.
\item  A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Dynkin class measure} if it satisfies \(\|U_1 \mu\|_{\infty, q} < \infty \). Denote by \(\mathcal{D}\) the set of all Dynkin class measures.
\item A Kato class measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Green-tight measure} for \(R_1\) if, for any \(\varepsilon >0\), there exists a compact set \(K\) such that \(\|R_1(1_{K^c}\mu)\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon\). Denote by \(\mathcal{K}_\infty= \mathcal{K}_\infty(R_1)\) the set of all Green-tight measures.

\item A Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_1(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0\) the set of all Radon measures of finite energy integrals.

\item When $(\form,\dom)$ is transient, a Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it \(0\)-order finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}\). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:45:17.650190+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c13cdf1ae89ace7e10968dd9d90bebdf0a5a3981f00c2bd17aa4dddc8ddd0b19","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defin:gammadef of arXiv:2604.08462, 'Convergence of $k$-point functions in\\ high dimensional percolation'] We introduce the notation $\Gamma(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ for the event $\{a_1 \leftrightarrow a_2 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow a_k\}$ that $a_1, \dots, a_k$ are in the same open cluster. We use the notation $\tau_k(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ for the $k$-point functions:
\[\tau_k(a_1, \dots, a_k) = \mathbb{P}(\Gamma(a_1, \dots, a_k))\ . \]
We occasionally overload notation, writing in case $A = \{x_1, \dots, x_k\}$
\[\Gamma(A) = \Gamma(x_1, \dots, x_k), \]
or
\[\Gamma(z, A) = \Gamma(z, x_1, \dots, x_k)\ ,\]
with similar extensions for e.g.~$\tau_k(A)$.

The open cluster $\mathfrak{C}(x)$ is the connected component of $x$ in the random open subgraph of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. In other words, $\mathfrak{C}(x) = \{y: \, \Gamma(x,y) \text{ occurs}\}$. We also introduce the notion of ``restricted'' connections and clusters. If $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$, we write $\{x \ensuremath{\,{\buildrel A \over \longleftrightarrow}\,} y\}$ for the event that $x$ and $y$ are connected by an open path lying entirely in $A$. We write $\mathfrak{C}_A(x) = \{y: \, x \ensuremath{\,{\buildrel A \over \longleftrightarrow}\,} y\}$ for the connected component of $x$ in the open subgraph of $A$.

We write $x \Longleftrightarrow y$ for the event that there are two edge-disjoint open connections from $x$ to $y$, and we write $x \stackrel{A}{\Longleftrightarrow} y$ for the event that there are two edge-disjoint connections from $x$ to $y$ lying entirely in the set $A$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.318510+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c1425fc50cf7d1f9ebff299ca6dda4e190fab5c3157b0c3ed92879419eb2caff","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma theorem4.4 of arXiv:2606.01664, 'Brown measure convergence for the spectrum of polynomials in Ginibre matrices'] In a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, let $E,Y\subset \mathcal{H}$ be linear subspaces. Denote by $P_{Y^\perp}$ the orthogonal projection onto $Y^\perp$ and define 
$$
T:=P_{Y^\perp}\mid_E:E\to Y^\perp.
$$For any threshold $\tau>0$, denote by 
$$
C_\tau(E,Y)\subset E
$$ the vector space spanned by all right singular vectors of $T$ with singular value at most $\tau$. Denote their dimensions by 
$$
c_\tau:=\dim_\mathbb{C}C_\tau(E,Y),\quad e:=\dim_\mathbb{C}E.
$$We then define the tuple 
$$
\mathcal{T}_\rho(E,Y):=\{x\in E:\|x\|\leq 2,\operatorname{dist}(x,Y)\leq\rho\}.
$$Then we have the following inclusion 
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{T}_\rho(E,Y)\subset (B_{C_\tau(E,Y)}(2))+\frac{\rho}{\tau}B_E(1).   
\end{equation}
More specifically, if we have the following orthogonal decomposition 
$$
E=C_\tau(E,Y)\oplus (C_\tau(E,Y))^\perp, 
$$then each element $x\in\mathcal{T}_p(E,Y)$ can be decomposed as 
\begin{equation}
x=x_0+x_1,\quad x_0\in C_\tau(E,Y),\quad x_1\in (C_\tau(E,Y))^\perp\cap E,
\end{equation}satisfying that $\|x_0\|\leq 2,\|x_1\|\leq\rho/\tau$.

Therefore, for every mesh size $0<\epsilon<1$, $\mathcal{T}_\rho(E,Y)$ has an $\epsilon$-net of cardinality at most 
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{N}_\epsilon(\mathcal{T}_\rho(E,Y))\leq \left(\frac{C}{\epsilon}\right)^{2c_\tau}\left(\frac{C\max\{\rho/\tau,\epsilon\}}{\epsilon}\right)^{2(e-c_\tau)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\mathcal{T}_\rho(E,Y)$ has an $\epsilon$-net $\mathcal{N}_\epsilon'$ contained entirely inside $T_\rho(E,Y)$ of cardinality
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{N}_\epsilon'(\mathcal{T}_\rho(E,Y))\leq \left(\frac{2C}{\epsilon}\right)^{2c_\tau}\left(\frac{2C\max\{\rho/\tau,\epsilon/2\}}{\epsilon}\right)^{2(e-c_\tau)}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.091718+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c14325f78e6c96fc5fdb6a81ceb83e6488d6b52c2c688742bdf4bb6719abc5c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 46 (One-step tilted spine law and its Beta limit) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Denote by $\mu_{k,t}$ the conditional law of $P_{\ell+1}$ under the spine measure
$\Q_t$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We have
$$
\mu_{k,t}\!\left(\left\{\frac{j}{m}\right\}\right)
=
\frac{\theta}{\beta_{m,t}(\theta)}\,
\frac{j^{t-1}}{m^t}\,
\frac{\Gamma(m+1)\,\Gamma(m-j+\theta)}
{\Gamma(m-j+1)\,\Gamma(m+\theta)},
$$
\item As $k$ goes to infinity, $\mu_{k,t}$ converges in distribution to a
    $\mathrm{Beta}(t,\theta)$ distribution with density 
    $$f_t(x) =
    \frac{\Gamma(t+\theta)}{\Gamma(t)\,\Gamma(\theta)}\,x^{t-1}\,(1-x)^{\theta-1}\,\mathbf
    1_{(0,1)}(x).$$
\item Consequently, if $ P\sim \mathrm{Beta}(t,\theta)$ and $X_{\ell+1} = -\log
    P_{\ell+1}$, then $X_{\ell+1}$ converges in distribution to $-\log P$.
 \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:43:45.383424+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c1491c663ad94b7bf8325c5de118fae0ca479e972d0a309d962b3c453635d47e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2609.04095, '2609.04095'] Let \(d\ge1\), let \(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_d>0\), and let
\(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d\ge0\) be log-concave with interval support
\(\{0,1,\ldots,e\}\), where \(1\le e\le d\).  Put
\[
 \pi_j:=\omega_j\lambda_j,
 \qquad
 M(t):=
 \frac{\sum_{j=0}^d j\omega_jt^j}
      {\sum_{j=0}^d\omega_jt^j}
 \quad(t>0),
\]
\[
 \bar\jmath:=
 \frac{\sum_{j=0}^d j\pi_j}
      {\sum_{j=0}^d\pi_j}.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item \(M\) is strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), and there is a
      unique \(t>0\) such that \(M(t)=\bar\jmath\).
\item For this \(t\), choose \(\kappa>0\) such that
      \[
       \widetilde\pi_j:=\kappa\omega_jt^j,
       \qquad
       \sum_j\widetilde\pi_j=\sum_j\pi_j,
      \]
      and put \(\Delta_j:=\pi_j-\widetilde\pi_j\).  Then
      \[
       \sum_j\Delta_j=\sum_jj\Delta_j=0,
      \]
      and \(\{j:\Delta_j>0\}\) is an interval.
\item \(\pi_0\le\widetilde\pi_0\).
\item
      \[
       \sum_jj^2\Delta_j\le0,
       \qquad
       \sum_j\frac{\Delta_j}{j+1}\le0.
      \]
\item If \(\rho>0\) and
      \(\lambda_{j+1}\le\rho\lambda_j\) for \(0\le j<d\), then
      \(t\le\rho\).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.414810+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c14e11946032186794e816a1686020bbcdc021aafd35983c07a1b558612c629b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 134 (Raw covariance-response first-jet selection) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Assume an admissible testing core in the sense of
\Cref{def:admissible-backward-testing-core}.  Then the backward
value--martingale response program selects the stable first-jet state
$\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}$ with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item Every energy-bounded covariance cross-response generates a unique
fiber-valued local jet $D_Q^{\rm pw}Y_t\in\mathscr E_{\mathfrak a_t}$ by Riesz
representation, with the regularized covariance-pseudoinverse formula
\eqref{eq:backward-pseudoinverse-factorization}.  The common-completion
condition \textup{(A2)} makes its active section a class in
$\mathbb H_{\cP}^2$, and under every law that class is the covariance-energy
class of the classical GKW coefficient.
\item The terminal martingale response calibrates the
$\mathbb H_{\cP}^2$ jet norm isometrically at every stopping horizon, while
the complete path response $(Y,I(Z))$ reconstructs the graph completion up to
stable-causal bi-Lipschitz equivalence.
\item No proper noninjective stable-causal quotient is lossless for
the complete first-jet response.
\item The completed first-jet state is a closed linear relation.  It is the
graph of a single-valued closed response operator exactly when its vertical
space vanishes.  Genuine compression to the inherited value-process topology
then occurs exactly when the value domain is closed; otherwise the recovery
operator is unbounded and the graph topology retains the jet.
\end{enumerate}
The derivative leg uses the covariance channel rather than skew area, while
the zero-order environmental state may still retain area.  Orthogonal
martingale components remain visible in the value trajectory but outside the
covariance jet.  Solver identification is governed separately by
\Cref{def:backward-compatible-interface}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.899215+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c1626cc50ea1f08795814dc1868b7c5f88e64cab461bfb93a5692eb6859312e2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eraGcont of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}\! \equiv \!  \textrm{and}\quad {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GHP}}\big( (T^n_{\! \mu_n, h_n} , d_n, \rho_n ,  \mathtt{P}_{T^n_{\! \mu_n, h_n}} \mu_n)\, &, \, (T_{\! \mu , h}, d, \rho, \mathtt{P}_{T_{\! \mu , h}} \mu) \big)  \longrightarrow 0\, .

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:22:20.957145+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c165a3b85729dd68acf7318654e2f3a256a37fe5a0e62bad40a3fb64af2f8e82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Recovery in the limit $\varphi\to1$) of arXiv:2604.20634, 'Distributional Statistical Models:\\ \large Weak Moments, Cumulants, and a Central Limit T'] Let $f\in L^1(\R)$ and let $\psi$ be measurable with $\psi f\in L^1(\R)$.

$\varphi_\varepsilon>0$, $\varphi_\varepsilon\to1$ pointwise as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and
\[

\;\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\downarrow0]{}\;
\int_\R\psi(x)f(x)\,dx .

{"assumptions":["uniform measure","f not identically 0 for the log statements"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:12:41.903316+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_c19d664cb5b6f18d70886236b05bd8deb91122fc23f5f0977fdb87209bee1268","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. RELLICH IDENTITY: for every u in C^2(closure of Omega) one has integral_Omega (x . grad u) Laplacian(u) dx = ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx - (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |grad u|^2 dS + integral_{boundary} (x . grad u)(du/dnu) dS. POHOZAEV IDENTITY: if in addition u = 0 on the boundary of Omega and -Laplacian(u) = f(u) in Omega with f continuous and F(t) = integral_0^t f(s) ds, then, since on the boundary grad u = (du/dnu) nu, the two boundary terms collapse and one gets ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx + (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |du/dnu|^2 dS = n integral_Omega F(u) dx. CONSEQUENCE (nonexistence): let n >= 3, let Omega be star-shaped with respect to the origin (x . nu >= 0 on the boundary) with C^1 boundary, and let f(u) = |u|^(p-1) u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2). Multiplying the equation by u gives integral |grad u|^2 = integral |u|^(p+1), while Pohozaev gives ((n-2)/2) integral |u|^(p+1) + (1/2) integral_{boundary}(x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = (n/(p+1)) integral |u|^(p+1). Since p >= (n+2)/(n-2) is exactly n/(p+1) <= (n-2)/2, the boundary term is <= 0 while star-shapedness makes it >= 0; hence it vanishes and integral |u|^(p+1) = 0 for p > (n+2)/(n-2).    	$\beta(t_1,t_2)\leq \beta(t_3,t_4)$ if $(t_1,t_2)\subset (t_3,t_4)$ and there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726188+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_c1ffc6c7824bf7e532852028244a4f3f17e1d97b6a2fce726d3b11f59a0d7c16","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x(R×R^n)} ≤ C‖f‖_{L²} the exponents must satisfy 2/q + n/r = n/2 exactly, and q ≥ 2 (and r ≥ 2). None of these can be relaxed, so an argument that 'interpolates' to a pair off the scaling line, or that uses a short-time-looking pair with q < 2, is wrong. Scaling: for f_λ(x) = f(λx) one has (e^{itΔ}f_λ)(x) = (e^{iλ²tΔ}f)(λx), hence ‖e^{itΔ}f_λ‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} = λ^{−2/q − n/r}‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} while ‖f_λ‖_{L²} = λ^{−n/2}‖f‖_{L²}. If 2/q + n/r ≠ n/2 the ratio of the two sides is λ^{n/2 − 2/q − n/r}, which is unbounded as λ → 0 or λ → ∞ for any fixed f ≠ 0. So an estimate off the scaling line fails for every nonzero f. Necessity of q ≥ 2 (the case r > 2; on the scaling line r = 2 forces q = ∞, so there is nothing to prove there): take φ ∈ S(R^n) and f_N = Σ_{k=1}^N e^{−i t_k Δ}φ with t_1 ≪ t_2 ≪ ... ≪ t_N separated enough that Σ_{j≠k}|t_k − t_j|^{−n(1/2−1/r)} is small for every k. Since |⟨e^{isΔ}φ, φ⟩| ≤ (4π|s|)^{−n/2}‖φ‖_{L¹}² → 0, the summands are almost orthogonal in L² and ‖f_N‖_{L²}² ≈ N‖φ‖²_{L²}; and for t within O(1) of t_k the dispersive estimate makes every term but the k-th small in L^r_x, so ‖e^{itΔ}f_N‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} ≳ N^{1/q}‖e^{itΔ}φ‖_{L^q_t([−1,1]) L^r_x}. The ratio is ≳ N^{1/q − 1/2}, unbounded when q < 2. Known excluded endpoints, where the pair is on the scaling line and q = 2 but the estimate is still false: (q,r) = (2,∞) for Schrödinger in n = 2 (Montgomery-Smith), and (q,r) = (2,∞) for the wave equation in n = 3 (Klainerman–Machedon). Also for the wave equation the Lebesgue-space estimate is stated with r < ∞; at r = ∞ one must pass to Besov spaces.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:52.493692+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c21a41315bc24d80ae4bd7020fe06ab73d18c4a9b3e069785ff80e5dc4979e72","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 256 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Assume $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ is realized by a bipartite gluing graph $\mathsf{G}$, with bipartition $\epsilon : [m] \rightarrow \{\pm 1\}$. Then the vector $\boldsymbol{v} = \epsilon_1\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_1}$ has $\mathfrak{G}$-orbit $\{\epsilon_i\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_i}\,\,|\,\,i\in [m]\}$, this orbit is good (\textit{cf.} Definition~\ref{def:goodor}) and has minimal size $m = \textnormal{rank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) + 1$. For any $i \in [m]$ and $h \in [H]$ we have
\[
T^{(h)}(\epsilon_i \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_i}) = \left\{\begin{array}{ccc}  \epsilon_i \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_i} && \textnormal{if}\,\,h \notin \mathcal{H}_i, \\[0.6ex] \epsilon_{i'_h}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{i'_h}} && \textnormal{if}\,\,h \in \mathcal{H}_i. \end{array}\right.

The genus of the spectral curve $\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ is $\mathsf{g}_{\boldsymbol{v}} = \textnormal{corank}(\boldsymbol{\Theta})$ and the group $\hat{\mathfrak{G}}$ is the Weyl group of type $A_{m - 1}$ (\textit{i.e.} the symmetric group in $m$ elements).

Its matrix of biresidues is \textbf{\foreignlanguage{russian}{B}} = $\textnormal{\textbf{Id}} - \boldsymbol{1}$, and the bidifferential itself is equal to
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{B}_{\boldsymbol{v}} = \mathcal{B}^{\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\mathcal{L}} - \frac{\dd z_1\dd z_2}{(z_1 - z_2)^2},
\end{equation}
where $(z_1,z_2) = Z_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{v}}}$, the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} \subset H_1(\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\amsmathbb{Z})$ is spanned by cycles around the components of the gluing locus (\textit{cf.} Definition~\ref{def:spcurv1}), and $\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\mathcal{L}}$ is the fundamental bidifferential of Section~\ref{sec:fund02}.

\[
\begin{array}{ccc} \textnormal{Ker}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) & \longrightarrow & H^1(\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}},\amsmathbb{C}) \\
\boldsymbol{v}' & \longmapsto & \mathfrak{u}_{\boldsymbol{v};\boldsymbol{v}'} \end{array}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.769101+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c21d93a68c67c686ea5a8cd2e99c7b889993d1a4ff262836889ebac6fb9aa426","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.31168, 'The anisotropic Michael-Simon inequality for surfaces in every codimension'] Let $m \geq 2$ and consider a vector field $S \in C_c^{\infty}(\bR^m;\bR^m)$.
For every sufficiently small $\tau> 0$, there exists a finite set $F_{\tau} \subset \bR^m$ and
\[
S_{\tau} \in C_c^{\infty}(\bR^m; \bR^m), \qquad \eta_{\tau} \in C_c^{\infty} (\bR^m), \qquad U_{\tau} \in C^{\infty}(\bR^m \setminus F_{\tau} ; \bS^{m-1})
\]
with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item We have $S_{\tau} = \eta_{\tau} U_{\tau}$ for $\eta_{\tau} \geq 0$, $U_{\tau}$ is a unit vector field, and, as $\tau \downarrow 0$,
    \[
    S_{\tau} \to S, \qquad \textup{div} \, S_{\tau} \to \textup{div} \, S \quad \text{in } \; L^1(\bR^m).
    \]
    \item We have $U_{\tau} = e$ outside a compact set, where $e \in \bS^{m-1}$ is any prescribed vector.
    Also, for every $p \in F_{\tau}$, there exist $r_p > 0$ and $Q_p \in O(m)$ such that
    \[
    U_{\tau}(x) = Q_p \frac{x-p}{|x-p|} \quad \text{for } \; 0 < |x-p| < r_p.
    \]
    The sign $\det Q_p = \pm 1$ is the local degree of the singularity.
    \item For $m=2$, depending on the index $\pm 1$ of the point $p$, we can moreover arrange
    \[
    U_{\tau}(z) = i \frac{z-p}{|z-p|} \quad \text{if $p$ has index $1$}, \qquad U_{\tau}(z) = i \frac{\overline{z-p}}{|z-p|} \quad \text{if $p$ has index $-1$}.
    \]
    Moreover, all but finitely many maximal integral curves of $U_{\tau}$ are defined for all time and are disjoint from $F_{\tau}$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:32:58.363785+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c226a2c7f1b05f071ff1d7d3b07885611556c5fba25a89c94df53037ad91759a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition H-reduced graph of arXiv:2506.06559, 'Bi-infinite incipient cluster in high dimensions'] Let $G$ be a multigraph, we say that an edge $\{x,y\}$ is \emph{H-reducible} if $x$ and $y$ both have an edge degree at least 3 in $G$ and $x$, $y$ are only connected by one edge. 

We define a multigraph $\tilde{G}$, called \emph{H-reduction of $G$ by $\{x,y\}$}, in the following manner:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $x$ and $y$ have degree 3, then $V(\tilde{G})=V(G)\setminus \{x,y\}$ and $E(\tilde{G})=E(G) \setminus (\{\{x,z\}; x\sim_G z\} \cup \{\{y,z\}; y\sim_G z\}) \cup \{e_{x\setminus y}, e_{y \setminus x}\}$ with $e_{x\setminus y}=\{z_1, z_2\}$ where $z_1,z_2$ are the neighbours of $x$ which are not $y$ (and a symmetrical definition of $e_{y\setminus x}$)
\item if $x$ has degree 3, $y$ has degree at least 4, then then $V(\tilde{G})=V(G)\setminus \{x\}$ and $E(\tilde{G})=E(G) \setminus (\{\{x,z\}; z\sim_G z\} ) \cup \{e_{x\setminus y}\}$.
\item if $x$ and $y$ both have degree at least 4, then  $V(\tilde{G})=V(G)$ and $E(\tilde{G})=E(G)\setminus \{x,y\}$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:47:07.706693+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c23f1f825a326fafd36306b68cf59d0681c5ae639e78a672c072a036a5ddf624","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 1 ({\cite[Lemma 2.1) of arXiv:2608.06232, 'The mean absolute deviation of the classical discrete distributions:\\ collapse identities'] {elezovic_mad}}]
	Let $\lambda_j,\mu_k>0$ and $u_j,v_k\in\R$, where $1\le j\le\rho$ and
	$1\le k\le\sigma$.  Put
	\[
		F(x)=\frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\lambda_jx+u_j)}
			{\prod_k\Gamma(\mu_kx+v_k)} .
	\]
	If $\Lambda:=\sum_j\lambda_j-\sum_k\mu_k=0$, then, as $x\to\infty$,
	\begin{equation}
		\log F(x)\sim \Theta\,x+U\log x+K
		+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n(n+1)}\,S_{n+1}\,\frac{1}{x^{n}},
	\end{equation}
	where
	\[
		\Theta=\sum_j\lambda_j\log\lambda_j-\sum_k\mu_k\log\mu_k,\qquad
		U=\sum_j\Bigl(u_j-\tfrac12\Bigr)-\sum_k\Bigl(v_k-\tfrac12\Bigr),
	\]
	\[
		K=\sum_j\Bigl(u_j-\tfrac12\Bigr)\log\lambda_j
		 -\sum_k\Bigl(v_k-\tfrac12\Bigr)\log\mu_k+\frac{\rho-\sigma}{2}\log2\pi,
	\]
	\begin{equation}
		S_{n+1}=\sum_{j}\lambda_j^{-n}B_{n+1}(u_j)-\sum_{k}\mu_k^{-n}B_{n+1}(v_k),
	\end{equation}
	and, for every $M$, the remainder after $M$ series terms is $O(x^{-M-1})$, uniformly for the
	shifts in compact sets and the scalings in compact subsets of $(0,\infty)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:26:40.351843+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c24518fdc9bb8c7d0548e84810d71223fe8017f26734138f246472f2715b9fe5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 ($\AS$) of arXiv:2511.07350, 'Decoupling of clusters in independent sets in a percolated hypercube'] Define the random independent set $\hat{I}$ in $\Qp$ via the following procedure.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $\cH$ be $\cE$ or $\cO$, with probabilities proportional to $e^{\Psi^\cE}$ and $e^{\Psi^\cO}$ respectively.
		\item Let $\tilde{S}$ denote a subset of $\cH$ which includes each $v \in \cH$ independently with probability
		$\fr{2^{-\N(v)}}{1 + 2^{-\N(v)}}$.
		\item If $\tilde{S}$ contains any triple of vertices which is \emph{2-linked},
        terminate the algorithm with a result of failure.
		Otherwise, remove all dimers from $\tilde{S}$ and let $S_1$ denote the resulting set of well-separated singletons (which share no neighbors).
		\item Let $S_2$ denote a collection of dimers constructed by including each $\{u,v\} \in \Dim^\cH$ independently with probability
		$\fr{2^{-\N(\{u,v\})}}{1 + 2^{-\N(\{u,v\})}}$.
		\item If any neighbor of a dimer in $S_2$ also neighbors a vertex in $S_1$, {or if any pair of dimers in $S_2$ overlap or share a neighbor,}
        terminate the algorithm with a result of failure.
		Otherwise, let $\hat{S} = S_1 \cup S_2$.
		\item Let $\hat{I}$ denote the independent set with $\hat{I} \cap \cH = \hat{S}$ and with every vertex in $\Q \setminus \cH$
		which does not neighbor $\hat{S}$ included independently with probability $\fr{1}{2}$ each.
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:29:08.524718+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2471f025e9ff4fdd0876a25b1c49abacb37c9c87a63abcb440a4c96f18cf150","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def-thin-disk of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $W\in(0, \frac{\gamma^2}{2})$. 
	    Sample $(\mathcal{W}, T) \sim \mathcal{M}^\mathrm{wed}(W) \times (1-\frac{2}{\gamma^2}W)^{-2}\textup{Leb}_{\mathbb{R}_+}$, and write $\mathcal{W} = \{(u, \mathcal{D}_u)\}$. The \emph{weight $W$ quantum disk} is the concatenation of the quantum disks $\{\mathcal{D}_u \: : \: u \leq T\}$ according to the ordering induced by $u$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:45:32.074836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c250ebe165fef6567b4cc6693b2f130eee07803853c8239ccc8d8163db983e46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm sharp of arXiv:2411.14236, 'Size of chaos for Gibbs measures\\of mean field interacting diffusions'] Suppose that the following three conditions hold true.
\begin{itemize}
\item
(Log-Sobolev inequalities)
There exists $\rho > 0$ such that the non-linear and linear
log-Sobolev inequalities hold:
\[
\forall m \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X),
\qquad
2\rho H(m|m_*)
\leqslant
\begin{cases}
I(m|\Pi[m]),~\text{and} \\
I(m|m_*).
\end{cases}
\]
\item
(Transport inequalities)
There exists $\gamma \geqslant 0$ such that
for both $\mu = m^{N,k|[k-1]}_{*,\bm{x}^{[k-1]}}$ and $\mu = m_*$,
the probability measure $\mu$ satisfies the transport inequality
\[
\forall \nu \in \mathcal P(\mathcal X),\qquad
\lvert \langle \nabla_1 W(x^k, \cdot),
\nu - \mu \rangle\rvert^2
\leqslant \gamma
H(\nu | \mu )
\]
uniformly in $k \in [N]$, $\bm{x}^{[k]} \in \mathcal X^{k}$.
\item
(Square integrability)
There exists $M \geqslant 0$ such that
\begin{align*}
\int_{\mathcal X^2} \lvert \nabla_1 W(x,y)
- \langle \nabla_1 W(x,\cdot), m_*\rangle\rvert^2
m^{N,2}_*(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} y) &\leqslant M, \\
\int_{\mathcal X} \lvert \nabla_1 W(x,x)
- \langle \nabla_1 W(x,\cdot), m_*\rangle\rvert^2
m^{N,1}_*(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x) &\leqslant M.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
Then for all $k \in [N]$,
\[
\int_{\mathcal X^{k-1}} H(m^{N,k|[k-1]}_{*,\bm{x}^{[k-1]}} | m_*)
m^{N,k-1}_*(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\bm{x}^{[k-1]})
\leqslant
\frac{36\bigl(1+\frac\gamma\rho\bigr)^3M}{\rho N^2}
\biggl( k + \frac{3\gamma}{\rho}\biggr),
\]
and consequently,
\[
H(m^{N,k}_* | m_*^{\otimes k}) \leqslant
\frac{18\bigl(1+\frac\gamma\rho\bigr)^3M}{\rho N^2}
\biggl( k^2+ \Bigl(1+\frac{6\gamma}{\rho}\Bigr)k\biggr).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:10:05.793585+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c26668dd768186d6a4e6905c8109b644377b9ffa1405486e290ba73c85be6817","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(a>1\) and \(r_a(\xi)=e^{-2\xi}-e^{-2a\xi}\), \(\xi>0\). \[

\]

\begin{equation}

        \int_0^\infty r_a(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_c26dbe1967eabd9968a58da43f41afdfaebe56d66241b6d5ae45dbc5bb37aa7a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Localized regime of the bounded-density conjecture for quadratic forms (Proposition 4). Let X_1..X_n be independent with densities <=1 and Q(x)=x^T A x with A symmetric. (a) If some 2x2 PRINCIPAL submatrix B of A (two original coordinates i, j) is definite, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/sqrt(det B). Proof: condition on the other n-2 ORIGINAL coordinates (independent, so Fubini is genuine); given them Q is a quadratic-plus-linear form in (X_i, X_j); complete the square (B invertible), which shifts (X_i, X_j) and keeps their joint density <=1; for definite B each set {s <= y^T B y <= s+h} is an elliptic annulus of area at most pi h/sqrt(det B), so the conditional density is at most pi/sqrt(det B); average. (b) Hence if A has a 3x3 PRINCIPAL submatrix A_[S] all of whose eigenvalues have modulus >= c>0, and A_[S] is definite or diagonal, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/c: for definite A_[S], Cauchy interlacing puts both eigenvalues of every 2x2 principal block of A_[S] at modulus >= c with one sign, so det >= c^2; for diagonal A_[S], two of the three diagonal entries share a sign and form a definite diagonal block with det >= c^2. This contains the separable case. (c) For other well-conditioned blocks the bound K/c is not proved. A block may have no definite 2x2 principal block at all, e.g. [[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0]] (eigenvalues 2, -1, -1), and the rank-3 coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K||rho||_inf^{2/3} is false for general bounded densities on R^3: a density rho <= B placed on a thin shell around {S = s} gives p_S of order B s^{1/2}/sqrt(l1 l2 l3) for a definite form, unbounded in s. So the localized regime is settled for forms with a definite 2x2 principal block of determinant >= c^2, in particular when a well-conditioned 3x3 principal block is definite or diagonal; the other localized forms stay open, together with the DELOCALIZED forms (every 3x3 principal block near-singular), which is the CLT regime.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:32:56.080729+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c27304041e46fa9dafcd902cb9ff9c6010b8d66033a4f82dbfc4896ce7d5f05b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm: DPP2 of arXiv:2411.12474, 'Multi-type branching processes with immigration generated by point processes'] Assume that immigration

		then 
		\[
		\frac{{Z_i}(t)}{e^{\delta t}}\xrightarrow[t \to \infty]{L^2} A_i:=
 K_\ast \lambda_\infty\int_0^\infty e^{-\delta x}\Ebb{Z_{\times,i}(x)}\mathrm{d} x,

		\item

		\[\frac{\boldsymbol{Z}(t) }{t}\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{d}

		\boldsymbol{v}  ,\]  where $Y\sim \Gamma(K(0,0)\lambda_\infty \beta,1/Q)$ with

		the Gamma law with shape $\alpha$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564752+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c27395fdd622af983c5bbb8bf266923ee0bca3378e79f11affe6bc9e95d19078","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (A sufficient condition for proxy-faithfulness) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Let transforms $A,B$ act on the same operand under a common grouping and produce group-RMS profiles with $\sum_g\sigma_g^2=S_A\ge S_B$ and per-group crest factors $M_g=\mathrm{CF}_g\,\sigma_g$ all lying in a band

for a group of size $G$). If that band is tight relative to the proxy gap,
$\bar c^2/\underline c^2 < S_A/S_B$, then the $L^2$ proxy $\sum_g\sigma_g^2$ and the
AbsMax step-size surrogate $\sum_g M_g^2$ rank $A$ and $B$ the \emph{same} way. When

concentrating transform induces, the ranking can \emph{invert}. {"assumptions":["mu and nu are measures on a common measurable space (X, Sigma); nu may be signed or complex","the epsilon-delta characterisation requires nu finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251367+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_c2889b5313a76c0af8fa3f49c365322c4a2e27291177d6ab0a182d09f34f8d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ be measures on the same measurable space $(X, \\Sigma)$, with $\\nu$ possibly signed or complex. $\\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\\mu$, written $\\nu \\ll \\mu$, if $\\nu(A) = 0$ for every $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ (for signed $\\nu$, equivalently $|\\nu|(A) = 0$, where $|\\nu|$ is the total variation). If $\\nu$ is FINITE (or finite signed/complex), this is equivalent to the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition: for every $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\\delta > 0$ with $|\\nu(A)| < \\varepsilon$ whenever $\\mu(A) < \\delta$; for infinite $\\nu$ the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition is strictly stronger (e.g. $\\nu(A) = \\int_A |x|^{-1}dx$ on $(0,1)$ has $\\nu \\ll$ Lebesgue but fails $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$). Any measure of the form $\\nu(A) = \\int_A f\\,d\\mu$ with $f \\geq 0$ measurable (or $f \\in L^1(\\mu)$ for signed $\\nu$) satisfies $\\nu \\ll \\mu$; the Radon-Nikodym theorem is the converse under $\\sigma$-finiteness. $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ are mutually singular, $\\mu \\perp \\nu$, if there is $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ and $\\nu(X\\setminus A) = 0$. Lebesgue decomposition: for $\\sigma$-finite $\\mu, \\nu$ there is a unique splitting $\\nu = \\nu_{ac} + \\nu_s$ with $\\nu_{ac} \\ll \\mu$ and $\\nu_s \\perp \\mu$. Related but different: a FUNCTION $F: [a,b]\\to\\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous iff its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure iff $F(x) = F(a) + \\int_a^x F'$ with $F' \\in L^1$; the Cantor function is continuous, increasing, but not absolutely continuous (its measure is singular). Sharp edge: $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ is not symmetric, and $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ with $\\mu \\ll \\nu$ (equivalence) does not make the density bounded or bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356302+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c28ac3ae4d8e7ea64f8166fb4e0c699b29ccee4086b9570d919c226f9391a1e9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 232 (truncated Lipschitz algorithm) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Consider an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with input $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$. Denote its output $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. For $a\in [M]$, define the random variable
	\[\fm_a\equiv
		\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)
		\equiv
		\frac{(\bg^a,\bx)}{N^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we recall that $\bg^a$ is the $a$-th row of $\bG$.
	For $K > 0$, define
	\[
		S_K(\cA_N) = \bigg\{
			a \in [M] : 
			\Big|\E\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)\Big|
			\ge K
		\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Let $\hbG \in \R^{M\times N}$ be a matrix of i.i.d. gaussians independent of $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$.
	Then define the \textbf{truncated algorithm} $\cA_{N[K]}$ as the function
	\[\cA_{N[K]}\Big(\bG, 
	\bg^{\aux+}

$\mathrm I^{P,(-1)}:=0$.  For every

\[
 h\longmapsto \mathrm I_{s,\cdot}^{P,(k-2)}\otimes h
\]
and a $2\alpha$-H\"older remainder.  On the modelwise canonical rough-path
domain one has, in $H^{\otimes_2 k}$ and simultaneously in the terminal time,
\begin{equation}
 \int_s^\cdot
 \mathrm I_{s,r}^{P,(k-1)}\otimes\dd\mathbf X_r^{S,P}
 =

 \mathrm I_{s,r}^{P,(k-1)}\otimes\dd X_r
 +\frac12\int_s^\cdot
 \mathrm I_{s,r}^{P,(k-2)}\otimes\dd Q_r.
\end{equation}
Consequently the rough integral is the Hilbert-valued Stratonovich integral,

 \int_s^t\mathrm I_{s,r}^{P,(k-1)}\otimes\circ\dd X_r
 -\frac12\int_s^t\mathrm I_{s,r}^{P,(k-2)}\otimes\dd Q_r
 =\mathrm I_{s,t}^{P,(k)}.
\end{equation}
On the modelwise canonical rough-path domain, the first integral in this last
display is the rough integral against $\mathbf X^{S,P}$ and the second is the

{"assumptions":["the transversal obstruction is for the cyclic square (Cayley table of Z_n) with n even; it does not transfer to arbitrary Latin squares of even order","Tarry's result is specific to order 6; orthogonal mates exist for every order other than 2 and 6","a transversal is a set of n cells, one per row, column and symbol"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048970+00:00","domain":"combinatorial designs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_c2a935feb9d5a1be9d3032095348234a9a1e5cc7691477012e8f97b64cdb76ec","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Tarry (1900) showed by exhaustion that no Latin square of order 6 has an orthogonal mate, so Euler's thirty-six officers problem has no solution; a pair of orthogonal Latin squares exists for every order n except n = 2 and n = 6 (Bose, Shrikhande, Parker 1960, refuting Euler's conjecture for all n congruent to 2 mod 4 beyond 6). A Latin square has an orthogonal mate if and only if it can be decomposed into n disjoint transversals. For the cyclic Latin square of order n (the Cayley table of the integers mod n): when n is odd the diagonals give n disjoint transversals, so it has an orthogonal mate; when n is even it has no transversal at all, because a transversal would be a complete mapping of Z_n and the sum of all elements of Z_n, n/2, is not zero (a parity obstruction), so in particular it has no orthogonal mate. The even-order cyclic result is a statement about the cyclic square only; other Latin squares of the same even order (n = 4, 8, 10, ...) can have transversals and mates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.487730+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2a9c143acf14884e7e7bf65ba91862dada2d77b3e9a7c21ab741649264bddd8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor lq-to-lr of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Fix $T > 0,p > 1$, $q \in (2,\infty]$ and suppose that $u_t,y_t^+,y_t^- \in L^p(\Omega;C([0,T];C(\overline D)_+))$ and there is $0 < \eta^* \leq 1/2$ such that, for all $r \in [2,q)$, $Z_t \in L^p(\Omega \times [0,T]; \gamma(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{B}_{\eta^*-1/2,r}))$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.678356+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2b679eedd00fea65e26f6164ec663223d01a1f098c3ad3c6e262298098c7172","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 23 (Orthogonally natural quadratic coefficient architecture) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] For each finite-dimensional real Hilbert space $E$, let
$\kappa_A^E$ be a norm on $\operatorname{Skew}(E)$ and let $\kappa_Q^E$ be a
norm on $\operatorname{Sym}(E)$.  The family
$\boldsymbol\kappa=(\kappa_A^E,\kappa_Q^E)_E$ is called an
\emph{orthogonally natural quadratic coefficient architecture} if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(A\arabic*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item for every orthogonal isomorphism $U:E\to F$,
\[
 \kappa_A^F(UKU^*)=\kappa_A^E(K),\qquad
 \kappa_Q^F(USU^*)=\kappa_Q^E(S);
\]
\item for orthogonal sums,
\begin{align*}
 \kappa_A^{E\oplus F}(K\oplus L)^2
 &=\kappa_A^E(K)^2+\kappa_A^F(L)^2,\\
 \kappa_Q^{E\oplus F}(S\oplus T)
 &=\max\{\kappa_Q^E(S),\kappa_Q^F(T)\};
\end{align*}
\item if $(e_1,e_2)$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^2$ and
$J_0=e_1\otimes e_2-e_2\otimes e_1$, then
$\kappa_A^{\mathbb R^2}(J_0)=\sqrt2$, while
$\kappa_Q^{\mathbb R}(1)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
By \Cref{thm:Brownian-calibration-rigidity} the Brownian gauges obey these laws;
the next proposition is their deterministic converse.","status":"unverified"}

and that $K$ is a proper subgraph 
of the graph $H\setminus e$,  
obtained from $H$ by

Then we have that $0\leqslant x\leqslant v(H)-2$
and 
\[
e(K) \leqslant \lambda(H)x, 
\]  
with equality if and only if 
either 
\begin{enumerate}

\item $x=v(H)-2$ and $e(K)=e(H)-2$.
\end{enumerate}
In all other cases, in fact, 
\[
e(K) \leqslant \lambda(H) x-\xi(H),
\] 
where $\xi(H)>0$ is as in 
Definition (D_xi of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.154577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2eb21a5cc39c0c3fffe3fb5b1b7a2350df0572a37ca7f08d6204162f254e734","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 (Product-shell bookkeeping) of arXiv:2609.01570, 'A Proof of Fraenkel's Conjecture'] For distinct \(a,b\in A\), write
\[
 d_{ab}=\normQ{ab^{-1}},\qquad P_{ab}=bd_{ab}.
\]
Then
\[
 P_{ab}\in\{a,Q-a,Q+a,2Q-a,2Q+a,\ldots\},
 \qquad \frac1{d_{ab}}=\frac b{P_{ab}}.
\]
For every \(a\in A\), every subset \(B\subseteq A\setminus\{a\}\),
and all real numbers \(L\ge0\) and \(T>0\), if
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}b\le L
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 P_{ab}\ge T\quad(b\in B),
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}\frac1{d_{ab}}\le\frac LT.
\]
Also, \(P_{ab}=a\) implies \(b\mid a\).

In the special case \(s=1\), call \(b\) good when
\(b\mid Q-1\) or \(b\mid Q+1\).  If such a good \(b\) satisfies
\(P_{ab}\in\{Q-a,Q+a\}\), then \(b\mid a-1\) or \(b\mid a+1\).
If moreover \(a>1\) and \(b>a\), this forces \(b=a+1\).","status":"unverified"}

\[
\tau_x = \inf\{n\ge1 : X_n > x\}.
\]
Assume that
\[
Q(x,\{x\}) = p \in [0,1), \qquad Q(x,(x,\infty)) = 1-p,
\]
and that, conditionally on $X_0=x$, the event $\{X_1>x\}$ has positive probability.

\[
\mathbb{P}_x(X_{\tau_x}\in A)
=
\frac{Q(x,A)}{Q(x,(x,\infty))}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:58:24.514330+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2f8db02d7eb1c61dc1b6bb055c1354744ee910a93674fac050707fe224f7e21","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm t:GPXi of arXiv:2601.09537, 'Gene genealogies in haploid populations evolving according to sweepstakes reproduction'] Suppose (equation eq:PXi of the paper) holds. Take   $K > 0$ and $\gamma > 1$  to be fixed. Let
$\underline{\textrm{Beta}}(z;2-\alpha,\alpha) $ denote the
density associated with the truncated Beta distribution with density function
$f(x;z,\alpha) =   x^{1-\alpha}(1-x)^{\alpha -1}\ensuremath{\mathds{1}_{\left\{ 0< x \le
z \right\}}} / \int_0^{z}t^{1-\alpha}(1-t)^{\alpha - 1}dt$.  Similarly let
\textrm{Beta}$(2-\alpha,\alpha) $ denote the density associated with the
untruncated beta distribution with density function $f(x;1,\alpha)$. 
Then the finite-dimensional distributions of the
process $(\xi_N^{(n,{\ensuremath{\mathds h} })}(\lfloor t/c_N \rfloor )$ converge to those of a
process $ \{ \xi^{(n, {\ensuremath{\mathds h} })}(t); t \ge 0 \}$ with
generator  $G$ with merger rates (equation eq:lambda of the paper) with $F$ given by 
\begin{equation}

F = \begin{cases}
 \delta_0 & \textrm{if $\alpha \ge 2$ or $\Psi(N) \ll N$,} \\
 \underline{\textrm{Beta}}(\tfrac{K}{K+m};2-\alpha,\alpha) & \textrm{if
 $1 < \alpha < 2$ and $\Psi(N) = KN$,} \\
\textrm{Beta}(2-\alpha,\alpha) & \textrm{if
 $1 < \alpha < 2$ and $\Psi(N) = N^\gamma$.} \\
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The unit of time $c_N$ is given in Prop.~(prop:cN of the paper) except for the case $1
< \alpha < 2$ and $\Psi(N) = KN$, where we rescale $c_N$ so that
\be
    N^{\alpha-1} c_N \to \frac{\alpha \underline{B}(
    \tfrac{K}{K+m}; 2-\alpha, \alpha) }{m^\alpha} 
\ee
where  $ \underline{B}( \tfrac{K}{K+m}; 2-\alpha, \alpha) = \int_0^{K/(K+m)}
t^{1-\alpha}(1-t)^{\alpha - 1}dt$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241752+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3092bf5adfd353dc1b6027a3f20a6ae44e2f31050c739a2a2102928d191e63b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (weak pullback calculus) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X$ be an orientation-preserving global bi-Lipschitz map as above.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $E_i$ is skew-adjoint on $L^2(\mu)$. In particular
  \[
   \int_{\Real_y^n}(E_if)\phi d\mu=-\int_{\Real_y^n}f(E_i\phi)d\mu
  \]
  whenever $f,\phi,E_if,E_i\phi\in L^2(\mu)$.
\item[(ii)] Let $F=F^i\eframe_i$ be a vector field along $X$ whose Cartesian components belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\Real^n_y;\Rn)$. If
  $q,c^{ij}\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$, then
  \[
   \Div_{\gmetric}F=q,
   \qquad
   (\curl_{\gmetric}F)^{ij}=c^{ij}
  \]
  in the conjugated distributional sense if and only if
  \[
   \partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aF^i)=Jq,
   \qquad
   \partial_a\!\left(J\Kmat_i^aF^j-J\Kmat_j^aF^i\right)=Jc^{ij}
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real^n_y).
  \]
  Equivalently, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Real^n_y)$,
  \begin{equation}
   \int q\varphi d\mu=-\int F^i\Kmat_i^a\partial_a\varphi d\mu,\qquad
   \int c^{ij}\varphi d\mu=-\int\bigl(F^j\Kmat_i^a-F^i\Kmat_j^a\bigr)
          \partial_a\varphi d\mu.
  \end{equation}
  With the convention in \eqref{eq:metric-tensor-divergence}, the same
  calculation gives, whenever
  $H:=\Div_{\gmetric}T\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$,
  \begin{equation}
   JH^j
   =\partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aT^{ji})
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_y^n)
  \end{equation}
  for every locally integrable tensor $T$.
\item[(iii)] If $\mathcal C_X^{-1}F\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ for some
  $1\le p\le\infty$, then 
  \begin{equation}
      \partial_aF^i=A_a^jE_jF^i,
  \end{equation}
  and the conjugated divergence and curl in
  (ii) agree almost everywhere with the pointwise formulas $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^i$ and
  $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^j-\Kmat^a_j\partial_aF^i$.
\item[(iv)] The conjugated derivatives commute on their common
distributional domain:
  \[
   E_iE_j=E_jE_i.
  \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:58:38.108170+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c33b0b0a59a72b6302cb401c7096979885697be83908601e3c5e16baa6945b73","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] Let \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) be a complete probability space supporting a family of \(d\)-dimensional
	Wiener processes \((W(\cdot,\xi))_{\xi \in [0,1]}\) and a family of initial random variables
	\((X_0(\xi))_{\xi \in [0,1]}\) taking values in \(\mathbb{R}^d\). A family of stochastic processes
	\(X=(X(\cdot,\xi))_{\xi \in [0,1]}\) is called a \emph{strong solution} to (equation eq:fibered-McKean-Vlasov-SDE of the paper) if
	the following conditions hold: 
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item For almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\), \(\mu^{\xi}=\mathrm{Law}(X(\cdot,\xi))\).  
		\item For almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\), the process \(X(\cdot,\xi)\) has continuous paths, is adapted to the filtration generated by the Wiener process \(W(\cdot,\xi)\) and the initial condition \(X_0(\xi)\), and satisfies the following integral equation \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.:
		\[
			X(t,\xi) = X_0(\xi) + \int_{0}^{t} b_{\xi}(s,X(\cdot,\xi),\mu) \,ds + \int_{0}^{t} \sigma_{\xi}(s,X(\cdot,\xi),\mu) \,dW(s,\xi), \quad t \in [0,T].
		\]  
	\end{enumerate}
	We say that \emph{strong uniqueness} holds if any two strong solutions \(X\) and \(X'\), defined on the same probability space, driven by the same family of Wiener processes, and starting from the same initial conditions, satisfy \(X(\cdot,\xi)=X'(\cdot,\xi)\) \(\mathbb{P}\)-a.s.\ for almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\).

	We say that \emph{uniqueness in law} holds if for any two strong solutions \(X\) and \(X'\), possibly defined on different probability spaces and driven by different Wiener processes but sharing the same fibered law for their initial conditions, one has that \(\mathrm{Law}(X(\cdot,\xi))=\mathrm{Law}(X'(\cdot,\xi))\) for almost every \(\xi \in [0,1]\).","status":"unverified"}

        \quad (j\ge1).

 \Prob(\deg A_j=h)

 (q-1)q^{-h}

 (1-q^{-1})q^{-(h-1)},
 \qquad h\ge1.
\]
Thus the case $r=1$ of

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is dissipative","the range condition Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) is the hypothesis at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772454+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, boundary value problems","id":"claim_c354d651b0d3d4c7e46b9aa4b5480a1f39abee205e5d85399db455e11dffea4d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: A is densely defined, dissipative, AND Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or at least dense) for some λ_0 > 0. What fails without the range condition: a dissipative operator can be closed and densely defined and still generate nothing. Counterexample: X = L²(0, 1), A f = f' with D(A) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. Then A is densely defined and closed, and Re⟨f', f⟩ = (|f(1)|² − |f(0)|²)/2 = 0, so A is dissipative (indeed both A and −A are). But solving λf − f' = g with f(0) = 0 gives f(x) = −∫_0^x e^{λ(x−s)}g(s) ds, and the second boundary condition f(1) = 0 forces the constraint ∫_0^1 e^{−λs} g(s) ds = 0: Ran(λ − A) is a closed subspace of codimension 1, not dense, for every λ > 0. Hence A is not a generator, although dropping one boundary condition (D = {f ∈ H¹ : f(1) = 0}) gives exactly the generator of the left shift semigroup. The range condition is what encodes 'the right number of boundary conditions'. What fails without density: X = C[0,1] with the sup norm, A f = f' on D(A) = {f ∈ C¹[0,1] : f(1) = 0}. Solving λ f − f' = g with f(1) = 0 gives f(x) = ∫_x^1 e^{λ(x−s)}g(s)ds, so ‖f‖ ≤ ‖g‖/λ: A is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0. Yet the closure of D(A) is {f ∈ C[0,1] : f(1) = 0}, a proper closed subspace, so A generates no C_0-semigroup on C[0,1] (generators are densely defined); it generates one on the smaller space. Density is automatic only when X is reflexive, which C[0,1] is not. Related trap: for the norm inequality version, dissipativity means ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 - checking it for a single λ, or checking Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 only on a core without knowing the operator is closed or closable there, proves nothing about the closure being a generator unless the range condition is verified on that same core.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.776894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c376a83c14ab39a3e30edd52614f64e087bad693ea56fcb12f7a04e6b75cd3e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:vector-poincare-goe-gradient of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Let $N\in\mathbb N$, let $\operatorname{Sym}_N$ be the set of symmetric matrices in $M_N(\mathbb R)$ equipped with the metric induced by $\schnorm{\cdot}$, and let $B\in \operatorname{Sym}_N$ be a normalized GOE matrix.
Let $(\mathcal H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\mathcal H)$ be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
Let $f,g: \operatorname{Sym}_N \to \mathcal H$ be locally Lipschitz with respect to $\schnorm{\cdot}$ on $\operatorname{Sym}_N$.
Then
\begin{equation}

\mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}\Bigl|\bigl\langle f(B)-\mathop{{}\mathbb{E}} f(B),\,g(B)-\mathop{{}\mathbb{E}} g(B)\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal H}\Bigr|
\ \leqslant\
\frac{2}{N^2}\,
\Bigl(\mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}\|df(B)\|_{\mathrm{HS}(\operatorname{Sym}_N,\mathcal H)}^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\,

\end{equation}
where $\|df(B)\|_{\mathrm{HS}(\operatorname{Sym}_N,\mathcal H)}$ is as given in \pref{def:frechet}, so that
\begin{equation}

\|df(B)\|_{\mathrm{HS}(\operatorname{Sym}_N,\mathcal H)}^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^N
\left\|
\frac{\partial f(B)}{\partial(B_{ii}/\sqrt N)}

+

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:49.836961+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c39df897f7f17ec37595ab70bb72f5b1a5ebd10761da85994bc976ec87c4d886","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2506.13571, '2506.13571'] {\rm (i)} \textup{(Wiener chaos)}  Fix $n\in\N_{\geq 1}$.
Given  $f\in \fH^{\odot n}\otimes K$, 

\noi
\begin{align} 
I_n(f) : = \sum_{i\geq 1} I_n(f_i) k_i \quad
\text{with}\quad f_i = \langle f, k_i\rangle_K
\end{align}
is well defined and also called the $n$-th multiple integral 
of $f$.\footnote{We use the same notation for the real setting 
and $K$-valued setting, which shall not cause any ambiguity
for readers. } 
For a {\rm(}deterministic{\rm)} vector $v\in K$, we put
$I_0(v) := v$.
And, the following orthogonality relation holds:
\begin{align}
\langle I_n(f) , I_m(g) \rangle_{L^2_\o K} = 
\ind_{\{ n=m\}} n! \jb{f, g}_{  \fH^{\otimes n}\otimes K  }
\end{align}
for any $m,n\in\N_{\geq 0}$ and for any $f\in \fH^{\odot n}\otimes K$
and $g\in \fH^{\odot m}\otimes K$.

\medskip

\noi
{\rm (ii)} \textup{(Chaos decomposition)}
For any $F\in L^2_\o K$, there exist 
unique kernels 
$f_n\in\fH^{\odot n}\otimes K$ for $n\in\N_{\geq 1}$
such that 

\noi
\begin{align}
F = \E[ F] +   \sum_{n\geq 1} I_n(f_n) , 
\end{align}

\noi
where the above series is convergence in $L^2_\o K$.
In particular, we have 

\noi
\begin{align}
 \| F - \E[F] \|^2_{L^2_\o K} =  \sum_{n\geq 1} n!   \| f_n \|^2_{\fH^{\otimes n} \otimes K}. 
 
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:06:42.683852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3b7e779e62c432a68ec0191123230a19ac04e5aa7494f32c23cf10738870265","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thmq of arXiv:2411.03942, 'Asymptotic expansions relating to the distribution of the product of correlated normal ran'] Let $\mu_X,\mu_Y\in\mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y>0$, $-1<\rho<1$ and $n\geq1$. 

Let $q=1-p$. 

\vspace{2mm}

\noindent 1. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow1$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=s(1+\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/q)+\frac{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}+\frac{n-3}{4}\ln(\ln(1/q))\nonumber\\
&\quad+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1+\rho)^{(n+1)/4}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\bigg)+\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X-r_Y)^2\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{n}{4}\frac{(r_X+r_Y)^2}{1+\rho}-\frac{n}{2(1-\rho^2)}\big(r_X^2+r_Y^2-2\rho r_X r_Y\big)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{(n-3)\sqrt{n}}{8}\frac{|r_X+r_Y|}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/q))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}}\bigg\}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 2. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow1$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=s(1+\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/q)+\frac{1}{2}(n-2)\ln(\ln(1/q))+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1+\rho)^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\bigg)-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}\bigg\}\nonumber\\
&\quad+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\ln(1/q)}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 3. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=-s(1-\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/p)+\frac{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}+\frac{n-3}{4}\ln(\ln(1/p))\nonumber\\
&\quad+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1-\rho)^{(n+1)/4}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\bigg)+\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X+r_Y)^2\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{n}{4}\frac{(r_X-r_Y)^2}{1-\rho}-\frac{n}{2(1-\rho^2)}\big(r_X^2+r_Y^2-2\rho r_X r_Y\big)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{(n-3)\sqrt{n}}{8}\frac{|r_X-r_Y|}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/p))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}}\bigg\}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 4. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=-s(1-\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/p)+\frac{1}{2}(n-2)\ln(\ln(1/p))+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1-\rho)^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\bigg)-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}\bigg\}\nonumber\\
&\quad+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\ln(1/p)}\bigg). 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:57:07.304779+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3c54296c57ccf48e84d5bb3fa45ac8546a72b43187f17e4a8b59d104658336b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2606.24090, 'Sparsity-adaptive concentration inequalities for random polynomials'] Let $A=(A_{i_1,\ldots,i_{2d}})$ be a $2d$-tensor. Fix
$I=\{k_1,\ldots,k_l\}\subseteq[d]$ with $k_1<\cdots<k_l$, and fix
$\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^l$. Let $T_{I,\varepsilon}A$ be defined by
\eqref{eq:B_T_I_epsilon_A}, and let $\rho_{I,\varepsilon}$ be defined by
\eqref{eq:B_rho_I_epsilon}.

Let $I_2\subseteq[2l]$ and set
\[
    F:=\rho_{I,\varepsilon}(I_2)\subseteq[2d].
\]
For a fixed $j_{I_2}$, denote by $j_F^\rho$ the corresponding fixed coordinates
of $A$, namely
\[
    i_{\rho_{I,\varepsilon}(s)}=j_s,
    \qquad s\in I_2.
\]
If $\mathcal J=\{J_1,\ldots,J_\kappa\}\in
\Pi([2l]\setminus I_2)$, define
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal K
    :=
    \rho_{I,\varepsilon}(\mathcal J)
    \cup
    \bigl\{\{t,d+t\}:t\in[d]\setminus I\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
Then $\mathcal K$ is a partition of $[2d]\setminus F$, and
\begin{equation}
    \bigl\|
    (T_{I,\varepsilon}A)_{j_{I_{2}^{c}}}
    \bigr\|_{\mathcal J}
    \le
    n^{(d-l)/2}
    \bigl\|A_{(j_F^\rho)^{\,c}}\bigr\|_{\mathcal K}.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $I_2=\varnothing$, then
\begin{equation}
    \|T_{I,\varepsilon}A\|_{\mathcal J}
    \le
    n^{(d-l)/2}
    \|A\|_{\rho_{I,\varepsilon}(\mathcal J),\,\{\{t,d+t\}:t\in[d]\setminus I\}}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:06:39.327545+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3cc37e35e819a155a5ed6033016030abfe119dafda82baef010d9f9f3f3555a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:local_smoothing_iteration_pressure_turbulent of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Let $Q=Q_{\varrho}(t_0,x_0)$ be a parabolic cylinder of side $\varrho\in (0,1]$ and center $(t_0,x_0)\in {\mathbb R}\times {\mathbb R}^d$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:19.991176+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3ccd1bf9fdf996f58aff1fbbbb9cb3cb4655e8e5fa0081e12bb7b1dfa0df511","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 (Action on measures) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] For a finite signed measure $h \in \Sign$ and a number $n \in \Nz$ we define
the finite signed measure $T^{n} \circ h \in \Sign$ by
\[
  (T^{n} \circ h)(A) := \int_{\XX} T^{n}(A \mid x)\, h(\dd x)
  \qquad (A \in \XXA),
\]
the integral of a bounded measurable map against $h$ being defined, as usual, as its
integral against $h^{+}$ minus its integral against $h^{-}$.
The map $h \mapsto T^{n}\circ h$ is a linear map $\Sign \to \Sign$ which
maps $\Prob$ into $\Prob$, and it satisfies
\[
  T \circ (T^{n} \circ h) = T^{n+1} \circ h \qquad (n \in \Nz),
\]
because for every bounded measurable map $g : \XX \to \R$ one has
$\int g \dd(T^{n}\circ h) = \int \bigl( \int g(z)\,T^{n}(\dd z \mid x) \bigr)
h(\dd x)$. That identity holds for indicator maps by the displayed formula, hence for
nonnegative simple maps by linearity, hence for every measurable
$g : \XX \to [0,\infty]$ by monotone convergence, applied to $h^{+}$ and to $h^{-}$
separately; a bounded measurable $g : \XX \to \R$ is then treated by writing
$g = g^{+}-g^{-}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.502877+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3d4b4660aa6f2b82a15ece3b96b209202d919a0b37be7c6e887135762207035","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 18 of arXiv:2607.04730, 'Variance gamma approximation to sums of triplewise independent random variables'] \cite[p. 3330]{Gaunt2017}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:01:56.372007+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c409b06dbbfd938e7ecb6038a179a5e4bfb533513a5da17631bf453aa4e996d5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop_omega_rk1 of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Suppose that $E$ is a complex of ``rank 1'' representations of $Q$, i.e.\ $\dim E_i^n\leq 1$ for all $i\in Q_0,n\in\bZ$.

\begin{align*}

&+\sum_{a\colon i\to j}\left(\alpha_a^n +(\alpha_a^n-\alpha_a^{n-1})(\beta_i^n-\beta_j^n)\varphi_2(\beta_i^n-\beta_j^n+\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_j^{n-1})\right) \\
&+\sum_{a\colon k\to i}\left(-\alpha_a^n+(\alpha_a^{n+1}-\alpha_a^{n})(\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_k^{n+1})\varphi_2(\beta_i^{n+1}-\beta_k^{n+1}+\beta_i^{n}-\beta_k^{n+2})\right)\Bigg)

Here, $d_i^n\colon E_i^{n-1}\to E_i^n$ and $\rho^n(a)\colon E_i^n\to E_j^n$ for $a\colon i\to j$ and $\alpha_a^n$, $\beta_i^n$ are considered as non-negative real scalars.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is measure-preserving on a standard Borel (Lebesgue) probability space","mu is T-invariant; entropies are Kolmogorov-Sinai entropies with values in [0, +infinity]","the ergodic decomposition is taken over the sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets","convex combinations are of T-INVARIANT measures only","no finiteness of entropy and no continuity of the entropy map is assumed or asserted"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732492+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_c423ff08a284a7ccfc7dc1d8f089019abb153806f7c00355fd50d003464125fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a STANDARD Borel (Lebesgue) probability space, and let I be the sub-sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets.

ERGODIC DECOMPOSITION. There is a measurable family x -> mu_x of T-invariant Borel probability measures on X such that (i) mu_x is a version of the conditional measure of mu given I, so mu(A) = integral of mu_x(A) d mu(x) for every A in B and integral of f d mu = integral over x of (integral of f d mu_x) d mu(x) for f in L^1(mu); (ii) mu_x is ERGODIC for mu-a.e. x; (iii) the family is essentially unique. Writing P for the law of the random measure x -> mu_x, one gets mu = integral of nu dP(nu) supported on the ergodic T-invariant measures -- the Choquet representation of mu in the simplex of invariant measures.

AFFINITY OF ENTROPY. Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is affine in the measure, with values in [0, +infinity]:
  for every finite measurable partition Q,   h_mu(T, Q) = integral of h_{mu_x}(T, Q) d mu(x);
  and                                        h_mu(T)    = integral of h_{mu_x}(T) d mu(x).
In particular, for T-invariant mu and nu and t in [0,1],  h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T) = t h_mu(T) + (1-t) h_nu(T).

SHARP EDGES. (1) AFFINE IS NOT CONTINUOUS: nu -> h_nu(T) is affine on the simplex of invariant measures but is in general NOT weak-* continuous; for expansive homeomorphisms it is upper semicontinuous, and in general it can fail even that. Do not use affinity to pass to weak-* limits. (2) The decomposition genuinely needs a standard/Lebesgue space; on a pathological measure space conditional measures need not exist and the statement can fail. (3) The convex combination must be of INVARIANT measures -- entropy is undefined for a non-invariant measure, so there is no affinity statement along an arbitrary path in the space of measures. (4) The identity holds in [0, +infinity]; if h_mu(T) = +infinity the integral is +infinity, and no finiteness is assumed anywhere. (5) The affinity is a property of measure-theoretic entropy, not of topological entropy: the variational principle gives h_top(T) = sup over invariant nu of h_nu(T), which is a supremum over the simplex, so it is attained (if at all) at ergodic measures precisely BECAUSE h is affine -- but h_top itself is not an average.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:53:51.331508+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c45839b77fb698462117e881e35da0431c1b272976e4e998592e65f0e133cec7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:exp-affine of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Let $X$ be an integrable solution with input $f$, let
$u:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded measurable (of arbitrary sign), and
suppose $\varpi\in C([0,1])$ solves~(equation eq:riccati of the paper); set
$\chi:=-u(1-\cdot)+\tfrac{\nu^2}{2}\varpi^2$.  Define, for
$0\le t\le s\le 1$, the forward curve
\[
\xi_t(s):=f(s)+\nu\int_0^tK(s-r)\,dM_r,
\qquad M_r=\int_0^r\sqrt{X_v}\,dW_v,
\]
and the exponent process
\[
H_t:=-\int_0^tu(s)X_s\,ds+\int_t^1\chi(1-s)\,\xi_t(s)\,ds .
\]
Then, almost surely, for all $t\in[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}
H_t=H_0+N_t-\tfrac12\langle N\rangle_t,
\qquad
N_t:=\nu\int_0^t\varpi(1-s)\sqrt{X_s}\,dW_s .
\end{equation}
Consequently $G:=e^{H}=e^{H_0}\,\mathcal E(N)$ is a positive local
martingale and supermartingale with
\[
G_0=\exp\Bigl(\int_0^1\chi(1-t)f(t)\,dt\Bigr),
\qquad
G_1=\exp\Bigl(-\int_0^1u(t)X_t\,dt\Bigr),
\]
so that
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\exp\Bigl(-\int_0^1u(t)X_t\,dt\Bigr)\Bigr]
\ \le\
\exp\Bigl(\int_0^1\chi(1-t)f(t)\,dt\Bigr),
\end{equation}
with equality if and only if $\mathcal E(N)$ is a true martingale on
$[0,1]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:46:36.165410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c45cdb92b570f500c30a620f417f35882d4e5b8a5f7044029ea51e456d6af3a0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Def_UniformlyFredholmMap of arXiv:2609.02848, 'The universal moduli space of non-degenerate $\Z/2\Z$~harmonic spinors'] Let ${\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{Y}}$ be tame Fréchet manifolds.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.388242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c48365866ce534c77114704d0db89b51cd9ee0418e1cdad2bbed722719835d1f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem homo multilinear recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Homogeneous Multilinear Recursion]

Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequences of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a permutation symmetric, homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix of degree $d$ as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\ a+b+c=d}} (48dt)^{4dt} \cdot L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t}^{4t}.
$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350409+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c49ed582047c4cb6f5e89c53325b0de3d7f6b9478d7f83ec9740f9f1a7410e51","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 179 (annealed second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ 
be defined by \eqref{e:barD} and \eqref{e:barD.plus} (see also \eqref{e:drift.error.II}). We have 
the second moment bound 
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}
		{p(q_d)}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS \delta}{N}\,,
	\]
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.
\begin{proof}
Recalling the notation from
\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.g} and \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y},
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}
		{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
Note that $\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$. 
It follows by applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} that 
	\[
	\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	=\frac{1}{M}\E\bigg[\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)^2
		\bigg]
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}}{M}
	\E\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|^2}{N}\,.
	\]
We then note that if $\ind_B\in\R^M$ is the indicator of the coordinates in $B$, then
	\[
	\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|
	=\bigg\| \bar{\bG}(q_d) \frac{\ind_B}{|B|^{1/2}}\bigg\|
	\le \|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|\,,
	\]
from which it follows that
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	\le
	\frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS 
		\E[\|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|^2]}{MN}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS}{N}\,,
	\]
where the last bound follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}.
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.507698+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4a29a9821f86641b73c9a2bd61db74a52d87562589038f7e6c1d25cbde5925f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 16 (From scalar wavelets to vector-valued wavelets) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $(\phi,\psi)$ be an orthonormal wavelet basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ associated with an MRA.
Fix $m\ge 2$ and set $D=2^m$. Define $\Phi,\Psi$ by \eqref{eq:Phi-def}--\eqref{eq:Psi-def}.
For $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $j\ge 0$ set
\[
\widetilde\Phi_k=\Phi(\cdot-k),
\qquad
\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}=D^{j/2}\Psi(D^j\cdot-k).
\]

Then the family
\[
\{\widetilde\Phi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}\ \cup\ \{\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\}_{j\ge 0,\ k\in\mathbb Z}
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] is an orthogonal wavelet basis of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m)$ (for the usual scalar $L^2$ inner product); moreover $\|\widetilde\Phi_k\|_{L^2}^2=\|\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\|_{L^2}^2=m$,
\item[(b)] is an $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--orthonormal system in the Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module
$\big(L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big)$, i.e.
\[
\big\langle \widetilde U_\alpha,\widetilde U_\beta\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,I_m
\quad(\alpha,\beta\in\{(0,k)\}\cup\{(j,k):j\ge 0\}),
\]
and it is a Parseval $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module frame with the canonical reconstruction
\[
f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Phi_k\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Phi_k
+\sum_{j\ge 0}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k},
\qquad f\in L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),
\]
with convergence in the module norm.
Moreover, each component inherits compact support, regularity and vanishing moments from $\phi$ and $\psi$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.562017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4a7efd4ffd532c6e9f1d326b2cbedbb130db89d3f3815a1d60f3704ee973b3b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:cond-Fokker-planck-a} is a measurable map
\[
    \tilde \P:\R_+\times\Xc\longrightarrow \Pc(\R^d),
    \qquad
    (t,x)\longmapsto \tilde\P_{t,x},
\]
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    For \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\), the map
    \(t\mapsto \tilde \P_{t,x}\) is weak continuous.

    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_\Xc
    \int_{\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,\tilde\P_{t,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(y)
    \right|^p
    \tilde\P_{t,x}(dy)\,\mu(dx)\,dt
    <\infty.
    \]

    \item 
    For every \(h\in C_c^\infty(\R^d; \R)\) and every \(t\ge0\), one has,
    for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\),
    \[
    \E^{\tilde\P_{t,x}}[h]
    =
    \E^{\tilde\P_{0,x}}[h]
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\tilde\P_{s,x}}\!\left[
    \nabla h(Y)\cdot
    \left(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,x,Y,\tilde\P_{s,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \right)
    +
    \Delta h(Y)
    \right]ds .
    \]

    \item 
    If
    $
    \P_t(dx,dy)
    :=
    \mu(dx)\,\tilde\P_{t,x}(dy),
$
    then, for a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}
    \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:24:45.963847+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4aad038f07c92b1df51f459a1a654560244c716889ca0dceed481fa50b3d26c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop: profile update of arXiv:2509.11384, 'The Horton-Strahler number of butterfly trees'] [Profile update]
    Let $\mathcal T_p$ (parent) and $\mathcal T_c$ (child) have profiles
    \[
    (h_p; L_p; R_p), \qquad (h_c; L_c; R_c),
    \]
    and define
    \[
    k^\star := \min\{k \ge h_c : (a_k^{(R_p)}, b_k^{(R_p)}) \neq (1,1)\}.
    \]
    
    Then $\mathcal T_p \oplus \mathcal T_c$ has profile $(h; L; R)$ as follows.
    
    \medskip
    
    \noindent\textbf{\textnormal{(i)} HS number.}
    \[
    h =
    \begin{cases}
    h_c, & h_c > h_p,\\
    h_p + 1, & h_c \le h_p \text{ and } k^\star = h_p + 1,\\
    h_p, & \text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    
    \medskip
    
    \noindent\textbf{\textnormal{(ii)} Right profile.}
    
    If $h_c > h_p$, then
    \[
    (a_k^{(R)}, b_k^{(R)}) = (a_k^{(R_c)}, b_k^{(R_c)}) \quad (k \le h_c),
    \qquad m^{(R)} = 1.
    \]
    
    If $h_c \le h_p$, then
    \[
    (a_k^{(R)}, b_k^{(R)}) =
    \begin{cases}
    (a_k^{(R_c)}, b_k^{(R_c)}), & k \le h_c,\\
    (1,0), & h_c < k \le k^\star,\\
    (a_k^{(R_p)}, b_k^{(R_p)}), & k^\star < k \le h_p,
    \end{cases}
    \]
    and
    \[
    m^{(R)} =
    \begin{cases}
    1, & k^\star = h_p,\\
    m^{(R_p)}, & \text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
    \]
    
    \medskip
    
    \noindent\textbf{\textnormal{(iii)} Left profile.}
    
    For all $k < h_p$,
    \[
    (a_k^{(L)}, b_k^{(L)}) = (a_k^{(L_p)}, b_k^{(L_p)}).
    \]
    
    At the top level:
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{If $h_c > h_p$:}
        \[
        (a_{h_c}^{(L)}, b_{h_c}^{(L)}) = (1,1), \qquad m^{(L)} = 0,
        \]
        and
        \[
        (a_{h_p}^{(L)}, b_{h_p}^{(L)}) =
        \begin{cases}
        (a_{h_p}^{(L_p)}, b_{h_p}^{(L_p)}), & m^{(L_p)} = 1,\\
        (0,0), & m^{(L_p)} = 0.
        \end{cases}
        \]
    
        \item \textbf{If $h_c \le h_p$ and $k^\star = h_p+1$:}
        \[
        (a_{h_p+1}^{(L)}, b_{h_p+1}^{(L)}) = (1,\, m^{(R)}), \qquad m^{(L)} = 0,
        \]
        and
        \[
        (a_{h_p}^{(L)}, b_{h_p}^{(L)}) =
        \begin{cases}
        (a_{h_p}^{(L_p)}, b_{h_p}^{(L_p)}), & m^{(L_p)} = 1,\\
        (0,0), & m^{(L_p)} = 0.
        \end{cases}
        \]
    
        \item \textbf{If $h_c \le h_p$ and $k^\star = h_p$:}
        \[
        (a_{h_p}^{(L)}, b_{h_p}^{(L)}) = (1,1), \qquad m^{(L)} = 0.
        \]
    
        \item \textbf{If $h_c \le h_p$ and $k^\star < h_p$:}
        \[
        (a_{h_p}^{(L)}, b_{h_p}^{(L)}) = (a_{h_p}^{(L_p)}, b_{h_p}^{(L_p)}),
        \qquad m^{(L)} = m^{(L_p)}.
        \]
    \end{itemize}
    
    \medskip
    
    \noindent The profile for $\mathcal T_p \ominus \mathcal T_c$ is obtained via
    \[
    \mathcal T_p \ominus \mathcal T_c = (\mathcal T_p^R \oplus \mathcal T_c^R)^R.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.336865+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4b0b3c78d60a8233c772b75e1763993f89eda62c0d6d97c1f53fbebf289d552","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 26 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] We collect the adjoint and interval-size differentiability statements in one proposition.

\textup{(i)} The formal adjoint is
\[
\cA_L^*v=d\int_{-L}^{L}J(x-y)v(y)\,dy-(qv)'(x)+b(x)v(x).
\]
It possesses a positive principal eigenfunction $\phi_L^*$ satisfying
\[
\cA_L^*\phi_L^*+\lambda_p(L)\phi_L^*=0\ \hbox{in }(-L,L),\quad \phi_L^*(-L)=0,
\]
and this eigenfunction is unique up to multiplication. For all $u,v\in C^1([-L,L])$ satisfying $u(L)=0$ and $v(-L)=0$,
\[
\int_{-L}^{L}v\cA_Lu\,dx=\int_{-L}^{L}u\cA_L^*v\,dx.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\phi_L'(L)<0,\quad \phi_L^*(L)>0,\quad \phi_L(-L)>0.
\]

\textup{(ii)} Let $\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}=(\alpha,\beta)$ and let $\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\Lp(\cA_{\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}})$. Assume the coefficients are $C^2$ and normalize the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions by
\[
\int_\alpha^\beta\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx=1.
\]
Then $\lambda$ is $C^1$ in $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
\[
\partial_\beta\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}'(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(\beta)<0,
\]
while
\[
\partial_\alpha\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=d\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\alpha)\int_\alpha^\beta J(x-\alpha)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx>0.
\]
Thus moving the outflow endpoint to the right and moving the inflow endpoint to the left both strictly decrease the principal eigenvalue, but the two shape derivatives have different structures.

\textup{(iii)} The maps $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ and, after pull-back to $(-1,1)$ and the above normalization, $L\mapsto\phi_L$, $L\mapsto\phi_L^*$ are continuous. On every compact interval $[L_0,L_1]\Subset(0,\infty)$ the convergence is uniform in $C^1$ for the eigenfunctions.

\textup{(iv)} The map $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is of class $C^1$ on $(0,\infty)$. With the normalization above,
\[
\partial_L\lambda_p(L)=q(L)\phi_L'(L)\phi_L^*(L)-d\phi_L(-L)\int_{-L}^{L}J(x+L)\phi_L^*(x)\,dx.
\]
In particular, $\partial_L\lambda_p(L)<0\quad L>0$.
Thus $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is strictly decreasing.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:51:44.808754+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4b3bee4bcfc8b9f25c991f9a899fd4cbcbe0a4e9f45ac41396ee7e4e9bd1856","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 35 of arXiv:2608.26823, 'Evolutes, involutes and parallels of Legendre curves in hyperbolic and de Sitter 2-spaces '] Let $(\bgamma_d,\bgamma_d^h):I\rightarrow\overline{\Delta}_1$ be a spacelike Legendre curve  with curvature $(m_d,n_d)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.866399+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4d843d3c7a55aae3efd96f6f9ef04c1f75fe248831807e0b531278a91a9c03d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def: Hermite process of arXiv:2609.03589, 'Correlated initialization of deep residual networks'] {Tudor13}}]
    
    The rank \(q\) {\it Hermite process with Hurst index} \(H \in (\frac12, 1)\) is defined as
    \[
        Z^{q,H}_t \coloneq A_{q, H} \int_{\mathbb{R}^q}' \int_0^t \prod_{j=1}^q (s-x_j)_+^{-(\frac12 + \frac{1-H}{q})} ds\, W(dx_1)\cdots W(dx_q),\quad t\geq 0,
    \]
    where \(W\) is the Wiener Gaussian white noise measure and \(\int'_{\mathbb{R}^q} (...) W(dx_1)\cdots W(dx_q)\) indicates a {\it multiple Wiener-Itô integral} of order $q$ (see [bluebook]). The normalizing
    constant \(A_{q, H}\) is selected so that
    \(\Exp{(Z^{q,H}_1)^2} = 1\) and is known explicitly [Tudor13].
    Equivalent representations are given e.g. in [Tudor13] and  [pipirasLongRangeDependenceSelfSimilarity2017].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:58:10.026941+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4d8671acedaf63b39ff467e0961d59e412b21c1716ab523b3829848b8541514","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop rrt-blob-input of arXiv:2607.21428, 'Subcritical percolation and network archaeology on random recursive tree substrate network'] Fix \(p\in(0,1)\).
