{"assumptions":["i.i.d. real summands","Lambda finite in a neighbourhood of 0, which makes Lambda^* a good rate function","the rate is exponential in n; polynomial prefactors are NOT captured"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.782174+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4dfaffbd4e619148e1df048b6bc2f3b8bb7627b05d4a288d55a3707d2b749ea","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with cumulant generating function Lambda(lambda) = log E[ exp(lambda X_1) ] and Legendre transform Lambda^*(x) = sup_{lambda in R} ( lambda x - Lambda(lambda) ). Assume Lambda(lambda) < infinity for every lambda in a neighbourhood of 0. Then the empirical means S_n/n satisfy the LARGE DEVIATION PRINCIPLE with speed n and good convex rate function Lambda^*: for every closed set C, limsup_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in C ) <= - inf_{x in C} Lambda^*(x), and for every open set G, liminf_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in G ) >= - inf_{x in G} Lambda^*(x). In particular, for x > E[X_1], (1/n) log P( S_n/n >= x ) -> - Lambda^*(x), so the Chernoff upper bound is exact at the level of the exponential rate although it can be off by polynomial factors: the sharper Bahadur-Rao asymptotic supplies a factor of order n^{-1/2}. The exponential moment hypothesis is what makes Lambda^* a GOOD rate function, meaning its sublevel sets are compact; on the real line the large deviation principle itself continues to hold without it, but the rate function may fail to be good and the statement must then be handled with care. Heavy-tailed laws with no exponential moments have Lambda^* identically 0 above the mean, and their large deviations are governed by a single big jump rather than by a rate function of this shape. [Cramer (1938); see Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.2.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.642553+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4e252b7a033cd99fd34781147ec03c758d618ba59d61bf0c7ad4e09060628ff","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:saddle of arXiv:2411.13875, 'Large deviations at the origin of random walk in random environment'] Fix $\kappa > 0$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_j \in \mathcal P_\mathbb V^{(\kappa)}$ be all distinct. {"assumptions":["i.i.d. (or stationary ergodic with care) elliptic environment on Z^d","The statement concerns the UNION of the two directional events","Directional 0-1 law is open for d >= 3"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.990370+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4f0b35296bb24abc03e25c08c3620d73cbcb1dad336577101e148e2359e4818","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Kalikow's zero-one law (1981; Zerner-Merkl 2001 for the sharp form): for random walk in an i.i.d. elliptic random environment on Z^d and a direction l, let A_l = {X_n . l -> +infinity}. Then P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) is 0 or 1. It does NOT say that P_0(A_l) itself is 0 or 1: the directional zero-one law P_0(A_l) in {0,1} is a theorem in d = 1 (Solomon) and d = 2 (Zerner-Merkl, using planarity: two walks in the same environment must intersect), and is an OPEN PROBLEM for d >= 3 (Drewitz-Ramirez Open Question 3.2; Kalikow's law is often misquoted as the directional one). Kalikow's proof: the event A_l union A_{-l} is invariant under a coupling of walks started at different points that follow the same environment after they meet in a slab, and its probability is a function of the environment's tail sigma-field, hence 0 or 1 by Kolmogorov. Consequences: under transience in some direction the regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner applies to the union event; Zerner's law of large numbers then gives X_n/n -> v or -c v. Typical failure: Treating Kalikow's zero-one law as if it determines transience, mistaking the statement that the probability is 0 or 1 for a claim that it equals 1; the theorem only rules out intermediate probabilities and leaves open, often genuinely unresolved, which side of the dichotomy holds for a specific environment law, which is precisely the content of the still largely open general ballisticity conjecture for random walk in random environment in dimension d>=2. Canonical reference: Kalikow, 1981, Annals of Probability; Zeitouni, 2004, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499560+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_c53552d7811e343a9c322a0f0f633c47f09d36f9fce8bd51339ed0e1ea11dbf9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"(1) One omitted value is not enough. The family {exp(nz) : n ≥ 1} on the unit disk omits the value 0 everywhere, but it is not normal, not even in the extended sense: on the left half of the disk exp(nz) → 0 while on the right half |exp(nz)| → ∞, and a locally uniform limit on the connected set D would have to be holomorphic throughout or identically ∞. Montel's fundamental normality test needs two distinct omitted values, and that is sharp. (2) When two values are omitted, the conclusion is normality in the extended sense: the constant functions f_n = n omit 0 and 1 and converge to ∞, so a proof that assumes the limit is a finite holomorphic function must first exclude the ∞ branch (typically by a bound at one point or by the maximum principle). (3) Pointwise bounds are not local bounds. Montel's first theorem needs a bound uniform on each compact set; pointwise boundedness of the family is genuinely weaker (Runge's theorem produces sequences of polynomials converging pointwise on C to a discontinuous function, so such a sequence is pointwise bounded and not normal). (4) Normality is not convergence: it only yields subsequences, and the limit may leave the class one is working in — the injective maps z/n converge to a constant, and the limit of a normal family of functions in some prescribed family need not satisfy the same constraint unless Hurwitz-type arguments are added.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.740138+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c55f9500cdeca03cb4b77499ccb95af5c483967bd4cd23872b823bd8043a11dc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 8 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] (\textbf{Bilateral trees}) 
$(\textbf{a})$ A non-empty subset $T \! \subset \! \overline{\bbU}$ is a \emph{bilateral tree} if it satisfies the following conditions. 
 
 \begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

 \item[$(\textbf{a1})$] There is $k\ino\bbZZ$ such that $T \backslash \{ \varnothing\} \! \subset \! \overline{\bbU}_k$.
 
\smallskip

\item[$(\textbf{a2})$] For all $u\ino T\backslash \{ \varnothing \}$, $\overleftarrow{u} \ino T$.   

\smallskip

 \item[$(\textbf{a3})$]  For all $u\ino T$, 
 $k_u (T)\!\!  : = \! \# \{ v\ino T\! : \! \overleftarrow{v}\eqo u\} \leko  \infty$ 
 and $\{ 1, \ldots , k_u (T)\}  \! =\! \{ \mathtt{end} (v)\, ; \, v\ino T\!   : \!    \overleftarrow{v}\! = \! u\}$ if $k_u (T) \! \geq \! 1$. 

\smallskip

 \item[$(\textbf{a4})$] For all $u,v\ino T $, there is $l\ino \bbZ$ such that $u_{\mathbf{|\! |}_{(-\infty, l]}} \! \! = \! v_{\mathbf{|\! |} _{(-\infty,  l]}}$. 
 
\end{compactenum}  
 
\smallskip 

\noi
$(\textbf{b})$  We denote by $\overline{\bbT}$ the set of all bilateral trees. For all $T\ino\overline{\bbT}$ distinct from $\{ \varnothing \}$, we define the \emph{depth $\bbn T \bbn_- $ of $T$} as the unique $k\ino\bbZZ$ such that $T\backslash\{\varnothing\} \! \subset \! \overline{\bbU}_k$.

\smallskip

\noi
$(\textbf{c})$ A \emph{pointed bilateral tree} is a bilateral tree $T\ino \obbT$ and a distinguished vertex $o\ino T$ that is interpreted as an origin when $T$ is viewed as a space (or a distinguished individual when $T$ is viewed as a family tree: in this case it is rather denoted by $\varrho$). Recall from (\ref{ancestral}) the notation $L_o$ for the ancestral line of $o$. For all integers $p \ino \bbZ$, we shall use the following notation.
\begin{equation}
 
 o (p) = o_{\lll_{(-\infty , -p]}}, 
\quad  \textrm{and} \quad 
\partial L_o  \! = \! \big\{ u\ino T \backslash \Loo : \overleftarrow{u}\ino \Loo  \big\}. 
\end{equation}
Here $\partial L_o$ is called the \emph{spine} of $(T, o)$. We denote by $\obbT^\bullet$ the set of pointed bilateral trees. \cq","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.100246+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c56ef7012a68ca3817605163ac67b912f6316ba2c63f6c2d28ac862d6d79eacb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:heterogeneous-packet of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a circuit state $\tau$, including a maximizing smoothing, all

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c574fba2347e734a070686822f78efb69bc3f308b61775e623e7cd7013108c3f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real parameter delta >= 0 the SQUARED BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta started at y >= 0, written BESQ^delta, is the unique strong solution of dY_t = 2 sqrt( |Y_t| ) dW_t + delta dt with Y_0 = y; the solution is nonnegative, and pathwise uniqueness holds despite the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient by the Yamada-Watanabe criterion, which requires only Holder continuity of exponent 1/2. When delta = d is a positive INTEGER, BES^d started at |x| has the law of the radial part |B_t| of a d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x - a fact that makes the family the natural interpolation of radial Brownian motion to non-integer dimension. ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For 0 <= delta < 2 the point 0 is reached from y > 0, and the BESQ^delta equation itself fixes what happens there: 0 is absorbing for delta = 0 and instantaneously reflecting for 0 < delta < 2, so the squared process needs no extra boundary convention (the equation for X = sqrt(Y) holds only while X_t > 0). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:01:22.604561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c58051e42f1cdb52d00da99d8a39d79eba60a06c0b7bae6dd919be3b622b9291","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:rplfbm of arXiv:2606.21049, '\textsc{Locality of rough path lifts}'] Let $H \in (0, \frac 12]$ and $0 < \eta <H$ with $1/\eta < \lfloor 1/H \rfloor + 1$.
A \emph{local $\eta$-H\"older rough path lift} (\emph{local $\eta$-RPL} for short) of $X$ is a random variable $\boldsymbol{X} \colon \Omega \to C^{\eta\text{-}\mathrm{H\ddot ol}}([0,1], \mathcal G^{\lfloor 1/H \rfloor}(\mathbb R^d))$ such that $\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)} = X$ and
for any $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n \in [d]$ with $n \leq \lfloor 1/H \rfloor$, denoting $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t} \coloneqq \boldsymbol{X}^{-1}_s\boldsymbol{X}_t$, it holds that $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t}^{\alpha_1 \ldots \alpha_n}$ is $\mathscr r_{s,t}^{-1}(\mathcal F^{\alpha_1\ldots \alpha_n}_{s,t})$-measurable. 
We furthermore say that $\boldsymbol{X}$ is square-integrable if $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t}^{\alpha_1 \ldots \alpha_n} \in L^2\Omega$ for all $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n \in [d]$.","status":"unverified"}

Let $x\in K$. Let $D,E$ be derivations on $K$.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The $p$-times composition 
        $D^{\circ p}=D^p$
        is a derivation on $K$.
        \item Derivations kill $p$-powers: 
        $$D(x^p)=0.$$
        In particular, all derivations are derivations over $k$.
        \item (Jacobson's formula) There exists a universal Lie polynomial $s$ such that 
        $$\left(D+E\right)^p=D^p+E^p+s(D,E).$$
        \item (Hochschild's formula) We have 
        $$\left(xD\right)^p=x^pD^p+\left(xD\right)^{\circ (p-1)}(x)D.$$
        \item We have
        \[
        [D,xE]=D(x)E+x[D,E].
        \]
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.026141+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5b407679b1fe1959a73a0566bb925060e9ec554806f1451d75afae06ecacbd7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $(\mathcal{L}_t)_{t=0}^{T}$ be a nonnegative process adapted to a filtration $(\mathscr F_t)_{t=0}^{T}$. Let $\mathcal G\subseteq \mathscr F_0$ be an initial sigma-field, and let $B$ be a nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable random variable such that $\mathcal{L}_0\leq B$. Fix $\kappa\in(0,1]$, and let $G_0,\ldots,G_{T-1}$ be events with $G_t\in\mathscr F_t$.

Assume that, for every $t=0,\ldots,T-1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (\textbf{Deterministic non-expansion}) $\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\leq \mathcal{L}_t$ almost surely.
\item (\textbf{Good-step contraction}) On $G_t$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\mid \mathscr F_t]\leq (1-\kappa)\mathcal{L}_t.
\]
\item (\textbf{Conditional bad-event control}) For deterministic numbers $\delta_t\geq0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(G_t^c\mid \mathcal G)\leq \delta_t.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then
\be
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_T\mid\mathcal G]
\leq \left((1-\kappa)^T+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\delta_t\right)B.
\ee","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.741936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5c435fc4dd319d710826c9d90551d7bad8fff793142f5b087fc68f2b821ed66","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 29 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] (\textbf{Continuous snakes)} 

Let $(E, d_E)$ be complete and separable. 
We equip the set
$ \bCpl  \times    \bC^0(\bbR_+, \bCqq)$ with the product topology, which is Polish. 
Then $(h(s), w_s(\cdot))_{s\in \bbR_+}\! \ino  \bCpl  \times    \bC^0(\bbR_+, \bCqq)$ is a \emph{snake} if the following conditions are satisfied.
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(a)$] For all $s\ino \bbR_+$ and for all $r\ino [h(s), \infty)$, $w_s (r)\! = \! w_s (h(s))\! =: \! \widehat{w}_s $. 

\smallskip

\item[$(b)$] For all $s_1, s_2 \ino \bbR_+$, 
$w_{s_1} (r)\! = \! w_{s_2} (r)$ for all  $r\ino [0,m_h (s_1, s_2)]$ where we have set 
$m_h (s_1, s_2)\!   =\!  \inf_{s\in [s_1\wedge s_2, s_1\vee s_2]} h(s)$. 

\smallskip

\end{compactenum}
\noi
$\bullet$ We refer to $(b)$ as to the \textit{snake property}. The function $h$ is called the \textit{lifetime process} of the snake and the function $(\widehat{w}_s)_{s\in \bbR_+}$ the \textit{endpoint process} of the snake.

\noi
$\bullet$ We denote by $\fSigma_q (\bbR_+)$ the space of snakes of $ \bCpl \! \times \!   \bC^0(\bbR_+, \bCqq)$. For all 
$\zeta \ino (0, \infty)$, we denote by $\fSigma_q ([0,\zeta])$ the snake with duration $\zeta$: namely snakes $(h,w)\ino \fSigma_q (\bbR_+)$ such that $h(s)\eqo 0$ for all $s\ino [\zeta, \infty)$. 

\noi
$\bullet$ To simplify notation, we also set $\fSigma (\bbR_+)\! :=\! \fSigma_1 (\bbR_+)$ and 
$ \fSigma ([0,\zeta]) \! := \! \fSigma_1 ([0,\zeta])$.  \cq","status":"unverified"}

      little output.  If
      $T_{S,\lambda,r}=\operatorname{Mat}_S(P_{\lambda,r}L_n(s,t))$ and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.355776+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5d27474344ed5fdaae075af027ac72392cf1fbcdd0588acdb0b5ff80e8817b7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 226 (\textbf{algorithmic threshold for perceptron model}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\phi\in C_b(\bbR;\bbR)$, recall the perceptron Hamiltonian $H_N$ from in \eqref{e:hamiltonian}. We have the following:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  
        For any $\iota> 0$, there exists $L$ large enough and $c$ small enough such that the following holds.
        For sufficiently large $N$, there exists a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ such that for $\bx = \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux})$,
        \[
            \bbP\bigg(\bx \in \Sigma_N(\iota), H_N(\bx) \ge M(\ALG-\iota)\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
        \]
        \item 
        For any $\iotaval > 0$, there exists sufficiently small $\iotasol > 0$ such that the following holds.
        For any $L$, there exists $c$ small enough that for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, and $\bx = \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux})$,
        \[
            \bbP\bigg(\bx \in \Sigma_N(\iotasol), H_N(\bx) \ge M(\ALG+\iotaval)\bigg) \le e^{-cN}\,.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.555614+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5ddb3d32441d883dcb835b60a7466b5c1c65f287fd9edf79a6bb28a3f276c0d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 20 (Limits of the Schrödinger--Bass problem) of arXiv:2604.02312, 'A weak transport approach to the Schrödinger--Bass bridge'] For $\beta > 0$, let $\pi^\beta \in \Cpl(\mu,\nu)$ be the primal optimizer of the Schrödinger--Bass problem~\eqref{eq:SB_limits.SB}.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item 
        Suppose there exists $\pi \in \Cpl(\mu,\nu)$ such that $H(\pi\,|\,\mu\otimes\gamma_{\bullet}) < \infty$.
        Then
        \[
            \lim_{\beta \uparrow \infty} V_{\rm SB}^\beta(\mu,\nu) = V_{\rm EOT}(\mu,\nu),
        \]
        and $\pi^\beta \to \pi^\infty$ weakly as $\beta \uparrow \infty$, where $\pi^\infty$ is the unique minimizer of $V_{\rm EOT}(\mu,\nu)$.

        \item 
        Let $\Cpl_{\rm BStr}(\mu,\nu)$ denote the set of minimizers of the Brenier--Strassen problem~\eqref{eq:BStr}. Then
        \[
            \lim_{\beta \downarrow 0} V_{\rm SB}^\beta(\mu,\nu) = V_{\rm BStr}(\mu,\nu)
        \]
        and $\pi^\beta \to \pi^0$ weakly as $\beta \downarrow 0$, where $\pi^0$ is the unique minimizer of 
        \[
            \inf_{\pi \in \cpl_{\text{\rm BStr}}(\mu,\nu)} \int \frac12 \Wcal_2^2(\pi_x,\gamma_{\bar\pi_x}) \, \mu(\rmd x).
        \]

        \item  Suppose that $\mu \le_{\rm cvx} \nu$. Then
        \[
            \lim_{\beta \downarrow 0} \frac1\beta V_{\rm SB}^\beta(\mu,\nu) = V_{\rm mBB}(\mu,\nu),
        \]
        and $\pi^\beta \to \pi^0$ weakly as $\beta \downarrow 0$, where $\pi^0$ is the unique minimizer of $V_{\rm mBB}(\mu,\nu)$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236391+00:00","domain":"numerical analysis","id":"claim_c5e1eefee3a99acd765d978e051f62579879b0225ba57349cf7cbd16a9d39226","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"An algorithm computing an approximation y_hat to y = f(x), for an input x in floating-point arithmetic with unit roundoff u, is backward stable if for every admissible input x the computed output equals the exact result of the same problem applied to a slightly perturbed input: y_hat = f(x_hat) for some x_hat with ||x_hat - x|| = O(u) * ||x||. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:11:57.316418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5e2294fec4f1778f0a7807ae65946d06987fa620d71eb33df8aac6607482cb0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23401, 'Limit Theorems for the Pitman-Yor Frequency Spectrum'] Let $J,k,n, (m_i)_{1\le i\le n}$ be integers

 $\big(X_{in}^{(J)}\big)_{1\le i\le  k^{(J)}}$ be i.i.d. with

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.837259+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5e2914dbde7f6e2918e8391c55dfcad61563ccb7cbfa37d71f53bca9022e7b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 14 of arXiv:2609.01965, 'A logarithmic Bogomolov--Sommese vanishing theorem on compact K\"ahler manifolds'] Let $X$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold of dimension $n$ and $D$ a reduced simple normal crossing divisor on $X$.
    The following statements hold.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Let $\mathcal{F}\subset T_X(-\log D)$ be a saturated coherent subsheaf of corank $r$, where $1\leq r\leq n$, and set
        $$\mathcal{Q}:=T_X(-\log D)/\mathcal{F}, \quad
        A_{\mathcal{F},D}:=\det(\mathcal{Q}^*)=(\wedge^r\mathcal{Q}^*)^{**}.$$
        If $A_{\mathcal{F},D}$ is pseudo-effective, then
        $\nd(A_{\mathcal{F},D})\leq r$.
        In particular, in the case of $r=1$, suppose that $\mathcal{F}\subset T_X$ is a saturated codimension-one foliation, and that every irreducible component of $D$ is $\mathcal{F}$-invariant. 
        Denote $$N_{\mathcal{F}}:=(T_X/\mathcal{F})^{**}.$$ 
        Then $A_{\mathcal{F},D}\simeq N_{\mathcal{F}}^*\otimes\mathcal{O}_X(D)$.
        If $N_{\mathcal{F}}^*\otimes\mathcal{O}_X(D)$ is pseudo-effective, then
        $$\nd(N_{\mathcal{F}}^*\otimes\mathcal{O}_X(D))\leq 1.$$
        
        \item Assume that $K_X+D$ is pseudo-effective. Then
        $$H^0(X,\wedge^pT_X(-\log D))=0 \quad \text{for every } n-p<\nd(K_X+D).$$
        In particular, if $\nd(K_X+D)=n$, then
        $$H^0(X,T_X(-\log D))=0.$$
        Thus $(X,D)$ has no nonzero infinitesimal automorphism.
        If $\nd(K_X+D)\geq n-1$, then
        $$H^0(X,\wedge^2T_X(-\log D))=0.$$
        Hence there is no nonzero logarithmic Poisson structure on $(X,D)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.329193+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5e5fe170c2f6d5f99326e0be1c1d66fef7a0e4f4f43e110ae6e22ad31077268","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The functor $\textup{diag}\colon\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}\to\cat{$\bm{G}$-OrthSp}$ sends $G$-global level weak equivalences to $G$-global weak equivalences and hence descends to ${\mathfrak d\kern-.25pt}{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}_\textup{$G$-lvl}\to{{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}_\textup{$G$-gl}$.
    \begin{proof}
        It is clear that $\textup{diag}$ sends acyclic fibrations (i.e.~maps $X\to Y$ such that each $X(V)(U)\to Y(V)(U)$ is an acyclic fibration in the $\mathcal G_{{\textup{O}}(U),{\textup{O}}(V)\times G}$-model structure) to $G$-global level weak equivalences. By Corollary~(cor:cofibrant-LSp-closed of the paper) it will therefore suffice to show that $\textup{diag}$ sends any $G$-global level weak equivalence $f\colon X\to Y$ such that $X$ and $Y$ are levelwise closed to a $G$-global weak equivalence. 
        
        Restricting along any homomorphism of compact Lie groups $\varphi\colon H\to G$ (and replacing $G$ by $H$), it suffices to show that $\pi_n^G(\textup{diag}\,f)$ is bijective for every $n\in{\mathbb{Z}}$. We will give the argument for $n=0$; the argument for general $n$ is analogous, but requires slightly more notation. For this we consider the functor $\Pi_X\colon s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\to\textbf{\textup{Sets}}$ sending $(V,W)$ to $[S^V, X(V)(W)]_*^G$ with the obvious functoriality in $V$ and $W$, and define $\Pi_Y$ analogously. If we write $\Delta\colon s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\to s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)$ for the diagonal embedding, then $\pi_0^G(\textup{diag}\,X)=\mathop{\textup{colim}}\Pi_X\circ\Delta$ and $\pi_0^G(\textup{diag}\,Y)=\mathop{\textup{colim}}\Pi_Y\circ\Delta$ by definition. As $\Delta$ is cofinal, it will therefore suffice to show that the map
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{(V,W)\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V,X(V)(W)]_*^G \longrightarrow 
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{(V,W)\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)\times s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V,Y(V)(W)]_*^G
        \]
        induced by $f$ is bijective, for which it is enough by the Fubini Theorem for colimits to prove bijectivity of the analogous map
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{W\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, X(V)(W)]_*^G
            \longrightarrow
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}\mathop{\textup{colim}}_{W\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, Y(V)(W)]_*^G.
        \]
        Arguing as in the proof of Lemma~(lemma:cotensoring-fully-homotopical of the paper), this may be identified with the map
        \[
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)]_*^G\longrightarrow
            \mathop{\textup{colim}}_{V\in s({\mathcal{U}}_G)}[S^V, Y(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)]_*^G
        \]
        induced levelwise by $f(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)\colon X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)\to Y(V)({\mathcal{U}}_G)$. As the latter is a $G$-equivariant weak equivalence, the claim follows.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:59:58.429950+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5f63169a5f0b5277765e55b52aea5c68d0689f3dcdb3e5458df04f981e1bb46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:decomp of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] For $L, M \in \mathscr{L}(T, d)$, we have 
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}^2(L, M) = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L,\, A_t^M\bigr).
\end{equation}

\begin{proof}
Fix $L,M\in\mathscr{L}(T,d)$. Applying (equation eqn:d.BW of the paper) to the column covariances $A_t^L=L_{\cdot,t}L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal}$ and $A_t^M=M_{\cdot,t}M_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal}$ yields
\[
\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_*.
\]
Summing over $t \in [T]$ gives
\begin{equation} 
\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \sum_{t=1}^T \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \sum_{t=1}^T \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_*.
\end{equation}
It remains to identify the three sums on the right-hand side of (equation eq:decomp.sum of the paper) with the corresponding terms in (equation eq:ABW of the paper). Since the block-columns $L_{\cdot,1}, \ldots, L_{\cdot,T}$ collect all the blocks of $L$, we have
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{s=1}^T \|L_{t,s}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \|L\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2,
\]
and likewise
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \|M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2.
\]
For the last sum, the $d\times d$ diagonal block of $L^{\intercal}M$ indexed by $t$ is
\[
(L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t}
=L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t}
=\sum_{s=1}^T L_{s,t}^{\intercal} M_{s,t}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_* = \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| (L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t} \bigr\|_*.
\]
Substituting these three identities into (equation eq:decomp.sum of the paper) gives
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \|L\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \|M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| (L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t} \bigr\|_* = \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}^2(L, M),
\]
where the last equality is the definition (equation eq:ABW of the paper) of $\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}$. This proves (equation eq:decomp of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.313136+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_c619e145faa54d71a70d2a407f2b55f1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family (A_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by a set I, there exists a function c on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently, every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function selecting one member of each set; every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; and every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting exactly one element from each. Over Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory ZF, AC is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, and Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC asserts existence, not a specified construction; Zermelo formulated it in 1904 in order to prove the well-ordering theorem. AC is independent of ZF, assuming ZF is consistent: Godel (1938) established relative consistency of ZF+AC using the constructible universe, and Cohen (1963) established relative consistency of ZF+not-AC by forcing. Choice for every finite index set is a theorem of ZF. Choice for arbitrary countable families of nonempty sets is not provable in ZF in general.","status":"unverified"}

For almost every fixed seed there are a balanced nonzero rank-one critical factor zstar=(bstar;astar), physical arrival times T_alpha>=0, positive numbers p_alpha->0, and fixed-in-time hidden orthogonal rotations Q_alpha such that, on every fixed compact shifted interval,
  [B_alpha(T_alpha+log(1/p_alpha)/s+t); A_alpha(T_alpha+log(1/p_alpha)/s+t)^T] Q_alpha
       -> Ustar(t).
Here s is the unique positive singular value of Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma, and the canonical limit Ustar has only two nonzero columns. It is a complete nonconstant factor-flow connection from [zstar,0,...] at t->minus infinity to a finite global-minimizing factor at t->infinity with product M.

The actual arrival Grams satisfy Z_alpha(T_alpha)->Z1=zstar zstar^T and
  liminf [v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v / ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-Z1||F]>0,
where v is the unit positive-growth residual vector. More precisely the chosen rotations give active parameter error O(p_alpha^2), dormant norm O(p_alpha), and dormant projected row norm p_alpha. Consequently a_alpha=v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v=p_alpha^2+O(p_alpha^4), so the Gram clock log(1/a_alpha)/(2s) is asymptotically equivalent to the displayed parameter clock.

No hypothesis of arrival alignment is imposed on the Gaussian seed. Sigma need not be a scalar matrix or commute with any target covariance. No gap assumption is imposed on the singular values of M Sigma^(1/2). The exclusion is the repeated origin singular value s1=s2, together with rank-deficient M or covariance. The first rank-one endpoint is allowed to be a saddle even within rank-one factors; the theorem does not incorrectly call every such endpoint a best rank-one product.

For ordinary data X in R^(2xN), Y in R^(2xN), this applies when XX^T is positive definite, M=YX^T(XX^T)^(-1) invertible, and the two singular values of YX^T/N are distinct, taking Sigma=XX^T/N. The irreducible least-squares residual adds a constant to the loss and leaves all gradients and strict energy comparisons unchanged. The first canonical endpoint is seed-independent: c1>0 changes its time shift, while c2!=0 supplies the remnant. The excluded dependent-origin-row event is a proper algebraic zero set. This is a restricted square-2x2 result, not the full T232 problem. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.273237+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c6313ef89d3318c169090499b8ef0a5658e4ce1768b103c2729b2f5e5902f330","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Satz thm:HigherOrderLSI of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on ${\mathbb R}^n$ which satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (equation eq:LSI of the paper) with constant $\sigma^2 > 0$, and let $f\colon {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}$ be a $\mathcal{C}^d$-smooth function with ${\mathbb E} f = 0$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:11:35.822150+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c642b24828726a0ede206189457052ae7f926a030ebc35c3a185e70482f8085f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:priority of arXiv:2607.22908, 'Epidemic Phase Transitions in the Zero-Range Process'] A \emph{priority assignment} for
  a configuration $\eta_0$ is a map that assigns to every particle a value in $\mathbb{R}$. We write $\xi(x,j) \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{\varnothing\}$ for the priority of the particle at the slot $(x,j)$, assigning priority $\varnothing$ to empty slots, and adopt the convention that smaller values correspond to higher priority and that $r < \varnothing$ for every $r \in \mathbb{R}$.

  Let $n(\xi, x) = \sum_{i=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{\xi(x, i) \neq \varnothing}$ denote the \emph{height} of
  the stack at $x$, and for $r \in \mathbb{R}$, let $n_{\le r}(\xi, x) =
  \sum_{i=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{\xi(x, i) \le r}$ denote the number of particles at $x$ with priority at most $r$.

  Let $\Xi_{\text{packed}} \subset (\mathbb{R} \cup \{ \varnothing \})^{\mathbb{Z}^d \times \mathbb{N}}$ denote the space of
  packed and priority-sorted configurations. 
  By being priority-sorted we mean that for every site $x$  the inequalities
  \begin{equation}
    \xi(x, 1) \le \xi(x, 2) \le \cdots \le \xi(x, n(\xi, x))
  \end{equation}
  hold, and $\xi(x, j) = \varnothing$ for all $j > n(\xi, x)$. 
  This implies that the particles with priority at
  most $r$ occupy slots $1, \ldots, n_{\le r}(\xi, x)$, a requirement which is compatible with any packed initial configuration $\eta_0$, since it only prescribes the ordering within each stack.

  The \emph{slot-priority dynamics} is given by the Markov process on $\Xi_{\text{packed}}$
  generated by
  \begin{equation}
    L^{\text{prio}} H(\xi) = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \sum_{i = 1}^{n(\xi, x)}  \lambda_i \sum_{y\sim x} \bigl[ H(\xi^{(x, i) \to y}) - H(\xi) \bigr],
  \end{equation}
  acting on local functions $H: \Xi_{\text{packed}} \to \mathbb{R}$. Here $\xi^{(x, i) \to y}$ is the
  priority configuration resulting from the particle in $(x, i)$ jumping to site $y$, defined as
  follows:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item The departing particle with priority $r = \xi(x, i)$ is removed from slot $(x, i)$.
    \item Every remaining particle at site $x$ in a slot $(x, j)$ for $j > i$ shifts down to slot $j - 1$, and we set $\xi(x, n(\xi, x)) = \varnothing$.
    \item At the target site $y$, the arriving particle is placed in slot $(y, k + 1)$, where
      $k=n_{\le r}(\xi, y)$. The particles originally at slots $(y, j)$ for $j \in \{k+1,
      \ldots, n(\xi, y)\}$ shift one slot up to $(y, j + 1)$.
  \end{itemize}

  Equivalently, in terms of the graphical representation, we associate to each slot $(x, i)$ and each nearest neighbor $y$ with $|y-x|=1$ an
  independent Poisson clock $\mathcal{P}_{x,y}^i$ with rate
  $\lambda_i$. When the clock $\mathcal{P}_{x,y}^i$ rings, if $i \le n(\xi, x)$, the system jumps to $\xi^{(x, i) \to y}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296313+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c663f0050fa00804b63b2073413d20b8a9c40d3970d812ab2b12faa032d9f2c2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm optimali of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] {\bf (P-2)}
Consider the secretary problem
with the  Mallows distribution with $q=q_n\in(0,1)$ in the case that the largest number is  of highest rank..

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
\noindent iii. Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac q{1-q}\le L<\frac 1{1-q}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=(1-q)q^{L-1}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.284240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c66ceef19aa9d88a35c37ed0c3b56b4596efc977ac22d9acc6e886344d586d94","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:smc of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $(Y_{\ell})_{\ell\ge0}$ be a Markov
jump process on $(0,\infty)$ with the following dynamics. When $Y_{\ell}=y$,
the process waits an exponential time $r(y)=y$ before jumping,
at which time the process takes on
the new value $Y'=Uy+Z$, where $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ is the
recombination time on the current tree expressed as a fraction of
the tree height, and $Z\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ is the additional coalescence
time after the recombination event. 

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$,
independent of the chain. Given $X_{n}$, define the holding time
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X_{n}}\ \sim\ \mathrm{Exp}(X_{n}),
\]
and jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\begin{align}
Y_{\ell} & :=X_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),\nonumber \\
X_{n+1} & :=U_{n}X_{n}+Z_{n},
\end{align}
where $(U_{n},Z_{n})$ are i.i.d.\ with $U_{n}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$
and $Z_{n}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$. In particular, $(Y_{\ell})$ is almost surely
piecewise constant.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.363242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c68c1fb2525dc9a7169cf8812969929d197893305f4e90acaec00bd283420031","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:dispersion of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $g$ be of bounded variation with a jump.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.191622+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_c6cd13253ab5596b8fea649dca02b296822ac3a4f35fabaaefac04021c453114","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In complex dynamics, the Julia set and the Fatou set are two complementary sets defined from a function. Informally, the Fatou set of the function consists of values with the property that all nearby values behave similarly under repeated iteration of the function, and the Julia set consists of values such that an arbitrarily small perturbation can cause drastic changes in the sequence of iterated function values. Thus the behavior of the function on the Fatou set is \"regular\", while on the Julia set its behavior is \"chaotic\".","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:48:00.292268+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c6d6c84b25f3c21d4801eca47a6fcff1a6980bf4c74c7fd028e9de4ce0b69fff","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:derivativeObjective of arXiv:2609.03094, 'Discrete Gromov--Wasserstein Duality: Algorithms and Isomorphism Testing'] For each $\varepsilon\geq0$, define $\ell_{\varepsilon}:u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}\to\mathbb R$ via
        \[
            \ell_{\varepsilon}(u) = \sup_{v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}}\left\{  \frac12\|u\|^2-\frac{1}{2}\|v\|^2 +\inf_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left( \mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1 v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal} x -\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}\right\}.
        \]
        Then, the Clarke subdifferential\footnote{The Clarke subdifferential [clarke1990optimization] generalizes  the  gradient for functions which are locally Lipschitz continuous. Given a locally Lipschitz continuous function $f:X\subset \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R$, its Clarke subdifferential at $x\in X$  is  
$
    \partial f(x)\coloneqq \left\{ \xi \in \mathbb R^n : \limsup_{\substack{y\to x,t\downarrow 0}}\frac{f(y+tv)-f(y)}{t}\geq \xi^{\intercal}v\text{ for all }v\in X\right\}.$ If $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x$, $\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}$.} of $\ell_{\varepsilon}$ at $u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}$ is given by 
        \begin{equation}
        
            \partial \ell_{\varepsilon}(u) = u-\mathrm{B}_0 \argmin_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\frac{1}{2}x^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1\mathrm{B}_1 x- u^{\intercal}\mathrm{B}_0 x-\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}.
        \end{equation}
        Furthermore, for any fixed $u\in\mathbb R^{r_0}$, the Clarke subdifferential of the function 
        \[
            f_{\varepsilon,u}: v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}\mapsto \frac12\|u\|^2-\frac{1}{2}\|v\|^2 +\inf_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left( \mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1 v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal} x -\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}
        \]
        at any $v\in\mathbb R^{r_1}$ is given by 
        \[
            \partial f_{\varepsilon,u}(v) = -v+\mathrm{B}_1 \argmin_{x\in\mathcal K}\left\{\left( \mathrm{B}^{\intercal}_1 v-\mathrm{B}_0^{\intercal} u\right)^{\intercal} x -\varepsilon\mathsf{H}(x)\right\}.
        \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:41:29.036405+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c6da2cc23a38d5c7bcae300382a84a46b867bff2dc69710e1156ad6f179a7d2e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 1 (Baseline invariance of the resampling law) of arXiv:2608.26585, 'GRAS: Guided Reduced-Variance Proposals\\ and Adaptive Selection for Training-Free\\ Rewar'] Fix a scale $c=\alpha\sigma>0$, and for increments $\{\Delta^k\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\R$ and baselines
$\{b^k\}_{k=1}^K$ define the resampling law $\hat w^k\propto\exp\!\big((\Delta^k-b^k)/c\big)$, with
$\mu=\tfrac1K\sum_j\Delta^j$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=1pt]
\item \textup{(Constant baseline.)} For any constant $b^k\equiv b$, the law
$\hat w^k=\mathrm{softmax}_k(\Delta^k/c)$ is independent of $b$ and depends on the group only through the
centered increments $\Delta^k-\mu$.
\item \textup{(Leave-one-out baseline.)} For $b^k=\tfrac{1}{K-1}\sum_{j\neq k}\Delta^j$, the log-weight
$\log\hat w^k$ equals its value in \textup{(i)} up to an additive $O\!\big(1/(K{-}1)\big)$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence the resampling law is invariant to the leave-one-out baseline up to $O(1/K)$, and exactly to any constant baseline; the only operative effect
of standardization is the replacement of the fixed temperature $\alpha$ by $\alpha\sigma$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\begin{enumerate}

    \[
    I_{\lambda,q}(s_B,s) = \int_{\text{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q}_q)} \phi_{s_B,q}^{k}(g^{-1}\lambda g)\Phi_q((0,1) g) |\det g|^{s} \: dg

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.148249+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c6ef8bc97d0e2ba86d2d190a1e68ef776ac1fcf4ee2a1f41caac17a559ca0e07","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem th:deficit1 of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] For all symmetric $f\in\mathcal{C}^\infty_c(\mathbb{C}^n_{\neq},\mathbb{R})$, 
  \begin{align}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.286124+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c701e0f19379c8e3a94d8c551ad2d0f9d80535cad1c30585cbf2ed22fc6bede1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma prob0 pure of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Assume that $\xi$ is pure $p$-spin. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $u\in(0,1)$, $q\in(0,1)$, $f\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\zeta\in \mathrm{Prefix}_2(u,q)$ where $\mathrm{Prefix}_2$ is as in Definition (def:nprefix of the paper).
		
		Let $\delta\in[\varepsilon,1)$ and $\mathbf{m}\in[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^N$. Suppose moreover that $q_\mathbf{m}\in (q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$ and
		$\mathrm{dist}\!\bigl(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\,\zeta|_{(q,1]}+\zeta([0,q])\,\delta_q\bigr)<\varepsilon$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  The gradient $\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})$ is a non-degenerate Gaussian vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Its log-density at $0$, tilted by
			\[
			u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right),
			\]
			satisfies
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				+\frac{N(p-1)}{2p\,\xi'(q)\,q}
				\!\left(
				\frac{1}{N}\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				-\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				\right)^{\!2}
				\\
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{multline}
			
			\item  Suppose moreover that
			\begin{equation}
				\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				=
				N\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t+O(N\varepsilon)
			\end{equation}
			and
			\begin{equation}
				\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(h_\zeta(q,m_i)-\partial_m h_\zeta(q,m_i)m_i\bigr)
				+N\int_0^q t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				+\frac{N}{2}\int_q^1 t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				=
				-Nf+O(N\varepsilon).
			\end{equation}
			Then the squared term in (equation eq:pure-prob0-main of the paper) is $O(N\varepsilon)$, so that 
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right),
			\end{multline}
			and, on the event $\{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0\}$,
			\begin{equation}
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.","0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.362761+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c701f819aa156cb392336f5dc77d31cdfefe98e256ab50479dcc6ee2e7e58553","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:56.347313+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c706d8393421a0192cb6c15eb46f18463c66299744b4433e392822f28e259bcc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2603.13798, 'Iterated Graph Systems (I): random walks and diffusion limits'] $\Psi:\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^K\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^K$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{(Monotonicity).}
If $\mathbf x\le \mathbf y$ coordinatewise, then
$
\Psi(\mathbf x)\le \Psi(\mathbf y).
$

\item \textbf{(Homogeneity).}
For all $t\ge 0$,
$
\Psi(t\mathbf x)=t\Psi(\mathbf x).
$

\item \textbf{(Continuity).}
The map $\mathbf x\mapsto \Psi(\mathbf x)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)^K$.
Moreover, for $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^K$ the limit
$
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\Psi(\mathbf x+\varepsilon\mathbf 1)
$
exists and defines an extension of $\Psi$ to $\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^K$.

\item \textbf{(Concavity).}
For all $\lambda\in[0,1]$ and all $\mathbf x,\mathbf y\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^K$,
\[
\Psi(\lambda\mathbf x+(1-\lambda)\mathbf y)
\ge
\lambda \Psi(\mathbf x)+(1-\lambda)\Psi(\mathbf y).
\]

\item \textbf{(Superadditivity).}
For all $\mathbf x,\mathbf y\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^K$,
$
\Psi(\mathbf x+\mathbf y)\ge \Psi(\mathbf x)+\Psi(\mathbf y).
$
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.822009+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c73143ec74e424ea68649a830e250439809c11442dd36f075e4edd190adabcb4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:finite-profile-transfer of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $H\geq1$ and $k\geq2$, and let $G$ be a nontrivial torsion-free abelian
group.  The following four collections of truncated profiles are identical:

(\Psi_{\delta}(\cdot), \aleph(\cdot, \cdot)) \in L^2_{\mathcal{F}_{\delta}}(r, \delta; H) \times L^2(r, \delta; L^2_{\mathcal{F}}(\delta, b; L_0^2)).
\]

The second special case of (equation f3.4 of the paper) is as follows: Let \( r = \delta \), and define

\[
X(t) := \lambda(t, t), \quad t \in [\delta, b], \quad \aleph(t, s) := \mu(t, s), \quad (t, s) \in [\delta, b]^2.
\]

Then equation (equation f3.4 of the paper) becomes

\begin{align}
X(t) = \Psi(t) + \int_t^b \eta(t, s, \aleph(t, s), \mathbb{E}[\aleph(t, s)]) \, ds - \int_t^b \aleph(t, s) \, dB_{s}, \quad t \in [\delta, b].

This is a specific case of a singular MF-BSVIE (equation r3 of the paper), where the generator \( \eta \) is independent of \( X(s) \) and \( \aleph(s, t) \). We can define \( \aleph(t, s) \) for \( (t, s) \in [\delta, b]^2 \) by using the martingale representation theorem:

\[
X(t) = \mathbb{E}[X(t) | \mathcal{F}_{\delta}] + \int_{\delta}^t \aleph(t, s) \, dB_{s}, \quad t \in [\delta, b].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.948244+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c762b62130a07ff83f75a496776fa59bc682951707dae65e832a374e046d5f5b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:genbackoff of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$, a non-negative integer~$\tau$, and 
a distribution~\newsym{D-cal-0}{birth distribution}{\mathcal{D}} on non-negative integers. 
Fix a (possibly random)
tuple $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^Z(\tau)$ of disjoint sets 
$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^Z(\tau) = (\mathbf{arr}^Z_{1}(\tau),\mathbf{arr}^Z_2(\tau),\ldots)$ where
each $\mathbf{arr}_i^Z(\tau) 
\subseteq \mathcal{B}(\tau)$.
A \emph{generalised backoff process}~\newsym{Z-roman}{generalised backoff process, Definition~(def:genbackoff of the paper)}{Z} with send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$\tau$,
birth distribution~$\mathcal{D}$, and 
initial population $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^Z(\tau)$ is defined as follows: First,
$\mathbf{b}^Z_0(\tau) = \emptyset$ and,
for all positive integers~$j$,
$\mathbf{b}^Z_j(\tau) = \mathbf{arr}^Z_j(\tau)$.
For each time step~$t>\tau$ and each bin $j\geq 0$, the process has random variables 
\newsym{Bjz-bf}{population of bin~$j$ in~$Z$ just before sends at $t$}{\mathbf{B}^Z_j(t)}, 
\newsym{sjz-bf}{balls that send from $j$ at $t$ in $Z$}{\mathbf{s}^Z_j(t)},
\newsym{ejz-bf}{balls that escape from $j$ at $t$ in $Z$}{\mathbf{e}^Z_j(t)}, and 
\newsym{bjz-bf}{population of bin~$j$ in~$Z$ just after step $t$}{\mathbf{b}^Z_j(t)} of respective sizes 
\newsym{Bjz}{$|\mathbf{B}^Z_j(t)|$}{B^Z_j(t)}, 
\newsym{sjz}{$|\mathbf{s}^Z_j(t))|$}{s^Z_j(t)}, 
\newsym{ejz}{$|\mathbf{e}^Z_j(t)|$}{e^Z_j(t)}, and 
\newsym{bjz}{$|\mathbf{b}^Z_j(t)|$}{b^Z_j(t)}.
By analogy to backoff processes, 
$\mathbf{b}^Z_j(t)$ is the population of bin~$j$ just after step~$t$ in~$Z$, 
$\mathbf{B}^Z_j(t)$ is the population of bin~$j$ just before the sends at step~$t$,
$\mathbf{s}^Z_j(t)$ is the set of balls that send from bin~$j$ at step~$t$, and $\mathbf{e}^Z_j(t)$ is the set of balls that escape from bin~$j$ at step~$t$.
The process evolves as   follows for $t>\tau$.
\begin{itemize}

\item   The quantity \newsym{n-z}{$|n^Z(t)|$}{n^Z(t)} is drawn from~$\mathcal{D}$.  If $n^Z(t) = 0$ then $\mathbf{n}^Z(t) = \emptyset$. Otherwise,
the set 
$\newsym{nz-bf}{set of balls born at $t$ in $Z$}{\mathbf{n}^Z(t)} = \{\mathcal{B}(t,0,1),\ldots,\mathcal{B}(t,0,n^Z(t))\}$.

\item $\mathbf{B}_0^Z(t) = \mathbf{n}^Z(t) \cup \mathbf{b}_0^Z(t-1)$.   
For $j\geq 1$, $\mathbf{B}_j^Z(t) =  \mathbf{b}_j^Z(t-1)$.   

 
\item    
For all $j\geq 0$,  the set $\mathbf{s}^Z_j(t)$ is formed
by taking each element of $\mathbf{B}_j^Z(t)$ independently with probability~$p_j$. 
$\newsym{sz-bf}{set of balls that send at $t$ in $Z$}{\mathbf{s}^Z(t)} = \cup_{j\geq 0}\ 
\mathbf{s}^Z_j(t)$
and $\newsym{sz}{$|\mathbf{s}^Z(t)|$}{s^Z(t)} = |\mathbf{s}^Z(t)|$.
 

\item For all $j\geq 0$, 
a random subset $\mathbf{e}^Z_j(t)\subseteq \mathbf{s}^Z_j(t)$ is drawn from some distribution (to fix a particular generalised backoff process this distribution will be specified).   
 

\item $\mathbf{b}^Z_0(t) = \mathbf{B}^Z_0(t) \setminus \mathbf{s}^Z_0(t)$.

\item Fix a (possibly random) tuple 
$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^Z(t)$ of disjoint sets
$\newsym{arr-bf}{end-of-step arrivals}{\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^Z(t)}  = ( \mathbf{arr}^Z_{1}(t),\mathbf{arr}^Z_2(t),\ldots)$
where each $\mathbf{arr}^Z_i(t) 
\subseteq \mathcal{B}(t)
\setminus  \cup_{k\geq 0} \mathbf{B}^Z_k(t)$. 

  

\item For all $j\geq 1$, 
$\mathbf{b}^Z_j(t) = \mathbf{arr}^Z_j(t) \cup (\mathbf{B}^Z_j(t) \setminus \mathbf{s}^Z_j(t)) \cup 
(\mathbf{s}^Z_{j-1}(t) \setminus \mathbf{e}^Z_{j-1}(t))$.
 
 
\end{itemize}

 

For $t\geq \tau$ we use the notation ${\overline{\mathbf{b}}}^Z(t)$ for the  tuple $(\mathbf{b}_0^Z(t),\mathbf{b}_1^Z(t),\ldots)$
and we use ${\overline{b}}^Z(t)$ for the tuple 
 $(b_0^Z(t),b_1^Z(t),\ldots)$. We define $\overline{\mathrm{arr}}^Z(t) = (\mathrm{arr}_1^Z(t), \mathrm{arr}_2^Z(t),\ldots)$ where $\newsym{arr-roman}{$|\mathbf{arr}^Z_j(t)|$}{\mathrm{arr}^Z_j(t)} = |\mathbf{arr}^Z_j(t)|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Pinned field and potential-kernel normalization as specified","For the maximum interpretation: bounded open D containing zero, finite connected/boundary components of positive boundary diameter","D_N contained in the infinity-distance >1/N interior and eventually containing every fixed positive-distance interior","Maximum depth test depends on finitely many coordinates with compact support"],"created_at":"2026-10-26T22:12:14.368434+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_c76665fcb3587093cd069e61f74c56d6431cbb01c3515ec07846f147bff7aa73","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let a be the Z^2 simple-random-walk potential kernel, normalized by a(0)=0, harmonicity off zero and a(x)=(2/pi)log|x|+O(1). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161307+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c76ff01d24ad4f8093e496a7b8036d62b53cda129bbff51ae8e0f650a7bc1740","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 11 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\ge0$, 
and for $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
the mapping
$(\lambda,\mu)\mapsto S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)$,
is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric $d_H$.

\begin{proof} Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\ge0$.
Recall the notation \eqref{e:lam.mu.delta.ball}, and suppose
$(\lambda',\mu')\in\Lambda$ and 
 $(\lambda,\mu)\in B_\delta(\lambda',\mu')$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:52.428087+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c7838ce2b13bbf1628cfb5c1e56b1bb1277468c626e6fbf5d4e4f73929fcf4c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 180 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Let $\nu$ be a complex measure on a surface whose support is a smooth compact curve $\gamma$, which has smooth density with respect to the Lebesgue measure relative to coordinate charts for $\gamma$, and which satisfies
\[
\int_{\gamma \times \gamma} \big|\textnormal{Gr}(p_1,p_2) \dd\nu(p_1)\dd\nu(p_2)\big| < +\infty.
\]
If we have a holomorphic function $z$ on the surface which is a local coordinate near every point of $\gamma$, we can also write $\dd\nu(p) = \mathbbm{1}_{\gamma}(p)\nu(p)\dd z(p)$ for some ``density'' $\nu(p)$ which is a smooth function of $p \in \gamma$.

The Gaussian free field on the surface is such that $\int \textnormal{GFF}(p) \dd \nu(p) = \int_{\gamma} \textnormal{GFF}(p) \nu(p) \dd z(p)$ is a well-defined Gaussian centered random variable. Moreover, if we have two such measures $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ supported respectively on curves $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$, then
\[
\amsmathbb{E}\left[\bigg(\int \textnormal{GFF}(p_1)\dd\nu_1(p_1)\bigg) \cdot \bigg(\int \textnormal{GFF}(p_2) \dd\nu_2(p_2)\bigg)\right] = \iint_{\gamma_1 \times \gamma_2} \textnormal{Gr}(p_1,p_2) \nu_1(p_1)\nu_2(p_2) \dd z(p_1) \dd z(p_2).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite subset distribution, nonzero nonnegative weights","Every coordinate appears with positive probability","0<alpha<=1","All positive external fields"],"created_at":"2026-10-26T23:41:26.318426+00:00","domain":"random graphs, entropy and fractional log-concavity","id":"claim_c78c4a21daabbf1f10d42733e1a8de8e26e24057545f9f665f38e6552961ad79","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Covariance criterion for fractional log-concavity in the Alimohammadi-Anari-Shiragur-Vuong framework: let mu be nonnegative weights on subsets S of a finite ground set [n], not all zero, and suppose each coordinate appears in some positively weighted subset. Put g(x)=sum_S mu(S) product_{i in S} x_i. For 0<alpha<=1, log g(x_1^alpha,...,x_n^alpha) is concave on the positive orthant if and only if C_theta<=alpha^(-1)D_theta for every positive theta, in positive-semidefinite order. Logs are natural. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.660635+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c78d3c3631b9ada9c50fde938d1a3eea11619a26e45983cc90a3597cefa36709","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 34 (Conditional convergence) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] Let either $W(\mu):=\mu(\varphi_0)$, with $\varphi_0\in\Cc$, $\varphi_0\not\equiv0$, fixed

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:29:14.945292+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c7ac7eae4275a9c4e496859dbfa42418153ee743f251e3655b0ff20762f05ec5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:BCSVH of arXiv:2606.14687, 'Lehner's operator norm formulas, semidefinite programming, and spiked matrix models'] For $\bm X$ defined as in (equation eq:X-gauss of the paper), define the quantities
\begin{align*}
\sigma(\bm X)^2
  &\colonequals \|\mathbb{E}(\bm X - \mathbb{E} \bm X)^2\| \\
  &= \left\| \sum_{i = 1}^n \bm A_i^2 \right\|, \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \\
v(\bm X)^2
  &\colonequals \|\mathbb{E} \mathsf{vec}(\bm X - \mathbb{E} \bm X)\mathsf{vec}(\bm X - \mathbb{E} \bm X)^{*}\| \\
  &= \left\|\sum_{i = 1}^n \mathsf{vec}(\bm A_i) \mathsf{vec}(\bm A_i)^*\right\|, \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation}  \\
\sigma_*(\bm X)^2
  &\colonequals \sup_{\|\bm u\| = \|\bm w\| = 1}\mathbb{E}[|\bm u^{*}(\bm X - \mathbb{E} \bm X)\bm w|^2] \\
  &= \sup_{\|\bm u\| = \|\bm w\| = 1} \sum_{i = 1}^n \left| \langle \bm u, \bm A_i \bm w \rangle \right|^2, \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation}  \\
  \widetilde v(\bm X)^2
  &\colonequals
v(\bm X) \cdot \sigma(\bm X). \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation}
\end{align*}
    There is a universal constant $C > 0$ such that
    \[
        \left|\mathbb{E}\lambda_{\max}(\bm X) - \Lambda_{\mathsf{sc}}(\bm A_0, \bm A_1, \dots, \bm A_n)\right|

    Also, if $\bm X = \bm X^{(d)} \in \mathbb{C}^{d \times d}_{\mathsf{herm}}$ is a sequence of such random matrices with $\bm X^{(d)} = \bm A_0^{(d)} + \sum_{i = 1}^n g_i\bm A_i^{(d)}$ for some $n = n(d)$, and one has, as $d \to \infty$,
    \[

    \]
    then the following convergence in probability holds as $d \to \infty$:
    \[
        |\lambda_{\max}(\bm X^{(d)}) - \Lambda_{\mathsf{sc}}(\bm A_0^{(d)}, \bm A_1^{(d)}, \dots, \bm A_n^{(d)})| \to 0.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:07.259805+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c7b271fba94d570bc446cff1d98eba6cc3ee0b0a57526188bd794431d459e37c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2604.19738, 'Phase Transitions in the Fluctuations of Functionals of Random Neural Networks \\'] Let $\widehat \kappa_L$ be as in \eqref{defkappahatL} and assume either \Cref{ass::CRI}, $\kappa'(1)>1$ and $\kappa'(b)\neq 0$, or \Cref{ass:cri-pot}. Then the following asymptotics holds for fixed $q\in\N$, $q\ge2$.

\smallskip
\noindent
If $q<d/(2\nu)$, as $L\to\infty$ we have
	\begin{equation*}
		\int_{-1}^1 \widehat \kappa_L(u)^q\,\di \mu(u)
		= v_L^{q}\Big(\beth_q+o(1)\Big)\,
	\end{equation*}
where
    $$\beth_q = \frac{1}{\beta_0^q} \int_{-1}^1 \widehat \beta(u)^q  \di \mu(u)\,,\,\,\,\qquad \widehat \beta:=\beta-\int_{-1}^1\beta(u)\di\mu(u)\,.
    $$
Moreover,  $\beth_q=0 \iff \kappa$ and $q$ are both odd.

\smallskip
\noindent
If $q\ge d/(2\nu)$ and $q$ is even whenever $\kappa$ is odd we have
$$ \int_{-1}^1 \widehat \kappa_L(u)^q \di \mu (u)\asymp
\begin{cases}
			v_L^q \log(v_L^{-1})&\textnormal{if } q=\frac{d}{2\nu} \\
			v_L^{d/(2\nu)}
            &\textnormal{if } q>\frac{d}{2\nu}
		\end{cases}\,\,\,\,\,\,.
        $$

\smallskip
\noindent
Moreover, we always have (with no restrictions on $q,\kappa$)
$$ \int_{-1}^1  |\widehat\kappa_L(u)|^q \di \mu (u)\lesssim
\begin{cases}
v_L^q &\textnormal{if } q<\frac{d}{(2\nu)} \\
			v_L^q \log(v_L^{-1})&\textnormal{if } q=\frac{d}{2\nu} \\
			v_L^{d/(2\nu)}
            &\textnormal{if } q>\frac{d}{2\nu}
		\end{cases}\,\,\,\,\,\,.
        $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, mu) and (Y, nu) are sigma-finite measure spaces","F is measurable with respect to the product sigma-algebra","F >= 0 (or the right-hand side is finite when F is complex)","1 <= p < infinity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.552266+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_c7e6ce33332ca204b69943ebb85d6c5977e07b252cd3daa2dcc9174662d19207","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, mu) and (Y, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces, 1 <= p < infinity, and F: X x Y -> [0, infinity] measurable for the product sigma-algebra. Then ( int_Y ( int_X F(x,y) dmu(x) )^p dnu(y) )^{1/p} <= int_X ( int_Y F(x,y)^p dnu(y) )^{1/p} dmu(x), both sides in [0, infinity]. Consequently, for complex measurable F with the right-hand side (computed with |F|) finite, int_X F(x,y) dmu(x) converges absolutely for nu-a.e. y and its L^p(nu)-norm is at most the right-hand side. In words: the L^p norm of an integral is at most the integral of the L^p norms. (For p = infinity the analogous statement with ess sup holds for F >= 0.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.845469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c81e16d14a6e51fc87da21e030a9ee34388bb31078a04202e7ace736392682c0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 15 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] A {\bf Ginibre Brownian motion} of size $N$ is an $\M_N(\C)$-valued diffusion process $Z^N(\cdot)$ of the form
    \[ Z^N(t) \equaldist \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X^N(t) + \i Y^N(t) ) \]
    where $X^N,Y^N$ are independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$.  Entrywise, this can be described simply: for $1\le i,j\le N$, 
    $\{\sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Re}Z_{i,j}^N, \sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Im}Z_{i,j}^N\}_{t\ge 0}$ are all independent standard Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$.

    The random matrix $Z^N(1)$, whose entries are all i.i.d.\ complex normal random variables, is called a {\bf Ginibre Ensemble} first introduced in \cite{Ginibre1965}. Equivalently, the law of $Z$ has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\M_N(\C)$ which is proportional to $Z\mapsto \exp(-N\mathrm{Tr}_N[Z^\ast Z])$.  Note that this density is invariant under $Z\mapsto UZV^\ast$ for any deterministic unitary matrices $U,V\in\mathrm{U}(N)$; thus, the law of the Ginibre ensemble is unitarily bi-invariant.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.241559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c835caa603445775a1fb28fb06d65938405a8ca8164ec960b5fd81186a095e1d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 (Riemannian $p$-harmonicity residual) of arXiv:2609.00571, '\textbf{Shape Optimization and Bernoulli Free Boundary Problems\\ for the Riemannian $p$-L'] For a diffeomorphism $\Psi:U\to V$, define the residual of the transported

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.492821+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c836ed719a8d442d6f73be266f4d6ec3c61685b613b2c110645479d676120e5a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 (Discrete Hessian and the $\De_i$ on $T_n$) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] Let $f: T_n \ra \R$ be a function.
\bit
\item Let $E_0(T_n)$ be the set of all parallelograms $e_0\subseteq T_n$ whose vertices are $\{(v_1, v_2),  (v_1 + 1, v_2),  (v_1 + 1, v_2 + 1),  (v_1 +2, v_2 + 1)\}.$

\hess f(e_0) := \De_0 f(e_0) :=  f(v_1, v_2) - f(v_1 + 1, v_2) - f(v_1 + 1, v_2 + 1) + f(v_1 +2, v_2 + 1).\nonumber\\
\hess f(e_1) := \De_1 f(e_1) :=  - f(v_1, v_2) + f(v_1 + 1, v_2) + f(v_1, v_2 + 1) - f(v_1 + 1,  v_2 + 1).\nonumber\\
\hess f(e_2) := \De_2 f(e_2) :=  f(v_1, v_2) - f(v_1+1, v_2+1) - f(v_1, v_2 + 1) + f(v_1 + 1, v_2 + 2).\nonumber\\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:45:17.704083+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c83b41327dd3fc7f3f989d767c4ebd8ab9b61b8d2c885e02e5e04efd04ac7e1c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:hypoexponential_derivative_properties of arXiv:2604.09509, 'An Improved Bipartition Cover Bound for the Multispecies Coalescent Model'] If we have positive, distinct rates $\{\lambda_i\}_{i = 1}^\infty$:

        \item At zero, the one-sided derivatives $F_k^{(m)}(0) = 0$ for $0 \leqslant m \leqslant k-1$. The nonzero derivatives take the form

        \[ h_r(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_k) := \sum_{1\leqslant i_1\leqslant i_2 \leqslant ...\leqslant i_r\leqslant k} \prod_{j=1}^r \lambda_{i_j}.\]

            \[F_k^{(k)}(0) = \prod_{i=1}^k \lambda_i, \qquad F_k^{(k+1)}(0) = -\left(\sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i\right)\left(\prod_{i=1}^k \lambda_i\right).\]

{"assumptions":["(a): f integrable on R","(b): the periodization converges everywhere to a continuous function AND the Fourier transform is absolutely summable over the integers","(c): f continuous with (1+|x|)^{-1-delta} decay of both f and its transform","integrability alone does NOT give the pointwise identity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.263262+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis on Euclidean space","id":"claim_c871045185872c50e3ad107b05bbe60ce99326ffffae1aec8481b784ad7e885a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Convention $\\hat f(\\xi)=\\int_{\\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-2\\pi i x\\xi}dx$. (a) (Always, as an $L^1$ identity) If $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R)$, the periodization $Pf(x)=\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f(x+n)$ converges absolutely for a.e. $x$, $Pf\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ with $\\|Pf\\|_{L^1(\\mathbb T)}\\le\\|f\\|_1$, and $\\widehat{Pf}(k)=\\hat f(k)$ for all $k\\in\\mathbb Z$. (b) (Pointwise identity) If in addition $\\sum_nf(x+n)$ converges for every $x$ to a continuous function and $\\sum_k|\\hat f(k)|<\\infty$, then $\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f(x+n)=\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z}\\hat f(k)e^{2\\pi i kx}$ for every $x$; taking $x=0$, $\\sum_nf(n)=\\sum_k\\hat f(k)$. (c) (Convenient sufficient condition) If $f$ is continuous and there are $C,\\delta>0$ with $|f(x)|\\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\\delta}$ and $|\\hat f(\\xi)|\\le C(1+|\\xi|)^{-1-\\delta}$, then (b) applies and both series converge absolutely; this holds for every $f\\in\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R)$. (d) Scaled and multidimensional forms: for $T>0$, $\\sum_nf(nT)=T^{-1}\\sum_k\\hat f(k/T)$; for $f\\in\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R^d)$ and the lattice $\\mathbb Z^d$, $\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z^d}f(x+n)=\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z^d}\\hat f(k)e^{2\\pi i k\\cdot x}$; more generally for a full-rank lattice $\\Lambda$ with dual $\\Lambda^*$ and covolume $|\\Lambda|$, $\\sum_{\\lambda\\in\\Lambda}f(\\lambda)=|\\Lambda|^{-1}\\sum_{\\mu\\in\\Lambda^*}\\hat f(\\mu)$. Classic application (Jacobi theta transformation): $\\sum_ne^{-\\pi n^2t}=t^{-1/2}\\sum_ne^{-\\pi n^2/t}$ for $t>0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:13:31.904720+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c87a764610fbe61ef1c23644c0f9f4938a21a1f9ccdb4efc4a33ff94d96de279","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:generalcoupling of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $\Omega$ and $\Sigma$ be two finite sets, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ be probability measures on $\Omega$ and $\Sigma$ respectively, and $f: \Omega \to 2^{\Sigma}$ be a function\footnote{Here, $2^{\Sigma}$ is the power set of $\Sigma$.}. For each $\eta \in \Sigma$, let
    $f^{-1}(\eta):=\{\omega \in \Omega \mid \eta \in f(\omega)\}.$
     Suppose that $ \sum_{\omega \in \Omega, \eta \in \Sigma} \rho[\omega] \gamma[\eta] 1\! \!1[\eta \in f(\omega)] > 0$ and then define a coupling probability measure on $\Omega\times\Sigma$ by
	\[\mathscr{P}[\omega,\eta]\propto \rho[\omega] \gamma[\eta] 1\! \!1[\eta \in f(\omega)],~\forall (\omega, \eta)\in\Omega\times\Sigma. \] 

	\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$, denoted by  $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}$, satisfies $ \mathscr{P}_{\Omega}[\omega]  \propto \gamma[f(\omega)]\rho[\omega]$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$. 
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$, denoted by $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}$, satisfies $ \mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta] \propto  \rho[f^{-1}(\eta)] \gamma[\eta] $ for each $\eta \in \Sigma$.   

\item[(c)] For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}[\omega]\neq 0$,  the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\cdot | \omega]$ on $\Sigma$ is $\gamma[\cdot \mid f(\omega)]$.
        \item[(d)]   For each $\eta\in\Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta]\neq 0$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\cdot|\eta] $ on $\Omega$ is $\rho[\cdot \mid f^{-1}(\eta)]$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543907+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c894786f1b55507dfb078a06491f9f69fe1f01bd76b485d4469c8716a85154c8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real parameter delta >= 0 the SQUARED BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta started at y >= 0, written BESQ^delta, is the unique strong solution of dY_t = 2 sqrt( |Y_t| ) dW_t + delta dt with Y_0 = y; the solution is nonnegative, and pathwise uniqueness holds despite the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient by the Yamada-Watanabe criterion, which requires only Holder continuity of exponent 1/2. The BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta, BES^delta, is X_t = sqrt(Y_t); for X > 0 it solves dX_t = dW_t + ((delta - 1)/(2 X_t)) dt. When delta = d is a positive INTEGER, BES^d started at |x| has the law of the radial part |B_t| of a d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x - a fact that makes the family the natural interpolation of radial Brownian motion to non-integer dimension. ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For delta < 2 the boundary point 0 is reached and a boundary convention (absorbing or instantaneously reflecting) must be specified; for delta >= 2 the point 0 is never reached from y > 0 and no convention is needed. [standard; e.g. Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Chapter XI]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.025842+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8b07daf74ce3b894cf8f7044bb5cf06d17b06e10113205e8971f490e4dc707f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:deformed_lattice of arXiv:2607.27810, 'Perturbed Beta Corners Process'] Given a top row $\mathbf{z}=(z_1>\cdots>z_N)$ and parameters
$\mathsf{a}=(\mathsf{a}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{a}_N)$,
the \emph{deformed $\infty$-corners lattice}
$\{\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^k\}_{1\le i\le k\le N}$ is defined by
$\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^N = z_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,N$, and the remaining
positions $\{\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^k\}_{1\le i\le k\le N-1}$ are the unique 
solution of the \emph{coupled optimality equations}:
\begin{equation}
	
	\sum_{\substack{j=1\\j\ne i}}^{k}\frac{1}{\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^k - \bar{\mathsf{y}}_j^k}
	- \frac{1}{2}\sum_{q=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^k - \bar{\mathsf{y}}_q^{k+1}}
	- \frac{1}{2}\sum_{p=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^k - \bar{\mathsf{y}}_p^{k-1}}
	= \frac{\mathsf{a}_k - \mathsf{a}_{k+1}}{2},
	\qquad i=1,\ldots,k,
\end{equation}
for $k=1,\ldots,N-1$, subject to \emph{strict}
interlacing.  That is, $\bar{\mathsf{y}}^k \prec
\bar{\mathsf{y}}^{k+1}$, and
$\bar{\mathsf{y}}^k_i\ne\bar{\mathsf{y}}^{k+1}_j$ for all
$1\le k\le N-1$, $1\le i\le k$ and $1\le j\le k+1$.
Equivalently, $\bar{\mathsf{Y}}\coloneqq
\{\bar{\mathsf{y}}_i^k\}_{1\le i\le k\le N-1}$ lies in
the open Gelfand--Tsetlin polytope, where every denominator
of~(equation eq:deformed_optimality of the paper) is nonzero.  Existence
and uniqueness 
of the solution to~(equation eq:deformed_optimality of the paper)
