{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.168228+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccc0df09822bfa3a5d90fb1bef1737321977369413bb52b928df8763118ba57f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 62 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\BOGP}(\alpha,q_0)$.
\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$, where $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$. Recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, this means there exists a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_j)^\circ$ (acting in $N_j$ dimensions) such that
    \begin{align} \nonumber 
    &\WERR( (\cA_j)^\circ,\mu)
 \le \epsilon\,,\\
        
   &     q_0(j)
        \equiv \chi_{ (\cA_j)^\circ}(0)
         \stackrel{j\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} q_0\,.
    \end{align}
    Let $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ be the perturbations of the $( (\cA_j)^\circ)_{j\ge 1}$ given by Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable}, which are also $L$-Lipschitz.
    Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} further yields
    \[
        \frac{1}{N} \bbE \Big[\| (\cA_j)^\circ(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) 
        	- \cA_j(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2\Big]
        \le \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2}\,.
    \]
Thus Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx} implies that for $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$ and $C_2(\alpha,L)$ given therein,
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_j,(\cA_j)^\circ)
	\le 
	\bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) \cdot \frac{2}{(1-q_0(j))L^2} + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j}
        \bigg\}^{1/2} 
        \le \epsilon \]
    where the last inequality holds if $L$ is sufficiently large depending on $\alpha,q_0,\epsilon$ (consistent with our assumptions), and $j$ sufficiently large depending on $q_0,\epsilon,L$. Hence, by omitting finitely many $j$, we can assume it holds for all $j$ that
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\cA_j,\mu)=
        \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_j), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_j), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\}
        \le 2\epsilon\,,
    \eeq
By passing to a further subsequence of the $j$'s, we can assume that for all $j$ we have 
    \[
         \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_j), \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_j), \mu^\Ising\Big)
        \bigg\}
         \le 3\epsilon
    \]
for some fixed $\mu^\Ising \in \cP(\{\pm 1\})$.
    By passing to a further subsequence, we can assume (as in Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}) that $\chi_{\cA_j}$ converges to a limiting function $\chi$, both pointwise and in $L^1$.
    Since Proposition~\ref{p:wlogable} ensures 
    \[
        \chi_{\cA_j}(0) = \chi_{\cA^\circ_j}(0) = q_0(j)\,,
    \]
    by \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.q0.limit} we have $\chi(0) = q_0$.

We now apply Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} to the sequence $(\cA_j)_{j\ge 1}$ where, treating $\epsilon$ as a function of $L$ tending to $0$ sufficiently slowly, the hypothesis \eqref{e:BOGP-hardness-main-hypothesis} holds by \eqref{e:Lip.in.BOGP.hardness.hypothesis}.
    Then, for some $\tilde\epsilon = \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon)$ tending to $0$ sufficiently slowly as $\epsilon\rightarrow 0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} provides controls $(q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conclusions of that theorem, where all $o_L(1)$ error terms are replaced by $\tilde\epsilon$. We assume without loss that $\tilde{\epsilon}\le1$. 
    We will now verify that for $C(L)$ given by Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main},
    \beq
        
         (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p\equiv \chi^{-1},\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) 
         \in \Adm^{\BOGP}\Big(
         \alpha,q_0;
         \tilde C = \max\{C(L),L^2\}, \tilde\epsilon 
         \Big)\,.
    \eeq
    Indeed, we verify each of the conditions from Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} specifying the $\Adm^{\BOGP}$ class:
    \begin{itemize}
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-Lip}
    implies condition~\ref{it:1.1bogp};

\item Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main}\ref{it:BOGP-hardness-main-diffusivity}
    implies condition~\ref{it:2.1}; 

\item We have $p(q_0) = 0$ because we defined $\chi(0) = q_0$. 
        Theorem~\ref{thm:BOGP-hardness-main} asserts $p(q_*) \le \tilde\epsilo (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.775784+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cceb8926ad8613162a17b69260373e15646c727032d01959ed3b249d6320261b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def: Berger_good_box_definition of arXiv:2608.00399, 'The Heavy-tailed Frog Model'] Let $Q$ be a $k$-block

    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=2pt]
    \item A $0$-block $Q$ is \textbf{good} if there is no directed edge $(u,w)$ with
    $u,w\in Q$ and $|u-w|>A_0/100$.

    \item For $k\ge1$, a $k$-block $Q$ is \textbf{good} if the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}, leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=2pt]
    \item there is no directed edge $(u,w)$ with
    $u,w\in Q$ and $|u-w|>A_{k-1}/100$;
    \item among the $(k{-}1)$-blocks (children) of $Q$,
    all but at most one are good;
    \item for every
    $v\in\{0,\pm A_{k-1}/2\}^d$, the shifted inner block $Q^{\mathrm{int}}+v$
    also satisfies \textup{(b)} (i.e., among its $(k{-}1)$-subblocks, all but at most
    one are good).
    \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352896+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccec066ffa0ec9499357e450b8a09d076a5e7a35b2314061cdccc3fc37f950af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 198 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, and let $\bx(q_d)$ be as defined by
\eqref{e:x.q.mean}. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\bigg|
    \frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}-q_{\min\{d,\ell\}}
    \bigg|\ge
    \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\bigg) 
    \le \exp(-N^{0.1})\,.
    \]

\begin{proof}
This follows easily from gaussian Lipschitz concentration (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}).
Indeed note that $\|\cA(\bG,  \bg^\aux)\|_2\leq N^{1/2}$ almost surely, while by definition $\bx(q_d)$
is an $L$-Lipschitz function of the gaussian vector $(\bG(q_d),\bg^\aux(q_d))$. It follows that for $\ell \le d$, the normalized inner product
    \[\frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}\]
is an 
 $O(LN^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz function of 
    \[\Big(\bG(q_\ell),
    \bg^\aux(q_\ell),
    \bG(q_d) - \bG(q_\ell),\bg^\aux(q_d) - \bg^\aux(q_\ell)\Big)\,.\]
 Therefore it concentrates around its mean by Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}, which gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:07:48.552657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccecdb2b3a682f61a22c6f6e603f65d48bccf2f7c9c088a4551638b51f29d639","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (Absolute Fourier estimate) of arXiv:2609.01413, 'Sharp Threshold for Universality of Rational Canonical Forms over a Finite Field'] Fix a positive integer $m$ and a constant $c>1$, and put
    $$
    \beta_n:=\frac{c\log n}{n}.
    $$
    Let $V$ be an $m$-dimensional $\F_p$-vector space, and let
    $\mu_{ij}$, $1\leq i,j\leq n$, be arbitrary
    $\beta_n$-balanced probability measures on $\F_p$. Fix a nontrivial
    additive character
    $$
    \psi:\F_p\longrightarrow\C^\times,
    $$
    and write
    $$
    \widehat{\mu}_{ij}(u)
    :=
    \sum_{a\in\F_p}\mu_{ij}(a)\psi(ua),
    \qquad
    u\in\F_p.
    $$
    Then
    \begin{align}
        
        &p^{-mn}
        \sum_{\substack{g_1,\ldots,g_n\in V\\
        \Span_{\F_p}\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}=V}}
        \ \sum_{\substack{h_1,\ldots,h_n\in V^\vee\\
        (h_1,\ldots,h_n)\neq(0,\ldots,0)}}
        \prod_{i,j=1}^n
        \left|
        \widehat{\mu}_{ij}\bigl(h_j(g_i)\bigr)
        \right|
        =
        o(1),
    \end{align}
    where the estimate is uniform over the choices of
    $\mu_{ij}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.896789+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccef04059d6280610b1564c3308a6d8a71f363cb89c359e9f2d289a5a3867c85","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition properased of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $(T, d, \rho, \mu)$ be a rooted finitely measured Polish $\mathbb{R}$-tree, let $h \! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+$ and let $\rho \! \in \!  \mathtt{t} \! \subseteq \! T$ be closed and connected. Then the following holds true. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$]  If $\mu (T\backslash \mathtt{t}) \! < \!  h$, then ${\cal E}_h \mu\! = \! {\cal E}_h \mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}} \mu$.  

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] For all connected components $C$ of $T \backslash \mathtt{t}$, 
${\cal E}_h \mu ( C)\! =\!  (\mu (C) \! -\! h)_+$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(iii)$] ${\cal E}_h \mu (T\backslash \mathtt{t}) \! \leq \! \mu (T\backslash \mathtt{t}) $. 

\smallskip

\item[$(iv)$] $\mathtt{Span}\,  (\mathtt{Supp}\,   {\cal E}_h \mu)$ is the compact set $ T_{\! \mu, h+}$, 
which is the closure of $\, \bigcup_{h^\prime >h} T_{\! \mu, h^\prime}$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(v)$] $({\cal E}_h )_{h \in \mathbb{R}_+}$ is a semigroup on $\mathcal{M}_f (T)$, i.e.~ 
$ {\cal E}_h \!  \circ\!  {\cal E}_{h^\prime} \! = \!  {\cal E}_{h+h^\prime}$ for all $h,h' \! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+ $.  

\smallskip

\item[$(vi)$] For all $h, h^\prime \! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+$ and all $\mu \! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_f (T)$, $d_{\mathtt{var}} ({\cal E}_{h+h'}\mu, {\cal E}_h\mu ) \! \leq \!  3 \mu(T) h^\prime / h$, where for all $\nu, \nu'\! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_f(T)$ we have set $d_{\mathtt{var}} (\nu, \nu')\! = \!   \sup_{B \in \mathscr{B} (T)} | \nu(B)\! -\! \nu'(B) |$. 
\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 versus (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 with left state 1 and right state 0","Rankine-Hugoniot: σ = [flux]/[density], so both entries matter","Chain-rule manipulations of the flux are valid only where the solution is C^1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418709+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_cd2c0cd0a6c998918c8d20dec220a3380322e8bf670c19046ddde117aec30ea3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and hence the whole notion of weak solution, is attached to a specific pair (conserved density, flux) — not to the PDE as an equation for smooth functions. Two equations with identical classical solutions can have different weak solutions. Counterexample: for smooth u, Burgers' equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is equivalent to (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 (multiply the first by u; conversely divide where u ≠ 0). But a jump from u_l = 1 (left) to u_r = 0 (right) travels with speed [f]/[u] = (1/2 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1/2 for the first form, and with speed (1/3 - 0)/(1/2 - 0) = 2/3 for the second: the two weak solutions are genuinely different. The same phenomenon makes the nonconservative form u_t + u u_x = 0 meaningless across a shock (the product u u_x is not a distribution for discontinuous u). Physically, the model must specify which quantity is conserved; numerically, only schemes written in the conservative form of the true conserved quantity (Lax-Wendroff theorem) converge to the correct shock speeds. Auditor's check: when a proof rewrites the flux (multiplying the equation by a function of u, changing variables u = φ(v), or using a chain rule), the manipulation is legitimate for smooth solutions only; across discontinuities it changes the answer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:52:17.579659+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cd52e1c002bbc25e77385abad22475754ded034dfa21a8d435c80a4947583a91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma eq:l:FullDomain:0 of arXiv:2411.14936, 'Massive Particle Systems,\\Wasserstein Brownian Motions,\\ and the Dean--Kawasaki Equation'] Let~$k\in {\mathbb N}$,~$F\in \mcC_b^\infty({\mathbb R}^k)$, and~$\left(f_i\right)_{i\leq k}\subset \msD(\mssE)$. 
For every choice of everywhere defined $\nu$-representatives~$\tilde{f_i}$ of~$f_i$, the function
\begin{equation}
\tilde{u}\colon \mu \longmapsto (F\circ\tilde{\mbff}^\star)(\mu)
\end{equation}
is well-defined on~$\msP$ and $\mcQ_\pi$-square-integrable. Its class~$u\eqdef \class[\mcQ_\pi]{\tilde{u}}$ is independent of the choice of representatives for the~$f_i$'s and satisfies
\[
u\in \msD(\mcE_\pi)\qquad \text{and} \qquad \mcG_\pi(u)=\sum_{i,j}^{k,k} (\partial_i F\cdot\partial_j F) \circ \tilde{\mbff}^\star \cdot \mathsf{\Gamma}(\hat f_i, \hat g_j)^\star \quad \mcQ_\pi\text{-a.e.}\,\mathrm{.}
\]

\begin{proof}
It suffices to show the statement for~$\tilde{u} = \tilde{f}^\star$. The conclusion for~$\tilde{u}$ as in~(equation eq:l:FullDomain:0 of the paper) follows by the diffusion property for~$\mcG_\pi$.
Let~$\left(f_n\right)_n\subset \msA$ be $\mssE^{1/2}_1$-convergent to~$f$ and consider the sequence~$\left(f_n^\star\right)_n$.
By Theorem~(t:TransferP of the paper)(i:t:TransferP:2 of the paper), by~(equation eq:l:DiffusionP:0.1 of the paper), and since~$f\mapsto f^\star$ is linear on~$\msA$,
\begin{align}
\nonumber
\mcE(f^\star_n-f^\star_m)=&\ \widehat\boldsymbol\mssE_\pi\big({(f_n^\star-f_m^\star) \circ\mathrm{em}}\big)
\\
\nonumber
=& \int \boldsymbol{\mathsf{\Gamma}}^\mbfs\paren{\sum_i s_i (f_n-f_m)({\,\cdot\,}_i)}_{(\mbfs,\mbfx)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\widehat\boldsymbol\nu_\pi(\mbfs,\mbfx)
\\
\nonumber
=& \int\!\!\!\!\!\int \sum_i s_i \mathsf{\Gamma}(f_n-f_m)_{x_i} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\nu(\mbfx)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi(\mbfs)
\\
\nonumber
=& \int \sum_i s_i \int \mathsf{\Gamma}(f_n-f_m)_{x_i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\nu(x_i)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\pi(\mbfs)
\\

=&\ \mssE(f_n-f_m) \,\mathrm{.}
\end{align}
Together with Lemma~(l:SimpleTridLp of the paper), the equality in~(equation eq:l:DomainCylinderF:1 of the paper) shows that~$\left(f_n^\star\right)_n$ is $\mcE^{1/2}_1$-fund\-amental.
As a consequence of Lemma~(l:SimpleTridLp of the paper)(i:l:SimpleTridLp:3 of the paper) there exists~$\lim_{n} f_n^\star= f^\star$, thus~$f^\star\in\msD(\mcE_\pi)$ by closability of~$(\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi))$.
The independence of~$\mcG_\pi(u)$ from the representatives~$\tilde{f_i}$'s is straightforward.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190407+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_cd8b3fd8a8f4ae722c7b30ce5ede1b8d61ec46e770d6d666a20852c38aba2023","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle, but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle. The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group which can be computed as isomorphic to the group where corresponds to an even number of twists, and to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:09:15.295467+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdae9cc92bbf3f2a2943670b41491a4758ca78aa99b5ab057a5ef4274d36139d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop bvp of arXiv:2411.05441, 'Sticky diffusions on star graphs : characterization and It\^o formula'] For every $\delta > 0$ and $f \in \bigoplus_{i=1}^N C_b([0,\delta))$, with $f_i(0) = f_j(0)$ for all $1 \leq i,j \leq N$, there is a unique $u \in \bigoplus_{i=1}^N C^2([0,\delta])$ such that
 \begin{equation}
  \begin{cases}
   L_i u_i(x) = f_i(x) \quad & \textnormal{for all } x \in (0, \delta), \, 1 \leq i \leq N, \\
	\eta L u (\mathsf{v}) - \sum_{i=1}^N \rho_i {u_i}'(0) = 0, \\
	u_i(\delta) = 0 \quad & \textnormal{for all } i \in \{1,\dots, N \}, \\
	u_i(0) = u_j(0) \quad & \textnormal{for all } i,j \in \{1,\dots, N \},
  \end{cases}
 \end{equation}
 given by
 \[
  u_i(x) = - \frac{\kappa_i  \alpha_i(x)}{\alpha_i(0)} - \beta_i(x) \quad \textnormal{for all } 0 \leq x \leq \delta,
  \]
  where
  \begin{align*}
  \kappa_i & = \left (\eta f(\mathsf{v}) - \sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\rho_j(\beta_1(0) - \beta_j(0))}{ \alpha_j(0)} \right ) \left (\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\rho_j}{\alpha_j(0)} \right )^{-1} + \beta_1(0) - \beta_i(0) \\
  \alpha_i(x) & = \int_x^\delta \exp \left (-\int_0^y \frac{2b_i(z)}{\sigma_i^2(z)} dz \right) dy \\
  \beta_i (x) & = \int_x^\delta \left ( \int_0^y \frac{2 f(z)}{\sigma_i^2(z)} \exp \left (\int_0^z \frac{2b_i(s)}{\sigma_i^2(s)} ds  \right) dz \right ) \exp \left (-\int_0^y \frac{2b_i(z)}{\sigma_i^2(z)} dz \right) dy
 \end{align*}
 for all $1 \leq i \leq N$.
 Furthermore, we have 
 \[
  \max_{1 \leq i \leq N} \max_{x \in [0,\delta]} \left \lvert u_i''(x) \right  \rvert = O(1) \quad  \textnormal{as } \delta \downarrow 0,
 \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.097667+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdd5f54e5bdf05094dcfb32b770057456e8982935a922cb313566d05d62f9dba","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Uniform local bound for zero-truncated Poisson sums) of arXiv:2604.26298, 'The Expiring Coupon Collector\\ Sliding-Window Surjection Flux and Rare-Entry Laws'] Let \(N\ge2\), \(m\ge N+1\), and let \(\tau=\tau_{N,m}>0\) be the unique
solution of
\[
        \frac{\tau}{1-e^{-\tau}}=\frac{m}{N}.
\]
Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_N\) be iid zero-truncated Poisson variables with parameter
\(\tau\):
\[
        \Pbb(D_i=k)=\frac{\tau^k}{k!(e^\tau-1)},\qquad k\ge1.
\]
Write
\[
        \mu_\tau=\Ebb D_i=\frac{\tau}{1-e^{-\tau}},
        \qquad
        \sigma_\tau^2=\Var(D_i),
        \qquad
        B=N\sigma_\tau^2.
\]
Assume \(0<\tau\le C_0\log N\). If \(B\to\infty\), then
\[
        \Pbb(D_1+\cdots+D_N=m)
        =
        \frac{1+o(1)}{\sqrt{2\pi B}},
\]
uniformly in this range. Consequently, for some constants \(c,C>0\),
depending only on \(C_0\),
\[
        \Pbb(D_1+\cdots+D_N=m)\ge c\,m^{-C}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(N\). If \(B\) is bounded, the same polynomial
lower bound still holds.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The conditioning events have positive probability.","The counterexample construction is reported, rather than proved within this record."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdd80b44a9454466067d131fab9489ca2a0e9f1127b0248a98cd8979f501f40a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the boundary and condensation part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Use Janson's balls-in-boxes setting with weights w_j, generating function Phi, radius rho, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), nu = lim_{t up to rho} Psi(t), m/n -> lambda, pi the tilted law at tau = rho when lambda >= nu, and N_d the number of boxes with d balls. In the two regimes not covered by the finite-variance mean-conditioning theorem, (c) lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and (d) lambda > nu, the natural analogue of the Gaussian limit has variance sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d). In (d) the constraint is absorbed by the condensate rather than by the bulk. The record asserts that this analogue holds under regular variation of the tail, by the argument of Thevenin's Theorem 6.7 in case (d), and fails in general. The failure rests on two constructions, Theorems A and B of the companion memo on Problem 20.2. Theorem A is a subcritical law conditioned at lambda = 1 > nu, that is, sum of the xi_i equal to n-1, for which (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) converges to a non-degenerate two-point law. Theorem B is a law with nu = 1 and sigma^2 = infinity, conditioned at lambda = 1, for which (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) converges to a mixture of two Gaussians. Assuming those two theorems, a Gaussian limit for the box counts in regimes (c) and (d) does not hold without a further regularity condition on the tail. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.037616+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cddf33c08cd90b9aef303fb27df6681c9ebd7af642b83aea8a737b6be7011ba1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 23 (Vertex condition) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The structure satisfies the \emph{vertex condition}
\textup{(V)} if there is $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ such that for
every active orbit $O$ and both of its sites $z\in O$,
\[
\varepsilon\,\mathcal W\bigl[\varphi_O,\,s(z;\cdot)\bigr](\gamma)>0
\qquad\text{for all }\gamma\in(0,1).
\]
Equivalently, since
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma}
\left(\frac{\varphi_O}{s_z}\right)
=\frac{\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s_z]}{s_z^{2}},
\qquad s_z>0,
\]
each ratio $\varphi_O(\gamma)/s(z;\gamma)$, $z\in O$, is strictly
monotone in $\gamma$, in the same direction for all orbits and both
orbit sites. Only these $2r$ scalar ratios
enter the theorem below, and the condition involves only scalar
functions of $\gamma$.

Two remarks on the shape of \textup{(V)}. First, it is stated
relative to the orbit representatives fixed once and for all in
Section~\ref{subsec:inherited-structure}: reversing the
representative of an orbit replaces $\mathbf d_O$ by
$-\mathbf d_O$, hence $\varphi_O$ by $-\varphi_O$ and both of that
orbit's Wronskians by their negatives. The genuinely invariant
content of \textup{(V)} is therefore the \emph{intra-orbit}
requirement that the two Wronskians of a given orbit share a sign;
the common value of $\varepsilon$ across orbits is a normalisation.
That it is always achievable is worth stating precisely: the choice
of representative is made \emph{independently in each orbit}, and
reversing it in a single orbit $O$ sends
$\mathbf d_O\mapsto-\mathbf d_O$,
$\varphi_O\mapsto-\varphi_O$, hence
$\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s(z;\cdot)]\mapsto
-\mathcal W[\varphi_O,s(z;\cdot)]$ at both $z\in O$ and leaves every
other orbit untouched. So if each orbit separately has a constant
Wronskian sign, the $r$ signs can be aligned one orbit at a time.
The substantive hypothesis is thus the intra-orbit one; the global
$\varepsilon$ follows. Second, and
consequently, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:vertex-sign} is
orientation-independent, since only the product
$\varepsilon\cdot\operatorname{sgn}[\mathbf d_O]_z$ appears there,
and that product is unchanged by a reversal.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is consistent","T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)","T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378582+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_cde8bcbf7d8ce7708f2314743185825fb5c4235f909300f46e471371d1a885c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A increasing and depending on finitely many coordinates","product measure with a common density p","for general events use the Margulis-Russo form with signed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543078+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce028eff08f7ef08cc636b492788f905d03b4c3fa8e4ee1b14f0bc0ea2dcd3a1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an INCREASING event depending on the states of a FINITE set E of edges, and let P_p be the product measure with density p. Equivalently the derivative is the TOTAL INFLUENCE. The monotonicity hypothesis matters: for a general event the correct statement is the Margulis-Russo formula d/dp P_p(A) = sum_e [ P_p(A with e open) - P_p(A with e closed) ], whose summands can be negative and which reduces to Russo's formula exactly when A is increasing. Russo's formula is the bridge from influence estimates - Kahn-Kalai-Linial, Talagrand, Friedgut-Kalai - to SHARP THRESHOLDS: a lower bound on the total influence of order log(1/(p(1-p))) forces P_p(A) to rise from eps to 1 - eps over a parameter window of width O(1/log n). {"assumptions":["The stated published minimum-location, tail, and limit theorems apply to this Poisson branching walk."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363927+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce056cd6340bc4912f6868fe54fad0f2450076e2feff0e1ef5d3b6511feace21","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the recursion is integrated exactly against two published closed-form values as a control] This is the campaign answer to Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1; layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. Let e be the base of the natural logarithm. There is a constant C_star in (0,infinity) such that bar_ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> C_star and ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> (1-exp(-1/e)) C_star. More precisely, if M_star denotes the distributional limit of M_k-[k/e+(3/(2e))log k] furnished by the cited branching-random-walk minimum theorem, then C_star=E[exp(-M_star)]. In particular both tails have order exp(-k/e) k^(-3/(2e)). The proof uses Addario-Berry and Ford's Poisson-Dirichlet branching random walks, Annals of Applied Probability 23 (2013), Theorems 1.1-1.2, and Aidekon's Convergence in law of the minimum of a branching random walk, Annals of Probability 41 (2013), as stated in the record. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.285568+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce2854bc46715b64a84e17e7e82c740cce538870a762eb52c14617533264e705","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21551, '\bf Sparse Separable Factor Analysis in the Complex Domain with an Application to Local Fi'] For $j=1,\ldots,d$, let $\Lambdab_j\in\CC^{p_j\times k_j}$ denote the true loading matrix and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ denote its estimate. Define the orthogonal projectors onto their column spaces by
\begin{align*}
  \Pb_j
  &=
  \Lambdab_j
  \left(
    \Lambdab_j^\star\Lambdab_j
  \right)^+
  \Lambdab_j^\star,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\Pb}_j
  =
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \left(
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \right)^+
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star,
\end{align*}
where $+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. The null-space projection error is
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  \left\|
    \left(
      \Ib_{p_j}-\widehat{\Pb}_j
    \right)
    \Pb_j
  \right\|_F^2.
  
\end{align}
Let
\begin{align*}
  r_j
  &=
  \operatorname{rank}(\Lambdab_j),
  \qquad
  \widehat{r}_j
  =
  \operatorname{rank}(\widehat{\Lambdab}_j),
  \qquad
  r_{\min,j}
  =
  \min(r_j,\widehat{r}_j).
\end{align*}
Denote the principal angles between the column spaces of $\Lambdab_j$ and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ by
\begin{align*}
    0
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)1}
  \leq
  \cdots
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)r_{\min,j}}
  \leq
  \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{align*}
Then,
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  r_j-r_{\min,j}
  +
  \sum_{i=1}^{r_{\min,j}}
  \sin^2\left(\theta_{(j)i}\right),
  
\end{align}
where the sum \eqref{eq:appendix-null-err-proj-angle} is interpreted as zero when $r_{\min,j}=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega open in R^n","a^{ij} = a^{ji}, b^i, c real functions on Omega","lambda|xi|^2 <= a^{ij} xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for uniform ellipticity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.147082+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations","id":"claim_ce331292e9dfb7e46eae58cc677d147b6511a99448713cb6fd049abdfc239c02","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega in R^n be open. A nondivergence-form operator is Lu = sum_{i,j} a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + sum_i b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} real (symmetry is no loss because D_{ij}u is symmetric) and b^i, c real. L is elliptic at x if the matrix (a^{ij}(x)) is positive definite; lambda(x) denotes its smallest eigenvalue. L is uniformly elliptic with constants 0 < lambda <= Lambda if lambda|xi|^2 <= sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for all x (a.e. x for measurable coefficients) and all xi in R^n. Sign convention: here L = +Laplacian when (a^{ij}) = I, b = 0, c = 0, so the maximum principle concerns Lu >= 0 and the favorable sign of the zeroth-order coefficient is c <= 0 (the opposite of the divergence-form convention -div(A grad u) + c u with c >= 0). A classical solution of Lu = f is u in C^2(Omega) with Lu = f pointwise; a strong solution is u in W^{2,p}_loc(Omega) for some 1 <= p <= infinity with Lu = f almost everywhere. If the a^{ij} are C^1 (or Lipschitz), a^{ij} D_{ij} u = D_i(a^{ij} D_j u) - (D_i a^{ij}) D_j u rewrites L in divergence form; for merely measurable a^{ij} the two forms are different theories (De Giorgi-Nash-Moser for divergence form, Krylov-Safonov for nondivergence form).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.746327+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce401aa64737a416098d32fd1fee2eeb8a1914d03a12deebec6ff992c91040bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (Frankenstein matching) of arXiv:2605.02499, '2605.02499'] Let $I \subseteq [N]$. For any $C \in \varSigma_I^R$, any $\alpha,\beta,\gamma \in [N]$ with $\alpha \neq \beta \leq \gamma \neq \alpha$, there exist two permutations 
$\sigma^\downarrow,\sigma^\uparrow$ on $\tilde{I} = I \cup \{\beta,\gamma\}$ and a bijection
$f:\{\downarrow,\uparrow\} \to \{\downarrow,\uparrow\}$ such that, denoting 
\[
\onintminus{\alpha}{\beta}{\gamma}^{(v,1)}(C)=\longtilde{C}_{\tilde{I}}^{(v,1)}, \qquad
   \onintminus{\alpha}{\beta}{\gamma}^{(v,2)}(C)= \longtilde{C}_{\tilde{I}}^{(v,2)},
   \qquad v \in \{\downarrow,\uparrow\},
\]
the sets
\[
\widehat{C}^{\ddownarrow}_{\tilde{I}}
   \coloneqq \longtilde{C}^{(\downarrow,1)}_{\tilde{I}}
   \cup \sigma^\downarrow\!\bigl(\longtilde{C}^{f(\downarrow),2)}_{\tilde{I}}\bigr),
\qquad
\widehat{C}^{\uuparrow}_{\tilde{I}}
   \coloneqq \longtilde{C}^{(\uparrow,1)}_{\tilde{I}}
   \cup \sigma^\uparrow\!\bigl(\longtilde{C}^{(f(\uparrow),2)}_{\tilde{I}}\bigr),
\]
are both $R$-cylinders, and we refer to them as \emph{Frankenstein cylinders}. Moreover, these two cylinders contain the same number of $R$’s as $C$, except in the following cases:

\begin{enumerate}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.333168+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce670b13671e47792346799c4d9c36f0f335b9c93728f51c70d8c7f3484183c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:lipschitz of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty domain. We call $\Omega$ a (strongly) \textit{Lipschitz domain} if $n=1$ or if for every $x\in \partial\Omega$, there is an open neighborhood $U_x \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ around $x$, an orthogonal matrix $O_x \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and a Lipschitz function 
    $\phi_x: \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\to \mathbb{R}$ with 
    \begin{align*}
       O_x (U_x\cap \Omega) = \{(\xi,y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times \mathbb{R}~|~ y < \phi_x(\xi) \}\cap O_x(U_x).
    \end{align*}

    
    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty, bounded Lipschitz domain, and let $\Omega_w,\Omega_h\subset \Omega$ be two disjoint, non-empty Lipschitz domains. If 
    $\overline{\Omega}=\overline{\Omega_w\cup \Omega_h}$, we call $(\Omega,\Omega_w,\Omega_h)$ a \textit{Lipschitz interface triple} with interface $\gamma.$ 
    In this case, we set
    $$\Gamma_w  \coloneq  \partial\Omega\backslash\partial\Omega_h, ~~\Gamma_h \coloneq \partial\Omega\backslash\partial\Omega_w,~~ \gamma \coloneq  \partial\Omega_w\backslash\overline{\Gamma_h} = \partial\Omega_h\backslash\overline{\Gamma_w}.$$
    Furthermore, we denote by $\nu_w,\nu_h$ the unit outer normal vectors on $\Gamma_w,\Gamma_h$, which exist almost everywhere due to Rademacher's Theorem for $n\geq 2,$ and trivially everywhere in the case $n=1.$

    
Our assumptions on $(\Omega,\Omega_w,\Omega_h)$ are weaker than the assumptions imposed in  [ines,zuazualongtime].

    \item Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a non-empty Lipschitz domain, and let $\Gamma\subset \partial\Omega$ be a non-empty, relatively open subset of the boundary.
    We call $(\Omega,\Gamma)$ an \textit{admissible} Lipschitz pair, if there exists some domain $\Tilde{\Omega}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ such that 
    $$(\Omega\cup \Gamma\cup \Tilde{\Omega}, \Omega, \Tilde{\Omega})$$ is a Lipschitz interface triple with interface $\Gamma$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496825+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce8217e70fdb06c744eabae51c069fc0b750d8aec4ee06dee28df6c628b24330","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 (Conditional first-break law and moments) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level from

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.513826+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cebac43e37aab5fd3a6ff3c520945d3e8cb4b923d1a12460d55a12c8c1761f6a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn H marginal of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] The locally commuting n chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa$ is a compatible family of measures $\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}$ on $n$ tuples of continuous non-self-crossing curves $\left(\eta^{(1)}, \eta^{(2)},\ldots,\eta^{(n)}\right)$ for all simply connected domain $\Omega$ with $\left(z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)$, and $\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)$ as above that satisfy additionally the conditions below. 

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Conformal invariance}: If $\varphi: \Omega \rightarrow \Omega^{\prime}$ is a conformal map fixing 0, then the pullback measure
$$
\varphi^* \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega^{\prime} ; \varphi\left(z_1\right), \varphi\left(z_2\right),\ldots,\varphi\left(z_n),\varphi(u)\right)\right)}^{\left(\varphi\left(U_1\right), \varphi\left(U_2\right),\right)}=\left(\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}\right) .
$$

Therefore, it suffices to describe the measure when $\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)=\left(\mathbb{H}; z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n,0\right)$.
We can extend our definition to arbitrary simply-connected domain $\Omega$ with a marked interior point $u$ by pulling back via a conformal equivalence $\phi:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ sending $u$ to $0$.

\item
\textbf{Domain Markov property}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1, x_2,\ldots,x_n\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots, U_n\right)}$ and we parametrize $\gamma^{(j)}$ by their own capacity in $\mathbb{H}$. Let $\mathbf{t}=\left(t_1, t_2,\ldots,t_n\right)$, such that $t_j$ is a stopping time for $\gamma^{(j)}$ and $\gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}$ is contained in the interior of $U_j$. Let
$$
\tilde{U}_j=U_j \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad \tilde{\gamma}^{(j)}=\gamma^{(j)} \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad j=1,2,\ldots,n; \quad \tilde{\Omega}=\mathbb{H} \backslash\left(\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}\right) .
$$

Then conditionally on $\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup  \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}$, we have
$$
\left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}, \tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}, \ldots, \tilde{\gamma}^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\tilde{\Omega} ; \gamma_{t_1}^{(1)}, \gamma_{t_2}^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma_{t_n}^{(n)}\right)}^{\left(\tilde{U}_1, \tilde{U}_2, \ldots,\tilde{U}_n\right)} .
$$

\item \textbf{Absolute continuity with respect to independent SLE($\kappa$)}:
 In $\mathbb{H}$-uniformization, let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n)\right.}$. 

We assume that there exist smooth functions $b_j: \mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where the chamber: $$\mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u)=\left\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{H} \mid x_1<x_2<\ldots<x_n, u \in \mathbb{H} \right\}$$ 
such that the capacity parametrized Loewner driving function $t \mapsto \theta_t^{(j)}$ of $\gamma^{(j)}$ satisfies
\begin{equation} 
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{~d} x_{j}(t)=\sqrt{\kappa} \mathrm{d} B_{j}(t)+b_j\left(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t),u\right) \mathrm{d} t \\
\mathrm{~d} x_{k}(t)=\frac{2}{x_{k}(t)-x_{j}(t)} \mathrm{d} t,  k\neq j
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $B_{j}$ is one-dimensional standard Brownian motion. 

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.167126+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cec6261eff7687e8f0ee5cb35fe0595b337ea131dee3666a40bb962b51879ea8","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Matrix concentration inequalities) of arXiv:2608.22595, 'Sparse Additive Off-Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning with Potentially Limited '] Let \(p_1,p_2\geq1\) and write \(D=p_1+p_2\).

\begin{itemize}
\item
Let \(\{\boldsymbol{Z}_j\}_{j=1}^m\) be independent, mean-zero
random matrices of dimension \(p_1\times p_2\). Suppose that
\(\|\boldsymbol{Z}_j\|_2\leq R\) almost surely, and define
\[
\nu^2
=
\max\left\{
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb{E}
\left(
\boldsymbol{Z}_j\boldsymbol{Z}_j^\top
\right)
\right\|_2,
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb{E}
\left(
\boldsymbol{Z}_j^\top\boldsymbol{Z}_j
\right)
\right\|_2
\right\}.
\]
Then, for any \(u>0\),
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{Z}_j
\right\|_2
>
\sqrt{2\nu^2\{u+\log D\}}
+
\frac{2R}{3}\{u+\log D\}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]
In particular, if \(\nu^2\leq mR^2\), then
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{Z}_j
\right\|_2
>
R\sqrt{2m\{u+\log D\}}
+
\frac{2R}{3}\{u+\log D\}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]

\item Let \(\{\boldsymbol{X}_j,\mathcal{F}_j\}_{j=1}^m\) be an adapted
sequence of random matrices of dimension \(p_1\times p_2\) satisfying
\(\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{X}_j\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1})
=\boldsymbol{0}\). Suppose that
\(\|\boldsymbol{X}_j\|_2\leq R_j\) almost surely, where
\(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) are deterministic. Then, for any \(u>0\),
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{X}_j
\right\|_2
>
\sqrt{
8\{u+\log D\}
\sum_{j=1}^m R_j^2
}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]
In particular, if \(R_j\leq R\) for all \(j\), then
\[
\Pr\left[
\left\|
\sum_{j=1}^m\boldsymbol{X}_j
\right\|_2
>
R\sqrt{8m\{u+\log D\}}
\right]
\leq
\exp(-u).
\]
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:46:25.368429+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cecaf155eb2c5db710fb3c1b6c45085b2515af8e32c50e6737304427803639ed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:convbls of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Consider a bounded simply-connected domain $D$ and sequence $(\widetilde D_m)_{m\geq 1}$ of approximating metric graphs via the lattice $\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{Z}^2$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.440231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cece4f2611afaaf20370001e0626301bb0096e2f920ab068ef79865cb50b5521","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 146 (Response presentation and response congruence) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] A \emph{response presentation} is a family
\[
 \mathfrak R
 =\bigl(X,(\mathsf Y_\alpha,\mathcal U_\alpha,R_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}\bigr),
\]
where $X$ is a set, each $(\mathsf Y_\alpha,\mathcal U_\alpha)$ is a complete
Hausdorff uniform space, and
$R_\alpha:X\to\mathsf Y_\alpha$ is a map.  No topology or uniformity is
assumed on $X$.

The \emph{joint response profile} is
\[
 \mathbf R:X\longrightarrow
 \mathsf Y:=\prod_{\alpha\in A}\mathsf Y_\alpha,
 \qquad
 \mathbf R(x):=(R_\alpha(x))_{\alpha\in A}.
\]
Two candidates are \emph{response-equivalent} if
\[
 x\sim_{\mathfrak R}y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathbf R(x)=\mathbf R(y).
\]
Write $X_{\mathfrak R}:=X/\!\sim_{\mathfrak R}$.  The induced injective map
\[
 \iota_{\mathfrak R}^0:X_{\mathfrak R}\longrightarrow\mathsf Y
\]
is called the \emph{response profile embedding}.  The initial uniformity on
$X_{\mathfrak R}$ induced by its coordinate responses is the
\emph{response-generated uniformity}; its topology is the
\emph{response-generated topology}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:01:01.740618+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cecfdcfe12e4ddd370526d20a2147db4cb20caa0a79caf88feb34ff3846a79fd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2609.00163, 'Decompositions and diagrams of symplectic surfaces in Weinstein domains'] Let $\mathcal{T}=(H_1,H_2,H_3;\tau_1, \tau_2,\tau_3)$ be the spine of a $b$-bridge bisection with divides and consider $\hat\phi_{i,i+1}$ be the pointed mapping class group of the tangle $\tau_i$. Let $\tau'_1$, $\tau'_2$, $\tau'_3$ be ($b+1$)-stranded braided tangles corresponding to the pointed monodromies:
\[\hat\phi'_{12}=ATB, ~ \hat\phi'_{23}=\hat\phi_{23}, \text{ and } \hat\phi'_{31}=\hat\phi_{31}, \text{ or }\]
\[\hat\phi'_{12}=\hat\phi_{12}, ~ \hat\phi'_{23}=\hat\phi_{23}, \text{ and } \hat\phi'_{31}=AT^{-1}B,\]
where $A,B$ are pointed mapping class group elements, $\hat\phi_{12}=AB$ or $\hat\phi_{31}=AB$, and $T$ is a positive half-twist involving the $(b+1)$-st puncture of the page. The resulting tuple of braided tangles $\mathcal{T}'=(H_1,H_2,H_3;\tau'_1,\tau'_2,\tau'_3)$ is called a \emph{positive braided perturbation} of $\mathcal{T}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.300287+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cee543072473629441b91ef51c460c6ff61a63e7f9c8c712992ffa41242103d2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 (Markov Kernels) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Fix $d\ge 1$. Let $I$ be any locally compact additive subgroup of $\mathbb R^d$, for example $I=\mathbb R^d$ or $I=A \mathbb Z^d$ where $A$ is some nonsingular $d\times d$ matrix. Let $\mathcal B(I)$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $I$. 
A \textit{Markov kernel} on $I$ is a continuous function from $I\to \mathcal P(I)$, where $\mathcal P(I)$ is the space of probability measures on $(I,\mathcal B(I))$ equipped with the topology of weak convergence of probability measures. 

Any Markov kernel $K$ on $I$ shall be written as $K(   x,A)$, which is identified with the continuous function from $I\to \mathcal P(I)$ given by $x\mapsto K(   x,\cdot)$. We denote by $\mathcal M(I)$ the space of all Markov kernels on $I$.

We equip $\mathcal M(I)$ with the weakest topology under which the maps $T_{f,   x}:\mathcal M(I)\to \mathbb R$ given by $$K\stackrel{T_{f,   x}}{\mapsto}  \int_I f(   y)\;K(   x,\mathrm d   y)$$ 
are continuous, where one varies over all $x\in I$ and all bounded continuous functions $f:I\to \mathbb R$. This topology endows $\mathcal M(I)$ with a Borel $\sigma$-algebra which allows us to talk about random variables taking values in the space of Markov kernels. For $   a\in I$ define the translation operator $\tau_a:\mathcal M(I)\to \mathcal M(I)$ by $(  \tau_{   a} K)(   x,A):= K(x+   a,A+   a)$ which is a Borel-measurable map on this space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.014637+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cef10872bc2f7d729fa12f1c6c789e180896bd4785f1feb1ccccd89e8218c046","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] A limiting point \(\xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T}\) is \emph{based at \(q\)} with
respect to the limiting morphism \(\pi\) if
\(\pi_*\mu_t\rightharpoonup\delta_q\).  Such a \(q\) is unique when it
exists, and we denote it by \(q_\pi(\xi)\).  It is
\emph{Type-I based at \(q\)} if there is \(C_\xi<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \int_Xd_\eta(\pi(x),q)^2\,d\mu_t(x)\le C_\xi(T-t)
 \qquad\text{for every }0\le t<T.
\end{equation}
If \(q\in Y^{\rm rv}\) and \(\rho_q\) is a localized
squared-distance barrier from \cref{def:squared-distance-barrier},
compactness and the defining comparisons for \(\rho_q\) show that this
is equivalent to
\[
 \int_X\rho_q\circ\pi\,d\mu_t\le C'_\xi(T-t).
\]
For an arbitrary holomorphic map, qualitative basing alone need not
imply this rate.  For the semiample K\"ahler--Ricci flow considered here,
\Cref{lem:automatic-label} proves that every limiting point is based at
a unique point \(q_\pi(\xi)\) and is Type-I based there.  Thus
\eqref{eq:label-moment} is never an additional hypothesis below.  When
\(q_\pi(\xi)\in Y^{\rm rv}\), we simply say that \(\xi\) is based at
the regular value \(q_\pi(\xi)\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:54:57.594106+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf1899ac7f2a0792890e7dab7a934cca0e3e20ef171ae09356f899bc3c410e1f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:main-func of arXiv:2412.03415, 'Critical first passage percolation on random graphs'] For any pair of vertices $u\neq v \in [n]$, let $\mathscr{P}_n(u,v)$ denote the collection of all (self-avoiding) paths from $i,j$. Let $T_n(u,v) = \min_{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \mathscr{P}_n(u,v)} T(\boldsymbol{\pi})$ denote the optimal passage time between these two vertices and 
\[\mathscr{P}_{\opt}(u,v) = \left\{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \mathscr{P}_n(u,v): \boldsymbol{\pi} = \arg \min T(\boldsymbol{\pi}) \right\},\]
denote the collection of optimal paths. Let 
$H_n(u,v) = \min \set{|\boldsymbol{\pi}|: \boldsymbol{\pi} \in \mathscr{P}_{\opt}(u,v) },$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.318398+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf257d2018b486e542b6a241bbb27a5623950121b56546fec58f4024c3514fb4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:LMTparallel of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] {LandryMinskyTaylor2025_TransverseSurfacesAndPseudoAnosovFlows_PUB}}]
Let \(\varphi\) be a pseudo-Anosov flow on \(M\), and let \(S_{1}\) and \(S_{2}\) be two isotopic embedded subsurfaces in \(M\) which are almost transverse to \(\varphi\).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:38:17.786796+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf28243606e831a2e9ba0712be1708014cf6a9dc76261bf3a1eda2382265f35c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:theta_exp_properties of arXiv:2507.22577, 'A Mean-Field Theory of $\Theta$-Expectations'] The operator $\mathfrak{E}[\cdot|\mathcal{F}_t]$ satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{(Dynamic Consistency):} For any $0 \le s \le t \le T$, it holds that $\mathfrak{E}[\xi|\mathcal{F}_s] = \mathfrak{E}\big[\mathfrak{E}[\xi|\mathcal{F}_t] \big| \mathcal{F}_s\big]$.
    \item \textbf{(Monotonicity):} If $\xi_1, \xi_2 \in L^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$ satisfy $\xi_1 \ge \xi_2$, $P_0$-a.s., then $\mathfrak{E}[\xi_1|\mathcal{F}_t] \ge \mathfrak{E}[\xi_2|\mathcal{F}_t]$, $P_0$-a.s. for all $t \in [0,T]$.
    \item \textbf{(Failure of Sub-additivity):} The operator $\mathfrak{E}[\cdot]$ is generally not sub-additive. That is, there exist terminal conditions $\xi_1, \xi_2$ for which the inequality $\mathfrak{E}[\xi_1+\xi_2] \le \mathfrak{E}[\xi_1] + \mathfrak{E}[\xi_2]$ is strictly violated.
    \item \textbf{(Failure of Translation Invariance):} The property of translation invariance, $\mathfrak{E}[\xi+c] \neq \mathfrak{E}[\xi]+c$, holds if and only if the driver $G(t,x,y,z,\mu)$ is independent of its argument $y$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.852191+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf4e894bd3d610bee648403add7690d7b5bd18b2231ba45c128f662a40570b6c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] For every $e\in E$, define

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.879788+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf7ceb7b9f663dd6dd55750949d787415cc1e49ab811d669ae7147b6c3730041","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d:p-dir-structure of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let $p \in (1,\infty)$.
		We say that $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E}_p, \mathcal{F}_p, \Gamma_p)$ is a $p$-Dirichlet structure if it satisfies the following properties:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item			\textbf{Probability space}: $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ is a probability space and $\mathcal{F}_p$ is a subspace of $L^p(X,\mu)$ such that $\mathds{1}_X \in \mathcal{F}_p$.
			\item \textbf{Completeness:} 
			$\mathcal{E}_p$ is a semi-norm on $\mathcal{F}_p$ such that $\mathcal{F}_p$ is a Banach space when equipped with the norm $\norm{f}_{\mathcal{F}_p}=(\norm{f}_{L^p}^p+\mathcal{E}_p(f))^{1/p}$.
			\item \textbf{Homogeneity:} For all $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$ there exists a finite non-negative Borel measure $\Gamma_p \langle f \rangle$ on $X$ such that $\Gamma_p \langle f \rangle(X)= \mathcal{E}_p(f)$   and for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle \lambda f\rangle = |\lambda|^p \Gamma_p\langle f\rangle.
			\]
			\item \textbf{Absolute continuity of energy measure}:  For all $f \in \mathcal{F}_p$, we have $\Gamma_p \langle f \rangle \ll \mu$.
			\item \textbf{Sublinearity:} For every $f,g\in \mathcal{F}_p$ and $A\subset X$, 
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle f+g\rangle(A)^{\frac{1}{p}}\le \Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(A)^{\frac{1}{p}}+\Gamma_p\langle g\rangle(A)^{\frac{1}{p}}
			\]
			\item \textbf{Chain rule:} For all $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$, $g\in \Lip(\mathbb{R})$ with $g(0)=0$,  we have $g \circ f \in \mathcal{F}_p$ and
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle g\circ f\rangle  \le \left((\Lip_a[g] \circ f)(x)\right)^p   \,\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle.
			\]
			Note that the measure $\left((\Lip_a[g] \circ f)(x)\right)^p   \,\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle$ is well-defined due to the absolute continuity of energy measure; that is, this measure does not depend on the choice of $f$ from the $\mu$-a.e.~equivalence class.
			\item \textbf{Locality:} For every $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$ and any measurable  set $A\in \mathcal{X}$, if $f|_A=c$ $\mu$-a.e., then $\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(A)=0$. In particular, $\Gamma_p \langle \mathds{1}_X \rangle$ is the zero measure.
			\item \textbf{Weak lower semicontinuity:} For every $f\in L^p(X)$, and for any sequence of functions $(f_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\in \mathcal{F}_p$ such that $f_n\to f \in L^p(X)$ with $\sup_{i\in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{E}_p(f_i)<\infty$, then $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$ and
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle f \rangle(A)\le \liminf_{i\to \infty} \Gamma_p\langle f_i \rangle(A)
			\]
			for every measurable set $A\subset X$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M a local martingale with M_0 = 0","for 0 < p < 1: M continuous","for p >= 1: cadlag suffices","constants depend on p only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627451+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf80a57cbccec160cd5893a5f18cbdc60f4fa6097c1a6f73d35f5f00697e2593","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let M be a local martingale with M_0 = 0, let M^*_T = sup_{t <= T} |M_t| for a stopping time T, and let [M] be the quadratic variation. There are constants 0 < c_p <= C_p < infinity depending ONLY on p such that c_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ] <= E[ (M^*_T)^p ] <= C_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ]. The admissible range of p differs by regularity: for CONTINUOUS local martingales the two-sided bound holds for every 0 < p < infinity; for general cadlag local martingales it holds for every p >= 1, and the case 0 < p < 1 genuinely requires continuity (Davis' theorem covers p = 1 in the general case). In discrete time the same holds with [M]_n = sum_{k <= n} (M_k - M_{k-1})^2 the square function, for 1 <= p < infinity. The constants are UNIVERSAL in the sense of depending on p alone - not on the martingale, the filtration, the time horizon or the dimension - and they blow up as p decreases to 0 and as p increases to infinity; explicit admissible choices grow like p for the upper constant. For p = 2 the inequality is an identity with c_2 = C_2 replaced by the Ito isometry together with Doob's L^2 maximal inequality, which is the cheap case one should reach for first. [Burkholder (1973), Davis (1970), Burkholder-Davis-Gundy (1972); see Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Theorem IV.4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Little: f entire and nonconstant","Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:45:15.353295+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_cfb6b34b04c740458f4aa7f731e3fa6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions. If f is entire and transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:58:38.161580+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cfd0bd8fc84223ef4ba30d42db11a9e7a3d97f279eda0de71ebe346b63501a73","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:GwithSeeds of arXiv:2606.24793, '\LARGE Random sequential nearest-neighbor coloring on trees'] Let $\mathcal G$ denote the genealogical graph of the coloring process on $\mathcal{T}$ without seeds. Write the decomposition of $\mathcal G$ into its connected components as:
$$
\mathcal G = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} \mathcal{C}_i.
$$
Fix $M\geq 1$ and vertices $\tilde{s}_1, \ldots \tilde{s}_M \in \mathcal{T}$ chosen as seeds. Let $\tilde{\mathcal{G}}$ denote the genealogical graph constructed\footnote{In this coupled construction of $\mathcal G$ and $ \tilde{\mathcal{G}}$, we also require ties (when there are multiple possible ancestors) to be broken in the same way, see Section (sec:constructionW of the paper) for more details.} with the same i.i.d.\ sequence of arrival times $(\tau_v,\, v\in \mathcal{T})$ except that now $\tau_{\tilde{s}_j}=0$ for all $1\le j\le M$. Then the decomposition of $\tilde{\mathcal{G}}$ into connected components satisfies
$$
\tilde{\mathcal G} = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} \tilde{\mathcal{C}}_i \sqcup \bigsqcup_{j = 1}^M\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j,
$$
where 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $i\in I$, $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_i$ is an infinite oriented subtree of $\mathcal{C}_i$. In particular, we have $\mathop{dir} \tilde{\mathcal{C}}_i = \mathop{dir} \mathcal{C}_i$.

    \item For each $j\in \{1,\ldots, M\}$, $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$ is an oriented tree rooted at $\tilde{s}_j$. Moreover, 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For $v \in \tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$, $v \neq \tilde{s}_j$, the set $\tilde{D}(v)$ of descendants of $v$ in $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$ is finite with $\mathbb{E}[\sharp\tilde{D}(v) \mid \tau_v] < \infty$.
\item The component $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$ is infinite if and only if $\tilde{s}_j$ has infinite degree. Furthermore, we have 
$$
\mathbb{P}(\mbox{$\tilde{s}_j$ has infinite degree in $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$})=
\begin{cases}
    1 & \mbox{if $\{v\in \mathcal{T}, d(v,\tilde{s}_j)=\min_{i\le M} d(v,\tilde{s}_i)\}$ is infinite}\\
    0 & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{cases}.
$$
\end{enumerate}    
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.387907+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cfde59fe258dc90a0905f631a27d3f3cd24dfbc1d981f8c747ab9091a2e616cb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem quadratic of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Quadratic Recursion]

Let $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequence of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{i,j}\}_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n}$ be a double sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define 
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) = \sum_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n} {\bf A}_{i,j} x_{i}x_{j}.
$$
Suppose that ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is also permutation symmetric, i.e.,\xspace ${\bf A}_{i,j} = {\bf A}_{j,i}$, $\forall (i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n$. Then for $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $2 \leq t < \infty$,
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t} ~ \leq ~ 2 (32t)^{2} \cdot \left( \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\a+b+c=2 }} L^c \cdot \norm{ {\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t} \right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["consistency of the finite-dimensional distributions under permutation and marginalisation","the state space Polish (or otherwise inner regular by compacts); the theorem fails for general measurable spaces","the conclusion is on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781981+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cff4b22d3f4e9f129de820bfc924fd6ae8ae16e1c64314c11984e1f4a5a4588a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be an arbitrary index set and suppose that for every finite subset {t_1, ..., t_n} of T a probability measure mu_{t_1, ..., t_n} on R^n (or on S^n for a Polish space S with its Borel sigma-algebra) is given. Suppose the family is CONSISTENT: (i) permuting the indices permutes the measure correspondingly, and (ii) the marginal of mu_{t_1, ..., t_n, t_{n+1}} on the first n coordinates is mu_{t_1, ..., t_n}. Then there is a probability measure P on the product space S^T equipped with the PRODUCT sigma-algebra whose finite-dimensional marginals are exactly the given family, and P is unique. TWO LIMITATIONS, both routinely forgotten. FIRST, the topological hypothesis is essential: for general measurable spaces the theorem is FALSE, and there are consistent families with no extension (Andersen and Jessen); what is really needed is that the marginals be inner regular in a suitable sense, which Polish spaces provide. SECOND, the resulting measure lives on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra, every member of which is determined by countably many coordinates. When T is uncountable, sets such as {the path is continuous}, {sup_t X_t <= c}, or {the path is bounded} are therefore NOT measurable for that sigma-algebra, so the theorem does not by itself construct Brownian motion as a continuous process; it constructs a process with the right finite-dimensional laws, and a separate regularity theorem - Kolmogorov's continuity criterion - is needed to produce a modification with continuous paths. [Kolmogorov (1933); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.21, and Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 36]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:40:26.988214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d002b3d6292344a530d5a7cd8debf8a8a352948623be67e2f20bed1cd6a350c6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:comb-estimates of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Under the setup above, the following hold.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
			\item \textup{(Continuation resistance)}\; For every $0\leq j\leq n{-}1$, one has $R_j\leq 2\,L_{j+1}$, and hence $V_j\leq 2\,I_{j+1}\,L_{j+1}$.
			\item \textup{(Trunk currents)}\; The trunk currents satisfy $I_1\geq 1/(4B)$ and $I_{j+1}\geq I_j/(2B)$ for every $1\leq j\leq n{-}1$. Consequently, $I_n\geq(4B)^{-n}$.
			\item \textup{(Total voltage mass)}\; There exists $C_{\mathrm{comb}}>0$ depending only on $B$ and~$\alpha$ such that
			\[
			\sum_{u\in D_{w,n}}g(u)\leq C_{\mathrm{comb}}\,I_n\,L_n^2\,.
			\]
			\item \textup{(Spike contribution)}\; Let $a\colon D_{w,n}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $a(u)\geq -b$ for all~$u$, for some finite $b\geq 0$, and set $K\coloneqq 2+2b\,(C_{\mathrm{comb}}+1)$. If a vertex~$v$ in the first half of the terminal pipe~$P_w$ (at distance at least $L_n/2$ from the boundary) satisfies $a(v)\geq K\,L_n-b$, then
			\[
			\sum_{u\in D_{w,n}}g(u)\,a(u)\geq I_n\,L_n^2\,.
			\]
			\item \textup{(Exponential growth)}\; $I_n\,L_n^2\geq\lambda^n/4$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477019+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d007b509b76b2574e8db1cb4d99bb511beec50788f3846f5da7d43e190951280","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For two probability measures mu and nu on a measurable space (S, A), the total variation distance is d_TV(mu, nu) = sup over A in A of |mu(A) - nu(A)|, a number in [0, 1]. If mu and nu have densities f and g with respect to a common reference measure lambda (which always exists, for instance lambda = mu + nu), then d_TV(mu, nu) = (1/2) integral |f - g| d lambda = 1 - integral min(f, g) d lambda, and the supremum is attained at A = { f > g }. Equivalent characterisations: d_TV is half the supremum of |integral h d mu - integral h d nu| over measurable h with |h| <= 1; and by the coupling characterisation, d_TV(mu, nu) = min P(X not equal to Y) over all couplings (X, Y) with X distributed as mu and Y as nu, the minimum being attained by the maximal coupling. Convergence in total variation is strictly stronger than weak convergence (point masses at 1/n converge weakly to the point mass at 0 but stay at total variation distance 1). The normalisation matters: some texts use the un-halved integral |f - g| d lambda, which lies in [0, 2].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Boundedness of Omega is essential (the embedding is never compact on R^n, by translating a fixed bump), and for W^{1,p} rather than W_0^{1,p} some boundary regularity is needed so that an extension operator exists.","Compactness FAILS at the critical exponent q = p*, which is exactly the loss of compactness behind concentration phenomena in critical problems."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.870307+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Sobolev spaces","id":"claim_d00bdbb3a32698c4ecb614feccf503f1db25275537f989f81c44012bb8fa3418","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with C^1 boundary (or any bounded extension domain, for instance a bounded Lipschitz domain), let 1 <= p < n and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. Then the embedding of W^{1,p}(Omega) into L^q(Omega) is COMPACT for every q strictly less than p*. At the endpoint q = p* the embedding is continuous but NOT compact. For p = n the embedding into L^q is compact for every finite q, and for p > n the embedding into C^{0,gamma}(closure of Omega) is compact for gamma < 1 - n/p. For the space W_0^{1,p}(Omega) no boundary regularity is needed: boundedness of Omega suffices.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:05:52.388847+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d00cd60998521663f3f5cf5226ad3a85bbf6847bfd36b1d600b90477fa9faf4a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition pr:tracking of arXiv:2504.11107, 'An Invariance Principle for some\\% Reaction-Diffusion Equations with a Multiplicative Ran'] For every $T>0$ let $u=u^{(T)}$ denote the solution to the parabolic Anderson model,
	\begin{equation*}\left[\begin{split}
		&\partial_t u = \partial^2_x u + \mu u  + \sigma u\dot{W}
			\hskip.95in\text{on $(T\,,\infty)\times\mathbb{T}$},\\
		&\text{subject to }u(0)=w(T)\hskip.9in\text{on $\mathbb{T}$}.
	\end{split}\right.\end{equation*}

	$L=L(k\,,f\,,g)>0$ and

	\]

	\[
		w_T(t\,,x) = w(t\wedge\tau(T)\,,x),\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.413234+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d01e9fd6f5dc66be51d583a10eeae66e3e2da0fe0e97e13aeb3758562c676ade","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:qRacah_tilings of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] We put a probability measure on the set of all
	nonintersecting path ensembles. The measure depends on the
	geometry of the hexagon (parametrized by $(T,S,N)$), and
	on two parameters $q>0$ and $\kappa\in
	\mathbf{i}\mathbb{R}$.
	The
	probability weight of a nonintersecting path ensemble is
	proportional to
	\begin{equation}
		
		\prod_{\textnormal{holes in the path ensemble}} \mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}\bigl( x-\tfrac t2+1\bigr),
		\qquad
		\mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}(j) \coloneqq \kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}-\frac{1}{\kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}}.
	\end{equation}
	Here the holes are points $(t,x)$ such that $x\notin X(t)$,
	but $x$ satisfies the inequalities
	(equation eq:hexagon_constraints of the paper). In other words,
	holes are lozenges of the type
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding box.south),scale=.25]
		\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.
	For example, in (fig:tiling_and_path_picture of the paper), right, the holes are $(1,2),(2,1),(2,4),(3,0),(3,2),(3,5),(4,2),(4,3),(5,3)$.
	The probability weights are normalized so that the total probability of all path ensembles is $1$.
	We call the resulting probability measure the \emph{$q$-Racah measure} on nonintersecting path ensembles
	(equivalently, on lozenge tilings of the hexagon).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["edges are present independently with the same probability p (the binomial model; the uniform model G(n,m) has the analogous statement with m = (n/2)(log n + c))","the statement is about the window p = (log n + c)/n with c fixed as n grows","the Poisson approximation is for the count of isolated vertices; other small components are negligible in this window"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049186+00:00","domain":"random graphs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_d041dda48ec32c5f52986ec651884b81edb7100fb10f41b597a06330618dfc66","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the binomial random graph G(n,p) with p = (log n + c)/n for a fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with mean e^{-c} (the method of moments: the factorial moments of the count converge to those of the Poisson law), and the probability that G(n,p) is connected tends to exp(-e^{-c}) (Erdos and Renyi 1959, 1960). The obstruction to connectivity in this window is isolated vertices alone: P(G connected) - P(G has no isolated vertex) tends to 0. Consequently p = log n / n is a sharp threshold: for p = (1 - epsilon) log n / n the graph is disconnected with probability tending to 1 (with a growing number of isolated vertices), and for p = (1 + epsilon) log n / n it is connected with probability tending to 1. Below the threshold at p = c'/n with c' > 1 the graph already has a unique giant component but is disconnected.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.454439+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d08be800ce38b6c8a7a10ab540a5a4b1d20f6f05e1c362c05fa8a0caabf00983","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{no_atoms_bigger_than_p}
Let $f \in \Sym$ with $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f)} \ge 3$. 
For all $y \ne 0$, $f(y) < p$. 
\begin{proof}
We separate the proof into two cases, when $y=1$ and when $y \ne 1$. 
In the case where $y \ne 1$, 
\begin{align*}
q f(-y+2) + p f(-y)
&=  f_{X+Y}(-y+1) \\
&= f_{X+Y}(y-1) = q f(y) + p f(y-2) 
\ge qf(y). 
\end{align*}
Dividing both sides by $p$ and adding $f(y)$, 
\[
f(y) + \frac{q}{p} f(-y+2) + f(-y) \ge \frac{q}{p}f(y) + f(y) = \frac{1}{p}f(y) .
\]
Since $\frac{q}{p} < 1$ and the values $y$, $-y+2$, and $-y$ are distinct, the left-hand side of the preceding equation is strictly bounded above by $1$. 

Similarly, when $y=1$, we have 
\[
qf(-1) + pf(-3) 
= f_{X+Y}(-2) 
= f_{X+Y}(2)
= qf(3) + pf(1) 
\ge pf(1) 
\]
so that
\[
f(-1) + f(-3) \ge \frac{q}{p} f(-1) + f(-3) \ge f(1) . 
\]
Adding $f(1)$ to both sides, we see that 
\(
1 \ge f(1) + f(-1) + f(-3) \ge 2f(1)
\);
in particular $f(1) \le \frac{1}{2} < p$. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["S symmetric positive semidefinite","the feasible set is nonempty (it always is: the simplex)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:16:12.170261+00:00","domain":"portfolio optimization / covariance estimation","id":"claim_d0a23007d09157190578bc34001ca8ab56a2324c0cee39b19878ff5e75ad0f46","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \\times M$ matrix (a sample covariance) and consider the long-only minimum-variance problem $\\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ and $w \\ge 0$. Let $w^+$ be a solution and $\\delta \\in \\mathbb{R}^M$, $\\delta \\ge 0$, the Lagrange multipliers of the nonnegativity constraints ($\\delta_m > 0$ only where $w^+_m = 0$). THEOREM (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003). $w^+$ is also the UNCONSTRAINED minimum-variance solution (subject only to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$) for the modified covariance $$\\tilde S = S - \\delta \\mathbf{1}^T - \\mathbf{1}\\delta^T,$$ which is symmetric, positive semidefinite on the relevant set, and differs from $S$ by lowering the covariances of the constrained (excluded) assets with every other asset by $\\delta_m$ and their variances by $2\\delta_m$. Imposing the no-short constraint is therefore equivalent to shrinking the large entries of the sample covariance toward zero by data-determined amounts - which is why the constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when the true covariance would not call for it (\"why imposing the wrong constraints helps\"): it acts as a covariance-shrinkage estimator whose amount is chosen implicitly by the optimisation, without cross-validation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:57.241898+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0b62de897cafe9c48c9b76cbc0eb4900d251b6263e3d4bb48b1b09f2255b869","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem teoScaleFnBV of arXiv:2604.08889, 'Matrix Representations for Scale Functions of Spectrally Negative Lévy Processes with Rati'] Let $X$ be a L\'evy process as in (equation eqnXTrajectories of the paper), with $\sigma=0$ and $d>0$. Then, for any $x\geq 0$ and $q\geq 0$ such that $\psi'(\Phi_q)>0$ we have
\begin{equation}
W^{(q)}(x) = \frac{1}{\psi'(\Phi_q)} \Big( \mathrm{e}^{\Phi_q x} - \bm{\Psi}\, e^{\bm{G}x}\,\bm{\nu} \Big), \qquad x \ge 0,
\end{equation}where $\bm{G}: = \bm{T} + \bm{t}\,\bm{\Psi}$, $\bm{\nu}:=(\Phi_q \bm I - \bm{T})^{-1}\bm{t}$ with $\bm I$ the identity matrix.
The matrix $\bm{\Psi}$ is a solution to 
\begin{equation}
\bm{\Psi} \big( (\lambda + q)\bm{I} - d\bm{T} - d\,\bm{t}\,\bm{\Psi} \big) = \lambda\, \bm{\alpha}.
\end{equation}Finally, $\bm{\Psi}$ can be obtained as the limit of the recursive equation
\begin{equation}
\bm{\Psi}_n
:=
\Big(\frac{\lambda}{d}\bm{\alpha} + (\bm{\Psi}_{n-1}\bm{t})\bm{\Psi}_{n-1}\Big)
\left(\frac{\lambda + q}{d}\bm I - \bm{T}\right)^{-1},
\end{equation}with  $\bm{\Psi}_0=\bm{0}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:27:14.770837+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0b6e82947acdaa6207ad9a5f4fb17f906067384734709b6b1ee453f07e8619c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2608.22693, 'Uniformity of extremal behaviour along geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\Phi \in (0,1/10)$ and $p_1 \in (0,1)$. With $\mathcal{H}_n = ((\varepsilon_n / 2)^{1/c_1} \ZZ^2) \cap U$, for all $\beta >0$, there exist (random) $0<\varphi < \psi < \beta /20$ depending only on $U$ and $\beta$ such that we have the following for all $n \in \NN$ large enough. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.649386+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0b953cde21bb02b4b8e3d38e587b807a952d847c7a7db4d0208735c2b3b09c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\gamma_L=(L-1)/\ell$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label={\normalfont(\arabic*)}]
\item The discrete in space processes DITP (resp. DFTP) converge, with quantitative control,  when $L$ tends to infinity, in Skorohod topology towards the continuous-space piecewise deterministic Markov process CITP (resp. CFTP).
\item The processes DITP and DFTP are exponentially ergodic with invariant measures converging as $L$ tends to infinity to the unique invariant measures of the CITP and CFTP.
\item The invariant measures of CITP and CFTP have a positive mass at $\{0\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$ and  $\{\ell\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$.
\item Let us define for a Markov process with semigroup $P_t$ and invariant measure $\pi$ its mixing time as

\item[\normalfont (b)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CFTP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)(\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta)(1+\alpha^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.415432+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0bc6885220b19ef0261a17e934955948a8f3ad5abcf8d4193f62d44839b7f8f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 139 (Boundary generation versus evolutionary value compression) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Put
\[
 \mathscr S_T:=\overline{\mathcal G_T^0(\mathscr T_0)}
 ^{\,\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}}
\]
and assume that this closed terminal solver range is invariant under the
first-jet truncations.  Terminal generation and evolutionary value compression
are different requirements:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item terminal generation asks whether
$\mathcal G_T^0:\mathscr T_0\to\mathscr S_T$ is Cauchy-continuous for the
terminal-data topology;
\item evolutionary compression asks whether
$\pi_Y|_{\mathscr S_T}$ is injective and has a stable-causal inverse
for the inherited $\mathbb S_{\cP}^2$ value topology.
\end{enumerate}
These conditions concern different maps, and neither implication is assumed
without additional comparison hypotheses.  The following comparison is
sufficient for boundary generation to
imply evolutionary compression.  Suppose
\eqref{eq:terminal-to-jet} holds and there is a nondecreasing modulus
$\chi$ with $\chi(0)=0$ and $\lim_{r\downarrow0}\chi(r)=0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 d_{\mathscr T}(\xi,\eta)
 \le\chi\bigl(\|Y^\xi-Y^\eta\|_{\mathbb S_{\cP}^2}\bigr),
 \qquad \xi,\eta\in\mathscr T_0.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|Z^\xi-Z^\eta\|_{\mathbb H_{\cP}^2}
 \le(\omega\circ\chi)
       \bigl(\|Y^\xi-Y^\eta\|_{\mathbb S_{\cP}^2}\bigr),
\end{equation}
and the induced closed terminal solver range is value-process compressible by
\Cref{prop:nonlinear-solver-range-compression}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:32:58.366231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0bd827569040d5647978204537a30a1d9504aab10442edd8df16ffbabae68a0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 33 of arXiv:2506.20146, 'Parabolic Anderson Model in the Hyperbolic Space.
