{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db9918fbc671f11eee90cd6406606fa76cc6077e21fc89d28df52ffb173bfd87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 237 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,K>0$ and any sequence of $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$,
	\[
		\lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big) 
		= \lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\sym}(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big)
		= 0\,.
	\]

\begin{proof}
	We only prove that the first limit is zero, as the second limit is proved analogously.
	Suppose for contradiction that there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta$ for infinitely many $N$.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, there exists $C = C(\alpha,L,K) > 0 $ such that for sufficiently large $N$, $\mu(\cA_{N[K]}) \in \cP_4(\R,C)$.
Then, for infinitely many $N$, we have
	\[\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\in
		S_\delta 
		\equiv \Big\{ \mu \in \cP_4(\R,C) : \bbW_2(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta 
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_4(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_2$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric, hence also compact. Therefore
 we may find $\mu \in S_\delta$ and a subsequence $(N_j)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big) = 0\,.
	\]
	As noted in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, we have $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j[K]}) = \mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j})$: thus, since each $\cA_{N_j}$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, so is each $\cA_{N_j[K]}$. It follows by omitting finitely many $j$'s that we have
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_{N_j[K]},\mu)
	=\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big),
	\bbW_2\Big(
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\cP(\{\pm1\})
		\Big)
	\bigg\}\le\epsilon
	\]
for all $j$. Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip} of  $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$, this implies
	\[
		\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\,,
	\]
	which contradicts that $\mu \in S_\delta$.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

\[

\[
    \mathcal U(T,x)\coloneqq
    \sup_{\tau\leq T}\mathbf E_x^{\rm BM}
    \bigl[Z(T,x)-Z(T-\tau,B_\tau)\bigr]\, ,
\]
where the supremum is over stopping times for Brownian motion. Then, for every $T>0$,
\[
    R^{-(2-d/2)}\,u^{(R)}_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}
    \Longrightarrow

    \qquad\text{in }C_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)\, ,
\]
where the field on the left denotes the multilinear interpolation from $R^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^d$ of the values
$x/R\mapsto R^{-(2-d/2)}u_{\lfloor TR^2\rfloor}(x)$.

\item \underline{\textup{Dimension four.}}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]

$\alpha>2$, the fields $\bigl(u_{t_R}-\mathbb{E} u_{t_R}(0)\bigr)^{(R)}$ at the

\end{enumerate}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.222647+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbd0d5759a727d7538da5d3816a778ec74338db6f0b32984dc664b1154ebf1eb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 7 (Conditional unique limit at infinite time) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Let $F\colon[0,\infty)\times\Sigma\to\Sph^3$ be a smooth MIWF of a

\[
 \inf_{t>0}\min_{x\in\Sigma}|A_{F_t}^0(x)|^2\geq c_0,
\]
and, in addition, that
\begin{equation}
 
 \int_0^\infty\sqrt{-W'(r)}\dd r<\infty.
\end{equation}
Then there are positive Radon measures $\mu_\infty$ on $\Sigma$ and

\]
as $t\to\infty$, and $\lambda_\infty=\lVert\Var_\infty\rVert$.
Writing $W_\infty:=\lim_{t\to\infty}W(t)$, one also has
\[
 H_{\Var_\infty}^{\R^4}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:41:28.173115+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbd1dca3c8072440538682ff80e8b1c8dd300ad26fc38ad37f7c4074747b89bf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Costly steps of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The $i$th step of the REA is called a {\it costly step}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.041687+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbecbcb9b13f161904a3293a0fba4ae24ea22a3e38c1603cc1251089b13c41ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 34 (Finite spectral reduction) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] The reduction space, \emph{in symmetrised coordinates}, is exactly
the odd sector:
\begin{equation}
\widetilde V:=D^{-1}V = E_{\mathrm{odd}},
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
V = D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}} .

\end{equation}
The distinction matters: $D$ does not commute with $S$ unless
$p=q$, so $D\,E_{\mathrm{odd}}\neq E_{\mathrm{odd}}$ for a biased
walk --- consistently with the fact, noted above, that it is
$\widetilde\psi$ and not $\psi$ that is antisymmetric. The space
admits the canonical decomposition
\begin{equation}
\psi(\gamma)=\sum_{k\ \mathrm{even}} f_k(\gamma)\,\mathbf m_k,
\qquad
\mathbf m_k := D\,P_k\,D^{-1}\xi = D\,P_k\,\widetilde\xi,
\qquad
f_k(\gamma)=\frac{t}{1-\lambda_k t},
\quad t=1-\gamma .

\end{equation}
The directions $\mathbf m_k$ are nonzero and linearly independent.
As for canonicity, the symmetrised directions $P_k\widetilde\xi$ are
determined by $(\widetilde P,S,\widetilde\xi)$; their
original-coordinate images are determined by $(P,S,\xi)$ alone. For
the present irreducible tridiagonal $P$ the positive diagonal
symmetriser is unique up to an overall scalar --- the ratios
$D_{z+1}/D_z$ being fixed by the neighbour relations --- and the
conjugation $D P_k D^{-1}$ is unchanged under $D\mapsto cD$; so no
normalisation of the symmetriser need be fixed. In particular $\dim V = r$, and all $\gamma$-dependence is
carried by the elementary scalars $f_k$.

The notation is deliberate: these $\mathbf m_k$ are \emph{not} the
normal directions $\mathbf n_\nu$ of Section~\ref{sec:finite-reduction}.
There are $N$ of the latter, one per spectral mode, spanning a space
of dimension $r$ and therefore dependent; there are exactly $r$ of the
former, indexed by the even $k$ alone, and they are independent. Both
families span $V$, which is all the two routes are claimed to share.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726371+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dbf122d5a238489aa083fdb44f89336d4d034fb877e0be5e3ba3b1dc4f1ae3c4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:38:04.499179+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dbf7aaa35f7e7882659db6f1452b6e56db52b21249d6de5f1f3d3e0981fbf86f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lemstable of arXiv:2607.12459, 'Renormalisation of Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] {\bf [Invariance property for positive stable weights]}

Let $\gamma\in(0,1)$, and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be i.i.d.\ standard positive $\gamma$-stable random variables, with Laplace transform
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda Y_1}] = \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda^\gamma}, \qquad \lambda\geq 0.
\]
Then
\[ 
m^{-1/\gamma}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i \stackrel{d}{=}Y_1.
\]
Consequently, for every $\delta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\eta\in[0,\infty)$, the inhomogeneous random graph with connection functions
\[
g^{\neq}_\delta(x,y)=\delta xy, \qquad g^{=}_\eta(x)=\eta x,
\]
and i.i.d.\ standard positive $\gamma$-stable weights is invariant in distribution under the renormalisation transformation, provided the aggregated weights are rescaled by $m^{-1/\gamma}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:39:18.525250+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc11e62301d1ade0d5da2d00d1c4119cf841891445c8ea274c0bf2514720eca0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 42 (Sublevel regular neighborhoods) of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] Let $T$ be a finite triangulation of the fixed PL sphere $S^n$, let $L$

Then $C(L,T)$ is a nonempty, proper, full subcomplex of $T$, and its
$0$--$1$-level function is $f_{C(L,T)}=1-f_L$.  Moreover, for every

 \Phi_c:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.600084+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc256567fe2e9178ffc3e664d5f0a3ae4ec6240edbfaa03b19b5239356ad256f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition proposition duality of arXiv:2412.05064, '\textbf{Sample path central limit theorem for the occupation time of the voter model on a '] For any integer $m\geq 1$, $y_1, y_2,\ldots, y_m\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, $0\leq t_1\leq t_2\leq \ldots\leq t_m$, $\eta\in \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ and function $G$ from $\{0, 1\}^m$ to $\mathbb{R}$, we have

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:24:20.958267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc583376f4907edc43358a9d1e4dfe128de06c6b2625dcb77e8829361bcce0e9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2508.12951, '\textbf{On the central limit question for strictly stationary, reversible Markov chains}'] {\rm (Doukhan, Massart, and Rio)}.

strictly stationary sequence of random variables such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.845617+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc6b41a2e65e311eaddb446d8f516a18f90158f9f11f93d80d67fed31fc2a608","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 17 (Elliptical Brownian motions) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $\rho>0$ and let $\zeta\in\C$ with $0<|\zeta|\le\rho$.  Define
\begin{equation}
    
    \theta = \frac12\arg \zeta \qquad a = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho+|\zeta|)} \qquad b = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho-|\zeta|)}. 
\end{equation}
Then $a^2+b^2=\rho$ and $e^{2\i\theta}(a^2-b^2)=\zeta$, so that $(a,b,\theta)$ satisfy \eqref{eq.rho.zeta}.  This yields a bijective mapping
\begin{equation} \{(\rho,\zeta)\colon 0<|\zeta|\le\rho\}\mapsto\{(a,b,\theta)\colon a>b\ge 0, \theta\in[0,\pi)\}. \end{equation}
We may extend the definitions of $a,b$ to allow $\zeta=0$, in which case $a=b$; here $\theta$ is undefined.

Let $(X^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$, $(Y^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$. 
We define the general {\bf elliptical Brownian motion} $(W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$ by
	\[ W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(aX^N(t) + \i b Y^N(t)\right). \]
    Similarly, if $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(y(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are freely independent free semicircular Brownian motion, the {\bf free elliptical Brownian motion $(w_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$} is defined as
    \[ w_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(a x(t) + \i b y(t)\right). \]
In both cases, when $a=b$ (i.e.\ $\zeta=0$), all values of $\theta$ yield the same distribution for the right-hand-side, so we may take canonically $\theta=0$ in this case.

Note that the laws of $W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ and $w_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ are invariant under $a\mapsto-a$, $b\mapsto-b$, and $(a,b,\theta)\mapsto(b,a,\theta+\frac{\pi}{2})$.  It then follows from \eqref{eq.bijection} that $\rho>0$, $|\zeta|\le\rho$ paramaterize the laws of all possible elliptical Brownian motions.

To lighten notation we will often drop the subscripts $\rho,\zeta$ if there can be no confusion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.478187+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc7f92a47f72e853d6ed6052ff3725a3345f24c23d06c222b2e1bdf27fc0359c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 (Parametric weighted lattice-corner expansion) of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Let $U$ be a compact interval. For each $p\in U$, let $Z_p$ be a random vector supported by a fixed finite subset of $\Zz^d$, with masses that are positive and $C^{r+2}$ in $p$. Assume that the additive group generated by differences of support points is $\Zz^d$. Put
\[
 M_p(\lambda)=\Ee e^{\langle\lambda,Z_p\rangle}.
\]
Suppose there is a $C^{r+2}$ map $\lambda:U\to(0,\infty)^d$ satisfying
\[
 \nabla_\lambda\log M_p(\lambda(p))=0.
\]
Let
\[
 I(p)=-\log M_p(\lambda(p)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma(p)=\nabla_\lambda^2\log M_p(\lambda(p)).
\]
Let $w:\Zz_+^d\to\Rr$ be bounded and define
\[
 W(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}
 w(z)e^{-\langle\lambda(p),z\rangle}.
\]
For independent copies $Z_{p,1},\ldots,Z_{p,n}$, put $S_{n,p}=\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{p,i}$ and
\[
 \mathcal T_n(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}w(z)\Pp(S_{n,p}=z).
\]
Then, for $\varepsilon_n=n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{3r+6}$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n(p)
 =\frac{e^{-nI(p)}n^{-d/2}}
 {(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p)}}
 \left[W(p)+O_{C^r(U)}(\varepsilon_n)\right].
 
\end{equation}
If $r\ge1$ and $I'(p_0)\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n'(p_0)
 =n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}
 \left\{-I'(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}+o(1)\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
If in addition $W(p_0)\ne0$, this may equivalently be written with a relative factor $\{1+o(1)\}$. If $r\ge2$, $I'(p_0)=0$, $I''(p_0)>0$, and $W(p_0)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n''(p_0)
 =-I''(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}
 n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}\{1+o(1)\}.
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:44:17.356494+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc8d79cdfad071f103b813a93714ffa464bbbc293c34fada78829a7ab5351568","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:fullconf of arXiv:2608.23638, 'Replicable Conformal Prediction'] Consider full conformal prediction with the $1$-nearest-neighbor score, calibration size $n\\ge2$, and data law $P$ absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\\mathbb{R}^{2}$. For every nonendpoint cutoff $m\\in\\{1,\\dots,n\\}$, two independent runs satisfy $\\mathbb{P}[\\widehat\\mathcal{C}^{(m)}_\\mathcal{D}\\equiv\\widehat\\mathcal{C}^{(m)}_{\\mathcal{D}'}]=0$ (map equality read in the completed law); with any shared seed $U$ and measurable cutoff $M(U)$, the agreement probability equals $\\mathbb{P}[M(U)\\in\\{0,n{+}1\\}]$ exactly. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.472254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc8da34479eed0193cb85c7afb8490a75b07f1957905bfef8d21c6764d0d5b80","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 158 (Simultaneous lawwise realization) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let \(E\) be Polish, let \(Z:\Omega\to E\) be Borel, and for every

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.762070+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc96ab0096b4ab4b2d523e56aa43e2fe0ed5dd706bf86b4ec82101823b9237c6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:frechet of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Let $\phi: U \to V$ be a function between two finite-dimensional normed vector spaces $U$ and $V$ with norms $\left\lVert{\cdot}\right\rVert_U$ and $\left\lVert{\cdot}\right\rVert_V$ respectively.
     If it exists, the Fr\'echet derivative of $\phi$ at a point $u \in U$ is the linear operator $d\phi(u): U \to V$ such that
     \[ \lim_{\left\lVert{h}\right\rVert_U\to 0} \frac{\left\lVert{\phi(u + h) - \phi(u) - d\phi(u)[h]}\right\rVert_V}{\left\lVert{h}\right\rVert_U} = 0. \]

     We write $\frenorm{\cdot}$ for the operator norm between the two tangent spaces of a Fr\'echet derivative.
     \[ \frenorm{d\phi(u)} := \sup_{\left\lVert{h}\right\rVert_U = 1}\left\lVert{d\phi(u)[h]}\right\rVert_V.\]
     
    When $V = M_n(\mathbb R)$, then unless otherwise specified, we will take the norm on $V$ to be the normalized Schatten-2 norm $\left\lVert{\cdot}\right\rVert_V \gets \schnorm{\cdot}$.
    We may write $\frenorm[\to \infty]{d\phi(u)}$ to indicate that the norm on $V$ is taken to be the matrix operator norm.

When applying the Poincar\'e inequality, we may consider the Hilbert-Schmidt norm
\[
\left\lVert{d\phi(u)}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}(U,V)}^2
:=
\sum_{\alpha}\|d\phi(u)[e_\alpha]\|_{V}^2,\]
where $\{e_{\alpha}\}$ is any orthonormal basis of $U$.
The point $u$ where we evaluate the Fr\'echet derivative $d\phi(u)$ will often be implicit---for example, $d\phi$ or $\left\lVert{d\phi}\right\rVert$.","status":"unverified"}

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Local existence for the characteristic IVP}}. 
Recall that the classical solution is $C^{\infty}$ on $\twoargMrough{[\timefunction_0,0],[- \rightu,\leftu]}{0}$
and therefore induces $C^{\infty}$ data on the characteristic surfaces
$\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\leftubar}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}, \, \outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\moreinterestingu_1}{[\leftubar,0]}$; see Appendix~\ref{A:DATASSUMPTIONS}.
Then there exists a  
$\ubarlocal \in (\leftubar,0)$, depending on the data, such the characteristic data launch a unique $C^{\infty}$ solution
on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$,
and the change of variables map $(u,\ubar,x^2,x^3) \rightarrow (t,x^1,x^2,x^3)$
is a diffeomorphism from $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$
onto its image in Cartesian coordinate space.

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Continuation criteria for the characteristic IVP}}.

Assume the following: 
\begin{itemize}
	\item The assumptions of Theorem\,\ref{T:EXISTENCEUPTOCAUCHYHORIZONBYCONTINUATIONCRITERIA} hold.
	\item $\ubarboot < 0$.
	\item The ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the wave variables $\wavearray$, and the acoustic geometry variables $u, \, \chi$, etc. are classical solutions on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$. 
	\item The bootstrap assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold for $(\ubar,u) \in [\leftubar,\ubarboot)\times[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]$. 
\end{itemize}

Then there exists a $\Delta \in (0,|\ubarboot|)$ such that the ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the solution variables $\wavearray, \, u$, and all of the other geometric quantities defined throughout the article can be uniquely extended to a strictly larger region of the form $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot + \Delta)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$ on which all of the bootstrap
assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U open with lambda_1 > 0 on H^1_0(U) (e.g. U bounded, or bounded in one direction, or of finite measure)","g in L^2(U)","u the weak solution of the Dirichlet heat equation with u(0) = g","the equality case requires the infimum defining lambda_1 to be attained, e.g. U bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105957+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dccca23e6eedae7c488796bf4490a59edff019e1d479e546a6dbd3a3e781c655","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^n$ be open with $\\lambda_1=\\inf\\{\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2}^2/\\|v\\|_{L^2}^2:v\\in H^1_0(U),v\\ne0\\}>0$; this positivity holds in particular when $U$ is bounded, when $U$ is merely bounded in one direction, and when $U$ has finite measure. Let $u$ be the weak solution of $u_t=\\Delta u$ in $U\\times(0,\\infty)$, $u=0$ on $\\partial U\\times(0,\\infty)$, $u(0)=g\\in L^2(U)$. Then $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2(U)}\\le e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\|g\\|_{L^2(U)}$ for all $t\\ge0$. \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:30:50.719777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcd322992c63443755363911b4d69ea7f9ffeda5c3b0026ee2759aab501144b5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:ensemble of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] Let $A_1,\dots,A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ be sketches applied to the same data.
\begin{romannum}
\item \emph{Converse.} Stacking gives one linear map of rank at most
$p=\min\{km,d\}$. For any joint decoder, the recoverable centered-distance
variance is at most $\alpha_p(\Sigma)$. In the isotropic case,
$\rho_{\mathrm{HGR}}\le\sqrt{p/d}$, with equality for independent Gaussian blocks and the
optimal joint decoder.
\item \emph{Explicit averaging decoder.} If the $A_i$ are independent
Gaussian maps and we average the $k$ rescaled squared distances they produce,
then the correlation, jointly over the maps and data, is
\[
\sqrt{\frac{km}{km+d+2}}.
\]
The ratio of this correlation to the HGR ceiling is
\[
\gamma_{k,m,d}
=\sqrt{\frac{km\,d}{(km+d+2)\min\{km,d\}}}
=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{d/(km+d+2)}, & km\le d,\\
\sqrt{km/(km+d+2)}, & km\ge d.
\end{cases}
\]
\end{romannum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176507+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2c5f1ca2ba7f115f24e4985d485e0ea81fbf2f9568b8bd5140a67410b7be1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 71 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For fixed $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $f \in L^\infty([q_0,1];[0,1/\alpha])$, the mapping $p \mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$, viewed as a function from $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ to  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)\Big)^2
        \le 6(1+\|f\|_\infty) \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1\,.
    \]
Here $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is metrized by  $\mathsf{dist}(p,\tilde p) = \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1$, and we recall that  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. 

\begin{proof}
Let $p,\tilde p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 = \delta$.
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows by integrating that $|p(t) - \tilde p(t)| \le \delta$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$, and so certainly we have $\|p-\tilde{p}\|_1\le\delta$. Recalling the notation of Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, let $(b,\sigma)\in \Adm(q_0;p,f)$. We will construct modified controls $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma) \in \Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$ such that the corresponding solutions to \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} approximate each other. Recall $s(t)\equiv (tp)'(t)^{1/2}$, and similarly denote
$\tilde{s}(t)\equiv (t\tilde{p})'(t)^{1/2}$.
We set $\tilde{b}=b$, and let $\hat \sigma$ be defined by the relation
	\[\hat{\sigma}_t-1
	= a(t) 
	(\sigma_t-1)\,,\quad
	a(t)
	\equiv 
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	\frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{\tilde{s}(t)}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$. We note that 
	\[
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	= \frac{[p(t) + tp'(t)]^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}} \ge 1\,,
	\]
so the ratio $a(t)$ can only be large if $p'(t)$ is very large, which occurs on a set of times of small measure. It is clear from the construction that $(\tilde b,\hat{\sigma})$ satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{e:budget-f} defining $\Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$, with the exception that $\hat{\sigma}$ is not necessarily non-negative. Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$, and $\hat X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(\tilde b, \hat \sigma)$. We couple these processes with the same initialization $X(q_0) = \hat{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. We will first show the endpoint laws of $X(1)$ and $\hat{X}(1)$ are close, then address the issue of $\hat{\sigma}$ being possibly negative. To this end, we recall from \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} that
  \[
        X(1) = \int_{q_0}^1 p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t)\,dB(t)
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t) (\sigma_t-1)\,dB(t)
        \,,
    \]
and similarly for $\hat{X}(1)$. This gives us a decomposition
$X(1)-\hat{X}(1) = \textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}+\textup{(c)}$, and we proceed to bound each of the three terms:
    \begin{align*}\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E \bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big) b_t\,dt\bigg)^2\bigg]
    \le \bigg(
     \int_{q_0}^1\Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg( \int_{q_0}^1 \E[(b_t)^2]\,dt\bigg) \\
    &\le\bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 |p'(t)-\tilde{p}'(t)|\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 f(t)\,dt\bigg) 
    =  \delta \|f\|_1 \,,
    \end{align*}
having used the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality along with the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f}. Next,
    \[\E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    = \int_{q_0}^1 \Big( s(t)-\tilde{s}(t) \Big)^2\,dt
    \le \int_{q_0}^1 \Big|s(t)^2 - \tilde{s}(t)^2\Big|\,dt
    \le \|p-p\|_1+\|p'-p'\|_1 \le 2\delta\,.\]
Lastly, using the above definition of $\hat\sigma$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\E[\textup{(c)}^2]
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \Big( s(t) (\sigma_t-1)-\tilde{s}(t)(\hat{\sigma}_t
    -1)\Big)^2\,dt\\
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}
    \E[(\sigma_t-1)^2]
    \cdot p(t)
    \bigg( 1- 
    	\frac{\tilde{s}(t)}{s(t)} a(t)
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt\\
	&\le
	\|f\|_\infty
	\int_{q_0}^1
	p(t)
    \bigg( 1- \frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}}
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt 
	\le \|f\|_\infty \delta\,,
	\end{align*}
having used the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f} along with the calculation from the bound on (a) above. Collec (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:52.417061+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce6b1c594de4677f728e5d51caa664dd86fb559de29744dbd43373916aeb29b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 100 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a variational datum satisfying Assumptions~\ref{Assumption_A}, \ref{Assumption_B} and \ref{Assumption_C} with segment filling fractions $\boldsymbol{n}^{0}$, such that each segment contains a single band of the equilibrium measure. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.455170+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcf5fcaa7413490dd1f78dfb73660e4b755af9b0b48d9d6e1a472fdf2a2744b5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem Entropic symmetrization resistance of Bernoulli of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:HY_exceeds_HX}
Let $X \sim \Bern(p,a,b)$ with $p \ne \frac{1}{2}$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}(X=b) = p$ and $\mathbb{P}(X=a) = 1-p$. 
Then, any independent symmetrizer $Y$ of $X$ satisfies $H(Y) \ge H(X)$, with equality if and only if $f_Y = f_{-X}$. 
\begin{proof}
By (lem:affine_invariance,cor:psymmetry of the paper) it is sufficient to consider $X \sim \Bern(p,-1,1)$ 

with $p > \frac{1}{2}$. 

Equality is attained when $f_Y=f_{-X}$ by (lem:support_size_one_or_two of the paper); therefore we only need to show that $H(Y) > H(X)$ when $f_Y \ne f_{-X}$, i.e., $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f_Y)} \ge 3$. 

In this case, by (calYzero_sufficient of the paper) either $H(f_Y) > H(X)$ or projecting $f_Y$ onto $\Sym^0$ does not decrease its entropy; therefore it suffices to consider 
$f_Y \in \Sym^0$. 
By (lem:calYzero_representation of the paper), we write $f_Y = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 = 1$. 
Then, 
$ f(0) = \alpha_1^0 \hat{f}_1^0(0) = \frac{\alpha_1^0}{2}$, 
so that $\alpha_1^0 > 2p > 1$. 
Note that $\alpha_1^0 = 1 - \sum_{i=2}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0$. 
But, by (lem:calYzero_negative_coefficient_control of the paper), $\sum_{i=2}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \ge 0$, so $\alpha_1^0 \le 1$, a contradiction. 

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:54:53.443469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd038426f703dde2403154a36724715d1981820c0aa7f4d5dc7cdb10eb9bd4aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Multispecies mixed Ising model) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let $N\geq 1$, $D\geq 1$ and $\Sigma_N=\{\pm 1\}^N$.
For all $\bmx\in\mathbb R^D$, define the covariance function
\[
    \xi(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \xi_k(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \sum_{\substack{\bm p\in\mathsf P_k}}
    \Delta_{\bmp}^2\prod_{d=1}^D x_d^{p_d}.
\]
where $\bmDelta=(\Delta_{\bmp}^2:\bmp\in\mathsf P_k,\, k\geq 1)$ is a family of nonnegative coefficients and
where
\[
    \mathsf P_k
    =
    \{\bmp=(p_1,\ldots,p_D)\in\mathbb Z_+^D:
      |\bmp|:=p_1+\cdots+p_D=k\}.
\]
We also assume that $\xi((1+\varepsilon)\bm{1})<\infty$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

For \(\sigma,\tau\in\SigN\), define the species overlap vector by
\[
    R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau)
    =
    \frac1N\sum_{i\in I_{N,d}}\sigma_i\tau_i,
    \qquad
    \bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)=(R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau))_{d=1}^D,
\]
where \(\bmI_N=\{I_{N,1},\ldots,I_{N,D}\}\) is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

The Hamiltonian of the \emph{multispecies mixed Ising model} is a centered Gaussian process
 \(H_N=(H_N(\sigma))_{\sigma\in\SigN}\)
with covariance
\[
    \mathbb E H_N(\sigma)H_N(\tau)
    =
    N\xi(\bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)),
    \qquad \sigma,\tau\in\SigN.
\]","status":"unverified"}

A random vector
	$Z\in\R^N$ is called a
	$(K_{\rm feat},\tau)$-regular feature, if $\E[Z]=0$, $\Cov(Z)=\Sigma$ with
	$\lambda_{\Sigma}=\|\Sigma\|_{\op}>0$, and the following holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
		\item[$\mathrm{(F1)}$] For every fixed $\theta\in\R^N$,
		\[
		\|\langle Z,\theta\rangle\|_{L^4}^2
		\le K_{\rm feat}^2\lambda_{\Sigma}\|\theta\|_2^2.
		\]
		\item[$\mathrm{(F2)}$] For every fixed symmetric matrix
		$T\in\R^{N\times N}$,
		\[
		\Var\left(Z^\top TZ\right)
		\le \tau^2\|T\|_F^2.
		\]
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

\[

\]

\[
        \sigma_g^2
        :=

\]
In particular, if the local gap defined in (equation gap definition invariant subspace of the paper)

        =

\]","status":"unverified"}

Thus a centered vector z has new z_i=0 and new z_j=(1-1/N)*z_j+z_i/N. A sweep is the explicit product of these N linear maps. Check: If the card is at i it moves uniformly; if it is at j different from i, it stays unless the random partner is j. Summing the two cases gives the formula, which preserves the uniform distribution. Adding a deterministic phase as a state coordinate would give a periodic phase marginal and cannot justify ordinary mixing of the augmented chain.     Let \(\{X_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) be a (time-homogeneous) Itô diffusion in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).  
The (infinitesimal) generator \(\mathcal{A}\) of \(X_t\) is defined by
\[
\mathcal{A} f(x) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\mathbb{E}^x[f(X_t)] - f(x)}{t}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\]
The set of functions \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) such that the limit exists at \(x\) is denoted by \(D_{\mathcal{A}}(x)\), while \(D_{\mathcal{A}}\) denotes the set of functions for which the limit exists for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.381897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd546742303e39ccdfe4081945a75a3f4c296215f9a48e8614db95e698e17d77","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:local-direction of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Fix an integer $\ell\in\{2,\dots,n\}$.  
A random direction $\rho\in S_n$ with law $q_\ell$ is generated as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Sample a starting index $i$ uniformly from $[n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}$.
  \item For $r=0,1,\dots,\ell-1$, define
  \[
    i_r \;:=\; 1 + \bigl((i-1+r)\bmod n\bigr)\ \in\ [n].
  \]
  \item Let $\rho$ be the $\ell$--cycle on these indices,
  \[
    \rho \;:=\; (i_0\ i_1\ \cdots\ i_{\ell-1}),
  \]
  i.e.\ $\rho(i_r)=i_{r+1}$ for $r=0,\dots,\ell-2$, $\rho(i_{\ell-1})=i_0$, and
  $\rho(k)=k$ for all $k\notin\{i_0,\dots,i_{\ell-1}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
We write $\rho\sim q_\ell$. The law $q_\ell$ is state independent (i.e.,
$q(\cdot\mid\sigma)\equiv q_\ell$ for all $\sigma\in S_n$) and is orbit--equivariant
in the sense of Definition~(def:direction-law of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.737824+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd74c2e2ed87bf25d22184ebc0aed046d4897dd743e65a167a5e5ee3fb679829","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.30089, 'On the Coefficients of Hurwitz-Type Matrix Polynomials'] Let \(\kappa\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}\), and let
\((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\) be a sequence of complex
\(q\times q\) matrices. For each \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), define the
block Hankel matrix
\[
H_n^{(\widetilde s)}
:=
(\widetilde s_{j+k})_{j,k=0}^{n}.
\]

The sequence
\((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\)
is called \emph{Hankel positive definite} if
\(H_n^{(\widetilde s)}\) is Hermitian positive definite for every
\(n\le\kappa\).

A sequence \((P_k)_{k=0}^{\kappa}\) of complex
\(q\times q\) matrix polynomials is called a
\emph{monic left orthogonal system of matrix polynomials with respect
to \((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\)} if the following conditions
are fulfilled:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(I)]
\(\deg P_k=k\) for all \(k\in\mathbb Z_{0,\kappa}\).
\item[(II)]
The leading coefficient of \(P_k\) is \(I_q\).
\item[(III)]
\[
Z_n^{[P_j]}
H_n^{(\widetilde s)}
\bigl(Z_n^{[P_k]}\bigr)^*
=
0_{q\times q},
\]
for all \(j\neq k\), where
\(n=\max\{j,k\}\).
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.805154+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd8339c15eb60a146d734dc5d86847af6ae6987a9980ee4e81dc9310adffeaf7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem th:main1 of arXiv:2609.01488, 'Stabilization by a background magnetic field: global well-posedness of the full compressib'] Let $\mathbf n\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy the Diophantine
	condition (equation Diophantine0 of the paper), and let $M,N$ be two  positive integers

	Then there is a constant $\epsilon>0$, depending only on

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.764803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd9208166dd05484a23daf9673b9aef5c8e7dea3fc0576c4ede0e2f0feef7150","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Consider the setup described just above where we let $\Gamma^\C$ be a nested whole-plane~\clekp{}. There exists a unique (up to a deterministic factor) collection of resistance forms $\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = ((\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C}))_{k \in \N}$ that is measurable with respect to $\Gamma^\C$ and satisfies the following properties. There is a further collection of resistance forms $((\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C}))_{V \in \metregions}$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
 \item For each $k \in \N$ we have that $(\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C})$ is a local, regular resistance form on $\Upsilon_k$. Its associated resistance metric $\rmetres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY[\Upsilon_k]$.
 \item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions[k]$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k = \Upsilon_k$. Then
 \begin{align*}
  \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C} &= \{ f : f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V_i}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ for each } i \} ,\\
  \text{and}\quad
  \rformres{k}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{\Gamma^\C} .
 \end{align*}
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions[k]$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \setminus \ol{V}$, then
\begin{align*}
 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} .
\end{align*}
 \item For each open set $U \subseteq \C$, the collection of forms $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ a measurable function of $\Gamma^\C|_U$.
\item For each $z \in \C$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \rform{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma^\C+z} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $T_{z} f = f(\cdot -z)$ denotes translation by $z$.
\item There exists a constant $\resexp > 0$ so that for each $\lambda > 0$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \lambda^{\resexp}\rform{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{\lambda\Gamma^\C} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $S_{\lambda} f = f(\lambda^{-1}\cdot)$.
\end{enumerate}
The analogous statement holds for the \clekp{} Brownian motion. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:52:45.034203+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd9eb2627997dc8728afc019a4ae8036c0b7cf57b972c52c4e03020b93d5b9f0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2606.07839, 'Bounds on Spectral Gaps for Non-Reversible Markov Chains with Applications to Temporal Dif'] Say that the system $(F,G)$ is controllable and all eigenvalues of $F$ have magnitude less than $1$.

  S=GG^\top +FSF^\top.
\end{equation}
\item

  $$

  $$

  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space over R or C","K: X -> X is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar (for lambda = 0 every assertion can fail)","in the Hilbert-space form, H is a Hilbert space and K* is the Hilbert adjoint, so the relevant homogeneous adjoint equation uses the complex conjugate of lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572093+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory, integral equations","id":"claim_ddaa1329528122fb80376912c0e3927070e563e1860806c39b21c8299d538814","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space over R or C, let K in K(X) be compact, let lambda be a nonzero scalar and set T = lambda I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional; (ii) ran T is closed; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T' = dim(X / ran T) < infinity, where T' = lambda I - K' on the dual X'; in particular T is Fredholm with ind T = 0; (iv) ran T = {y in X : f(y) = 0 for every f in ker T'}. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.305272+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddb69fa4ac2dca24303c692875b45bda2840bdd38da39af39e9463a71c18c3a6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Xi of arXiv:2411.06089, '{\Large \bf Averaging principle for semilinear slow-fast rough partial differential equati'] Let $\mathbf B= ( B, B^2) $ be a $\mathscr{C}^\gamma([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$-valued random variable for $\gamma \in (1/3, \gamma_0)$ and $\{W_t\}_{t\in [0,T]}$ is a $m$-dimensional BM.

$$W_{t,s}^2:= \int_s^t \delta W_{r,s} \otimes dW_r,  ~~~~ \delta W_{r,s}=W_r-W_s,$$
where the stochastic integration is understood in the sense of It\^{o} integral.

Then $\mathbf W=(W,W^2)$ is an It\^{o}-type Brownian rough path
and for any $\gamma \in (1/3, 1/2)$, $\mathbf W=(W,W^2) \in \mathscr{C}^\gamma ([0,T]; \mathbb R^m)$, $\mathbb P$-a.s..

$$I[B,W]_{t,s}=\int_s^t \delta B_{r,s} \otimes dW_r$$

$$I[W,B]_{t,s}=\int_s^t \delta W_{r,s} \otimes dB_r=\delta W_{t,s} \otimes \delta B_{t,s} -\int_s^t dW_r \otimes \delta B_{r,s} $$
by imposing integration by parts.

w_2(s)=\frac{2^{-s}}{1+2^{-s}},
\qquad s\ge 0.
\]
Fix $\theta\in(1/2,1)$ and set
\[
s_\theta:=\log_2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}\right).
\]
Then the expected quorum time has the explicit form
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{w_1(s)}+\dfrac{1}{w_2(s)}-1\right), & 0\le s\le s_\theta,\\[1.0em]
\dfrac{1}{\lambda\, w_1(s)}, & s>s_\theta.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover:
\begin{itemize}
\item the map $s\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]$ is strictly increasing on $[0,s_\theta]$;
\item the map $s\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]$ is strictly decreasing on $(s_\theta,\infty)$.
\end{itemize}
Hence global monotonicity in the aligned heterogeneity parameter is false.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:09.065822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd0b46475877dc9486644e9b067179e200769ed65364bf4c41a494cfa208634","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 (Properties of the limit process) of arXiv:2606.27117, 'Occupation-Time Fluctuations of an Age-Dependent Branching System Driven by Poisson Immigr'] $\,$  
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item The limit process $\X$ is self-similar with self-similarity index
$\frac{3+\gamma-d/\alpha}{2}$, that is, for every $a>0$,
\[
\{\X(at),\ t\ge0\}
\stackrel{d}{=}
\left\{a^{\frac{3+\gamma-d/\alpha}{2}}\X(t),\ t\ge0\right\}.
\]
   
   
\item For every $0\le s<t$, we have $C(s,t)>0$. In particular, the covariance functional of $\X$ is strictly positive.
    
       
\item For every $0\le s\le t$,
\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\left(4-2^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}\right) s^{\gamma}(t-s)^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}
\le

\le

\end{equation}
In particular, $\X$ is not a semimartingale.
    
    
\item $\X$ has Hölder-continuous sample paths of any order less than
$\frac{3-d/\alpha}{2}$; that is, for every
\(
\varepsilon\in\left(0,\frac{3-d/\alpha}{2}\right)
\)
and every $L>0$, there exists a random variable $K_{\varepsilon,L}\ge0$ such that, almost surely,
\[
|\X(t)-\X(s)|
\le
K_{\varepsilon,L}
|t-s|^{(3-d/\alpha)/2-\varepsilon},
\qquad s,t\in[0,L].

\item $\X$ is not Markovian.

\[

=
\frac{2-d/\alpha}{\gamma(1+\gamma)}
(t-s)\big(v^{1+\gamma}-r^{1+\gamma}\big).

  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.649094+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddd4e20bfd3dd49b8d37a8d98a3fb70fd6d7867fa0b97356656ac3de70c53df1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 14 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] Put $(\sR/p)_{\red}:=(R/\sqrt{pR},N)$

characterized as follows. For

 (\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)^0/p)_{\red},L_P

{"assumptions":["Standard Borel covariate; strictly positive measurable score almost surely, finite mean score.","Fixed retention fraction strictly between zero and one.","Conditional unbiasedness and the mean positive-weight retention budget; no claim about estimator asymptotics."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:15.363712+00:00","domain":"Statistical data selection and inverse-probability weighting","id":"claim_ddd5fc36f48265162995ac3142dd2378fa412c120b9b084e148942e78dec54b7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon optimal unbiased selection, strictly positive-score specialization. Let X take values in a standard Borel space, let Z(X)>0 almost surely be measurable with E Z(X)<infinity, and fix 0<gamma<1. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). There is a unique c>0 such that E pi_star(X)=gamma. The minimum is E[Z(X)/pi_star(X)]=E[max(Z(X),sqrt(Z(X))/c)]<infinity. Uniform random retention has objective E Z/gamma; the optimal objective is strictly smaller unless Z is almost surely constant. This is the convex allocation problem in Proposition4.2 and AppendixB of Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon, with the strict-positive-score restriction stated explicitly to avoid zero-score conventions. \[

and
\[

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure","phi : X -> G is Borel measurable","the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.731878+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products and cocycles","id":"claim_ddecdf9c38acba7f9d1a20280128c4273217092304e304e1c131cecbf3f30d61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:36.759114+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de0dd49514b8ded9d2e4c73d52cbd3d315da2f69fc7285efd35d4357a5fa3c28","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 58 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $l\in \N_0, \delt \in (0,1], \Thet := [0,1]\times [0,T] \times \R^d$ and suppose we are given functions

	\end{align*}
	Let $X : \Om \times [0,T]\times \Thet \to \R^d$ be the unique solution to the family of \tSDE s
	\[X_t^{\ep,s}(x) = x + \int_s^t b_u^\ep(X_u^{\ep,s}(x))\,du + \int_s^t\si_u^\ep(X_u^{\ep,s}(x))\,dW_u, \quad t\in[0,T],\]
	with the convention that $\int_s^t\,du = \int_s^t\,dW_u = 0$ for $s > t$.
	Then,
	\[X : \Om \times [0,T]\times \Thet \to \R^d, (\om,t,(\ep,s,x))\mapsto X_t^{\ep,s}(x) \in \Lip^{l+\delt}(\Thet,\Lfininfad).\]
	Further, for all $k,m\in \N_0$ and every multi-index $\al$ with $|\al| \leq l - k - m $, $\der^\al_x \der_\ep^k \der_s^m X$ satisfies the \tSDE{}

	Here,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.746107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de12232140b00c54f654a321a766291084b9267f14677bea219692b0e6f96eed","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Define 5 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] \begin{description}
  \item[ \rm (i)] ({\em Identical distribution}) Let $\bm X_1$ and $\bm X_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined
respectively in sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{H}_1, \mbE_1)$
  and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{H}_2, \mbE_2)$. They are called identically distributed, denoted by $\bm X_1\overset{d}= \bm X_2$  if
$$ \mbE_1[\varphi(\bm X_1)]=\mbE_2[\varphi(\bm X_2)], \;\; \forall \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^n). $$
 A sequence $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ of random variables is said to be identically distributed if $X_i\overset{d}= X_1$ for each $i\ge 1$.
\item[\rm (ii)] ({\em Independence})   In a sub-linear expectation space  $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mbE)$, a random vector $\bm Y =
(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ is said to be independent to another random vector $\bm X =
(X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ , $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$ under $\mbE$  if for each test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n)$
we have
$ \mbE [\varphi(\bm X, \bm Y )] = \mbE \big[\mbE[\varphi(\bm x, \bm Y )]\big|_{\bm x=\bm X}\big].$
 \item[\rm (iii)] ({\em Independent random variables}) A sequence of random variables $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$
 is said to be independent, if  $X_{i+1}$ is independent to $(X_{1},\ldots, X_i)$ for each $i\ge 1$.
 \item[\rm (iv)](m-dependence) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be $m$-dependent if there exists an integer $m$ such that for every $n$ and every $j\geq m+1$, $(X_{n+m+1},\cdots,X_{n+j})$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)$. In particular, if $m=0$, $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is an independent sequence.
\item[\rm (v)](stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+p},\cdots,X_{n+p})$.
\item[\rm (vi)](linear stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be linear stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $X_1+\cdots+X_n\overset{d}{=}X_{1+p}+\cdots+X_{n+p}$.
 \end{description}","status":"unverified"}

Then, under the asymptotic uniform distribution on reduced population vectors $(1, x, y)$, with $1<x<y$,  the probability of a quota violation is the same as the probability of a quota violation caused by states guaranteed nonzero allocations and is calculated by:
$$P(A(1,x,y) \text { has a q.v.}) = \sum_{k = \lceil M/2 \rceil}^{M-1} M\left( \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k + D(k)} \right)$$
where $k$ indexes the integer values of $\lfloor \tilde{q}_3 \rfloor$, where 
$$\tilde{q}_3 = \frac{2M}{3-3\tau}, \qquad \tau = \frac{\mathrm{mean}(1,x,y)-\mathrm{median}(1,x,y)}{\max(1,x,y)}=\dfrac{1 - 2x + y}{3y}.$$ and

{"assumptions":["Finite exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P","Fixed finite real matrices A_i, vectors b_i and constant step alpha","Finite second moment of xi_0","Conditional independence of z_(k+1) and xi_k given z_k","Columnwise vectorization and stacking by chain state"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:05:57.431397+00:00","domain":"reinforcement learning; Markov jump linear systems","id":"claim_de1b5940314d04a7ddcbc45caa566cc8e834b108f83b393e8aa92596fbff4e17","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let z_k be an exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain on {1,...,N}, with p_ij=P(z_(k+1)=j|z_k=i). Fix real d-by-d matrices A_i, real d-vectors b_i and a constant alpha. Set H_i=I+alpha A_i and let xi_(k+1)=H_(z_k)xi_k+alpha b_(z_k). Assume xi_0 has finite second moment and that, conditional on z_k, the next chain state is independent of xi_k (in particular deterministic initial xi_0 with the natural chain filtration suffices). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. Then p_(k+1)=P^T p_k, q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i q_k^i+alpha p_k^i b_i], and Q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i Q_k^i H_i^T+alpha(H_i q_k^i b_i^T+b_i(q_k^i)^T H_i^T)+alpha^2 p_k^i b_i b_i^T]. For stacked q_k and v_k=(vec(Q_k^1),...,vec(Q_k^N)), columnwise vectorization gives q_(k+1)=H11 q_k+alpha(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_d)b and v_(k+1)=H22 v_k+H21 q_k+alpha^2(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_(d^2))b2, where b stacks b_i, b2 stacks b_i tensor b_i, H11_(j,i)=p_ij H_i, H22_(j,i)=p_ij(H_i tensor H_i), and H21_(j,i)=alpha p_ij[b_i tensor H_i+H_i tensor b_i]. In particular H22=(P^T tensor I_(d^2))diag_i(H_i tensor H_i); the update factor uses the departure state i. The raw second moment is sum_i Q_k^i and E||xi_k||^2=sum_i trace(Q_k^i); these Q_k^i are not centered conditional covariances. No irreducibility, stationarity, or zero stationary mean of b is needed for these finite-time identities.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627278+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_de27015aaa0fed8be3e6e4717dc3b361b73aac1ab1054852f520fd6389b23345","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:30:07.876882+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de2e9fcb830b0dce242036c59270968aa9a4dc9ee9dcd48146d2b1374a1a3efd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_regular of arXiv:2608.09105, 'Longest convex chains with i.i.d.\ points'] Given a convex chain $\mathcal{C}$, let $f_\mathcal{C}\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be the maximal convex function starting at $f_\mathcal{C}(0)=0$ and satisfying $f_\mathcal{C}(x)=y$ for every $(x,y)\in\mathcal{C}$.
That is, $f_\mathcal{C}$ is piecewise linear with corners at the elements of $\mathcal{C}$, and $f_\mathcal{C}(1)=1$ unless $(1,y)\in\mathcal{C}$ for some $y\in[0,1)$.

Given $\rho\in(0,\frac12)$, we say $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{$\rho$-regular} if $f_\mathcal{C}(1-\rho)\geqslant\rho$ and $f_\mathcal{C}(1)=1$.
Otherwise we say $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{$\rho$-irregular}. 
Note that if $\mathcal{C}$ is $\rho$-regular, then it is $\rho'$-regular for every $\rho'\in(0,\rho]$.
\hfill\ensuremath{\square}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:49:06.312525+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de3141a8e31cc9aa5ff14d447e41493418eac0d1ddc3c32cdf34ea44ed8b8700","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:orthogonal-inv of arXiv:2601.07759, 'The value of random zero-sum games'] We consider the block decomposition of a matrix $Q\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$
$$Q = \begin{pmatrix}
Q_1 & Q_2 \\
Q_3 & Q_4
\end{pmatrix}$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.971369+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de328d4affc1b2116dd4522a152a1caec37e53541a285635fa249b293925c321","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:elem_diff1 of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] First, we associate to each labelled tree $\underline{\tau} \in \boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$ the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \bigotimes_{n \in N(\underline{\tau})} \R^{{\mcb{m}}}$. 
We introduce this notation since it is natural to write $j$-multi-linear functionals of the noise using duality pairings in $(\R^{{\mcb{m}}})^{\otimes j}$, and since in our trees each node will represent an occurrence of the noise.
We also write 
\[
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] \eqdef C^{\infty}\Big( (\R^{{\mcb{n}}})^{N(\underline{\tau})}, \R^{{\mcb{n}}} \otimes \mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}}\Big)\;.\]

The elementary differential corresponding to a labelled tree $\underline{\tau}$ will be a map $\underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}} \in {\mcb{B}}[\underline{\tau}]$ inductively defined by setting, for $\underline{\tau}$ as in (equation eq:product_of_trees of the paper), and $x_{N(\underline{\tau})} = (x_{n})_{n \in N(\underline{\tau})} \in (\R^{{\mcb{n}}})^{N(\underline{\tau})}$, 
\begin{equ}
\underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau})}) 
=
\big( \mathrm{d}^{k}V(x_{r(\underline{\tau})}) \big) \big[ \underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}_{1}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_1)}),\cdots, \underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}_{k}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_k)}) \big]\,,
\end{equ}
where $\mathrm{d}$ here represents taking a differential on $\R^{{\mcb{n}}}$.
The the base case for this induction given by the above formula when $k=0$, that is when $\underline{\tau} = \circ_{r}$, so
\begin{equ}
\underline{\Upsilon}^{\circ_{r}}(x_{r})
=
V(x_{r})\;.
\end{equ}
and we use the canonical isomorphism $\mathcal{L}(\R^{{\mcb{n}}},\R^{{\mcb{m}}}) \simeq \R^{{\mcb{n}}} \otimes \R^{{\mcb{m}}}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356404+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de6ed04e0e0829407fc76e9f9053d5e379c62e487fac745c92001f9f22aa70f4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 233 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $\cA_N$ is a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm.
	Then there exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ depending on only $\alpha$ and $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
			 \le C(\alpha)
			\,\,\text{and}\,\,
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
	Furthermore, for any $k\ge 1$, there exists $C(\alpha,k)$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$,
	\beq
		\max\bigg\{
			\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op})^k]}
				{N^{k/2}}, 
			\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^k]}{N^{k/2}}
		\bigg\} \le C(\alpha,k)\,.
	\eeq
\begin{proof}
	By Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}, there exists $C(\alpha)$ such that 
	\beq
		
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
		 \le C(\alpha)
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Since the mapping $(\bG,\bg^\aux) \mapsto \|\bx\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian.
	Combined with the equality $\E[\|\bx\|^2] = N$ from Definition~\ref{d:Lip}, this readily implies
	\[
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bx\|}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 \le 2\bigg) 
		 \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
which gives \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail}.
	By Jensen's inequality,
	\[
		\frac{\E\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}}
		\le 
		\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^2]^{1/2}}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 = 1
		 \,.
	\]
Since $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian, for any $u\ge1$ we have
	\[\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg)
		\le \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\| - \E\|\bx\|]}{N^{1/2}} \ge u - 1
		\bigg) 
		\le \exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}
		\bigg)\,.\]
Integrating this bound gives
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le 2^k + \int_{2^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt
		= 2^k + \int_2^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du \\
		&\le 2^k + \int_2^\infty \exp\bigg(-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du 
		\le 2^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	Since the mapping $\bG \mapsto \|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-subgaussian.
	Then \eqref{e:confinement.wishart.restated} implies that $\E[\|\bG\|_{\op}] \le C(\alpha) N^{1/2}$. Then, by a similar calculation as above, we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt \\
		&= (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1} \,du \\
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty
		\exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-C(\alpha))^2 N}{2}
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du
		\le (2C(\alpha))^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	This proves \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

With A_n = 2^(2^n) and w_n = 2^(-n-2) exp(-A_n^2), the measure mu = (1 - W) delta_0 + sum_n w_n delta_{-A_n} has finite exponential moments of every order, and for every alpha in (0,1) and t > 0 neither mu * S_t nor mu boxplus T_t is unimodal. In the classical case the convolution density is strictly decreasing on intervals arbitrarily far to the left; in the free case the density vanishes inside each late gap of mu while staying positive at the images of the atoms on either side (Huang-Wang, arXiv:2203.00421). At alpha = 1/2 this answers the question raised for the positive 1/2-stable law. The cases alpha in [1,2) and the two-sided laws remain open. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:53:30.611446+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_debf0ec4147801c4bf959828eaa726698651e800f58807efa7427f774c637460","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def-point process of class QL of arXiv:2505.24043, 'Weak solutions of Navier-Stokes Equation with purely discontinuous L\'evy Noise'] Let us assume that  that $(X, \mathscr{B}_X) $ is a non-empty measure space  and that
\[
\tilde{\mathfrak{A}}=\bigl( \tilde{\Omega}, \tilde{\mathscr{F}}, \tilde{\mathbb{P}}, \tilde{\mathbb{F}}  \bigr), \mbox{ with } \tilde{\mathbb{F}}=(\tilde{\mathscr{F}}_t)_{t\geq 0} ,
\]
is a filtered probability space. 
An $\tilde{\mathbb{F}}$-adapted and $\sigma$-finite  point process \[p: \tilde{\Omega} \to \Pi_X,  \]
 is of \textbf{(QL)} class   if and only if there exists a family
\[
\widehat{\eta}_p=\Bigl\{ \widehat{\eta}_p(t,U): \, t>0, \;U\in \Gamma_p \Bigr\}
\]
such that the following conditions are satisfied.
\begin{trivlist}
\item[(i)] For every $U\in \Gamma_p$,
\[(0,\infty) \ni t \mapsto \widehat{\eta}_p(t,U)
\]
is a continuous $\tilde{\mathbb{F}}$-adapted  and increasing process .
\item[(ii)] For every $t>0$,  $\tilde{\omega} \in \tilde{\Omega}$,
\[\mathscr{B}_X \niU \mapsto \widehat{\eta}_p(t,U;\tilde{\omega}) \]
is, $\tilde{\mathbb{P}}$-a.s.,  a $\sigma$-finite measure on $(X,\mathscr{B}_X)$.
\item[(iii)] If $U \in \Gamma_p$,  the process
\begin{equation}

\tilde{\eta}_p(t,U):=\eta_p((0,t]\timesU)-\widehat{\eta}_p(t,U), \;\; t>0,
\end{equation}
is an $\tilde{\mathbb{F}}$-martingale.
\end{trivlist}
The family $\widehat{\eta}_p(t,U)$ is called the \textbf{compensator} of the point process $p$, or the \textbf{compensator} of the integer valued random measure $\eta_p$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.974155+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dec516930bba9db6dd4e2b2facaf1814e8cf8f8e593d06d54f06d2a35b357538","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:forests of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Define $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}\eqdef\mathcal{T}\times\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2\}$, and denote by $\tilde\tau=(\tau,r,u)$ an element of $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}$. 
We introduce a set of (ordered, unlabelled) forests
\begin{equs}
\text{$   \widehat\mathcal{T}$}\eqdef
\Big\{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde {\tau}_1,\dots,\tilde{\tau}_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})
=
\Big( (\tau_1,r_1,u_1), \dots, (\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},r_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},u_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}) 
\Big)\in\text{$\mathcal{T}$}_1^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}:p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\in[P]
\Big\}\,. 
\end{equs}

For two forests ${\boldsymbol{\tau}},{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and a tuple $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{|I|})$ consisting of distinct elements of $[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we define the forest ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{I}$ by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}_I\eqdef\big(\tilde\tau_{i_1},\dots,\tilde\tau_{i_{|I|}}\big)\,,
\end{equs}
and we define the forest  ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, the concatenation of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\eqdef(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},\tilde\sigma_1,\dots,\tilde\sigma_{p({\boldsymbol{\sigma}})})\,.
\end{equs}
Fix ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and
suppose that for every $i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we are given tuples of times $(t_{i},s^{\tau_i})\in(-\infty,1]\times\R^{\mathfrak{s}(\tau_i)}$.
We then write
\begin{equs}
    t_{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef (t_{\tau_1},\dots,t_{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}})  \in (-\infty,1]^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,\;\text{and}\;s^{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef(s^{\tau_1},\dots,s^{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}}) \in \R^{\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,
\end{equs}
where $\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{$\mathfrak{s}$}(\tau_i)$ is the \textit{size} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$. We also write $\mathfrak{l}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})+\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})$. 

Finally, we define the \textit{scaling} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by
\begin{equs}    |{\boldsymbol{\tau}}|\eqdef\big(p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})-1\big)+\sum_{i=1}^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}|\tau_i|\,,
\end{equs}
the \textit{order} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by $\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef \sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}(\tau_i) $, and set $r({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}r_i$ and $u({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}u_i$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.642694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dedb47cb49ca03e3d809abd5685ffdbcbde13bd9575f46646317a0119f60760b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 13 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(Z\) be a subordinator with Laplace exponent \(\psi\), and let \(\mu_Z\) be the random measure on \([0,\infty)\) induced by \(Z\), namely
\[
\mu_Z((a,b]) := Z_b-Z_a
\quad (0\le a<b<\infty).
\]
Let \(A\subset [0,\infty)\) be a Borel set with \(\lambda(A)<\infty\), where \(\lambda\) denotes the Lebesgue measure.
Then
\begin{align}
  E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0). 
\end{align}
In particular,
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{\lambda(A)},
\]
and if \(A,B \subset [0,\infty)\) are disjoint, \(\mu_{Z}(A)\) and \(\mu_{Z}(B)\) are independent.
More generally, if \(A\) is a random Borel set independent of \(Z\), then
\[
E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}\mid A]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0),
\]
and hence, if \(\lambda(A)=a\) almost surely for some \(a\ge0\), then
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{a}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["symmetric bounded density with power tail exponent alpha in (3,4)","variance normalized to one","iid entries","N_m ~ gamma m"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:16:40.830214+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_df0f816418e26d78ae50f2947f682cea76273333c6a93f89a7846eca995095ff","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"There is a symmetric law $\\xi$ with a bounded density, variance one and $\\mathbb{E}|\\xi|^3 < \\infty$ for which the rectangular operator norm is NOT tight on the scale $\\sqrt{m}$: if $A_m \\in \\mathbb{R}^{N_m \\times m}$ has iid entries of law $\\xi$ and $N_m \\sim \\gamma m$, then $\\|A_m\\|_{\\mathrm{op}}/\\sqrt{m} \\to \\infty$ in probability. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:28.471206+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df0f93cfa7b11e293ca8d2bf6a84f57507e49a000a32b09be9146170bc69f5c7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 35 (Finite-dimensional operator-valued multiple integral) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let $m\ge1$.  Let $F\subset\cH$, $\cC_0\subset\cC$, and
$\cE_0\subset\cE$ be
finite-dimensional subspaces, and let $F_\C$ be the complexification of
$F$.  The \emph{operator-valued multiple Wiener--It\^o integral of order
$m$} is the unique linear map
\begin{equation}

  I_m(\,\cdot\,;W):
  F_\C^{\otimes m}\otimes\conj{\cC_0}\otimes\cE_0
  \longrightarrow L^2(\Omega;\Sch_2(\cC,\cE))
\end{equation}
determined on elementary tensors by
\begin{equation}

  I_m(f\otimes\kappa;W)
  :=I_m^{\mathrm{scal}}(f;W)\,\Theta_{\cC,\cE}(\kappa).
\end{equation}
Multilinearity gives the unique linear map in
\eqref{eq:operator-valued-wiener-integral-map}; we write $I_m(K)$ when $W$
is fixed.

Equivalently, if $(h_i)_{i=1}^N$ is an orthonormal basis of $F$ and
\begin{equation}

  K=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_m=1}^N
  h_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes h_{i_m}
  \otimes\kappa_{i_1\cdots i_m},
\end{equation}
then, with
$K_{i_1\cdots i_m}:=
 \Theta_{\cC,\cE}(\kappa_{i_1\cdots i_m})$ and
$g_i:=W(h_i)$,
\begin{equation*}
  I_m(K;W)
  =\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_m=1}^N
  K_{i_1\cdots i_m}\,
  \wick{g_{i_1}\cdots g_{i_m}}.
\end{equation*}
For $m=0$ and $T\in\Sch_2(\cC,\cE)$, set $I_0(T)=T$.
The construction is compatible with inclusions of the supporting subspaces
$F$, $\cC_0$, and $\cE_0$; it therefore defines $I_m(K;W)$ for every
operator-valued kernel $K$ of finite-dimensional support.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0108-optimal-quadratic-littlewood-offord-bound","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.047056+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df127cd92d4f0a6377ef899b08d31441efa3f90b37f5b0c3d7e81be6e1922774","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.423843+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df1930d3b5c69ff5b5722eeedfab44e38cb855f8473318a6f8cc104559b4a8a5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:weibull-degree-window of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:weibull-bulk}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.198334+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df26d27bad5c5d1eeef1c6602c0d167196e97df45a91ccf2597a76b1fb895a00","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 125 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $J\equiv J(p,2\tep,\lambda/2)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. Then the coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:cts.coeffs} satisfy the estimates 
	\[
	\max\left\{
	\begin{array}{c}
	|\tbbb(t,y)^2
		-\Tbbb(t,y)^2|,\\
	|\tvvv(t,y)-\Tvvv(t,y)|,\\
	|\tuuu(t,y)^2-\Tuuu(t,y)^2|
	\end{array}
	\right\}
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \lambda
	\]
for all $(t,y)\in( [q_*,1]  \setminus J)\times\R$. 

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} gives
	\[\begin{aligned}
	\tB(t,y)&=\tB^N(t,y)+o_N(1)\,,\\
	\Tbbb(t,y)&=\Tbbb^N(t,y)+o_N(1)
	\end{aligned}\]
for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$. Recall that $(p^N)'(t)$ converges to $p'(t)$ for almost every $t$. Therefore, for \emph{every} $t$, we can find $s\in[t-\tep,t+\tep]$ such that $(p^N)'(s)$ converges to $p'(s)$. If $t\notin J$, then $t\notin J^N$ for sufficiently large $N$ by Lemma~\ref{l:bad.times.JN.J}, so $p'(s)$ differs from $p'(t)$ by at most $\lambda/2$, while $(p^N)'(s)$ differs from $(p^N)'(t)$ by at most $\lambda$. Therefore, for $t\in[q_*,1]\setminus J$, we have
	\[
	\Big|\tbbb(t,y)-\tbbb^N(t,y)\Big|
	=\bigg|\frac{\tB(t,y)}{p'(t)^{1/2}}
	-\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2}}\bigg|
	\le o_N(1)
	+ \bigg( \frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda\,,
	\]
using the bounds on $\tB^N$ and $\tB$ implied by Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}.
Additionally, since $t\notin J^N$,
Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} bounds the discrepancy between $\tbbb^N(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb^N(t,y)$.
Sending $N\to\infty$ gives the claimed bound on the discrepancy between $\tbbb(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb(t,y)$. The other bounds follow by similar arguments:
	\begin{align*}
	\Big|\tvvv(t,y)-\tvvv^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|
	\frac{\tV(t,y)}{p(t)}
	-\frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t)}\bigg|\,,\\
	\Big|\tuuu(t,y)-\tuuu^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\tU(t,y)}{[ p(t)
		\cdot t p'(t)]^{1/2}}
		-\frac{\tU^N(t,y)}{[ p^N(t)
		\cdot t (p^N)'(t)]^{1/2}}
		\bigg|\,.
	\end{align*}
Note in these cases that in the factor $L^{O(1)}$ appearing in the final bound, the $O(1)$ exponent can depend on the constant $\breve{c}$ from \eqref{e:breve.q.bounds}. We will remark on this point again in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Lipschitz-SDE-approx}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df2ec02ab8113e2c74344a7c95930cb4ecc1735b76c9be1b5407fe24fca67876","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 234 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exist $C(\alpha) > 0$ and $C(\alpha,L,K) > 0$, such that the following holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	If $\cA_N$ is an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm and $\cA_{N[K]}$ is as in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, then 
	\begin{align}
		
		\max\{

		,\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2
		\}
		 &\le C(\alpha)\,, \\
		
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4 &\le C(\alpha,L,K)\,.
	\end{align}
	Furthermore, for $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2 \le C(\alpha)
			\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof $c > 0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha,L$ which may change line by line. Recall that we abbreviate $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
	We prove \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} first. Recalling the definition of $\fm$ from Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, note that
\beq
		\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		=\frac{\|\fm\|^2}{M} 
		= \frac{1}{M} \bigg\|\frac{\bG \bx}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\|^2
		\le \frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2}{MN} \,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the above is
	\[
	\le \frac{C(\alpha)^2 N \cdot 4N}{MN} 
		= \frac{4C(\alpha)^2}{\alpha}\,.
	\]
	This proves \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.
	Next, note that
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		= \E \|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		= 
		\frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M} 
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.step1}}{\le} 
		\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2]}{MN} \,.
	\]
By H\"older's inequality and the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{\E [(\|\bG\|_{\op})^4]^{1/2} \E[\|\bx\|^4]^{1/2}}{MN}

		= \frac{C(\alpha,4)}{\alpha}\,,
	\]
	for $C(\alpha,4)$ defined in Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}.
This proves the first part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$. For the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}, we split into cases depending on whether $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$. Recall that the truncated algorithm $\cA_{N[K]}$ resamples the rows indexed by $S_K(\cA_N)$. If $a\notin S_K(\cA_N)$, then $\tilde{\fm}_a$ is equidistributed as $\fm_a$, so they have the same second moment. If $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$, then 
	\[\tilde{\fm}_a
		= \frac{(\bg^a, \tilde{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
where $\bg^a$ is independent of $\tilde{\bx}$, as $\cA_{N[K]}$ does not use the input $\bg^a$.
	Thus, the distribution of $\tilde{\fm}_a$ conditional on $\tilde{\bx}$ is a (one-dimensional) centered gaussian random variable with standard deviation $\|\tilde{\bx}\| / N^{1/2}$. It follows in this case that
	\[

	= \frac{\E[\|\tilde{\bx}\|^2]}{N}=1\,.
	\]
Altogether this gives
	\[
	\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|^2
	=\frac{ \E[\|\tilde{\fm}\|^2]}{M}
	\le
	\frac{ \E[\|\fm\|^2 + M]}{M}

	\]
This proves the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.

	\[

To this end, we will show that there exists $C(\alpha,L,K)$ such that

		\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^4] \le C(\alpha,L,K)
	\eeq
	for all $a\in [M]$, which implies \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}.

Let $\mathbb{D} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be an open set and let $t_0 < t_1$ be real numbers.
    Suppose the It\^o process $X_t \in \mathbb R^n$ satisfies $X_{t_0} \in \mathbb{D}$ and also satisfies the SDE 
    \[dX_t = \mu_tdt +\sigma_tdB_t\]
    with $\mu_t \in \mathbb R^n$ and $\sigma_t \in \mathbb R^{n \times n}$ when $t \in (t_0, t_1)$ and $X_t \in \mathbb{D}$.
    Suppose that $f_t(x)$ is a vector-valued function that is continuously differentiable in $t \in [t_0, t_1]$ and continuously twice-differentiable in $x \in \mathbb{D}$.
