{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.852796+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec046ef5bfbae7d7c5f49984291891d74af12d504cff7374a41c044c4d9ece2f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 17 (Eigenvector master equation — Wishart case) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Fix integers $N, T \ge 1$, and let $\{\lambda_i^{(N)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ 
denote the (ordered, positive) eigenvalues of the Wishart matrix 
\(
W^{(N)} := X_{N}^{\!\top} X_{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
\)
Let $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{(N)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ be the associated orthonormal eigenvectors. 
Consider the rank–one extension
\[
X_{N+1} = \big( X_N \;\; g \big),
\qquad g \in \mathbb{R}^{T},
\]
that is, $X_{N+1}$ is obtained by appending the column vector $g$ to $X_N$.
Let $W^{(N+1)} = X_{N+1}^{\!\top} X_{N+1}$, with eigenvalues 
$\{\lambda_i^{(N+1)}\}_{i=1}^{N+1}$ and eigenvectors $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{(N+1)}\}$.
We define
\(
g_i^{(N)} \;=\; \langle v_i^{(N)},\, g \rangle,
\)
where $v_i^{(N)}$ denotes the eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue 
$\lambda_i^{(N)}$ of the matrix $X_N X_N^{\!\top}$.

\smallskip
\noindent
Then the overlap coefficients
\(
\Omega^{(N)}_{ij} := 
\big\langle \mathbf{u}_i^{(N+1)},\, \mathbf{u}_j^{(N)} \big\rangle
\)
satisfy the relation
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Omega^{(N)}_{k j}}{\Omega^{(N)}_{k i}} 
&= 
\frac{g_j^{(N)}}{g_i^{(N)}}
\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_j^{(N)}}{\lambda_i^{(N)}}}
\frac{\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)}}{\Delta_{k,j}^{(N)}},
\qquad 1 \le i,j \le N, \qquad
\frac{\Omega^{(N)}_{k,\,N+1}}{\Omega^{(N)}_{k i}} 
&= 
\frac{\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)}}{g_i^{(N)}}
\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda_i^{(N)}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where
\(
\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)} := \lambda_k^{(N+1)} - \lambda_i^{(N)}.
\)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.707487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec0bac36bb42256900aa5e2f7f0f606691963f8b054eda059b123828712ca568","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:angular-moments-comp of arXiv:2609.00698, 'Kinetic Wedge Layers and Diffusive Limit of Neutron Transport in Polygonal Domains'] Let $\phi$ be a smooth scalar function on $\Omega$ and let $q\geq0$ be an integer. Then the angular moments of the directional derivatives of $\phi$ satisfy, pointwise in $\Omega$,
\begin{align}
 \mathbf P\bigl((w\cdot\nabla)^{2q+1}\phi\bigr)
 &=0,
 \\
 \mathbf P\bigl((w\cdot\nabla)^{2q}\phi\bigr)
 &=c_q\Delta^q\phi,
 \qquad
 c_q=\frac{(2q)!}{2^{2q}(q!)^2}.
 
\end{align}
Let now $k\geq0$, let $\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_k$ be smooth and harmonic in $\Omega$, and let $U_0:=\rho_0$ while $U_\ell$ is defined recursively by (equation eq:interior-recursion-comp of the paper) for $1\leq\ell\leq k$. Then the profiles are given explicitly by a finite alternating sum of derivatives of the densities, and their velocity averages obey the solvability identities:
\begin{align}
 U_\ell
 &=
 \sum_{j=0}^{\ell}
 (-1)^j(w\cdot\nabla)^j\rho_{\ell-j},
 \qquad 0\leq\ell\leq k,
 \\
 \pkU_\ell
 &=
 \rho_\ell,
 \qquad
 \mathbf P(w\cdot\nablaU_\ell)=0,
 \qquad 0\leq\ell\leq k.
 
\end{align}
Therefore, the recursively defined profiles satisfy (equation eq:interior-coefficient-equations-comp of the paper), and $\mathbf P(w\cdot\nablaU_k)=0$ is the compatibility condition needed to continue the construction to order $k+1$. Only $\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_{k-1}$ are required to be harmonic for these identities at order $k$, which is the precise sense in which harmonicity is the solvability condition of the next order rather than an ansatz.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.155594+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec0f6d093f41e4be9467d6e9fa5464dee78c1ad78af1b3785ec7ea17a4cf83a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, let $\mu$ be its 
Haar probability measure and $Y$ be a random variable on $G$ with density $f_Y \in L^2(G)$. Let $S$ be a set of positive Haar measure and

\begin{equation} 
    \int_{G}(f_Y\ast g_S(x) - 1)^2\, dx \leq \eta_S\int_{G}(f_Y(x)-1)^2\, dx,
\end{equation}
where,
$$\eta_S = \left(\frac{\sin(\pi \mu(S))}{\pi \mu(S)}\right)^2.$$
Equivalently, 
\begin{equation} 
\chi^2(Y+U_S\,\|\,U_{G}) = \chi^2(Y+U_S\,\|\,U_{G} +  U_S)
\le
\eta_S\,\chi^2(Y\,\|\,U_{G}),
\end{equation}
where
$U_{G}$ is uniformly distributed on $G$ and independent of $U_S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:15:08.952685+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec214d36c45f14904c0ade077e85e245ac0134eb43375087c297ce075f537c03","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:bIs of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] For $x>0$, and $h, g\ge 0$, we define
\[
\mathbf F(x;h,g) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}} \left( \exp\left(-\frac{(g-h)^2}{2x}\right)-\exp\left(-\frac{(g+h)^2}{2x}\right)\right),
\]
and
\[
\mathbf I(x;h,g) = \mathbf F(x;h,g)\mathbb E\left[ \exp\left( \beta^{-1}\int_0^x B(y) \mathrm d y \right) \right],
\]
where $B:[0, x]\to \mathbb R$ is a Brownian bridge with $B(0)=g$ and $B(x)=h$, conditional on $B\ge 0$. We also define
\[
\mathbf F_0(x;h) = \frac{2h}{\sqrt{2\pi x^3}} \exp\left(-\frac{h^2}{2x}\right), \qquad
\mathbf I_0(x;h) =\mathbf F_0(x;h)\mathbb E\left[ \exp\left( \beta^{-1}\int_0^x B_3(y) \mathrm d y \right) \right],
\]
where $B_3:[0, x]\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}$ is a Bessel$_3$ process, conditional on $B_3(x)=h$.
Finally,
\[
\mathbf F_{0,0}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi x^3}}, \qquad \mathbf I_{0,0}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi x^3}} \mathbb E\left[ \exp\left( \beta^{-1}\int_0^x B_e(y) \mathrm d y \right) \right],
\]
where $B_e:[0, x]\to \mathbb R_{\ge 0}$ is a Brownian excursion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.671750+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec285511def467c9a0f5b4cc56a7440330929154434848666fd8fb693871fd96","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 13 (Polynomial continuity on bounded sets) of arXiv:2608.04824, 'Strong Convergence for a General Class of Random Matrix Models'] Let \(Q=\sum_w\alpha_ww\) be a noncommutative \(*\)-polynomial in
\(d\) variables.  For \(M\geq1\), set
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}_M(Q)
 =\sum_{|w|\geq1}|\alpha_w|\,|w|M^{|w|-1}.
\]
If two tuples \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\) and \(B=(B_1,\ldots,B_d)\) satisfy
\[
 \max_\kappa\bigl(\|A_\kappa\|,\|B_\kappa\|\bigr)\leq M,
 \qquad
 \delta=\max_\kappa\|A_\kappa-B_\kappa\|,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 \|Q(A,A^*)-Q(B,B^*)\|\leq\operatorname{Lip}_M(Q)\delta.
\end{equation}
The same right-hand side bounds the difference of the normalized traces when
\(A\) and \(B\) are matrix tuples of the same size.
More generally, if \(Q=\sum_w C_w\otimes w\) has coefficients in a fixed
matrix algebra, the conclusions hold with
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}_M(Q)
 =\sum_{|w|\geq1}\|C_w\|\,|w|M^{|w|-1}
\]
and with the tensor-product operator norm and normalized trace.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.058463+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec3b1dfe821e432397e4573f4925e5d3f43f99f4e05b2d65be66449ea4fb8fdb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:pure-time-gaussian-reduction of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] There is a matrix field

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:53:39.158814+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec3e2559e793e477d54fa1865ee129c000506d3dd3086d1eba0ff285193f0915","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 35 of arXiv:2608.26953, '2608.26953'] Let \(M\) be a finite-dimensional left \(A_S\)-module and choose \(\{( \omega_e, \varphi^e)\}_{ e \in S_1}\) as in \eqref{eq:right-dual-base}. Let \( \nabla \colon M \rightarrow \Omega_S^{1}\otimes_{A_S} M\) be a left connection and define \( T_e  \coloneq  (\varphi^e \otimes \mathrm{id}_M)\circ \nabla \colon M \rightarrow M. \) Then:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item For all \(x\in M\), \( \nabla(x) = \sum_{e\in S_1} \omega_e \otimes T_e(x) \) uniquely and \( T_e(x) \in M_{ d_0(e) } \) for every \(x\in M\).
\item For \(f \in A_S\) and \(x\in M\),
\begin{equation} 
T_e(fx)=\partial_e(f)\cdot x + f(d_1(e))T_e(x),

\end{equation}
\item For each $e\in S_1$, there is a unique map \( R_e\in \operatorname{Hom}_\Bbbk\bigl(M_{d_1(e)},M_{d_0(e)}\bigr)\) such that \[
T_e=\delta_{d_0(e)}-R_e\delta_{d_1(e)}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:24:20.972422+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec4a3fae9f4316dd7c0085e0492d99f9f6a83276f5c88b6f273b9b2d54049fce","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def6.4 of arXiv:2508.12951, '\textbf{On the central limit question for strictly stationary, reversible Markov chains}'] Suppose $\varepsilon$ and $\theta$ satisfy ((eq6.311 of the paper)).

(i) its state space is $\{-1, 0, 1\}$, \hfil\break
(ii) its (invariant) marginal probability vector is the vector 
$\pi^{(\varepsilon)}$ in ((eq6.331 of the paper)), and \hfil\break
(iii) its one-step transition probability matrix is the matrix
$\mathbb P^{(\varepsilon, \theta)}$ in ((eq6.341 of the paper)).

   That is [under Condition ${\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \theta)$],

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:53:51.338619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec71c22ff6e741882fa6560c61dd70df01801ba7e0e6d750508e56869b94ff98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:regions_in_limit_shape of arXiv:2605.03896, 'Dimer models on astroidal zig-zag graphs'] We say that \((x,y)\in \mathcal D_c^\circ\):

\begin{enumerate}
\item lies in the \emph{rough region} \(\mathcal L\) if \(\lambda_c(x,y)\) has a
\(\sigma\)-conjugate pair of zeroes. In this case, there is a unique zero
\(\zeta\in \Sigma_+^\circ\), and we define
\[
\Omega:\mathcal L \to \Sigma_+^\circ,
\qquad
\Omega(x,y):=\zeta.
\]

\item lies in the \emph{frozen region} \(\mathcal F_{(\alpha,\beta)}\), where
\((\alpha,\beta)\subset A_0\) is the open interval between two consecutive
angles \(\alpha,\beta\) with \(e(\alpha)\neq e(\beta)\), such that
\(\lambda_c(x,y)\) has exactly two simple zeroes in \((\alpha,\beta)\) when
the vertex \(e(\alpha)\cap e(\beta)\in V(N)\) is convex, and {two or} three
simple zeroes when it is concave.

\item lies in the \emph{quasi-frozen region} \(\mathcal Q_{(\alpha,\beta)}\),
where \((\alpha,\beta)\subset A_0\) is the open interval between two consecutive
angles \(\alpha,\beta\) with \(e(\alpha)=e(\beta)\), if \(\lambda_c(x,y)\) has
three simple zeroes in \((\alpha,\beta)\).

\item lies in the \emph{smooth region} \(\mathcal G_j\), for \(1\le j\le g\), if
\(\lambda_c(x,y)\) has four simple zeroes in \(A_j\).

\item lies on the \emph{frozen-rough boundary}
\(\mathscr{A}_{(\alpha,\beta)}\), where
\((\alpha,\beta)\subset A_0\) is the open interval between two consecutive
angles \(\alpha,\beta\) with \(e(\alpha)\neq e(\beta)\), if \(\lambda_c(x,y)\)
has a zero \(\zeta\) of order two or three in \((\alpha,\beta)\). In this case,
\(\zeta\) is unique, and we define
\[
\Omega:\mathscr{A}_{(\alpha,\beta)}\to (\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\Omega(x,y):=\zeta.
\]
If \(\zeta\) is a zero of order three, which can occur only when the vertex
\(e(\alpha)\cap e(\beta)\in V(N)\) is concave, we call \((x,y)\) a
\emph{frozen cusp}.

\item lies on the \emph{quasi-frozen-rough boundary}
\(\mathscr{A}_{(\alpha,\beta)}\), where
\((\alpha,\beta)\subset A_0\) is the open interval between two consecutive
angles \(\alpha,\beta\) with \(e(\alpha)=e(\beta)\), if \(\lambda_c(x,y)\) has
a zero \(\zeta\) of order two or three in \((\alpha,\beta)\). In this case,
\(\zeta\) is unique, and we define
\[
\Omega:\mathscr{A}_{(\alpha,\beta)}\to (\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
\Omega(x,y):=\zeta.
\]
If \(\zeta\) is a zero of order three, we call \((x,y)\) a
\emph{quasi-frozen cusp}.

\item lies on the \emph{smooth-rough boundary} \(\mathscr{A}_{A_j}\), for
\(1\le j\le g\), if \(\lambda_c(x,y)\) has a total of four zeroes in $A_j$ (counted with multiplicity), one of which is a zero \(\zeta\) of order two or three. In this case, \(\zeta\) is unique: if \(\lambda_c(x,y)\) had
two double zeroes on \(A_j\), then it would have constant sign on \(A_j\),
forcing
\[
\int_{A_j}\lambda_c(x,y)\neq 0,
\]
contradicting imaginary-normalization. We therefore define
\[
\Omega:\mathscr{A}_{A_j}\to A_j,
\qquad
\Omega(x,y):=\zeta.
\]
If \(\zeta\) is a zero of order three, we call \((x,y)\) a
\emph{smooth cusp}; an order four zero is excluded by the same argument that rules out two double zeroes.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.510111+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec989b1b804669d2846baf00bbc8b3dc7cb5672b8ac452b438cfb17baaccdbf2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 44 of arXiv:2608.18075, '2608.18075'] Let $T<\infty$, $b>2$, $p>4$, and
$\tilde w\in L^p(0,T;H^b)$. 
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\partial_t\rho=L_{\tilde w}(t)\rho$, then
\begin{align}

 +\nu\int_0^T\|\rho_t\|_{H^1}^2\,\dd t
 \le e^{C\Lambda_T(\tilde w)}\|\rho_0\|_2^2.
\end{align}
\item Let $f_i\in L^p(0,T;H^b), i=1,2$,

Then
\begin{align}

 \left(\|\eta_i\|_2^2

 \|\eta_{12}\|_2^2
 +T^{1-4/p}\|f_{12}\|_{L^{p/2}(0,T;H^b)}^2\|\rho_0\|_2^2
 \notag\\
 &\hspace{26mm}
 +T^{1-2/p}\sum_{i=1}^2

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.346134+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec9b5314aaf7bd4dfc0748469c33282c018b14d0dc36a6f0693538eeecdaf744","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:weights of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $f \in \mathcal{D}_{+}^{2}$ and suppose the rank profile

		the regularly varying tails of Theorem~(thm:singularity of the paper), for

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:21:28.762883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ecaf1a40e0ebab9fdc676c21912c154f4b333ed66b8633def22e016a43eb40e7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:mixed-lipschitz-gradient of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Fix $\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$.  Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric and let
$a,\widetilde a\in[0,1]$.  Let $W,\widetilde W\in\mathcal D_n((0,1])$ and set
$D:=W^{-1}$ and $\widetilde D:=\widetilde W^{-1}$.  Let $T,\widetilde T\in\mathcal D_n(\mathbb R)$
satisfy $\schnorm{T}\leqslant 1$ and $\schnorm{\widetilde T}\leqslant 1$.
Define
\[
X:=aI_n-\beta A + D,\qquad \widetilde X:=\widetilde a\,I_n-\beta A + \widetilde D,
\]
and assume $\ensuremath{\left\lVert \beta A \right\rVert_\mathsf{op}} \leqslant 1 - \gamma$.
For each triple $(a,W,T)$ define the scalar functional
\[
\Phi_{a,W,T}(A)
\;:=\;
\operatorname{tr}_n\left(
T\,E_{\mathcal D_n}\bigl[D\,(a-\beta A + D)^{-2}D\right]
\Bigr)
=
\operatorname{tr}_n\left(T\,D\,X^{-2}D\right),
\]
where the equality holds since $T$ is diagonal and $E_{\mathcal D_n}$ is trace-preserving.

Let $\nabla_A \Phi_{a,W,T}(A)\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ denote the gradient with respect to the
Hilbert structure $\langle U,V\rangle=\operatorname{tr}_n(UV)$ on $M_n(\mathbb R)$, i.e.
$d\Phi[H]=\langle \nabla_A\Phi,\,H\rangle$ for all symmetric directions $H$.
Then
\begin{equation}

\schnorm{\nabla_A \Phi_{a,W,T}(A)-\nabla_A \Phi_{\widetilde a,\widetilde W,\widetilde T}(A)}
\ \leqslant\
2\beta\left(
\frac{12}{\gamma^4}\,|a-\widetilde a|
\;+\;
\frac{32}{\gamma^4}\,\ensuremath{\left\lVert W-\widetilde W \right\rVert_\mathsf{op}}
\;+\;
\frac{4}{\gamma^3}\,\schnorm{T-\widetilde T}
\right).
\end{equation}
In other words, the map $(a,W,T)\mapsto \nabla_A\Phi_{a,W,T}(A)$ is Lipschitz in $\schnorm{\cdot}$ with constants depending only on
$\beta,\gamma$ and the operator bound $\ensuremath{\left\lVert A \right\rVert_\mathsf{op}}$, and independent of $n$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.367475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eccdf2d90953cab8ac02197ca5ce7eddd2d2316e2435ce25f0af8054e2300c80","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 116 (Euler-generated It\^o field and state equivalence) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let
$\varnothing\ne\mathcal P_{\rm sp}
 \subset\mathfrak S_{\Lambda,0}^{0,T}(H)$
have the uniform spatial trace-tightness profile $(P_m,\vartheta_m)$ fixed
above.  Let
\[
 b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m,
 \qquad
 \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathcal L(H,\mathbb R^m)
\]
be deterministic and continuous.  Assume, uniformly in time, that they are
globally Lipschitz in the state variable and have linear growth, with the
operator norm used for $\sigma$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item For every deterministic $(s,y)$, every $1\le r<\infty$, and every
sequence of deterministic partitions $|\pi_n|\to0$, the schemes
$Y^{\pi_n;s,y}$ converge, independently of the partition sequence, in
\[
 \mathbb L_{\mathcal P_{\rm sp}}^r
 \bigl(C([0,T];\mathbb R^m)\bigr)
\]
to a common It\^o solution $Y^{s,y}$.  Under every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\rm sp}$ its projection is the unique classical strong
solution
\begin{equation}
 Y_t^{s,y}
 =y+\int_s^t b(u,Y_u^{s,y})\,\dd u
   +\int_s^t\sigma(u,Y_u^{s,y})\,\dd X_u,
 \qquad t\in[s,T].
\end{equation}
The stochastic term is the common integral of
\Cref{thm:uniform-BDG-extension} and its modelwise projections are understood
in the corresponding bracket-energy quotient.

\item There is a total jointly Borel raw-causal field
\[
 \Phi:\Omega\times\Delta_T\times\mathbb R^m\longrightarrow\mathbb R^m
\]
whose fixed-parameter sections represent the limits in part~\textup{(i)}.
For every $R$, the polar-equivalence class of the frozen fixed-parameter
family admits a compatible Borel representative
$\Phi^R:\Omega\to\mathscr B_R$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \Phi^R\in\bigcap_{1\le r<\infty}
 \mathbb L_{\mathcal P_{\rm sp}}^r(\mathscr B_R).
\end{equation}
One diagonal of continuous finite-parameter interpolation fields, each built
from finitely many maps \eqref{eq:raw-Euler-starting-pair}, selects $\Phi$.
There are a Borel full-capacity set $G_{\rm E}$ and an increasing compact core
such that, simultaneously in every model and parameter,
$(s,t,y)\mapsto\Phi_{s,t}(x,y)$ is locally continuous on $G_{\rm E}$ and the
raw-path/parameter field is jointly continuous on compact parameter sets over
each core.  On $G_{\rm E}$, $\Phi$ and every $\Phi^R$ agree throughout their
parameter domains, and
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{s,t}(x,y)
 =\Phi_{u,t}\bigl(x,\Phi_{s,u}(x,y)\bigr)
\end{equation}
for every $x\in G_{\rm E}$, $0\le s\le u\le t\le T$, and
$y\in\mathbb R^m$.

\item Suppose additionally that
\begin{equation}
 b(t,y)=V_0(y),\qquad \sigma(t,y)=V(y),
\end{equation}
where $V_0$ is bounded globally Lipschitz and, for some
$p_{\rm rp}\in(1/\alpha,3)$ and $\rho>p_{\rm rp}$,
\[
 V\in\operatorname{Lip}^{\rho+1}
 \bigl(\mathbb R^m;\mathcal L(H,\mathbb R^m)\bigr).
\]
Let $\Psi$ be the bracket-corrected state flow of
\Cref{thm:common-Ito-flow} on $G_*^{\boldsymbol\vartheta}$, totalized by
$\Psi_{s,t}(x,y)=y$ on its complement.  There is one Borel
$\mathcal P_{\rm sp}$-polar set $N_{\rm id}$, independent of
$P,s,t,y$.  Define
\begin{equation}
 G_{\rm id}
 :=\bigl(G_{\rm E}\cap G_*^{\boldsymbol\vartheta}\bigr)
   \setminus N_{\rm id},
\end{equation}
Then $G_{\rm id}$ is Borel with polar complement, and
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{s,t}(x,y)=\Psi_{s,t}(x,y)
 \qquad
 (x\in G_{\rm id},\ 0\le s\le t\le T,\ y\in\mathbb R^m).
\end{equation}
Thus the independent first-level Euler construction and the corewise
continuous state propagation produce the same common It\^o cocycle.  If
$p_{\rm rp}>1/\eta$, the latter is the full-state continuous readout of
\Cref{cor:full-state-flow-readout}.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation on a locally finite TRANSITIVE infinite graph","the exponential-decay statement is asserted for finite-range models","the mean-field bound is quoted in the form stated in the paper's abstract"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ece8d7f1c3d22584194ee5dead73ab7ab9a536555aea7cc7a03d5465c516a331","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For Bernoulli percolation on an arbitrary locally finite transitive infinite graph, the phase transition is SHARP: (a) for every p < p_c the susceptibility is finite, chi(p) = E_p |C(0)| < infinity, and for FINITE-RANGE models the probability of an open path from the origin to distance n decays exponentially in n; (b) for every p > p_c the mean-field lower bound P_p(0 <-> infinity) >= (p - p_c)/p holds. There is therefore no intermediate regime in which the cluster size has a heavy polynomial tail without an infinite cluster - the subcritical decay is exponential right up to p_c. The same paper proves the corresponding statements for the Ising model, with finiteness of the susceptibility below the critical inverse temperature and the mean-field magnetisation bound above it. Historically this recovers the Aizenman-Barsky and Menshikov theorems by a much shorter argument based on a differential inequality for a well-chosen family of finite-volume quantities. The result is about BERNOULLI percolation on a TRANSITIVE graph; the transitivity hypothesis is used and the statement is not asserted here for general graphs. [Duminil-Copin and Tassion (2016), Comm. Math. Phys. 343; arXiv:1502.03050]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a finite, irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e","the two states a, b are distinct vertices of the graph","the graph is connected, so hitting and commute times, and R_eff, are all finite","consistent normalization of the total conductance c_G matching the specific convention used for R_eff"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993395+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ecfa965d432e2bd30d8bada02d7468db0f78ae6ff3009f102b45977594aa17a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e and total conductance c_G equal to the sum of conductances over all edges, the commute time C(a,b) = E_a[tau_b] + E_b[tau_a] between two vertices a, b satisfies the exact identity C(a,b) = 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), where R_eff(a,b) is the effective resistance in the associated electrical network. The identity is derived by checking that h(x) = P_x(hit a before b) is harmonic away from {a,b} and coincides with the network's voltage function, then relating expected hitting times to the network's energy dissipation. It converts questions about hitting, commute, and cover times of a reversible random walk into purely electrical or combinatorial resistance computations, enabling resistance-based bounds via series-parallel laws, Rayleigh monotonicity, or the Nash-Williams inequality on infinite graphs, on quantities such as cover time and mixing time. It does not directly give the individual one-way hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone, only the symmetrized commute time; and it is specific to reversible chains, since non-reversible walks lack the electrical-network correspondence and require substantially different techniques. Typical failure: Using the commute-time identity to bound a one-directional hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone by simply halving C(a,b), which is valid only under a separate symmetry argument between a and b; in general E_a[tau_b] and E_b[tau_a] can differ substantially even though their sum equals 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), so treating the identity as giving each one-way time individually, without additional justification, is a common overreach. Canonical reference: Chandra, Raghavan, Ruzzo, Smolensky and Tiwari, 1996, Random Structures and Algorithms; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["2D DGFF in admissible domains; extremal process with Poisson-cluster structure (Biskup-Louidor)","Exchange of limits requires uniform integrability not currently available"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed315b917a49a5586e8545dda8762df7dee0b7d1acded753da3ac58be204b190","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.666852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed3996b98d5415426cfd1f66d7ecdd8bdf7d751880578f07c083a451db55d37c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Censored two-source exploration of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Initially,
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_1(0)=\{0\},
 \quad
 \widehat \mathsf{T}_1(0)=0,
 \quad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_2(0)=\{U_n\},
 \quad
 \widehat \mathsf{T}_2(U_n)=0,
\end{align*}
and every other vertex is unlabelled.

Suppose that $q$ is an exploration time immediately after a vertex addition. For $i\in\{1,2\}$, define the active oriented boundary of label $i$ by
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\partial_i(q)
 :=
 \big\{(a,b):
 a\in\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q),\
 b\notin\widehat\mathcal{A}_1(q)\cup\widehat\mathcal{A}_2(q),\
 \{a,b\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}
 \big\}.
\end{align*}
If an unlabelled vertex remains, the next vertex-addition time is
\begin{align*}
 q^+
 :=
 \min_{i\in\{1,2\}}
 \min_{(a,b)\in\widehat\partial_i(q)}
 \big\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_i(a)+\go_{a,b}\big\}.
\end{align*}
On $\Omega_*$, this minimum has a unique minimizing triple $(i,a,b)$.
At time $q^+$, assign label $i$ to $b$ and set
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathsf{T}_i(b):=q^+,
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q^+)
 :=\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q)\cup\{b\},
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_{3-i}(q^+)
 :=\widehat\mathcal{A}_{3-i}(q).
\end{align*}
The labelled sets remain unchanged between successive vertex-addition times.

An edge is called a \emph{bridge} once its endpoints carry different labels. From that time onward, the bridge is censored: its weight is not tested against any further threshold, and the edge is never used for a subsequent vertex addition. The exploration is run without stopping at the first collision. After all vertices are labelled, the process is held fixed.

In rescaled time, define for $s\geqslant0$
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal{C}_i(s):=\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell ),
 \qquad
 N_i(s):=|\mathcal{C}_i(s)|,
 \quad i=1,2,
\end{align*}
and let the bridge set and its cardinality be
\begin{align*}
	\mathcal{B}_s:=\big\{\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}:u\in\mathcal{C}_1(s),\ v\in\mathcal{C}_2(s)\big\},
 \qquad
 B_s:=|\mathcal{B}_s|.
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.430489+00:00","domain":"first-order PDE","id":"claim_ed54d7f2f7b7a7d96dbbc8a67228d4b6ca38b4b45884e2cb0b37af76ddb0e0a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a first-order quasilinear PDE a(x,y,u) partial u/partial x + b(x,y,u) partial u/partial y = c(x,y,u) for unknown u(x,y), the method of characteristics reduces the PDE to a family of ODEs. Parametrize characteristic curves (x(s),y(s)) together with z(s)=u(x(s),y(s)) along them by dx/ds=a(x,y,z), dy/ds=b(x,y,z), dz/ds=c(x,y,z). Along a solution of this system, u is automatically consistent with the PDE, since the chain rule gives dz/ds = (partial u/partial x)(dx/ds) + (partial u/partial y)(dy/ds) = a(partial u/partial x)+b(partial u/partial y), which equals c(x,y,z) exactly when the PDE holds. Solving the PDE with data prescribed on a noncharacteristic initial curve reduces to solving the characteristic ODEs from each point of that curve and assembling the resulting family into the solution surface, then, where the map from characteristic parameters to (x,y) is invertible, reading off u(x,y). The same idea extends to fully nonlinear first-order PDE F(x,u,Du)=0 via characteristic ODEs derived from F, which also propagate Du along the curves.","status":"unverified"}

 \sum_{n\geq0}b_nr^n\,\mathrm d\log r
 \right)&=b_0e_\rho.
\end{align*}
These are chain maps and
\(\pi_\rho\iota_\rho=\Id\).  The degree \(-1\) operator
\[
 H_\rho
 \left(
 \sum_{n\geq0}b_nr^n\,\mathrm d\log r
 \right)
 =
 \sum_{n\geq1}\frac{b_n}{n+h}r^n,
 \qquad H_\rho|_{\mathcal A}=0,
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \nabla_{\rho,h}H_\rho+
 H_\rho\nabla_{\rho,h}
 =
 \Id-\iota_\rho\pi_\rho.

\end{equation}
Therefore \(\mathsf K_{\rho,h}^\bullet\) is a strong deformation retract
of \(\widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\rho,h}^\bullet\), and
\[
 H^0(\widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\rho,h})=0,
 \qquad
 H^1(\widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\rho,h})\simeq R_0/(h).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:27:32.354372+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed57b4f180cc69b9c9546b15383284d42808233005536637f4e78d3d1a98da54","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Propn PR3 of arXiv:2509.20657, 'Scaling limit for Brownian motions \\\\ on the $l$-level Sierpinski gaskets: \\\\ The fractal '] There exist constants $c_1$ and $\\gamma$, independent of $l$ and $\\lambda$, such that if $f_l:\\mathrm{SG}(l)\\rightarrow\\mathbb{R}$ is a bounded, measurable function, then\n\\[\\left|U^l_\\lambda f_l(x)-U^l_\\lambda f_l(y)\\right|\\leq c_1 \\left(\\tau^l+\\lambda^{-1}\\right) \\left(\\left|x-y\\right|\\vee l^{-1}\\right)^{\\gamma} \\|f_l\\|_\\infty,\\qquad\\forall x,y\\in\\mathrm{SG}(l).\\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.747035+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed581388fad192fa6e9c8864deb4a8c8567e01328d7f749d001c0ddead79debf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 25 (Supercritical shape) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1 / m)$ then $p \, (1-p)^m \,
  (T_{m,p} - m \log{m})$
  converges in law to an exponential distribution with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Recall from Lemma \ref{thm:coupling} that we can
    decompose $p \, (1-p)^m \, (T_{m,p} - m \log{m})$ as
    the sum of independent random variables
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m, 0} - m\log{m})$
    and $p\,(1-p)^m \, (T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$.
    The second random variable~has an exponential limit
    by Theorem~\ref{thm:supercritical}.

    The classical problem has mean
    $\E T_{m, 0} = m\log{m} + O(m)$ and
    variance $\Var(T_{m,0}) = O(m^2)$. Therefore,
    the first random variable's mean is 
    \[
      \E \left[ p\,(1-p)^m\left(T_{m,0} - m\log{m}\right) \right] = p \, (1-p)^m \, O(m) =
      O\left((p\,m) \, e^{-pm}\right) = o(1),
    \]
    and its variance is
    \[
      \Var\left( p\,(1-p)^m\,\left(T_{m, 0} - m\log{m}\right) \right) =
      p^2 \, (1-p)^{2m} \, O(m^2) =
      O\left((p\,m)^2 \, e^{-2pm}\right) = o(1).
    \]
    This implies $p\,(1-p)^m \, (T_{m,0} - m \log{m}) 
    \stackrel{P}{\to} 0$.
    Extend the convergence result using Slutsky's theorem.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:30:07.956801+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed5e3a50a1132e73e1f8165fbbde316114c64f9f9b71bf6396311094cda9f6ba","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:F-function of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Let \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}\) be the semicircle distribution on \([-2,2]\), with
density
\[
    f_{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2\pi}.
\]
We define
\[
    F(x):=2x_+
    =
    \begin{cases}
        2x, & x\in[0,2],\\
        0,  & x\in[-2,0].
    \end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
    P_j(x):=U_j\left(\frac{x}{2}\right),
\]
where \(U_j\) is the \(j\)-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind.  Then
\(\{P_j\}_{j\ge0}\) is an orthonormal basis for
\(L^2([-2,2],\mu_{\mathrm{sc}})\), with \(P_0=1\) and \(P_1=x\).

We write the Chebyshev expansion of \(F\) as
\[
    F(x)=C_F+x+\sum_{j\ge2}b_j \cdot P_j(x),
\]
where
\[
    C_F=b_0=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}}[F(X)]
    =\frac{8}{3\pi},
    \qquad
    b_1=1,
\]
and, for \(j\ge2\),
\[
    b_j\coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu_{\mathrm{sc}}}[F(x)]
\]","status":"unverified"}

Zhao, Theorem 6.5.1 (lopsided local lemma): let A_1, ..., A_n be events and for each i let N(i) ⊆ [n] be such that P(A_i | ∧_{j∈S} Ā_j) ≤ P(A_i) for all S ⊆ [n] \\ (N(i) ∪ {i}) (6.1). If there are x_1, ..., x_n ∈ [0,1) with P(A_i) ≤ x_i Π_{j∈N(i)} (1 − x_j) for all i, then P(none of the events A_i occur) ≥ Π_{i=1}^n (1 − x_i). Corollary 6.5.2: if |N(i)| ≤ d and P(A_i) ≤ p for all i, and ep(d+1) ≤ 1, then with positive probability none of the events occur. A graph with these neighbourhoods is called a negative dependency graph; Zhao's example is the random injection model of Lu and Székely (2007).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent and mean zero","each X_i sub-exponential with finite psi_1 norm K_i","no boundedness and no identical distribution required","c is an absolute constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627795+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eda4180819f0b7157752389f126936b1be16f6ab1c12b592bae8cb80e5ad04c2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent, mean-zero, SUB-EXPONENTIAL random variables, and write K_i for the Orlicz norm ||X_i||_{psi_1} = inf{ s > 0 : E exp(|X_i|/s) <= 2 }. Then there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every t >= 0, P( | sum_{i=1}^N X_i | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - c min( t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N K_i^2 , t / max_i K_i ) ). The bound has TWO regimes and that is intrinsic, not an artefact: for small t the tail is Gaussian with variance proxy sum K_i^2, and for large t it is exponential with rate 1/max_i K_i. No almost sure bound on the summands is assumed, which is what distinguishes this from the classical bounded-summand Bernstein inequality; the price is that the sub-Gaussian regime ends at t of order sum K_i^2 / max K_i rather than continuing forever. Squares of sub-Gaussian variables are sub-exponential, which is why this is the inequality behind chi-square tail bounds and the Hanson-Wright inequality. The constant c is absolute and no attempt should be made to read a specific numerical value out of this statement. [standard; e.g. Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 2.8.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.660216+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_edb1719bbf891ca09a000a2aeddc3b01b83a954c684d37ff15859bbb70863c52","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 24 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let $\mathbf X \in G\Omega_p(V)$. For each $N\in\mathbb N$ and each $1\le i\le d$, let
\(
A_i^N:\Omega\to\mathfrak h_N
\)
be a Hermitian random matrix defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. Assume that the following hold.

First, for every $k\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{1\le i\le d}\sup_{1\le m,l\le N}
\mathbb E\big[|A_i^N(m,l)|^k\big]\le c_A(k)<\infty,
\]
and moreover
\[
\mathbb E[A_i^N(m,l)]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[|A_i^N(m,l)|^2]=1.
\]

Second, there exists $K>0$ such that, for every $r\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{0\le s<t\le T}
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{1}{N^{r/2}}\|A_i^N(m,l)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^r\right]
\le K^r\Gamma\!\left(\frac{r}{2p}+1\right).
\]

Finally, assume that the sigma-algebras
\[
\bigvee_{i=1}^d \sigma(A_i^N(m,l)),
\qquad 1\le m\le l\le N,
\]
are independent, and that
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[A_i^N(m,l)A_j^N(m,l)\right]=0,
\qquad i\ne j.
\]

Define
\[
M^N\in\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb R^d,\mathfrak h_N),
\qquad
M^N(\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^d A_i^N\,\eta^{(i)}.
\]
Let $Z^N(\mathbf X)\in\mathcal D^p([0,T],U(N;\mathbb C))$ denote the solution of
\begin{equation} 
dZ^N(s,t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt N}M^N(d\mathbf X_t)\,Z^N(s,t),
\qquad
Z^N(s,s)=I_N.
\end{equation}

Then, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$ and for $\xi_N \in \mathcal{P}(\mathfrak{h}^d_N)$ denoting the law of the hermitian matrices $A^N_i$, the limit
\[
K(s,t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\,
\mathbb E_{\xi_N}\!\left[\operatorname{Tr}(Z^N(s,t))\right]
\]
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
K(s,t)=\sum_{|L|=0}^\infty i^{|L|}\varphi(L)\,S^{(L)}(\mathbf X)_{s,t}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, \(K\) solves the two-parameter RDE
\begin{equation}
K(s,t)=1-\int_s^t\int_s^r f(K(s,u),K(u,r))\,d\mathbf X_u\,d\mathbf X_r,
\end{equation}
where
\[
f:\mathbb R^2\to \mathrm{Hom}(V\boxtimes V, \mathbb{R}),
\qquad
f(z_1,z_2)[\eta,\xi]=z_1z_2\langle \eta,\xi\rangle_V.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.565836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_edb174ddd52e6e40217e85e1bab471e626931cb7a894a95c484100acbcd94105","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 (Projective-plane incidence class) of arXiv:2608.26516, '2608.26516'] For every integer $m\ge2$, let
\[
    q_m:=2^{m+10},
    \qquad
    N_m:=q_m^2+q_m+1,
    \qquad
    d_m:=q_m+1.
\]
Since $q_m$ is a prime power, a projective plane of order $q_m$ exists.

Take three disjoint vertex sets $V_0^{(m)},V_1^{(m)},V_2^{(m)}$, each of cardinality $N_m$. For every $r\in\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, place an oriented copy of the point-line incidence graph from $V_r^{(m)}$ to $V_{r+1}^{(m)}$. For $v\in V_r^{(m)}$, write $\Gamma^+(v)\subseteq V_{r+1}^{(m)}$ for its outgoing neighborhood and put $\mathsf S(v):=\{v\}\cup\Gamma^+(v)$. The projective-plane axioms imply
\begin{equation}

    |\mathsf S(v)\cap\mathsf S(w)|
    \le 1
    \qquad
    \text{for every pair of distinct vertices }v,w.
\end{equation}
Indeed, two vertices in the same part have exactly one common outgoing neighbor, whereas the cyclic supports of vertices in different parts permit at most one intersection.

For every vertex $v$, create the Boolean-cube block $Z_v:=\{0,1\}^{\Gamma^+(v)}$. The $m$th incidence component and the full domain are
\[
    \CX_m^{\mathrm I}
    :=
    \bigsqcup_{v\in V_0^{(m)}\sqcup V_1^{(m)}\sqcup V_2^{(m)}} Z_v,
    \qquad
    \CX^{\mathrm I}
    :=
    \bigsqcup_{m\ge2}\CX_m^{\mathrm I}.
\]
Introduce a private label $\tau_u$ for every vertex $u$, with all such labels distinct across components. For a vertex $u$ in the $m$th component, define $g_u$ on that component by
\begin{equation}

    g_u(v,z)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \starlabel,
            & u=v,\\
        \starlabel,
            & u\in\Gamma^+(v)\text{ and }z_u=0,\\
        \tau_u,
            & \text{otherwise},
    \end{cases}
    \qquad
    (v,z)\in\CX_m^{\mathrm I},
\end{equation}
and extend $g_u$ by $\dollarlabel$ outside its component. Let $h_{\dollarlabel}$ be the all-$\dollarlabel$ hypothesis, and set
\[
    \Hinc
    :=
    \{h_{\dollarlabel}\}
    \cup
    \{g_u:u\text{ is a vertex in some incidence component}\}.
\]
We call $\Hinc$ the \edefn{projective-plane incidence class}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A_n and A are self-adjoint on a common Hilbert space H","the mode of convergence (strong or norm resolvent) is as in the definition of resolvent convergence","in (a) the function f is continuous and vanishes at infinity","in (b) the function f is continuous and bounded on R","f(A) means the bounded functional calculus supplied by the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091074+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, functional calculus","id":"claim_edb40d994798192517bbbdee299a16a72daef10511a135ab38712d7a8be01de0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A_n and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, with no assumption relating their domains. (a) If A_n -> A in the NORM resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) in operator norm for every continuous f : R -> C vanishing at infinity. (b) If A_n -> A in the STRONG resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) strongly for every BOUNDED CONTINUOUS f : R -> C, where f(A) is given by the functional calculus of the spectral theorem. In particular exp(i t A_n) -> exp(i t A) strongly for every real t, and for a fixed vector the convergence is uniform for t in compact sets. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) 'bounded continuous' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded Borel'. On H = C take A_n = multiplication by 1/n and A = 0 (convergence in every sense) and f the indicator of (0, infinity): then f(A_n) = 1 for every n while f(A) = 0. Convergence of spectral projections therefore needs a separate hypothesis - typically that the endpoints of the interval carry no spectral mass for A - and even then it is only strong convergence. (ii) In (b) one gets strong, never norm, convergence, because strong resolvent convergence does not imply norm resolvent convergence: on l^2 let P_n be the orthogonal projection onto the coordinates with index at least n and set A_n = P_n, A = 0; then A_n -> 0 strongly and in the strong resolvent sense, while the resolvent difference has constant operator norm. (iii) Unbounded f is outside the theorem and the natural statement is false: strong resolvent convergence does not give A_n psi -> A psi, even for psi in every domain (rank-one examples with growing coefficients show this). (iv) Nothing is assumed about domains - that is exactly why the hypothesis is phrased through resolvents rather than as pointwise convergence of the operators.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818122+00:00","domain":"probability, Brownian motion, ergodic theory","id":"claim_edd3ee191057c39ca763758870773c942f09e028e8ea0142c98e648c2215a077","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Burdzy and Scheutzow, Forward Brownian motion (arXiv:1302.6958), Problem 7.5 (p. 26) asks: for any process {X_t, t >= 0} whose law is equivalent to Brownian motion, can one find a random piece to put in front of X so that the new process is a Brownian motion? Our result (id P0032, 2026-09-08): YES - and under absolute continuity rather than equivalence, which is weaker than the problem assumes. The mechanism is a filling-scheme lemma: for theta an invertible ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard Borel space (E, P) and Q = f P, there is an almost surely finite integer N >= 0 with law(theta^N Z) = Q for Z distributed as P. Apply it with E = C_0(R) under two-sided Wiener measure and (theta w)(t) = w(t+1) - w(1), lifting the one-sided density of X's law to two-sided paths; the lemma returns a finite N for which {Z(N+t) - Z(N)} has X's law while {Z(t) - Z(0)} is a Brownian motion whose first N units are exactly the prefix. Verification as the source words it: the filling construction was implemented on a finite ergodic system (Z/n with the +1 shift) for n = 5, 7, 12, 60 with random densities - total accepted mass 1.000000000000 every time, the law of theta^N Z matching f P to about 1e-16, E[N] finite - and the negative control is the informative one, since with a non-ergodic theta exactly half the mass is ever accepted and half survives forever. The L^1 ergodic-theorem step in the infinite-dimensional setting was not verified, only read; it is standard but checked by eye only. NOVELTY IS THE WEAK POINT and the campaign's own proof file volunteers it: the lemma is a filling construction related to classical work of Chacon-Ornstein, Rost and Thorisson - sound mathematics, very likely a known consequence. X's law absolutely continuous with respect to Brownian motion (weaker than the problem's equivalence) theta the unit shift with recentering on two-sided Wiener space, ergodic and invertible","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a measurable geodesic selection","resampling copy independent of the field"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T02:29:08.000000+00:00","domain":"probability (resampling / first-passage percolation)","id":"claim_edd981dfa102db4ee88acfca56d0bbbea4e9975c6dae0d792b6f1c6546fd094e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be the passage time between fixed endpoints and X^L its value after resampling a block L, and let U_L be the event that the geodesic uses an edge of L. If the geodesic avoids L then the original path survives unchanged in the resampled field, so X^L <= X on the complement of U_L. Hence the positive part (X^L - X)^+ vanishes off U_L, and any functional of the form E[1(U_L) f((X^L - X)^+)] with f(0) = 0 equals E[f((X^L - X)^+)] - the indicator carries no information. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:15:16.654974+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ede87e85ab88b50d85698211cc2e4fc95319ba63dc471ed5ec8f3229248bc55a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 27 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Let
\(
  u_0:\Sigma\to S
\)
be an orientation-preserving covering of degree \(d\) between
closed surfaces, and let \(X_g\in\mathcal T(\Sigma)\) be the conformal
structure determined by the domain metric \(g\). Denote by
\(u_0^*\Delta_q\) the pullback measured foliation on \(\Sigma\). Then
\begin{equation}

  \mathscr E_{\Delta_q}(u_0)
  =
  \frac12\,
  \operatorname{Ext}_{X_g}\!\left(u_0^*\Delta_q\right).
\end{equation}
More explicitly, write the pullback  multicurve as
\(u_0^*\Delta_q=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{a=1}^{r_i}\widehat\delta_{i,a}\). Let
\(\widehat\Phi=\Phi_{u_0^*\Delta_q,X_g}\) be the Hubbard--Masur

actual conformal modulus, then
\begin{equation}

  \mathscr E_{\Delta_q}(u_0)
  =
  \frac12\int_{X_g}|\widehat\Phi|
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{a=1}^{r_i}

\end{equation}

Suppose, in addition, that the  conformal structure on $\Sigma$ is the pullback
of the initial target structure, namely \(X_g=u_0^*X_0\in T(\Sigma)\). Then
\begin{equation}

  \mathscr E_{\Delta_q}(u_0)
  =

  \sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac1{M_i}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:49:15.475043+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_edf32a2bac89d6234b6fb24909230c5760fa4e020b225f32bac46de19693cda4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The functor $((eq:ext-orth-spc of the paper))$ is topologically enriched.
    \begin{proof}
        Recall that mapping spaces in enriched functor categories are topologized as a subspace of the product. By the universal property of the latter, the claim therefore amounts to saying that
        \[
            \textbf{\textup{maps}}_{\cat{$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}}(X,Y)\to\textbf{\textup{maps}}_{\textbf{\textup{Top}}}(\overline{X}(V),\overline{Y}(V))
        \]
        is continuous for all $X,Y\in\cat{$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}$ and $V\in{\widehat{{\smash{\textbf{\textup{L}}}\vphantom{t}}\kern-1.75pt}\kern1.75pt}$. Adjoining over and plugging in the definition of $\overline{X}(V)$, this is equivalent to continuity of
        \[X(U)\times\textbf{\textup{maps}}_{\cat{$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Top}}(X,Y)\to \overline{Y}(V)\]
        for all finite-dimensional $U\subset V$. But this map is simply the composite
        \[
            X(U)\times\textbf{\textup{maps}}(X,Y)\xrightarrow{\;X(U)\times\ev_U\;}X(U)\times\textbf{\textup{maps}}(X(U),Y(U))\xrightarrow{\;\ev\;} Y(U)\xrightarrow{\;\;}\overline{Y}(V),
        \]
        and each of these maps is evidently continuous.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\begin{equation}
 [\gamma_u]
 =
 \sum_{\alpha=1}^{\mu}
 C^{\mathrm{Betti}}_{u\alpha}[\Gamma_\alpha].
 
\end{equation}
Consequently
\[
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}\in
 \operatorname{Mat}_{N\times\mu}(\mathbb Z)
\]
is locally constant on \(\mathfrak C\).  If the representatives are
transverse, then
\begin{equation}
 C^{\mathrm{Betti}}_{u\alpha}
 =
 \#_{\mathrm{or}}
 \bigl(\gamma_u\pitchfork\check\Gamma_\alpha\bigr),
 
\end{equation}
the finite signed intersection count.  Its rank, integral kernel,
cokernel, and elementary divisors are therefore computed exactly by the

Across a Stokes wall, write the change of integral descending basis as
\[
 \boldsymbol\Gamma^+

 S_{\mathrm{top}}\boldsymbol\Gamma^-,
 \qquad
 S_{\mathrm{top}}\in\operatorname{GL}_\mu(\mathbb Z).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^+
 =
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}^-S_{\mathrm{top}}^{-1}.
 
\end{equation}
Along a generic path crossing successively walls with matrices
\(S_1,\ldots,S_k\),
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}(\lambda_1)
 =
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}(\lambda_0)
 S_1^{-1}\cdots S_k^{-1}.
 
\end{equation}

If an analytically normalised thimble frame is related to the integral
frame by
\[
 \boldsymbol\Gamma^{\mathrm{an}}
 =
 G\,\boldsymbol\Gamma^{\mathrm{top}},
 \qquad
 G\in\operatorname{GL}_\mu(\C),
\]
then its selected-cycle coordinate matrix is
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{sel}}
 =
 C_{\mathrm{Betti}}G^{-1}.
 
\end{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:19:00.881825+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee6fbfab0d5fae71ae7efeb21249e1bcdbf67dba6d0c494f66bb0e4850ff9acf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 40 (Optional stopping for nonnegative supermartingales) of arXiv:2608.20337, 'Information on trajectories:\\ martingales and random times'] Let $(M_t)$ be a nonnegative supermartingale and $\tau$ a stopping time (possibly infinite, with $M_\infty := \liminf_{t\to\infty} M_t$).
Then
\[
  \E[M_\tau] \leq M_0 .
\]
If $(M_t)$ is a nonnegative martingale, the matching equality $\E[M_\tau] = M_0$ holds in each of the following cases.

Integrability of $M_\tau$ alone does \emph{not} suffice: a nonnegative martingale can leak mass to $\{\tau = \infty\}$, so that $\E[M_\tau] < M_0$ even though $\E[M_\tau] < \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["One FCFS server","Poisson arrival rate lambda>0","Independent exponential service rate mu>lambda","Deterministic nonnegative setup tau and grace g","Setup is never cancelled; setup arrivals queue"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:07:30.221932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee901e9ab6079a52e8000f515d63eeed51c6cfe36449a529fc20f5c928a510cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Consider one FCFS server with Poisson arrival rate lambda>0 and independent exponential service rate mu>lambda. After becoming empty it remains on for deterministic grace g in [0,infinity], then switches off. A cold arrival triggers deterministic setup tau>=0, which is never cancelled; arrivals during setup wait. Put p=exp(-lambda g), x=lambda tau, rho=lambda/mu and y=p/(1+xp), with p=0 at g=infinity. The stationary mean queueing wait is lambda/[mu(mu-lambda)] + tau(1+x/2)y. If busy, on-idle, off and setup powers are B,I,O,U, average power is rho B+(1-rho)I+(1-rho)[O+xU-(1+x)I]y. Hence varying the grace period traces an affine waiting-power curve. The formula includes arrivals during setup and the subsequent busy period. It addresses k=1 and does not claim the many-server frontier or optimality among other policies.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.851897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee995522ed1e15c70f74b190d4e70387624f9742de07d15197ca3b2f7a63597a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 (Hard edge, \(q=1\)) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Fix \(K\in\mathbb{N}\) and an integer \(\alpha > K\).
Let \(T - N = \alpha\).
For each \(s\in\{0,\dots,K\}\), let \(\{\lambda^{(s)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N+s}\) denote the spectrum of the matrix \(X_{N+s}^\top X_{N+s}\),
and define the point process
\[
\Theta_{N}^{(s)} \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N+s} \delta_{\,4N\,\lambda_{j}^{(s)}}.
\]
Then the process \(\big(\Theta_{N}^{(s)}\big)_{s=0}^{K}\) forms a Markov chain in \(s\) and converges in distribution to the Markov chain driven by the operator \(\mathcal{T}\).
The limiting point process of eigenvalues
\(
\Theta^{(s)} \;=\; \lim_{N\to\infty} \Theta_{N}^{(s)}
\)
is the \emph{Bessel point process} of parameter~\(\alpha\), describing the universal statistics at the hard edge of the spectrum. \cite{forrester1993hard,tracy1994bessel,forrester2010log} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:45:10.120657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eeb1ede202905a69c010b7a27531edd642bba0c9a3f90f02e0930060574d855c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:basic_properties_of_PPPs of arXiv:2505.07145, 'Nonamenable Poisson zoo'] Let $\mathcal{X} = \sum_{i \in I} \delta_{(x,H)_i} \sim \mathcal{Q}_{\nu}^\lambda$ be as in Definition (def:Poisson_zoo_as_PPP of the paper) and given any $A \in \mathcal{Z}$ introduce the restricted measure $\nu_A(\cdot) := \nu ( \cdot \cap A)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.527446+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eec33edf4ae78009e0b5b174b9c69aad0c4d069c0fef2aa28876ddd785928871","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 8 of arXiv:2604.01748, 'Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$'] \begin{itemize}
   \item[(D1)] Let $b_{n} = n (\log n)^{-2}$ and $M = (\log n)^{2}.$ We divide the time interval $[0,n]$ into $M$ subintervals of equal length ($= b_{n}$) as follows. Let 
$$I^{1} (j) = \big[ n - j b_{n}, n - (j-1) b_{n} \big] =: [t^{1}_{j}, t^{1}_{j-1}] \ \ \ \text{ for \ \  $j =1, 2, \cdots , M$.} $$
 Note that $ 0 = t^{1}_{M} < t^{1}_{M-1} < \cdots < t^{1}_{1} < t^{1}_{0} = n. $

Similarly, we divide the time interval $[n,2n]$ in the same way as follows. Let 
$$I^{2} (j) = \big[ n + (j-1) b_{n}, n + j b_{n} \big] =: [t^{2}_{j-1}, t^{2}_{j}] \ \ \ \text{ for \ \  $j =1, 2, \cdots , M$.}$$
 Note that $ n= t^{2}_{0} < t^{2}_{1} < \cdots < t^{2}_{M-1} < t^{2}_{M} = 2n.  $

\item[(D2)] We set 

$$ L^{1} (j) = \text{len} \, \Big( \text{LE}^{\ast} \big( S [t^{1}_{j}, t^{1}_{j-1}  ] \big) \Big) \ \ \ \text{and } \ \ \ L^{2} (j) = \text{len} \, \Big( \text{LE}^{\ast} \big( S [t^{2}_{j-1}, t^{2}_{j}  ] \big) \Big). $$

As in (20) of \cite{DS-SW-4d}, we let 
$$ L^{\ast} = \max \big\{ j + k \ : \ I^{1} (j) \leftrightarrow I^{2} (k) \big\} $$
denote the size of the longest intersection. Here, for two intervals $I, J \subset [0, \infty)$, we write 
$$ I \leftrightarrow J \ \ \text{ if } \ \ \{ S(i) \ : \ i \in I \} \cap \{ S(j) \ : \ j \in J \} \neq \emptyset.$$
Clearly, $ 2 \le L^{\ast} \le 2M $. 

\item[(D3)] Set 
$$ L_{n}' = \text{len} \, \Big( \text{LE}^{\ast} \big( S[n,2n] \big) \Big). $$
Note that $L_{n}$ and $L_{n}'$ have the same distribution.

\item[(D4)] A time $k \in [0,n]$ is called a cut time (up to $n$) if $S[0,k] \cap S[k+1,n] = \emptyset$.

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.359645+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eec83666d4540435c0cbc9338be88813d17adac64ba25bc87e580084160f651f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] In Example (ex:different-stability-in-each-environment of the paper), the mixed process is exponentially ergodic for any choice of $\kappa>0$.
\begin{proof}
    Fix $\kappa>0$, and consider the function defined by
    \[
        h_\kappa(x,i)=\begin{cases}
            90 x^{\kappa/3} & i=1\\
            57 x^{\kappa/3} & i=2
        \end{cases}.
    \]
    Notice that
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal L_\kappa h_\kappa(x,1)
        &=(2x+1)(90(x+1)^{\kappa/3}-90x^{\kappa/3})
        +x(90(x-1)^{\kappa/3}-90x^{\kappa/3})
        +\kappa(57x^{\kappa/3}-90x^{\kappa/3})\\
        &=(2x+1)(30\kappa x^{\kappa/3-1}+o(x^{\kappa/3-1}))
        -x(30\kappa x^{\kappa/3-1}+o(x^{\kappa/3-1}))
        -33\kappa x^{\kappa/3}\\
        &=-3\kappa x^{\kappa/3}+o(x^{\kappa/3}),
    \end{align*}
    and similarly
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal L_\kappa h_\kappa(x,2)
        &=(x+1)(57(x+1)^{\kappa/3}-57x^{\kappa/3})
        +3x(57(x-1)^{\kappa/3}-57x^{\kappa/3})
        +\kappa(90x^{\kappa/3}-57x^{\kappa/3})\\
        &=(x+1)(19\kappa x^{\kappa/3-1}+o(x^{\kappa/3-1}))
        -3x(19\kappa x^{\kappa/3-1}+o(x^{\kappa/3-1}))
        +33\kappa x^{\kappa/3}\\
        &=-5\kappa x^{\kappa/3}+o(x^{\kappa/3}).
    \end{align*}
    The desired result follows from Theorem (thm:Lyapunov-exponential-ergodicity of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.715881+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ef095a49f503ad492533cca63bb96ad7bee3cc63a6898959f6f9783656701479","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Truth lemma of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $L \supseteq \textbf{FIK}$,
  then for any $x = (\Gamma_x, \Delta_x) \in W_L^*$ and any $\varphi \in \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$,
  $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \varphi$ iff $\varphi \in \Gamma_x$.
  \begin{proof}
    We use an induction on the construction of $\varphi$.
    We shall only consider the cases for $\to$, $\Box$, and $\Diamond$, as the other cases are trivial.

    If $\varphi = \psi \to \chi$, then we shall prove it in both directions.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[($\Rightarrow$)]
            Suppose $\psi \to \chi \notin \Gamma_x$, then by Proposition (prop:truth-lemma-imp-left of the paper),
            there is $x' = (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x') \in W_L^*$ such that $x \leq^* x'$, $\psi \in \Gamma_x'$, and $\chi \in \Delta_x'$.
            Here, $x' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$ and $x' \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \chi$ by the induction hypothesis.
            Therefore, $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi \to \chi$.
      \item[($\Leftarrow$)]
            Suppose $\psi \to \chi \in \Gamma_x$ and take any $x' = (\Gamma_x', \Delta_x') \in W_L^*$ such that $x \leq^* x' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi$,
            then $\psi \in \Gamma_x'$ by the induction hypothesis, and $\psi \to \chi \in \Gamma_x \subseteq \Gamma_x'$ by the definition of $\leq^*$,
            so $\chi \in \Gamma_x'$ by Corollary (cor:saturation of the paper).
            Therefore, $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_{\mathfrak{M}_L^*} \psi \to \chi$.
    \end{itemize}

    If $\varphi = \Box \psi$, then we shall prove it in both directions.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[($\Rightarrow$)]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.018469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ef0e055983c45f9e84e4f03798dc1e5f1c33166be79eb5ba51218262b537df3c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(n\ge2\).  Every tangent space at \(\xi\) is a metric soliton
flow with a distinguished probability measure.  Its time-\((-1)\) model
has the following properties.
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Metric-flow conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
series=limitingpackage]
\item The regular locus \(\mathcal R\) is connected and dense,
\(d|_{\mathcal R}\) is its intrinsic length distance, and \(Z\) is a
complete locally compact length space equal to the metric completion of
\(\mathcal R\).
\item There is a smooth function \(f\) on \(\mathcal R\) for which
\begin{equation}
 \Rc_g+\nabla^2f=\frac12g\qquad\text{on }\mathcal R;
\end{equation}
the distinguished probability measure satisfies
\begin{equation}
 d\mathfrak m=(4\pi)^{-n}e^{-f}\,dV_g\quad\text{on }\mathcal R,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z\setminus\mathcal R)=0,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z)=1,
\end{equation}
and \(\mathfrak m\) has finite second moment.
\item The tangent space is an exact self-similar metric soliton flow.
On regular convergence charts, in time-compatible gauges, the rescaled
metrics and distinguished densities converge smoothly to \(g\) and the
positive density in \eqref{sp:eq:measure}.
\item For every compact \(K\subset Z\) and every \(p\in(2,4)\), the
zero extension of \(r_{\rm Rm}\) is one-Lipschitz and
\begin{equation}
 \Vol_g\bigl(\{r_{\rm Rm}<\varepsilon\}\cap K\cap\mathcal R\bigr)
 \le C_{K,p}\varepsilon^p,
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<1;
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{K\"ahler conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
resume=limitingpackage]
\item The regular soliton \((\mathcal R,g,J)\) is K\"ahler, \(J\) is
parallel and time invariant, and the rescaled complex structures converge
smoothly to \(J\) on regular convergence charts.
\item If \(n=2\), then \(Z\) is a K\"ahler orbifold and
\(\Sing Z\) consists of isolated orbifold points.
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Complex-analytic conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
resume=limitingpackage]
\item The space \(Z\) is a normal klt complex space.  Its analytic and
metric topologies agree, and its analytic and metric regular loci
coincide.  The regular K\"ahler form extends locally across \(\Sing Z\)
as a positive current with bounded potential.  Every point has a local
closed analytic embedding \(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) such
that, on \(V\cap\mathcal R\),
\begin{equation}
 \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}|_V.
\end{equation}
\item The function \(f\) extends uniquely to a locally Lipschitz function
on \(Z\).  The flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete, preserves
\(\mathcal R\), and extends to a one-parameter group of biholomorphisms
of \(Z\).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

\[

where each $\mathbf{L}_{t,s}$ has $K$ column blocks $\mathbf{L}_{t,s}^{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$. For $a \in \mathbb{R}^{Td}$ and $\mathbf{L} \in \mathscr{L}_K(T, d)$, define the filtered process
\[

{"assumptions":["Deterministic initial coordinates with h_j e0,j squared=j^-gamma","Bt mutually independent fresh Gaussian inputs with covariance diag(j^-alpha)","Finite expected risk at deterministic t; finite-variance independent centered label noise","Updates lie in the span of observed inputs; data-dependent coefficients allowed","Independent review pending; optional optimal-step corollary depends on unaudited C02/C03."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:59:03.292447+00:00","domain":"stochastic optimization","id":"claim_ef32f8b8a5c7f1a6674c7630d45b5382c9f5f570bddb934911b55c4caa2768ce","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF (UNAUDITED), w741-T422-C06 v1. Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 2: a finite-sample-span upper confidence bound

Status: proof (unaudited), C06 v1. The constants below are explicit but the
bound is not asserted to have the sharp epsilon exponent of a typical noise
scale. The fixed-time theorem does not depend on C02 or C03; its final optional
optimal-step corollary inherits their unaudited status.

## Statement

Use the fresh Gaussian online least-squares model: H=diag(h_j),
h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1, deterministic initial errors satisfying
h_j e_0,j^2=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Gaussian L2 predictions are used if the
coefficient vector is not in ordinary l2, as explained in model_conventions.md.
Labels have independent centered noise of finite variance sigma2>=0.
Each of t>=1 deterministic steps uses B>=1 independent fresh samples,
B an integer. A fixed positive step suffices. More generally, the proof
only requires that every update be a finite linear combination of that
step's input vectors, that the Bt inputs remain mutually independent with
law N(0,H), and that expected risk at t is finite.

For ell=1,2 define

    V(e)=sum_j h_j e_j^2,
    W_(ell+1)(e)=sum_j h_j^(ell+1)e_j^2,
    v_t=E V(e_t), Z_r=zeta(r),
    R_ell(e)=1+Z_(ell alpha)(V(e)+sigma2)/W_(ell+1)(e).

These are the single-example instantaneous noise scales: ell=1 is unweighted,
ell=2 is Hessian-weighted. Fix confidence parameter theta in (0,1), and put

    K=Bt, d=K+1,
    A_d=sum_(j=1)^d e_0,j^2/h_j=sum_(j=1)^d j^(2alpha-gamma)>0,
    L_den=h_d^(ell+2) A_d theta^2/(16d)>0.

Then

    P(W_(ell+1)(e_t)>=L_den)>=1-theta/2.                  (S1)

Consequently, with probability at least 1-theta, e_t!=0 and

    1+Z_(ell alpha) <= R_ell(e_t)
      <=1+[16d Z_(ell alpha)/(h_d^(ell+2)A_d theta^2)]
                   [2v_t/theta+sigma2].                  (S2)

The probability of e_t=0 is zero. If t is a finite first EXPECTED-risk
hit v_t<=epsilon Z_gamma, substitute that upper bound for v_t in (S2).
The hitting index is deterministic here; a realized-risk stopping time
requires an additional argument.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:14:57.719523+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ef5880d642179271a2a05bcc6de6a1b9a16fae55691fc18aeb34dde63f8df92b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defin def:spect of arXiv:2605.31054, 'On the empirical spectral distribution of matrix perpetuities'] \ 
    For any $N\times N$ real  random matrix ${\mathbf Y}$ with eigenvalues $(\lambda_k({\mathbf Y}))_{k=1}^N$, we define the empirical spectral distribution and the expected empirical spectral distribution by $\hat{\mu}_{{\mathbf Y}}$ and $ \mu_{{\mathbf Y}}$ respectively, by 
    \[
    \hat{\mu}_{\mathbf Y} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N \delta_{\lambda_k({\mathbf Y})},\qquad \mu_{{\mathbf Y}}={\mathbb E}[\hat{\mu}_{\mathbf Y}],

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean zero, variance one (finite second moment suffices for the almost-sure convergence in the Bai-Silverstein form)","the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","Sigma and Z independent (Sigma may be random)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:53:48.737960+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_ef9d87ff35f4c090aed907a91632374e92ff38ec27c2bf7bbb3585b46a41183e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X = Z\\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \\times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \\frac{1}{n}X^T X$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.357815+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_efb2b986b6fe624f2e4292375b08dfc23949dd7d8ed64d88f7f754414b70d840","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop evanescent of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] Let $X$ be a CTMC on $\mathbb S\subseteq \mathbb Z^d$, and let $x\in\mathbb S$. Then $x$ is evanescent for $X$ iff when started from state $x$ with positive probability the process never enters a recurrent state.
\begin{proof}[Proof Sketch]
    First, assume that $\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*}{X(t)}_{\ell^1}\to\infty$ occurs with positive probability. Given this event, the process almost surely does not enter a recurrent state because if a recurrent state is visited once then it is a.s.~visited infinitely many times [Norris_1997].
    
    For the reverse implication, suppose that $\liminf\limits_{t\to\infty}\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*}{X(t)}_{\ell^1}$ is finite with probability one. Note that for all $R\in\mathbb R$, the event that the process ever enters a recurrent state contains, up to a set of measure zero, the event that $\liminf\limits_{t\to\infty}\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*}{X(t)}_{\ell^1}\le R$. Indeed, otherwise we could use the fact that $\{y\in\mathbb Z^d:\@ifstar{\oldnorm}{\oldnorm*} y_{\ell^1}\le R\}$ is finite to conclude that there existed a specific transient state $y$ which was visited infinitely often with positive probability, contradicting transience of $y$. Sending $R\to\infty$, the result follows from continuity of probability. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134016+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_efbdb008ccb6e350f19afa4b831a7f5eb8be29254ef907e1f0e1aedf7377ba81","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Then M(q) = sum over nonempty S of [1 - (1 - q)^|S|] w_S = Var(f) - J(1 - q), with J the Bernoulli reveal profile, and M(q) = (1/2) E[(f(X) - f(X^(A_q)))^2], where X^(A) redraws X_A independently from its own law. For every r >= 1, (-1)^(r+1) M^(r)(q) = sum_{k=r}^n (k)_r (1 - q)^(k - r) W_k >= 0 with (k)_r = k(k - 1)...(k - r + 1); so M is increasing and concave, M'(0) = sum_k k W_k = sum_i E Var(f | X_{-i}), and the derivatives at any q determine the spectrum. \[
K_{\mathrm{fac}}^N(q)

\right\}\,du

and

The derivative identities used below require only finite moments: for every $n\ge1$ with $\mathbb{E}[C(\mathbb{R})^n]<\infty$ and bounded compactly supported $f_0,\ldots,f_{n-1}$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} f_j(t_j)\,

whereas
\[

\mathbb{E}\sum_{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}\in C}

Equivalently, for $n\ge2$,
\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:58:01.581348+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f005a16c2578467f8120ac4ffbda0cca52795b28e495fd11270552b131d1bf53","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 55 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Fix $N,n\ge1$, $K_{\rm feat}<\infty$, $\beta>0$, and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.516900+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f01dc5eef7bf6f6e35fb169c089c433a1ee54ef7f465d58e7e53f8cc31f2d4ee","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm conformal invariance aut H of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] For conformal map $\tau \in {\rm Aut}(\mathbb{H})$, the drift term

   \log(\psi)-\log(\psi \circ \tau)+\frac{\kappa-6}{2\kappa}\sum_i \log(\tau'(z_i)) = F(\tau,u)

    and $F$ satisfies the following functional equation:
   \begin{equation}

   \end{equation}

    \[
   \psi_2 = g(u) \cdot \psi_1.
    \]

    \begin{itemize}

    \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542735+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f03dd267f4dbe993abe345addd53bd73d98a6535068e27ed077b61bcdaa98a66","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In BOND percolation on a graph G with parameter p in [0,1], each edge is declared open with probability p and closed otherwise, independently; P_p denotes the resulting product measure on {0,1}^{E(G)}. The open cluster C(x) of a vertex x is the set of vertices reachable from x through open edges. Write theta(p) = P_p( |C(0)| = infinity ) for a fixed origin. Coupling all parameters on a common family of independent uniform variables - edge e open at level p exactly when U_e <= p - shows theta is nondecreasing, so the CRITICAL PROBABILITY p_c(G) = sup{ p : theta(p) = 0 } = inf{ p : theta(p) > 0 } is well defined. SITE percolation is defined analogously with vertices; the two have different critical values on the same graph, and p_c^{bond} <= p_c^{site} on any graph. On Z^d with d >= 2 one has 0 < p_c < 1, with the explicit elementary bounds 1/(2d-1) <= p_c^{bond}(Z^d) < 1. The value is known exactly only in special cases, most famously p_c^{bond}(Z^2) = 1/2. Whether theta(p_c) = 0 in every dimension is a celebrated open problem: it is known for d = 2 (Harris and Kesten) and, by lace-expansion methods, in high dimensions - Hara and Slade for large d, later reduced to d >= 11 by Fitzner and van der Hofstad - and it was still open for the intermediate dimensions 3 <= d <= 10 at the time this node was written. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Chapters 1 and 8]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d, d >= 2","F(0) < p_c(d), so the time constant is a norm and the shape is bounded","E min{t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d} < infinity, equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity for Y the minimum of 2d independent copies of tau_e - and this condition is necessary, not just sufficient","no curvature, strict convexity or differentiability of B_nu is asserted; those are open"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f04b0c4ede53c43a4b671c5940e1cf1f891850e48c1cc9a9a34d6b9355fd1e2f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, d >= 2, with edge-weight law nu. Assume the two conditions (i) E min{ t_1^d, ..., t_{2d}^d } < infinity, where the t_i are 2d independent copies of tau_e - equivalently E[Y^d] < infinity where Y is the MINIMUM of 2d copies, the two being the same because x -> x^d is increasing on [0, infinity) - and (ii) F(0) < p_c(d). Let B(t) = {x : T(0, x) <= t}, the random ball. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c the time constant vanishes (Kesten) and B_nu is all of R^d; zero-weight edges percolate when F(0) > p_c, but at F(0) = p_c they do not in d = 2 or in high dimensions, so it is the vanishing time constant, not percolation of zero-weight edges, that unbounds the shape. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:28.085608+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0573dd07fb8534f7fee514596b37ff67d349a9ebfd80976a37683e5bb0670da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 13 of arXiv:2607.13849, 'Rearranged Stochastic Heat Equation with an Entropy Gradient Structure'] For $\delta >0$, let $(X_t, W_t,\zeta_t,{\mathscr J}_t)_{0 \le t \le T}$ be a weak limit in $\mathbb{D}([0,T], \mathcal{H}^{-1}_{\mathrm{Sym}}(\mathbb{S})\times L^2_{\mathrm{Sym}}(\mathbb{S})

Moreover,
    $$\mathbb{E}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:28.476762+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f064cd342b4c03d2daf177636f53a327072c70d4a37c0d79a334181de191517a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 83 (Reconstruction-lattice tensor--Pfaffian transfer) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let $E$ be a separable real Hilbert space, fix $2\le\sigma<\infty$ and
$\rho>0$, and let $A\in\Sch_2(E)$ be a strongly measurable random
skew-adjoint operator.

\emph{(a) Decoupled branch.}  For every $N\ge1$, let
$I_N^{\rm dec}$ be a countable two-sided block system and let
$\mathsf E_N^{\rm dec}(I_N^{\rm dec})$ be an order-continuous
$\sigma$-reconstruction lattice with reconstruction constant
$C_N^{\rm dec}$.  Let $(K_{2N;i})_{i\in I_N^{\rm dec}}$ be order-$2N$
block coefficients with input $\C$ and output $\wedge^{2N}E$, and put
\[
 b_{2N;i}^{\rm dec}:=\Prof_{2N,\sigma}(K_{2N;i}),
 \qquad
 R_{2N}^{\rm dec}:=C_N^{\rm dec}
 \big\|(b_{2N;i}^{\rm dec})_{i\in I_N^{\rm dec}}\big\|_{\mathsf E_N^{\rm dec}}.
\]
Assume $(b_{2N;i}^{\rm dec})_i\in\mathsf E_N^{\rm dec}$, let
$\mathbf K_{2N}:=\sum_iK_{2N;i}\in\mathfrak T_{2N,\sigma}$ be the
reconstructed coefficient, realize all decoupled evaluations on one common
product Gaussian space, and set
$\Xi_{2N}:=\cT_{\mathbf K_{2N}}^{(2N)}$.  Suppose that, on one event of
probability one,
\begin{equation}

 (\alpha_A)^{\wedge N}=\frac{N!}{2^N}\Xi_{2N}
 \qquad(N\ge1).
\end{equation}
If
\begin{equation}

 \mathcal L_{\rho,\sigma}^{\rm dec}
 :=\sup_{N\ge1}N^{1/\rho}(R_{2N}^{\rm dec})^{1/N}<\infty,
\end{equation}
then, for every finite $p\ge1$,
\begin{equation}

 \bigl\|\|A\|_{\Sch_{\rho,\infty}}\bigr\|_{L^p}
 \le C_\rho(1+p+\sigma)\mathcal L_{\rho,\sigma}^{\rm dec}.
\end{equation}

\emph{(b) Same-field branch.}  For every $N\ge1$, let
$I_N^{\rm W}$ be a countable two-sided block system and let
$\mathsf E_N^{\rm W}(I_N^{\rm W})$ be an order-continuous
$\sigma$-reconstruction lattice with reconstruction constant
$C_N^{\rm W}$.  Let $(L_{2N;i})_{i\in I_N^{\rm W}}$ be symmetric block
kernels, all evaluated by one real isonormal Gaussian process, and put
\[
 b_{2N;i}^{\rm W}
 :=\Prof_{2N,\sigma}(\Dec_{2N}L_{2N;i}),
 \qquad
 R_{2N}^{\rm W}:=C_N^{\rm W}
 \big\|(b_{2N;i}^{\rm W})_{i\in I_N^{\rm W}}\big\|_{\mathsf E_N^{\rm W}}.
\]
Assume $(b_{2N;i}^{\rm W})_i\in\mathsf E_N^{\rm W}$, let
$\mathbf L_{2N}:=\sum_iL_{2N;i}\in\mathfrak W_{2N,\sigma}$ be the
reconstructed same-field coefficient, and set
$\Xi_{2N}:=I_{2N}(\mathbf L_{2N})$.  Retain
\eqref{eq:reconstruction-lattice-pfaffian-compatibility}.  If
\begin{equation}

 \mathcal L_{\rho,\sigma}^{\rm W}
 :=\sup_{N\ge1}N^{1+1/\rho}(R_{2N}^{\rm W})^{1/N}<\infty,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}

 \bigl\|\|A\|_{\Sch_{\rho,\infty}}\bigr\|_{L^p}
 \le C_\rho(1+p+\sigma)\mathcal L_{\rho,\sigma}^{\rm W},
 \qquad 1\le p<\infty.
\end{equation}
Both estimates are dimension free.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:23.338984+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f078cf83609ed2d9bd2aed521d1d5181cc133405cb3d1b3bf45468da67038da4","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 15 of arXiv:2512.05687, '$L^p$-Boltzmann-Gibbs principle \\ via Littlewood-Paley-Stein inequality'] (Iteration lemma,
cf.\ Lemma 5.5 of \cite{BFS})
Let $p\ge 4$ and let $f$ be a local $L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})$ function on
$\mathcal{X}_N$ for some $p'>p$ depending only on $\eta_{\La_{\ell_0}}$ 
such that $\tilde f(u_0)=0$ and $\tilde f'(u_0)=0$.
Then, there exists a constant $C=C(u_0, \ell_0)>0$ such that, for $\ell \geq \ell_0$,

\begin{align}  
&E_{\mu_{u_0}}\Big[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\Big|\int_0^t\sum_{x\in{\T_N}} h(s,x) \\

\int_0^T \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in{\T_N}} |h(t,x)|^p dt.
\notag
\end{align}
On the other hand, when only $\tilde f(u_0)=0$ is known, we have

\notag \\
&\hskip 10mm  \leq \ CT^{(p-2)/2} N^{-p/2} \ell^p \|f\|^p_{L^{p'}(\mu_{u_0})}
\int_0^T \frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in{\T_N}} |h(t,x)|^p dt.

\end{align}","status":"unverified"}
