{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:46:25.368236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0a55cb3301770f006ba55fd2ddd09f040b5e72894962c83a8b49b7e136449cf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop CLEcoupling1 of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Consider a zero boundary GFF $\Phi_D$ on $D$ and the nested CLE$_4$ determined by exploring consecutively two-valued sets $A_{-2\lambda, 2\lambda}$. Then, for all boundary conditions $v \in 2\lambda \mathbb{Z}$, we have the following properties in coupling with $\Phi_D + v$: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The labels $s_\ell \in \{-2\lambda, 2\lambda\}$ attached to each loop $\ell \in \text{CLE}_4^{n}$ are i.i.d. symmetric conditionally on the loops, 
and in terms of distributions,
$$\sum_{\Gamma \in \text{CLE}^{\rm nest}_4}(v1_{\Gamma \text{ outermost}}+s_\Gamma)
\1_{\operatorname{Int}(\Gamma)} = \Phi_D +v.$$
\item 
We assign the height $v$ to the boundary of the domain. Thereby, each gasket in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ can be uniquely attached a height corresponding to the sum of labels of loops $s_\ell$ in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ strictly surrounding this gasket, including the boundary of the domain. If this sum equals $h$, then we say that the gasket is at height $h$. Equivalently we can attach a height to each loop in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ by considering the sum of labels of loops surrounding and including this loop and the boundary. This way the height of the gasket corresponds to the height of its outermost loop.   
\item In this coupling, conditionally on the loops, for each $z \in D$, the heights $h$ of the gaskets in 
CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ surrounding $z$ form a simple symmetric random walk $S^z(m)$ with step-size $2\lambda$ and starting point $v$. 
\item For $v \neq 0$, consider $A_0$, the first passage set of $\Phi_D + v$ with boundary values $0$. Then $A_0$ is almost surely equal to taking the connected component of the boundary of the closed union of all gaskets of non-zero height. In particular, for each $z \in D \cap \mathbb{Q}^2$, the boundary of the connected component of 
$D \setminus A_0$ containing $z$ is constructed as follows: we consider the nested loop sequence surrounding $z$ until the first time that a loop of height $0$ appears and that is the boundary. 
\item Further, the sign excursion sets of $\Phi_D + v$ have the following description using nested CLE$_4$: we consider the closed union of all the gaskets in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ of height different than zero. The connected components have then the law of sign excursion sets.
\item Finally, the dual of the excursion sets, i.e. the complement of the excursion sets in $D$, is given by the disjoint union of all the gaskets of height $0$ in the nested CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$. 
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:47:32.871096+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0afe268d180a6d8173a1598b426836aab1df7356089b0d17665fa3e0f8edcc5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 (Chebotarev density theorem) of arXiv:2609.02444, 'The Hasse norm principle for $A_4$-quartic extensions of global function fields'] Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\phi \colon X \to Y\) a \(G\)-torsor defined over \(\FF_q\), and \(\Phi \subset G\) a conjugacy class.
  \begin{enumerate}
      \item  Suppose that \(X\) is geometrically connected.
  Then
  \[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{|\{y \in Y(\FF_{q^m}) \mid \varphi(y) = \Phi\}|}{|Y(\FF_{q^m})|} = \frac{|\Phi|}{|G|}. \]
  \item More generally, suppose that \(Y\) is geometrically connected and \(X\) has \(r\) geometric components, all defined over \(\FF_q\).
  Then
  \[ \lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{|\{y \in Y(\FF_{q^{m}}) \mid \varphi(y) = \Phi\}|}{|Y(\FF_{q^{m}})|} \leq r\frac{|\Phi|}{|G|}, \]
  with equality if and only if $\Phi$ is contained in the stabiliser of a geometric component of $X$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:58:38.059781+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0b26a2fc30c94c70681f66708903515cb14d89bda4e0b00d14641f974860b5f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem kernel of arXiv:2606.19507, 'The $t$-Split Two-Periodic Aztec Diamond Model'] Let $-N \leq \xi,\xi' \leq -1$ and $0 < m, m' < N$. The correlation kernel $t$-split two-periodic Aztec diamond of size $2N$ with $t < 1/2$ can be written as a piecewise expression depending on whether $m' \leq tN$ or $m' > tN$. For $0 < m' \leq tN$ the kernel is:
    \begin{multline} 
        \left[\mathbb{K}_N(4m',2\xi'+j;4m,2\xi+i)\right]_{i,j=0,1} = -\frac{\1_{m>m'}}{2\pi \mathrm{i}} \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z} z^{\xi'-\xi}\phi_{m'\to m,N}(z)\\
        +\frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1} \mathrm{d}w \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\alpha,1}(w)^{tN-m'}F_{\alpha,1}(w) \\
        \times \Phi_{\beta}(w)^{(1/2-t)N} \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z) \\
        + \frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1}\mathrm{d}w\oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\alpha,2}(w)^{tN-m'} c(w) F_{\alpha,2}(w) F_{\beta,1}(w)F_{\alpha,1}(w) \\
        \Phi_{\beta}(w)^{(1/2-t)N} \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N} \Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z).
    \end{multline}
    For $tN < m' < N$ the kernel is:
    \begin{multline} 
        \left[\mathbb{K}_N(4m',2\xi'+j;4m,2\xi+i)\right]_{i,j=0,1} = - \frac{\1_{m>m'}}{2\pi\mathrm{i}} \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z} z^{\xi'-\xi} \phi_{m' \to m,N}(z) \\
        + \frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1} \mathrm{d}w \oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\beta,1}(w)^{N/2-m'} F_{\beta,1}(w)\\
        \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z) \\
        + \frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\oint_{\gamma_1}\mathrm{d}w\oint_{\gamma_{0,1}} \frac{\mathrm{d}z}{z(z-w)}\frac{w^{\xi'+N}(z-1)^N}{z^{\xi+N}(w-1)^N}r_{\beta,1}(w)^{(2t - 1/2)N - m'}c(w)F_{\beta,1}(w)F_{\alpha,1}(w)F_{\beta,2}(w)\\
        \times \Phi_{\beta}(z)^{(t-1/2)N}\Phi_{\alpha}(z)^{-tN}\phi_{0\to m,N}(z). 
    \end{multline}
    In both cases, $\gamma_1$ is a simple, positively oriented contour surrounding $1$ but not $0$, while $\gamma_{0,1}$ is a simple, positively oriented contour surrounding both $0$ and $1$ with $\gamma_1$ in its interior. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:52:17.367281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0b64d641d2fecddf18779b3093b50a23be7617297afe293177f05f01bf46552","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 8 (Trajectory lemma, simplified form) of arXiv:2606.02856, 'Geometric Routing in Geometric Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] Let \(w_0\) and \(D_0\) be sufficiently large constants, and let \(M:=\min\{w_0,D_0\}\). Let \(\om{1} \leq f_0(n) \leq \oh{\log\log n}\) be any growing function. Suppose that the geometric path \(P\) first enters
\(\overline{V}(w_0,D_0)\) at a vertex \(u_1\). Then, with probability
\(1-\Oh{M^{-\Omega(1)}}\), the following holds:

\(P\) follows the layered trajectory: it visits the layers in the prescribed order, visiting each first-phase layer and each second-phase layer at most once, except possibly the layer \(A_{2,\star}\), which may be visited twice. Moreover, before leaving the main part, \(P\) reaches a vertex \(u_\ell\) s.t.
\[
	\mathbb{E}_{<D_0}\big[\,\abs{N(u_{\ell}) \cap V_{<D_0}}\,\big] = \Om{M^{\Om{1}}},
\]
where the expectation is w.r.t. uncovering the vertices whose distance to target is at most \(D_0\), conditioned on the position and weight of \(u_\ell\). The number of hops from \(u_1\) to \(u_\ell\) is at most
\[
	\frac{1+\oh{1}}{\abs{\log(\tau-2)}} \left( \log\log_{w_0}(D_{u_1}^d) + \log\log_{D_0}(D_{u_1}) \right) 
	+\Oh{f_0(n)}.
\]
In particular, since \(D_{u_1}\le n^{1/d}\), this is at most \( \frac{2+\oh{1}}{\abs{\log(\tau-2)}}\log\log n\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:01:01.728852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0c5f4cb5165d85588c360487926993569f14315f5d88387f2e6e8060015bf74","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary projected-unit-sphere of arXiv:2609.00108, 'The double sphere solution in the liquid drop model'] Let
		\(
		\bar g=\bar g(\omega_3)
		\in C^{0,\beta}(S)
		\)
		be axially symmetric. Define
		\begin{equation}
			{\rm c}[\bar g]
			=
			-
			\frac{
				\displaystyle
				\int_S\bar g\,\omega_3\,d\sigma
			}{
				\displaystyle
				\int_S\omega_3^2\,d\sigma
			}.
		\end{equation}
		Then there exists a unique axially symmetric
		\(
		\bar h\in C^{2,\beta}(S)
		\)
		satisfying
		$$
		J_S[\bar h]
		=
		\bar g
		+
		{\rm c}[\bar g]\,\omega_3,
		\qquad
		\bar h(P_S)=0.
		$$
		Moreover,
		\begin{equation}
			\|\bar h\|_{C^{2,\beta}(S)}
			+
			|{\rm c}[\bar g]|
			\le
			C
			\|\bar g\|_{C^{0,\beta}(S)}.
		\end{equation}
		We denote this linear solution operator by
		\begin{equation}
			\mathcal T_S[\bar g]
			=
			(\bar h,{\rm c}[\bar g]).
		\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378087+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_f0d630daf2b020660e71ada6912cbc65cadaabb956acfe1ff58ddf76f6278e47","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family {A_i : i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by any set I, there exists a choice function c defined on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently: every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting one element from each. Over the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms ZF, the axiom of choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma and to the well-ordering theorem, and also to Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC is independent of ZF: Godel (1938) showed ZF plus AC is consistent if ZF is (constructible universe), and Cohen (1963) showed ZF plus the negation of AC is consistent if ZF is (forcing). Countable and finite choices do not follow from ZF alone in general, but AC is provable in ZF for finite index sets I by induction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.144882+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f0fc6f2de4695ac93f905fa80028c07ca29602ec265ab1ffc97fa70d2fa10760","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (EPI on compact groups) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a compact and metrizable topological abelian group, equipped with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Assume that $G$ has no open subgroups except $G$ itself and possibly $\{0\}$. Let $X,Y$ be independent random variables on $G$ with finite entropies. Then
$$h(X+Y)-\frac{1}{2}h(X)-\frac{1}{2}h(Y) \geq 0.$$
Moreover:
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(i)$]
If $G$ is connected, then there is equality if and only 
if $X$ and $Y$ are both uniform on $G$.
\item[$(ii)$]
If $G$ is finite, then there is equality if and only if 
either both $X$ and $Y$ are uniform on the whole group $G$ 
or both $X$ and $Y$ are deterministic.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

given by the same formulas. In particular $\Aut(X_{\Delta_1})$ and $\Aut(X_{\Delta_2})$ are isomorphic as ind-groups, while $X_{\Delta_1}\not\cong X_{\Delta_2}$. Consequently, the fully exposed hypothesis cannot be removed from \cref{thm:main}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.492911+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f1049bf4169b66ec7c6384db8ed87960c912531b374b2a5583e3cd6a99db9c4f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 (Rhombus concavity) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{def:rhomb}
Given a function $h:T \ra \R$, and a positive integer $n$,  let $h_n$ denote the function from $T_n$ to $\R$ such that for $(nx, ny) \in T_n$, $h_n(nx, ny) = n^2 h(x, y).$
A function $h:T \ra \R$ is called {\bf rhombus concave} if for any positive integer $n$, 
and any $i$, $\De_i h_n$ is nonpositive on $E_i(T_n),$ and $h$ is continuous on $T$.
The corresponding function $h_n$ is called {\bf discrete (rhombus) concave}.  
Note that a necessary and sufficient condition for a function $h_n$ from $T_n$ to $\R$ to be discrete concave,  is that the piecewise linear extension (which we denote $\tilh_n$) of $h_n$ to $nT$ is  concave.
Here each piece is an isosceles right triangle with a $\sqrt{2}-$length  hypotenuse parallel to the vector $(1, 1).$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:15:16.652975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f109537594b0900804d470c77d7ea62e778c46fc9f5f9d964e6ab5f7804411a6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Set
\(
  U_1
  :=
  |\Phi_1|_{\sigma_0}^2
  =
  \frac{|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}.
\)
Then
\begin{equation}
  \dot H_0=0,
  \qquad
  \ddot H_0
  =
  -4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}U_1.
  
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $k\ge 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \sigma_0
  +2t\operatorname{Re}\Phi_1
  \\
  &+
  \frac{t^2}{2}
  \left[
    2\operatorname{Re}\Phi_2
    +
    \left(
      2U_1-4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}U_1
    \right)\sigma_0
  \right]
  +O_{C^k}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}
Here $O_{C^k}(t^3)$ means that, after subtracting the displayed
terms up to order two, the remainder $R_t$ satisfies
\(
  \|R_t\|_{C^k(X_0,\sigma_0)}\le C_k |t|^3
\)
for $|t|$ sufficiently small. Equivalently, all covariant derivatives
of $R_t$ up to order $k$, computed with respect to $\sigma_0$, are
uniformly $O(t^3)$.
Equivalently, in the coordinate $z$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \rho\,dz\,d\bar z
  +
  t\left(
    \phi_1\,dz^2+\overline{\phi_1}\,d\bar z^2
  \right)
  +
  \frac{t^2}{2}
  \Bigg[
    \phi_2\,dz^2+\overline{\phi_2}\,d\bar z^2
  \\
  &+
    \left\{
      \frac{2|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}
      -
      4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}
      \left(
        \frac{|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}
      \right)
    \right\}
    \rho\,dz\,d\bar z
  \Bigg]
  +O_{C^k}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

We define a quiver $Q^\star$ with $\theta_i^\star$, $i\in Q^\star_0$, and a representation $E^\star$ of $Q^\star$ over $\bC$ as follows.

The $\lambda_{a,k}$ are as before and, by Lemma~(lem:limsvd of the paper) and its proof, are the well-defined values where the increasing filtration $\cF^-(\rho(a))_{\lambda}$ (equivalently: the decreasing filtration $\cF^+(\rho(a))_{\lambda}$) jumps.

    \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:38:17.807299+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f1332f234bebcc04988ea5b58332f523fbdaa4e35b9adf75d34a53db6ff832c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d.zdef of arXiv:2510.07682, 'From tug-of-war to Brownian Boost: \\ explicit ODE solutions for player-funded stochastic-'] For a sequence $h$, write as usual $\prod_{i=0}^k h_i = h_0 \cdots h_k$ for $k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. A device extends this notation to negative $k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$: we set 
$$\prod_{i=0}^k h_i \, = \, \begin{cases}
  \, 1  &  \text{for $k=-1$} \\
 \,  h_{k+1}^{-1} \cdots h_{-1}^{-1}  &  \text{for $k \leq -2$} \, .
\end{cases}
$$
Let $x \in (0,\infty)$. This parameter will index four real-valued  sequences 
$$
a^{\rm def}(x),b^{\rm def}(x),m^{\rm def}(x),n^{\rm def}(x) :\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \to (0,\infty)
$$ 
which we denote in the form $\big\{ *^{\rm def}_i(x): i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \big\}$  for $* \in \{a,b,m,n\}$. The resulting~$(a,b,m,n)$ is a normalized or `default' quadruple that (as we will state shortly) solves the \textrm{ABMN}  system. 

We first specify $m^{\rm def}(x):\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$. This increasing sequence is given by
\begin{equation}
m^{\rm def}_{-\infty}(x) = 0 \, , \, \, \, \, \textrm{and} \, \, \, \, m^{\rm def}_{k+1}(x)- m^{\rm def}_k(x) \, = \,  \kappa \prod_{i=0}^k \big( c_i(x) - 1 \big) \, \, \,  \textrm{for $k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$} \, ,
\end{equation}
in the notation of Definition~(d.stabc of the paper).
Note that $m^{\rm def}_0(x) - m^{\rm def}_{-1}(x) = \kappa$ in view of the product notation.

The decreasing sequence   $n^{\rm def}(x):\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ satisfies 
$$
n^{\rm def}_\infty(x) = 0 \, , \, \, \, \,   \textrm{and} \, \, \, \, n^{\rm def}_k(x)- n^{\rm def}_{k+1}(x)  \, = \, x \prod_{i=0}^k \big( d_i(x) - 1 \big) \, \, \,  \textrm{for $k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$} \, . 
$$
Note that $n^{\rm def}_{-1}(x) - n^{\rm def}_0(x) = \kappa x$.

To specify $a^{\rm def}(x),b^{\rm def}(x):\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \to (0,\infty)$, we set 
$$
M_i(x) = m^{\rm def}_{i+1}(x) - m^{\rm def}_{i-1}(x)
  \, \, \, \, \textrm{and} \, \, \, \, N_i(x) = n^{\rm def}_{i-1}(x) - n^{\rm def}_{i+1}(x)
$$ 
for $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$. We further write 
$$
a^{\rm def}_i(x) = \frac{\kappa \rho \, M_i(x)^{1+\rho} N_i(x)^\rho}{\big(M_i(x)^\rho+N_i(x)^\rho\big)^2} \, \, \, \, \textrm{and} \, \, \, \, 
b^{\rm def}_i(x) = \frac{\kappa \rho  \,  M_i(x)^\rho N_i(x)^{1+\rho}}{\big(M_i(x)^\rho+N_i(x)^\rho\big)^2} \, .
$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:44:17.354839+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f13ef1ad37c0db5419e6beff185f5037637a535c11b9320ebe6221c593e18d4b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:cond-pr-remask of arXiv:2608.23554, 'Provably adaptive sampling with uniform and remasking \\ discrete diffusion models'] Consider the remasking process with parameter \(p_M\) and let \(\rho = \sqrt{1 - p_M}\).
    Let \(0 \leq u < \ell\) with \(\Delta = \ell - u > 0\) and \(a, b \in \cV\). Then,
    \begin{equation*}
        \Pr(X_{\ell}^i = b \mid X_u^i = a) = \begin{cases}
             e^{-\Delta} \bI\{a = b\} + \frac{e^{-\Delta}}{S} (\cosh(\Delta \rho) - 1)&\text{if } a,b \in [S] \\
             e^{-\Delta} \rho \sinh(\Delta \rho)&\text{if } a \in [S], b = \mathrm{REMASK} \\
             1 - e^{-\Delta}(\cosh(\Delta \rho) + \rho \sinh(\Delta \rho))&\text{if } a \in [S], b = \mathrm{MASK}, \\

             1 - e^{-\Delta}\left(\cosh(\Delta \rho) + \frac{\sinh(\Delta \rho)}{\rho}\right)  &\text{if } a = \mathrm{REMASK}, b = \mathrm{MASK} \\
             1 &\text{if } a = b = \mathrm{MASK} \\
             0 &\text{otherwise.} \\

    \end{equation*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Integer d>=2; original drift 0<p<1/2","One active root frog, one sleeping frog at each non-root vertex","Independent common biased walk laws","Root stopping and single-entry restrictions in the lower model"],"created_at":"2026-10-26T22:39:34.229026+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f19b9e72825d301858e8887d4ca9dd34b97bcb066602f14bea251ccf2c298e93","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix integer d>=2 and original inward drift p in (0,1/2). A newborn frog in the coupled non-backtracking model moves up with probability pi; after an upward move its next upward probability is beta=pi/(pi+(1-pi)(d-1)/d)=p/(1-p), with its remaining probability divided uniformly among the other d-1 children. && D_{1}(n,p,\vartheta,R_{0}):=D(n, p) e^{\frac{2 p+1}{2 p-1} \vartheta R_{0}} R_{0}^{\frac{2p}{2 p-1}},  \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ D(n, p):=\frac{n(n-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2 p-1}}(2 p-1)^{\frac{p}{2 p-1}}}{(2 p-n)^\frac{3p-2}{2p-1}},    \\

{"assumptions":["Abel: sum a_n converges","Tauber: f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below and n a_n -> 0 (Littlewood: a_n = O(1/n) suffices, with a harder proof)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476957+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f1cba3555b43f0874b98c5a0afc289242890ff7c78565e100e36b9d11679d3e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Abel's theorem (the Abelian direction): if the series sum a_n converges to s, then the power series f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1 and f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below. The converse is false in general: f(x) = sum (-1)^n x^n = 1/(1 + x) tends to 1/2 while sum (-1)^n diverges. Tauber's theorem (the Tauberian direction): if f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1, f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below, and n a_n -> 0, then sum a_n converges to s. Littlewood strengthened the condition to a_n = O(1/n) (Littlewood's Tauberian theorem, 1911), and Hardy and Littlewood showed that a one-sided bound n a_n >= -C also suffices. 'Abelian' theorems pass from a summability method's convergence to a weaker one; 'Tauberian' theorems go back under an extra growth condition on the terms.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:57:07.304129+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f1d46960c6d62b35183a7af58fd40405eef057473203829635afbe23b3cf3c7d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Distance theorem for sparse simple random tensors) of arXiv:2606.24090, 'Sparsity-adaptive concentration inequalities for random polynomials'] Let \(0<\alpha\le 1\), \(p\in(0,1]\), and let
\[
     X=X^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{(d)}\in\mathbb R^{n^d},
\]
where \(X_i^{(k)}=\delta_i^{(k)}\xi_i^{(k)}\), the variables \(\delta_i^{(k)}\) are i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\), and the variables \(\xi_i^{(k)}\) are independent, mean zero, variance one, and satisfy  $\|\xi_i^{(k)}\|_{\Psi_\alpha}\le 1$. All variables are assumed to be mutually independent.
Set
\[
    \Lambda_{n,p,d}:=\max_{0\le s\le d-1}(np)^{s/2}.
\]
Then for every deterministic nonzero matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{n^d\times n^d}\) and every \(t\ge 0\),
\begin{align}
&\mathbb P\left\{
\left|\|B X\|_2-p^{d/2}\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\right|\ge t
\right\}\nonumber\\
&\qquad\le 2\exp\left[
-c_{\alpha,d}
\min\left\{
\frac{t^2}{\Lambda_{n,p,d}^2\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2},
\left(\frac{t}{n^{(d-1)/2}\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\right)^\alpha,
\left(\frac{t}{\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\right)^{\alpha/d}
\right\}
\right].
\end{align}
In particular, if \(np\ge 1\), then
\[
    \Lambda_{n,p,d}=(np)^{(d-1)/2}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is trace class, or the kernel is continuous and positive semidefinite (Mercer) on a compact space with a finite Borel measure of full support","the kernel is a continuous representative, so that its diagonal values are defined","an L^2 kernel alone determines only a Hilbert-Schmidt operator, whose diagonal is undefined"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573486+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, integral operators, operator ideals","id":"claim_f1fc0fc20e90cd54d10bec9762389999f830637cbe5b30da36ffa8f104d5b56e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For an integral operator T_k on L^2 with kernel k, the formula tr T_k = integral of k(x,x) dx is not a definition and not automatic. (1) An L^2 kernel is an equivalence class modulo null sets, and on a nonatomic space the diagonal is a null set, so k(x,x) has no meaning at all without choosing a distinguished representative; different representatives give different 'diagonal integrals'. (2) Continuity of the kernel is not enough for trace class. Carleman's example: there are continuous 2pi-periodic functions g whose Fourier coefficients are not absolutely summable. The convolution operator (T f)(x) = (1/(2 pi)) times the integral over the circle of g(x - y) f(y) dy has the continuous kernel k(x,y) = g(x - y)/(2 pi), is normal with eigenvalues the Fourier coefficients of g and eigenfunctions the exponentials, so its singular values are the moduli of those coefficients; hence T is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, while the naive diagonal integral is the finite number g(0). (3) What does hold: if T is trace class on L^2([a,b]) and has a continuous kernel on [a,b] x [a,b], then tr T = integral of k(x,x) dx; and by Mercer's theorem, if k is continuous, symmetric and positive semidefinite on a compact interval (more generally on a compact metric space with a finite Borel measure of full support), then the associated operator is trace class, the eigenfunction series converges absolutely and uniformly, and tr T = integral of k(x,x) dx = sum of the eigenvalues. So the safe routes are positivity plus continuity (Mercer), or an independent proof of trace class plus continuity; 'the kernel is nice' by itself is not a proof.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:04:55.814822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f211d8d5a884c11a94d5b23a1548d9dddc603bcb6167e91690ca0ebdb92424ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop p:efron-stein-classical of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] Let $X_0,X_1,\dots,X_n, Y$ be random vectors (possibly with different and/or infinite lengths) on the same probability space, such that $X_0,\dots,X_n$ are conditionally independent given $Y$.
    Write $\mathbf{X} \coloneqq  (X_0,\dots,X_n)$.
    Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = (\widetilde{X}_0,\dots,\widetilde{X}_n)$ be a conditionally independent copy of $\mathbf{X}$ given $Y$.
    Write
    \begin{align*}
        \widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)} \coloneqq  (X_0,\dots,X_{k-1},\widetilde{X}_k, X_{k+1},\dots,X_n).
    \end{align*}
    Note that we have the equality of unconditional joint laws
    \begin{align*}
        (\mathbf{X},Y)\overset{d}{=} (\widetilde{\mathbf{X}},Y) \overset{d}{=} (\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(0)}, Y)\overset{d}{=} \cdots \overset{d}{=} (\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(n)},Y).
    \end{align*}
    

    Let $Z=Z(\mathbf{X},Y)$ be a square-integrable function of $(\mathbf{X},Y)$.
    Then
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}[\Var(Z \mid Y)]
        = \frac12
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            \left(
                Z(\mathbf{X},Y)
                - Z(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}},Y)
            \right)^2
        \right]
        &\leqslant
        \frac12
        \sum_{k=0}^n 
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            \left(
                Z(\mathbf{X},Y)
                - Z(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)},Y)
            \right)^2
        \right].
    \end{align*}
    In fact, the above holds almost surely with $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,|\,Y]$ in place of $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.836982+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f212a955617f67401fa3ee364172c3cf3f3dcf3634c453a30fb36e4f9d32ab1e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 9 of arXiv:2607.20646, 'The Independence-Preserving Property and Planar Web Geometry'] Let $(\mu_X,\mu_Y,\mu_U,\mu_V)$ be probability measures on $(0, \infty)$ having positive continuous density.
Then $\HIp|_{(0,\infty)^2}$ preserves their independence if and only if there exist $p,q,r\in\R$ with $\max\{p, 0\} < \min\{q, r\}$ such that
\begin{alignat*}{3}
    \mu_X(\dd x)
        &\propto (1 + \alpha x)^{p}\Big(\frac{1}{1+x}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{\alpha x}{1+\alpha x}\Big)^r\frac{\dd x}{x} &
        &\propto x^{r-1}(1+x)^{-q}(1+\alpha x)^{p-r}\,\dd x,\\
    \mu_Y(\dd y)
        &\propto (1 + \beta y)^{p}\Big(\frac{\beta y}{1+\beta y}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{1}{1+y}\Big)^r\frac{\dd y}{y} &
        &\propto y^{q-1}(1+y)^{-r}(1+\beta y)^{p-q}\,\dd y,\\
    \mu_U(\dd u)
        &\propto (1 + \alpha u)^{p}\Big(\frac{\alpha u}{1+\alpha u}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{1}{1+u}\Big)^r\frac{\dd u}{u} &
        &\propto u^{q-1}(1+u)^{-r}(1+\alpha u)^{p-q}\,\dd u,\\
    \mu_V(\dd v)
        &\propto (1 + \beta v)^{p}\Big(\frac{1}{1+v}\Big)^q\Big(\frac{\beta v}{1+\beta v}\Big)^r\frac{\dd v}{v} &
        &\propto v^{r-1}(1+v)^{-q}(1+\beta v)^{p-r}\,\dd v.
\end{alignat*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:03:35.764879+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f21945168965d91d3814c75ca2e8370abe9f7795ba4ae1acefba822be9fb5225","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:commutator-transfer of arXiv:2608.22910, 'A Commutator Framework for Selective Spectral Alignment in Deep Neural Networks'] Fix \(t\geq0\) and \(\ell\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\), and set
\[
C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}:=[\mathcal S_\ell,\mathrm{NFM}_\ell],
\qquad
C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}:=[Q_\ell,P_\ell].
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}
=W_\ell^\top C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}W_\ell
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}\|_F
\leq
\|W_\ell\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F.
\end{equation}
If \(W_\ell\) has full row rank, and \(\sigma_{\min}(W_\ell)\) denotes
its smallest singular value, then
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{\min}(W_\ell)^2\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F
\leq
\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}\|_F
\leq
\sigma_{\max}(W_\ell)^2\|C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}\|_F,
\end{equation}
and hence \(C_\ell^{\mathrm{feat}}=0\) if and only if
\(C_\ell^{\mathrm{int}}=0\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.527139+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f21b6b4a30fcf2fdbf0d3cf2b443cc6e31a477a82f71378cf8829c651b8aba99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 4 of arXiv:2604.01748, 'Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$'] Let $\lambda = [\lambda(0), \lambda(1), \cdots, \lambda(m)]$ be a path of length $m$ in $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$. We define the chronological loop-erasure of $\lambda$, denoted by $\text{LE} (\lambda)$, in the following manner. First, set
$$ t_0 \coloneqq \max\{t \ge 0 \, : \, \lambda(t) = \lambda(0)\}.$$
For each $i \geq 1$, define
$$ t_i \coloneqq \max\{t \ge 0 \, : \, \lambda(t) = \lambda(t_{i-1}+1)\}. $$
Let 
$$n = \min\{i \, : \, t_i = m\}.$$
    Then, the chronological loop-erasure of $\lambda$ is given by
    $$\text{LE} (\lambda) \coloneqq [\lambda(t_0), \lambda(t_1), \ldots, \lambda(t_n)].$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.375742+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f228afb5fec46a77ed7a68dc1f47d716ae8d82f9cf50f0d93b7eb9f226275609","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $S_1\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(n-\sqrt{n})^{1/2}$
    \begin{proof}
        We may compute $S_1$ explicitly. We have, via a combinatorial identity,
        \[S_1=\frac{n-2m-3}{2^{n-2m-4}}\binom{n-2m-4}{\frac{n}{2}-m-2}\]
        By a special case of Stirling's estimate, we have
        \[\binom{n}{n/2}\sim 2^n(\pi n/2)^{-1/2}\] 
        This gives
        \[S_1\sim \frac{(n-2m-3)(2^{n-2m-4})}{(2^{n-2m-4})\sqrt{\pi(\frac{n}{2}-m-2)}}=\frac{(n-2m-3)}{\sqrt{\pi(\frac{n}{2}-m-2)}}\]
        \[=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{n-2m-3}{\sqrt{n-2m-4}}\right)\]
        \[=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{n-\left\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\right\rceil-2}{\sqrt{n-\left\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\right\rceil-3}}\right)\]
        \[\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(n-\sqrt{n})^{1/2}\]
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined nonnegative counting or indicator-sum random variable X = sum_i X_i","a computable or boundable first moment E[X]","a computable or boundable second moment E[X^2], in particular control of the pairwise correlations E[X_i X_j]","the correlation sum not growing asymptotically faster than (E[X])^2"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.982598+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f22c0577c492845332c3c1bfdcfe54194e3ac9704f0f1fdb3d81ba1f6e0e27d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a nonnegative random variable X, typically a count of some combinatorial structure written as X = sum_i X_i for indicator random variables X_i, the Paley-Zygmund inequality gives P(X > 0) >= (E[X])^2 / E[X^2]. Expanding E[X^2] = E[X] + sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j], the method succeeds in proving P(X>0) is bounded away from 0 exactly when the pair-correlation sum sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j] is of the same order as (E[X])^2, that is, when correlations between the indicators do not overwhelm the square of the mean. This is the standard route to existence results, such as an infinite cluster, a long crossing, or a large clique, once a first-moment computation has already established that E[X] is large or diverging, complementing the first-moment method, which by Markov's inequality only ever gives upper bounds on P(X>0). The method does not give any rate of convergence beyond the crude Paley-Zygmund ratio, gives no lower bound at all if the correlation structure is not controlled, and can produce a vacuous (near-0) bound whenever the variance is dominated by rare, strongly correlated configurations even though the mean itself is large. Typical failure: Computing a large or diverging first moment E[X] and declaring existence of the structure without bounding E[X^2]; if the indicators X_i are strongly positively correlated (a common situation for overlapping structures), the pair-correlation term can dominate (E[X])^2, making the Paley-Zygmund bound vacuous even as E[X] -> infinity, which is exactly the situation where a large first moment gives a false sense of near-certain existence. Canonical reference: Paley and Zygmund, 1932, Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society; Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition, Wiley.","status":"unverified"}

\[
 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)
 =

one has the polynomial identity
\begin{equation}
 M_{P,r}(\Sigma)

where

 N(E)

In particular, every complete contraction of copies of the tensors

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.301657+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f23500ba6eafb72371f9f1e55e0c5f4bd85d3c08580b94d7a7300674b0832c2f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2604.22130, 'Reflected Stochastic Differential Equations Driven by $G$-Brownian Motion with Nonlinear C'] (i) A mapping $X:\\Omega_T\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ is said to be quasi-continuous if, for each $\\varepsilon>0$, there exists an open set $O$ in $\\Omega_T$ such that ${c}(G)<\\varepsilon$ and $X|_{O^c}$ is continuous.\n\n\\noindent (ii) We say that $X:\\Omega_T\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ has a quasi-continuous version if there exists a quasi-continuous function $Y:\\Omega_T\\rightarrow \\mathbb{R}$ such that $X=Y$, q.s.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:32:20.021850+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f23551d1d6ce286a848c4a114798a230aaed7866f5fe5c8fbdd9a751ae99fd49","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 37 (Convergence, stated with a reference measure; Theorem \ref{thm:posdens}) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $\XX$ be a set, $\XXA$ a $\sigma$-algebra on $\XX$, and $\lambda$ a
$\sigma$-finite measure on $(\XX,\XXA)$. Let
\[
  p : \XX \longrightarrow [0,\infty)
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \tau : \XX\times\XX \longrightarrow [0,\infty), \quad (x,y) \longmapsto \tau(y \mid x),
\]
be measurable, respectively $\XXA\otimes\XXA$-measurable, and define the probability
measure $\pi$ and the Markov kernel $T$ by
\[
  \pi(A) := \int_{A} p \dd\lambda,
  \qquad
  T(A \mid x) := \int_{A} \tau(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y)
  \qquad (A \in \XXA,\ x \in \XX),
\]
where $\int_{\XX} p \dd\lambda = 1$ and $\int_{\XX}\tau(y \mid x)\,\lambda(\dd y) = 1$
for every $x \in \XX$. Write $\Xp := \{ y \in \XX : p(y) > 0 \} \in \XXA$ and assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,topsep=3pt]
  \item \emph{(invariance)} $\displaystyle\int_{\XX} \tau(y \mid x)\,p(x)\,\lambda(\dd x) = p(y)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $y \in \XX$;
  \item \emph{(the support is not left)} for every $x \in \XX$: $\ \tau(y \mid x) = 0$ for $\lambda$-almost every $y \in \XX\setminus\Xp$;
  \item \emph{(positivity)} $\tau(y \mid x) > 0$ for $(\lambda\otimes\lambda)$-almost every $(x,y) \in \Xp \times \Xp$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$, and
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty} \tv{T^{n}\circ\mu - \pi} = 0 \qquad\text{for every } \mu \in \Prob .
\]
Theorem \ref{thm:posdens} of the introduction is the special case in which $p > 0$
everywhere, so that $\Xp = \XX$ and hypothesis (ii) is vacuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:29:27.943404+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f23d98100da55908526d0c38bdf0f2cee3febcce48ec6c39ebfcc30c223adf71","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.24549, 'Persistent Cross Entropy'] A map $k:\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}\to(0,1]$ is called a
\textbf{similarity function} if it satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\textit{\roman*})]
\item there exist a metric $\rho$ on $\mathcal{Z}$ and a strictly decreasing function
$h:[0,\infty)\to(0,1]$ with $h(0)=1$ and
$\lim\limits_{r\to\infty}h(r)=0$ such that
$$
k(u,v)=h(\rho(u,v));
$$

\item $k$ is Lipschitz in its second argument: there exists $L_0>0$ such that
$$
|k(u,v)-k(u,v')|
\leq
L_0\Vert v-v' \Vert
$$
for all $u,v,v'\in\mathcal{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:22:48.868818+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f25330ccb17a2bdea4a968591cbb16cfbff2a560539b000697aab4eb9d53e94c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 4 of arXiv:2608.29148, '2608.29148'] A $\Theta$-metric $g$ on $(\ol X, [\Theta])$ is called an {\it asymptotically complex hyperbolic (ACH) metric} with CR infinity $(M, H, J)$ if it satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]  For any boundary defining function $r$, we have 
\[
\Bigl|\dfrac{dr}{r}\Bigr|^2_g=\dfrac{1}{4}\quad \textrm{on}\ M,
\]
or, equivalently, $|\nu|^2_g=4$. 
\item[(ii)] For any $p\in M$, the map
\[
L_p\longrightarrow {}^\Theta T_p \ol X, \quad Z\longmapsto [\nu_p, Z]
\]
gives the identity map on $L_p$.
\item[(iii)] For any contact form $\th$ on $M$, we have 
\[
\lambda_\th^*(g|_{L})=2h_{\a\ol\b}\th^\a\cdot\th^{\ol\b},
\]
where the right-hand side denotes the Levi form on $H$ associated with $\th$.
\end{enumerate}
We call $(\ol X, [\Theta], g)$ an {\it ACH manifold}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite simple undirected graph","Distinct initially nonadjacent vertices; add one unweighted edge","Positive degrees only for the displayed random-walk normalization"],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:58:04.168957+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_f2569a3986968c562214a71cba396aaa39befdc5d1f2317620db9a01ebb02a19","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G be a finite simple undirected graph on labeled vertices, with combinatorial Laplacian L_G=D_G-A_G. If distinct vertices u,v are not adjacent, form G_plus by adding their single unweighted edge, and let b=e_u-e_v. Then L_(G_plus)=L_G+b*b^T and E_(G_plus)(f)=E_G(f)+(f(u)-f(v))^2 for every real f. Consequently every ordered combinatorial Laplacian eigenvalue is nondecreasing under this edge addition. This identity concerns the combinatorial Laplacian. For ordinary simple random walk the transition matrix is D^(-1)A whenever all degrees are positive, so a single-edge addition changes both A and D; the associated symmetric matrix I-D^(-1/2)A D^(-1/2) must use the new degrees. Adding one edge to a regular graph does not generally preserve regularity or the uniform stationary law.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:47:12.026502+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f25c31164f52aee7d95a5487832ff8ba214c01e8a796f43bdd2590ffb2003181","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:doubling-metric-dim of arXiv:2512.06984, 'Infinite Dimensional Multifractal Analysis of the Wiener measure'] Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space.
		
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (A)] (Doubling $\Rightarrow$ finite metric dimension)
Assume that there exists an integer $N\ge 1$ such that for every $x\in X$ and $R>0$, the ball $B(x,R)$ can be covered by at most $N$ balls of radius $R/2$.
Then $(X,d)$ is $(C,s)$-homogeneous in the sense of Assouad, with
\[s=\log_2 N, \qquad C=N,\]
hence $\Dim(X,d)<\infty$.
			
\item[\rm (B)] (Finite metric dimension $\Rightarrow$ doubling)
Assume that $(X,d)$ is $(C,s)$-homogeneous: for all $0<a<b$ and all $Y\subset Z\subset X$ with $\mathrm{diam\, }(Z)\le b$ and $Y$ $a$-separated, one has $\#Y\le C(b/a)^s$.
Then $(X,d)$ is doubling: every ball $B(x,R)$ can be covered by at most
\[N_0:=C\,2^{s}\]
balls of radius $R/2$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:14:57.697915+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f28cced144ddd8d12a6fff5a14ac4b95f1bf1902889b9a579971a1efe1c90cdb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma area Lemma of arXiv:2605.29095, 'Asymptotics of the number of components of random polynomial lemniscates'] [Area Theorem] [Ahlfors], [crane-polynomialpreimage] 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let \( f \) be a univalent (injective holomorphic) function on a domain \( D \subseteq \mathbb{C} \), and let \( K \subset D \) be a measurable set. Then the area of the image \( f(K) \) is given by:
\[
\text{Area}\big(f(K)\big) = \int_K |f'(z)|^2 \, dA(z),
\]
where \( dA(z) = dx \, dy \) denotes the Euclidean area element in \( \mathbb{C} \).
\item Let \( p \) be a polynomial of degree \( n \) over \( \mathbb{C} \), and let \( K \) be any measurable subset of the complex plane. Let \( n(z, p, K) \) be the number of preimages of \( z \) under \( p \) that lie in \( K \) counted with multiplicity. Then,
\begin{align}
    \int_{\mathbb{C}} n(z, p, K)\, dA(z) = \int_K |p'(z)|^2\, dA(z).
\end{align}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:25:55.483668+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2991593485a090bd936f4f599c64c9da74c0b91a4aecf8f1115a9545f752b32","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.28578, 'On two differing geometric descriptions of the passage from microscopy to macroscopy in Ma'] Let $M$ be a connected closed Riemannian manifold, let $\Prob^{\infty}_+(M)$ be its Fr\'echet manifold of smooth positive probability densities and let $\Hspace_k\hookrightarrow C^1(M;TM)$ be a vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Then the following statements hold.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item The continuity operator $\Aop_{\rho}v=-\Div(\rho v)$ is the differential of the pushforward action, is surjective on the smooth core and identifies a density tangent with a particle velocity modulo the $\rho$ divergence free kernel.
		\item The weighted $L^2(\rho)$ norm and the reproducing kernel Hilbert norm produce fibrewise Otto and Stein tangent--cotangent Hilbert pairs by quotient and Riesz representation; their Onsager maps factor as $\Kop^{\bullet}_{\rho}=\Aop_{\rho}\Bop^{\bullet}_{\rho}$.
		\item Let $\Mop_{\rho}=\mathsf{P}^{\mathrm{hor}}_{\rho}\Iop_{\rho}\Iop_{\rho}^{*}$ on the Otto horizontal space. A regular covector $[f]$ induces the Otto tangent $\Aop_{\rho}\grad f$ and the Stein tangent $\Aop_{\rho}\Mop_{\rho}\grad f$. These tangents agree exactly when $\Mop_{\rho}\grad f=\grad f$, whilst the particle fields agree exactly when $\Iop_{\rho}\Iop_{\rho}^{*}\grad f=\grad f$.
		\item Positive proportionality of the two tangents gives the same unparametrised law curve, equality after a differentiable observation gives the same prescribed evolution of that observation, and spectral bounds on $\Mop_{\rho}$ compare dissipation and tangent cost. Agreement for every regular force in a closed force space is equivalent to $\Mop_{\rho}=\id$ there. Any positive self-adjoint response on a finite dimensional smooth force subspace can be realised by a finite rank reproducing kernel.
		\item Relative entropy supplies the common covector $[\log(\rho/\pi)]$. Its Wasserstein and Stein descents agree according to the preceding criterion; equality of their instantaneous dissipations is weaker than equality of their law tangents.
		\item Every regular minimal exponential family has smooth gradient solutions of the required Stein equations on the closed-manifold core. {"assumptions":["rows i.i.d. with finite fourth moments","M/n -> c > 0, m/n -> r in (0,1)","the two parts of the split are disjoint (independence of V_1 and S_2 is what carries the argument)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.563112+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation","id":"claim_f2a2a51ee2fc2c34c5acc49ed5282836e853f6346ca1c35a46bb72807e699342","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X$ be $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^M$ with covariance $\\Sigma$. Split the rows into two independent parts of sizes $m$ and $n - m$ with sample covariances $S_1 = V_1\\Lambda_1 V_1^T$ and $S_2$. The nonparametric eigenvalue-regularised covariance estimator is $\\hat\\Sigma = V_1 \\operatorname{diag}(V_1^T S_2 V_1)\\, V_1^T$, averaged over $K$ random splits. Then: (i) $\\mathbb{E}[V_1^T S_2 V_1 \\mid V_1] = V_1^T \\Sigma V_1$, so each diagonal entry $v_i^T S_2 v_i$ is an unbiased estimate of the population variance in the direction $v_i$ - the Ledoit-Peche oracle $d_i^* = v_i^T\\Sigma v_i$ evaluated on independent data; (ii) as $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $M/n \\to c > 0$ and $m/n \\to r \\in (0,1)$, $\\hat\\Sigma$ is asymptotically optimal in Frobenius loss among estimators of the form $V_1 D V_1^T$ with $D$ diagonal (Lam 2016, Theorem 1); (iii) $\\hat\\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite and carries no bandwidth, floor or shrinkage constant beyond the split fraction (Lam recommends choosing $m$ by minimising $\\|\\hat\\Sigma_m - S\\|_F$ over a grid; $m = n/2$ is the usual default). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:49:15.471319+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2b87cd018f9801b0ddac9848c660f98aadc52683de59ff173dd2aff5f050a10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem presym reduc corank 1 of arXiv:2608.28278, 'Reduction of symmetric time-dependent Hamiltonian systems I: presymplectic principal $\R$-'] [GUTIERREZSAGREDO]
    Let $\phi: G \times M \to M$ be a Hamiltonian presymplectic action of a Lie group $G$ for a presymplectic structure $(\omega, R)$ of corank $1$ on $M$ with $G$-equivariant momentum map $J: M \to \mathfrak{g}^*$. Then,
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(i)] There exists a unique closed $2$-form $\omega_\nu$ on $M_\nu$ such that

{"assumptions":["E and C symmetric p x p; the estimator class is restricted to the eigenvectors of E"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943255+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_f2c72c8f5c4a1fb5da7d3fb5c8cdf44405907d5be714dd864209131af7efd314","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E$ be a symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix with eigen-decomposition $E = \\sum_k \\lambda_k u_k u_k^T$ (for instance a sample covariance) and let $C$ be any symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix (the population covariance). Among all estimators of the form $\\Xi = \\sum_k \\xi_k u_k u_k^T$ - the same eigenvectors as $E$, free eigenvalues - the Frobenius loss $\\|\\Xi - C\\|_F^2$ is minimized by the oracle choice $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, the projection of the population matrix onto the $k$-th sample eigenvector, with minimal loss $\\|C\\|_F^2 - \\sum_k (u_k^T C u_k)^2$. In particular the oracle eigenvalues are convex combinations of the population eigenvalues (they lie between the smallest and largest population eigenvalue) and their sum equals $\\operatorname{tr} C$: a rotationally invariant estimator that is optimal in Frobenius loss never moves the trace and always shrinks the spread of the sample spectrum toward the population spread.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.756992+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2c8ae5ef5ac85c776bfa5f4ce43dd5aa65d1dc2314cc459488cebd658f030a8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 11 of arXiv:2512.03884, '2512.03884'] Let $\alpha$ be a quadratic irrational, let $ax^2+bx+c$ be its minimal polynomial with $a,b,c \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\mathrm{gcd}(a,b,c)=1$ and $a>0$, and let $Q(x,y)=ax^2+bxy+cy^2$ be the corresponding binary quadratic form. For any constant $\theta>1$ and any integer $M \ge 1$, we have
\[ \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{1}{m^{\theta} \| m \alpha \|^{\theta}} = c(\alpha, \theta) \log M +O(1) \]
with an implied constant depending only on $\alpha$ and $\theta$. The constant $c(\alpha, \theta)$ is given by
\[ c(\alpha, \theta) = \frac{D^{\theta/2}}{\log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{n \in \mathbb{Z} \\ n \neq 0}} \frac{R_Q(n)}{|n|^{\theta}}, \]
where $D=b^2-4ac>0$ is the discriminant, $R_Q(n)$ is the number of primary representations of $n$, and $\varepsilon=(t_0+u_0\sqrt{D})/2$ with the smallest positive solution $(t_0,u_0)$ of Pell's equation $t^2-Du^2=4$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:07:17.249409+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2d6391f59833740293808b811f91c84a58e6e86c5a2835f4556e601d7e426f5","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:VEB-escape of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] There exists a real number $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/2)$ such that the following holds. Consider any $\lambda \in (0,\lambda_0)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ such $p_0=1$ and, for all $i \ge 1$, $W_i \le (4/\lambda)^i$. Suppose that $\overline{p}$ has finitely many bins which are strongly exposed. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with
birth rate~$2 \lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set~$\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
Let $j_0\geq 5$ be a sufficiently large positive integer such that all strongly-exposed bins are in $[j_0-1]$.
Let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$ be the event that, for every step $t' \in [T^{\overline{p},j_0}]$, $n^{X^B} \ge 2$. 
We will condition on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$.
Let
$\tau_0 =  T^{\overline{p},j_0}$. 
Let
$\Psi_0$ be the  initialising high-level state   
with $\tau^{\Psi_0} = \tau_0$ and $j^{\Psi_0} = j_0$. 
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be   the $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule from Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-rule of the paper) and let $\ensuremath{\Psi^{\mathrm{BB}}(\Psi_0)}$  (Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-state-space of the paper)) be the  $\Psi_0$-closure (Definition~(def:hls-closed of the paper)) of~$\mathrm{hls}$.  
The $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule~$\mathrm{hls}$ is a transition rule (Definition~(def:transition-rule of the paper)) by Observation~(obs:BB-bounding-is-transrule of the paper) and 
it is $\ensuremath{\Psi^{\mathrm{BB}}(\Psi_0)}$-valid (Definition~(def:valid of the paper)) by
Lemma~(lem:backoff-bounding-valid of the paper).

Conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$,
the VEB-coupling (Definition~(equation def:VEB-couple of the paper)   couples $X$ with a volume process $V$ from $\Psi_0$ with  transition rule $\mathrm{hls}$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$ and with a sequence $E_1, E_2,\ldots $ of escape processes with send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$. 
The coupling uses $b_i^{E_0}(\tau_0+1)$ as a synonym for $\mathbf{e}_i^X(\tau_0+1)$.

With probability at least~$2/3$,  
both of the following hold.
 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item for all $t> \tau_0$ such that 
$\textup{type}^{\Psi(t)}  = \textup{advancing}$
and the $S\in \mathcal{S}^{\Psi(t)}$,
$\sum_{k \in  S } p_kb_k^{E_{g^{\Psi(t-1)}}}(t) \leq \lambda | S  |/80$. Moreover, $S$ is non-empty.
\item for all $t> \tau_0$ such that 
$\textup{type}^{\Psi(t)} \notin \{\textup{failure},\textup{advancing}\}$ and all $k \in [j^{\Psi(t-1)}-1]$ such that $W_k \ge (j^{\Psi(t-1)})^\chi$, $p_kb_k^{E_{g^{\Psi(t-1)}}}(t) \le \lambda/80$. Moreover, there is at least one such $k\in [j-1]$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:52:57.674209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2ed3477afc3d07457bef4a154dbb7751193b6e2f0e726f426a90c07f78cebfd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 3 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional Finsler metric measure manifold. && \leq  \left(\frac{n-1}{(2 p-1)(2 p-n)}\right)^{\frac{p-1}{2p-1}}\left(\left\|{\rm Ric}_{\infty}^{K}\right\|_{p, R, \vartheta}(x_{0})\right)^{\frac{p}{2p-1}} \int_{r}^{R} \frac{1}{\sin^{2}(\sqrt{K} s)} ds.

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a martingale with respect to (F_n)","for the optional stopping consequence: tau an almost surely finite stopping time and the martingale uniformly integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3381e7ccdd3a3ab4f50fa4aa3f0083f4b6eac81113da66a80d044e9f35491f6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n)_{n >= 0} be a martingale for a filtration (F_n) and let F_infinity be the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the F_n. The following are equivalent: (i) the family {X_n} is uniformly integrable; (ii) X_n converges almost surely AND in L^1 to some X_infinity; (iii) there exists Y in L^1 with X_n = E[Y | F_n] almost surely for every n, that is the martingale is CLOSED. When these hold one may take Y = X_infinity, and X_infinity = E[Y | F_infinity]. Consequences: for a UI martingale, E[X_infinity] = E[X_0], and the optional stopping identity E[X_tau] = E[X_0] holds for EVERY almost surely finite stopping time tau, with no boundedness assumption on tau or on the martingale - this is a genuinely stronger conclusion than the standard three sufficient conditions (bounded tau, bounded martingale, or E[tau] finite with bounded increments). An L^1-bounded martingale need not be UI, and then only the almost sure half of (ii) survives. For p > 1, an L^p-bounded martingale is automatically UI by de la Vallee Poussin and converges in L^p as well; p = 1 is the exceptional case. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorems 13.3 and 14.1]","status":"unverified"}

        \[

For $E\in\R$ and $N\geq1$, denote
\[\Omega_N(E,\Delta):=\{x\in\Lambda^N:E\leq H_N(x)<E+\Delta\},\quad G_N(E,\Delta):=\#\Omega_N(E,\Delta).\]
Whenever $G_N(E,\Delta)>0$, define the windowed microcanonical ensemble as the uniform measure
\[\mu^{\mc}_{N,E,\Delta}(x):=G_N(E,\Delta)^{-1}\one_{\Omega_N(E,\Delta)}(x)\]
on $\Omega_N(E,\Delta)$, and define its entropy as $R_{N,E,\Delta}^{\mc}:=\log G_N(E,\Delta)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite d,q; H constant SPD with 0<m<=lambda(H)<=M","A in C1(R^d,R^{q x q}), A^T A=H; sup sum_i ||partial_i A||_op^2<=D^2","Fresh iid labels: E z=0, E zz^T=I_q; only finite second moments; no central symmetry required","Deterministic u0, v0=0; sigma>=0; 0<rho<2; 0<eta<=rho/M","F in C_b^2 on all ambient space; F2, Fvv, Fuv as in the complete statement","Covariance proportional to loss Hessian on v=0 only; explicit SGD recursion in statement"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:49:18.681296+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_f352559210980586d3a503006032dcc6bc9cc4a6393ff741b69c4afe3aa09c8e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Status: proof (unaudited). A:R^d -> R^{q x q} be C^1, A(u)^T A(u)=H, and

    h_{k,i}:=u_{k+1,i}-u_{k,i}=-eta sigma z_k^T partial_i A(u_k)v_k,

{"assumptions":["each f_n Riemann integrable on the compact interval [a,b]","uniform bound |f_n| <= M","pointwise convergence to f, AND f Riemann integrable - an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752811+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f36289c5312e1ca03cfca5ba87601f4ac8063f5554a56039a9f33e45b9a5702a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be Riemann integrable, uniformly bounded (|f_n| <= M for all n), and suppose f_n -> f pointwise on [a,b] where f is ALSO Riemann integrable. Then integral_a^b f_n -> integral_a^b f. The Riemann integrability of the limit must be ASSUMED and does not follow: enumerate the rationals of [0,1] as q_1, q_2, ... and let f_n be the indicator of {q_1, ..., q_n}. Each f_n is Riemann integrable with integral 0, the family is bounded by 1, and f_n increases pointwise to the indicator of the rationals, which is not Riemann integrable. This is the essential defect that the Lebesgue integral repairs: the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem needs only measurability of the limit, which is automatic for a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Historically Arzela proved this in 1885 by a direct and rather delicate covering argument, before the Lebesgue theory existed. [Arzela (1885); see e.g. Luxemburg, 'Arzela's dominated convergence theorem for the Riemann integral', Amer. Math. Monthly 78 (1971)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:26:40.361341+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f37bff03ece2c067d6056469a0ba4bb794ee80373ec4455c04f963ec5c1de767","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 49 (Trunk paths and vertices) of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] Under $\q^m_n$, we have 
\[
X_j = m, \quad \text{for all } \bar{h} \le j \le \bar{h} + \lfloor c_0 n \rfloor.
\]
In other words, for each $j$ between $\bar{h}$ and $\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n\rfloor$, there are exactly $m$ vertices in $\cX_j$. These vertices belong to $m$ distinct ancestral lineages that remain separate at height $\bar{h}$. 
Let $\mathsf{T}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{T}_m$ be the $m$ coalescent subtrees at height $\bar{h}$.  
For $\bar{h}\le j \le \bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor$ and $1\le i\le m$, denote by 
\(z^j_i \in V(\mathsf{T}_i)\)
the unique vertex of $\mathsf{T}_i$ at height $j$. 
The sequence
\[
Z_i := \big(z^{\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor}_i, z^{\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor-1}_i, \ldots, z^{\bar{h}}_i\big)
\]
is called the trunk path of $\mathsf{T}_i$, and its elements are referred to as the trunk vertices of $\mathsf{T}_i$.  
The remaining $q_n(j)-m$ non-trunk vertices at height $j$ are denoted by $y^j_1, \ldots, y^j_{q_n(j)-m}$, where the subscripts are assigned arbitrary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:10:43.703233+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3b83ea240c36229c7a0d31a7e0cd6cb9e0bcb693ab32ee5382356dd5770e8ec","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition M1 of arXiv:2412.04212, 'Rectangular Gilbert Tessellation'] Let 
$\mathcal{V}$ be a locally finite set of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (i.e., within any finite square, there is a finite number of points of $\mathcal{V}$ ), and let a constant $0<p<1$ be fixed arbitrarily. For each $u\in \mathcal{V}$ 
a random vector $$d_u \in \{(0,1), (1,0)\}$$ is assigned independently of the rest with the probability
\begin{equation}\notag
\mathbb{P}\{d_u= (0,1) \}=p=1-\mathbb{P}\{d_u= (1,0) \}.
\end{equation}
Set 
$G(0):=\mathcal{V}.$
At time $t=0$, from every point $u\in \mathcal{V}$ into each side of the assigned direction ($\pm d_u$), a ray $\mathcal{L}^{\pm}_{u,d_u}(t)$
grows
with constant speed $1$ until it reaches another ray;
at this moment, the growth stops, and the ray remains unchanged thereafter. 

For any $t>0$, we define a collection of 
rays
\begin{equation}
G_{\mathcal{V}}(t):=  \left\{ \mathcal{L}^{+}_{u,d_u}(t),
\mathcal{L}^{-}_{u,d_u}(t),
u\in \mathcal{V}
\right\}.
\end{equation}
We call process $\left( G_{\mathcal{V}}(t), \ t\geq 0\right)$ 
the process of planar quadrangulation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.667215+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3d0f4a43e1234f642677f9825b3630dc54cd55f6fb84c3189154d5d54f82428","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn eq:Ae-def of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Let $e=\{u,v\}$ be a bridge, where $u$ has label $1$ and $v$ has label $2$. 
Its original activation time and the lower bound recorded at activation are
\begin{align*}
 \gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \max\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u),\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\},\\
 L_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
The corresponding residual in the cumulative-hazard scale is
\begin{align*}
 R_e
 := H(\go_e)-H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) 
 = \go_e^\theta-(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta.
\end{align*}

For $q\geqslant\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the collision threshold
\begin{align*}
 L_e(q)
 :=
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
In particular, $L_e(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}})=L_e^{\mathrm{act}}$.

For $s\geqslant\mathfrak{a}_\ell\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the rescaled bridge age by
\begin{align}
 A_e(s)
 :=
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align}
Then $ L_e(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell)=\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}$.

The cumulative bridge hazard at rescaled time $s$ is
\begin{align}
 \gL_s
 &:= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}
 \left[ H\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}\right) - H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) \right]
 =\sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}\left[\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell }\right)^\theta
 -(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta\right]
 \notag\\
 &=\int_0^s \frac{2\theta}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell ^\theta}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_q} A_e(q)^{\theta-1}\,\mathrm d q.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149599+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_f3f681977eb9ae940809b4e58a616eac3c6360d8024519e4cff1f440e2681399","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: an interior ball touching the boundary at the point x0 in question (and, for the strong maximum principle, the fact that such a ball can always be produced inside the open set where the solution is strictly below its maximum). Without it the conclusion 'the inward derivative at a boundary minimum is strictly positive' is false. Counterexample at a convex corner: in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with 0 < beta < pi and u(r, theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta). Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous on the closure, u > 0 inside and u = 0 on both straight edges, so 0 is a strict boundary minimum of u; but pi/beta > 1, so for every direction e pointing into Omega the difference quotient (u(te) - u(0))/t = O(t^{pi/beta - 1}) tends to 0: there is no Hopf gain at the vertex. No interior ball touches the vertex, exactly as the hypothesis requires. How far the hypothesis can be relaxed: the interior sphere condition may be replaced by an interior C^{1,Dini} (or interior paraboloid/cone-with-Dini) condition, but not by mere C^1 regularity of the boundary; there are C^1 domains where a positive harmonic function vanishing on the boundary has vanishing gradient at a boundary point - for instance the image of the upper half-plane near 0 under the conformal map z -> z log(1/z), whose boundary is C^1 but not Dini smooth at 0, and for which the inverse map has derivative tending to 0. Practical rule for an auditor: a proof that invokes Hopf's lemma (to get strict inequality, strict monotonicity, a sign of the normal derivative, simplicity of the first eigenvalue, or the strong maximum principle at the boundary) must say why the domain has the interior ball property at the relevant point; convex corners and cusps of the domain are where this silently breaks.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:50:44.858929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3f8e5198bcffc3acec71c1de3b41d54ef5f7797d612937121e45b4fb514f3ca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Admissible local-footprint family) of arXiv:2607.16502, 'Asymptotic Behavior of Path Functionals for Vector-Valued Gaussian Processes at High Level'] For \(E\in\mathcal K\) and \(F\in\mathcal K_0\), equip
\(C(E+F,\R^d)\) with the uniform norm and let
\[
  \Gamma_{E;F}:C(E+F,\R^d)\to\R
\]
be Borel measurable.  If coordinate deletion is used, the notation
\(\Gamma_{E;F}(\bm f_{K^c},\bm\infty_K)\) denotes a separate Borel map
\(\Gamma_{E;F}^{(-K)}:C(E+F,\R^{|K^c|})\to\R\), as above.
We call \(\{\Gamma_{E;F}\}\) an admissible local-footprint family, with
admissible levels \(\mathcal L\) and exponent \(\lambda_\Gamma\), if the
following conditions hold whenever the displayed restrictions are defined.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(\namedlabel{LF1}{\(\mathbf{LF}_1\)})]
  \textbf{Long-set union structure.}  For every fixed \(F\in\mathcal K_0\),
  all \(A,B\in\mathcal K\), \(L\in\mathcal L\), and
  \(\bm f\in C((A\cup B)+F,\R^d)\),
  \[
    \Gamma_{A;F}(\bm f)>L
    \Longrightarrow
    \Gamma_{A\cup B;F}(\bm f)>L
    \Longrightarrow
    \Gamma_{A;F}(\bm f)>L
    \quad\hbox{or}\quad
    \sup_{t\in B}\min_i f_i(t)>0,
  \]
  and
  \[
    \Gamma_{A;F}(\bm f)>L
    \Longrightarrow
    \sup_{t\in A}\min_i f_i(t)>0.
  \]
  No inclusion, monotonicity, or decomposition property is imposed in the
  footprint variable.

  \item[(\namedlabel{LF2}{\(\mathbf{LF}_2\)})]
  \textbf{Joint affine scaling.}  For all \(a>0\), \(b\in\R\),
  \(E\in\mathcal K\), \(F\in\mathcal K_0\), and \(L\in\mathcal L\),
  \[
    \Gamma_{aE+b;aF}(\bm f)>a^{\lambda_\Gamma}L
    \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
    \Gamma_{E;F}\bigl(\bm f(a\,\cdot+b)\bigr)>L.
  \]

  \item[(\namedlabel{LF3}{\(\mathbf{LF}_3\)})]
  \textbf{Local regularity for the exact limiting element.}  On each pair
  \(([0,S],F)\) used in a theorem, let \(\mathcal W_{\bm x}\) denote the
  coordinate-reduced shifted limiting path appearing in the corresponding
  local constant, regarded as a random element of
  \(C([0,S]+F,\R^d)\).  Then, for every \(L\in\mathcal L\) and
  Lebesgue-a.e. shift vector \(\bm x\),
  \[
    \pk{\Gamma_{[0,S];F}(\mathcal W_{\bm x})=L}=0,
    \qquad
    \pk{\mathcal W_{\bm x}\text{ is a continuity point of }
       \Gamma_{[0,S];F}}=1.
  \]
\end{enumerate}
As in Remark~\ref{rem:scaled-level-B1}, Assumptions~\ref{LF1}--\ref{LF2}
imply the long-set union structure at the scaled level
\(a^{\lambda_\Gamma}L\) for the scaled footprint \(aF\).  This is the form used
for a physical footprint \(\rho_uF\).
The coordinate-reduction property analogous to Assumption~\ref{B5}, when it
is used, is required only for the path coordinates and with \(F\) fixed.
A one-set family canonically lifts to a local-footprint family by
\[
  \Gamma_{E;F}(\bm f)=\Gamma_E(\bm f|_E),
\]
provided its affine scaling is read in the equivalent threshold-scaled form
used in~\ref{LF2}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.706252+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4177cd22fe68cf91c4fe2f17a2753cff7d031ce3e67b55d54b5041efda274b9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop shape of arXiv:2609.00672, 'Deciding superellipticity and computing the Weierstrass normal form'] Let $g\ge2$, let $C:y_2^2=f(x_2)$ with $f\in K[x_2]$ separable of degree $2g+1$ or $2g+2$, let $n\in\{2g+1,2g+2\}$, and put $m=n-1$. \[
f_t=a\,(x-\beta)^n+b,\qquad a,b\in K^\times,\ \beta\in K .
\]

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item There are $u,v\in K(C)$ with $K(u,v)=K(C)$ and $v^n=(u^2-b)/a$ for some $a,b\in K^\times$ if and only if $T_n\ne\emptyset$.

\begin{equation}
m\,p_t\,p_t''=(m-1)\,(p_t')^2 .
\end{equation}

The coefficients of $m\,p_t\,p_t''-(m-1)(p_t')^2$ as a polynomial in $x$ are polynomials in $t$ over $K$, not all zero, and $T_n\cap K$ is the set of their common roots in $K$.

{"assumptions":["i.i.d., or otherwise well-structured, entries of the non-Hermitian matrix M with matching moment and normalization conditions, e.g. mean 0, variance 1/n","convergence, for almost every z or in an appropriately averaged sense, of the empirical singular-value distribution of M-zI, established via Hermitian random matrix methods","a uniform bound preventing the smallest singular values of M-zI from concentrating excess mass near 0, i.e. a least-singular-value or anti-concentration estimate","sufficient regularity to justify exchanging limits with the singular logarithm in the potential-theoretic identity"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997859+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4189aeabe1f62c5a51a59e2d74be239517995bf2c0f01ad54eb33b87fa93fe6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To study the empirical spectral distribution of a non-Hermitian random matrix M, such as an i.i.d.-entry matrix in the circular law problem, Girko's Hermitization method associates to each z in C the 2n x 2n Hermitian matrix H_z with off-diagonal blocks M-zI and (M-zI)^*, whose eigenvalues are plus and minus the singular values of M-zI. The identity log|det(M-zI)| = (1/2) sum_i log(s_i(M-zI)^2) relates the real part of the logarithmic potential of M's empirical spectral distribution at z to the empirical distribution of singular values of M-zI, a Hermitian and hence more tractable object accessible via Stieltjes transform and local law techniques from Hermitian random matrix theory. Establishing, first, convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI for almost every z, and second, a uniform bound preventing accumulation of small singular values near 0, needed because log is singular there, together imply, via potential-theoretic uniqueness, convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of M itself, for example to the circular law for i.i.d. entries. It does not work without the delicate small-singular-value control, typically the hardest and most technical part of the proof, requiring separate anti-concentration or least-singular-value estimates, and the method inherently gives information about the logarithmic potential, from which the actual distribution is recovered only via a separate potential-theoretic uniqueness argument. Typical failure: Establishing convergence of the singular-value distribution of M-zI and concluding convergence of the eigenvalue distribution of M without separately proving the required small-singular-value control; without a quantitative lower bound on the least singular value, which can be genuinely delicate for matrices with dependent or heavy-tailed entries, the logarithmic potential argument can fail even though the easier half of Girko's method has been verified, historically the main obstruction in proving circular-law universality under weak entry assumptions. Canonical reference: Girko, 1984, Theory of Probability and its Applications; Bai, 1997, Annals of Probability; Tao and Vu, 2010, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:36.751148+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f443a441abcb2ab63f7ba1dcbb31cf06d84bbec648f76b0329ac8e2ceda42a2d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 48 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $F$ be a Hölder-type graded \tFre{} algebra, $l\in \N_0$, $m,p,d\in \N$, $e\in \N^*$, $U\subseteq \R^d$ and $V\subseteq \R^m$ convex, and $\delt, \ga \in [0,1)$. 		\item $\nrm{cf + g}{\Lip^{l+\delt}}\leq c\nrm f {\Lip^{l+\delt}} +\nrm g {\Lip^{l+\delt}}$, $f,g \in \Lip^{l+\delt}(U,F^{\Pi e})$.

		\item $\nrm{\innp fg}{\Lip^{l+\delt}_b,p} \lesssim \nrm{f}{\Lip^{l+\delt}_b,pq} \nrm{g}{\Lip^{l+\delt}_b,pr}$, uniformly over $f, g \in \Lip^{l+\delt}_b(U,F^{\Pi e})$. Here, $q,r\in \N \cup \set{\infty}$ with $\frac1q + \frac1r = 1$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.495670+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f4450b784da6e0938f0a47fa2c1b4558192e92c1177f2731452ea5e06519a583","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 36 (Weight) of arXiv:2605.09459, 'Multipoint connectivity in the branching interlacement process'] Given a tree $T$ equiped with functions $\varphi : V(T) \to \mathbb{Z}^d$, and $\alpha : E(T) \to \mathbb{R}$, we define the \textit{weight} of $T$, as
  \[
    p^{\alpha}_\varphi(T) = \prod_{(u,v) \in E(T)} \frac{1}{1 + \|\varphi(u)-\varphi(v)\|^{\alpha(u,v)}}.
  \]
  For a tree $T$ with vertices in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, we write $p^{\alpha}(T)$ for $p^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{Id}}(T)$. When there is no possible ambiguity, we omit the exponent $\alpha$. Furthermore, if the weight is constant equal to $c$, we simply write $p^c_\varphi$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:11.960170+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f446830f9c11f4c5fbfdcd3a5d25d8bc5064c5742878fb4ae88217c4fa051570","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main-result of arXiv:2607.24018, 'Jeu de taquin forests \\ and the inverse infinite RSK correspondence'] Let $T$ be a Plan\-che\-rel-distributed random IYT, and let 
	$(z_1,z_2,\ldots) = \RSK^{-1}(T)$ be the associated sequence of i.i.d.
	$U(0,1)$-distributed random variables. The following statements hold almost
	surely:
	
	\begin{enumerate}
	
	\item Each of the trees $\tau$ in $\Phi(T)$
possesses an asymptotic direction $\alpha_\textnormal{asym}(\tau)$ (see
(subsec:asymptotic-direction of the paper) for the definition).
	
	\item We have the equality of sets
	\[
	\left\{ \alpha_\textnormal{asym}(\tau) \,:\, \tau \textrm{ is a tree in }\Phi(T)
	\right\}

	\]

	in particular, the map $\tau \mapsto \alpha_\textnormal{asym}(\tau)$
	is a bijection between the set of trees of $\Phi(T)$

	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.678710+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f452b52a8962e47a5006920bf17ac68960ee9e12c01202ce995e7d1408f8b518","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 26 (Schatten classification from orthogonal direct-sum laws) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $1\le r\le\infty$.  Replace the area square-sum law by the $\ell^r$ block
law and normalize a standard skew two-plane by $2^{1/r}$ for $r<\infty$, or by
$1$ for $r=\infty$.  Then the finite-dimensional coefficient norm is
$\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal S_r}$.  The analogous symmetric law, normalized in one
dimension, also gives $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal S_r}$.  On finite-rank state
coordinates the dual gauge is the Schatten $r'$ gauge; completing finite ranks
gives $\mathcal S_{r'}$ when $r'<\infty$ and $\mathcal K(H)$ at the endpoint
$r'=\infty$.

For the principal pair $(r_A,r_Q)=(2,\infty)$, the state geometry is therefore
$\mathcal S_2/\mathcal S_1$.  At the coefficient endpoint $r_Q=\infty$, the
finite-rank norm completion is $\mathcal K(H)$, while the full normal test space
may be taken to be $\mathcal L(H)=\mathcal S_1(H)^*$; both unit balls induce the
same trace norm on $\mathcal S_1(H)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:18.001232+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f452f2800b6332b691764ee66440ee19b144a20a9507b6b8e23cceeca77f87b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:volume-process of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] (short version of Definition~(def:volume-process-ext of the paper), without the explanation)
Fix a real number $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. 
Fix an initialising state 
$\Psi_0 = (0, \tau_0,j,\overline{z},\emptyset,\textup{initialising})$.
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be a transition rule on a set of high-level states which includes~$\Psi_0$. Let $\Psi^*$ be the $\Psi_0$-closure of~$\mathrm{hls}$. Suppose that $\mathrm{hls}$ is $\Psi^*$-valid.
A \emph{volume process} $V$ 
from $\Psi_0$ with transition rule~$\mathrm{hls}$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$ is defined as follows. 

Choose the initial population as follows.
Choose 
a random vector 
$\overline{\mathrm{arr}} = (\mathrm{arr}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{arr}_j)
\sim\mathsf{Po}(F_{[j]}^{\Psi_0}(\tau_0))$.
Let $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^V(\tau_0)$ be a tuple
of $j$~disjoint sets
$\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^V(\tau_0) = (\mathbf{arr}^V_1(\tau_0),\ldots,\mathbf{arr}^V_j(\tau_0))$ 
where each $\mathbf{arr}^V_i(\tau_0) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\tau_0)$ and has size 
$\mathrm{arr}^V_i(\tau_0)$.

Let ${\overline{\mathbf{b}}}^V_{[j]}(\tau_0) = \overline{\mathbf{arr}}^V(\tau_0)$.
For all $i>j$, let   ${\mathbf{b}^V_i}(\tau_0) = \emptyset$. 
Let the initial high-level state 
$\Psi(\tau_0)$ be~$\Psi_0$. 
 

For all $t> \tau_0$ the evolution of 
$\newsym{V}{Volume process - Definition~(def:volume-process of the paper)}{V}$ at step~$t$ is as follows, having 
already defined $\Psi(t-1)$ and  ${\overline{\mathbf{b}}}^V(t-1)$.

\begin{itemize}

\item Let $j = j^{\Psi(t-1)}$.

\item Let
$\newsym{Y-t}{part of volume process
- Definition~(def:volume-process of the paper)
}{Y_{t-1}}$ be a $j$-jammed process with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$, start time~$t-1$, 
birth rate~$\lambda$, and initial population  $\mathbf{arr}^{Y_{t-1}}(t-1) = {\overline{\mathbf{b}}}_{[j]}^V(t-1)$.

 

 
\item  Let $\newsym{Psi-t}{high-level state determined by volume process - Definition~(def:volume-process of the paper) }
{\Psi(t) }
= \mathrm{hls}(\Psi(t-1), {\overline{b}}^{Y_{t-1}}_{[j]}(t), t)$.

 

\item Let ${\overline{b}}^V_{[j]}(t) = \phi_{\Psi(t-1),\Psi(t),t}({\overline{b}}^{Y_{t-1}}_{[j]}(t))$.

  

\item  For all $i\in [j]$,  let  $\mathbf{b}_i^{V}(t)$ be the lexicographically least
subset of $\mathbf{b}_i^{Y_{t-1}}(t)$ 
of size $b^V_i(t)$. 
 

\item {For all $i > j$, let $\mathbf{b}^V_i(t) = \emptyset$.}
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:16:46.719152+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f45385609796b7b234389683d8eeaf64657c8d428d56206a9686cbb83bf8523a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem theo.SRWBRW of arXiv:2411.19145, 'On the intersection of critical percolation clusters and other tree-like random graphs'] Let $(R_\infty^k)_{k\ge 1}$, and $(\mathcal R_c^k)_{k\ge 1}$, be respectively SRW and critical BRW ranges on $\mathbb Z^d$.

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
