{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.177619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f6cf902830d44196232726e732f11132c890f43f7349e2277ad075f47de1989b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 78 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\hat{Y}$ the stopped martingale defined above, we can construct a deterministic time change $\tilde{Y}$ that can be expressed as the stochastic integral
    \[
    \tilde{Y}(t)
    =\tilde{Y}(q_0) + \int_0^t \tilde{w}_t\,d\tilde{W}(t)
    \]
for $t\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$,
where
$\tilde{Y}(q_0)=\hat{Y}(q_0)=Y(q_0)$,
$\tilde{W}$ is a standard Brownian motion, and $\tilde{w}$ satisfies
the constraint $\E[(\tilde{w}_t)^2]=1$ for all $t\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$.

\begin{proof} We will construct a  martingale $\tilde{Y}$ to essentially be the deterministic time-change of $\hat{Y}$ such that $\E[\tilde{Y}(t)^2]=t$ for all $t\in[q_0,\gamma(1)]$. Then, for $t\in[\gamma(1),1]$, we will take $\tilde{Y}$ to be any martingale ending at $\pm1$ almost surely, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lem:Yt-process-always-is-completable} below. To formalize the time reparametrization, since $\gamma:[q_0,1]\to[q_0,\gamma(1)]$ is nondecreasing, we can define its right-continuous generalized inverse 
\[\lambda:[q_0,\gamma(1)]\to[q_0,1]\,.\]
As a consequence of \eqref{e:gamma.prime} we must have $\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)\le t-s$ and $\lambda(t)-\lambda(s)\ge t-s$ for all $q_0 \le s\le t\le1$. It  follows by combining these inequalities with Proposition~\ref{p:gamma-1} that
    \beq
    \begin{aligned}
    s &\ge \gamma(s) \ge \gamma(1)+s-1 \ge s-4\epsilon^{1/2}\,,\\
    t &\le \lambda(t) \le \lambda(\gamma(1)) + t-\gamma(1)
    =1+t-\gamma(1) \le t+4\epsilon^{1/2}
    \end{aligned}
    \eeq
for all $s\in [q_0,1]$, and $t\in [q_0,\gamma(1)]$. It is clear from this that we must define $\tilde{Y}(t) = \hat{Y}(\lambda(t))$, so that
we will have $\E[\tilde{Y}(t)^2] = \E[\hat{Y}(\lambda(t))^2] = \gamma(\lambda(t))=t$. Since
    \[
    \hat{Y}(\lambda(t)) = Y(q_0) + \int_{q_0}^{\lambda(t)}
        w_u \ind\{u\le\tau\} \,dW(u)\,,
    \]
by considering the change of variables $u=\lambda(s)$ it is natural to define
    \beq
    \tilde{W}(t) = \int_{q_0}^{\lambda(t)} \gamma'(u)^{1/2} dW(u)\,.
    \eeq
Then $\tilde{W}$ is a local martingale with quadratic variation
    \[
    \langle \tilde{W}\rangle_t 
    = \int_{q_0}^{\lambda(t)} \gamma'(u)\,du
    = \gamma(\lambda(t))-\gamma(q_0) = t-q_0
    \]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$, so by the L\'evy characterization it is a standard Brownian motion on $t\in[q_0,1]$, and is progressively measurable with respect to the time-changed filtration
$\tilde{\cF}_Y(t)\equiv\cF_Y(\lambda(t))$. We then define the modified control
    \[
    \tilde{w}_s
    \equiv
    \frac{w_{\lambda(s)}}{\gamma'(\lambda(s))^{1/2} }
      \ind\{\lambda(s)\le \tau\}\,,\]
where we define $\tilde{w}_s\equiv1$ in the case $\gamma'(\lambda(s))=0$ --- by Lemma~\ref{l:generalized.inverse.fn}, the set of such times $s$ is of measure zero. If $\gamma'(\lambda(s))=0$ then clearly we have $\E[(\tilde{w}_s)^2]=1$, and otherwise 
\eqref{e:gamma.prime} gives
	\[\E[(\tilde{w}_s)^2]
    =\frac{\E[(w_{\lambda(s)})^2 \ind\{
        \lambda(s)\le\tau\}]}
        {\gamma'(\lambda(s))}
    = 1\,.
    \]
We can then express the desired process as
    \[
    \tilde{Y}(t)
    = \hat{Y}(\lambda(t))
    =\tilde{Y}(q_0) + \int_{q_0}^t \tilde{w}_s\,d\tilde{W}(s)\,,
    \]
where $\tilde{Y}(q_0)=\hat{Y}(q_0)= Y(q_0)$. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.719078+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f6eba7d20cf15f2978075642c099f507acb92ae1e47b9510c6abae0b1d005602","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:modal-gg-translation of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {das_intuitionistic_2023}}] 
  We inductively define the \emph{modal (G\"odel--Gentzen) double negation translation}
  $(\cdot)^N: \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond} \to \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$:
  \begin{align*}
    \bot^N &\coloneq \bot, &
    p^N    &\coloneq \neg \neg p, \\
    (\varphi \land \psi)^N &\coloneq \varphi^N \land \psi^N, &
    (\varphi \lor \psi)^N  &\coloneq \neg(\neg \varphi^N \land \neg \psi^N), \\
    (\varphi \to \psi)^N &\coloneq \varphi^N \to \psi^N, \\
    (\Box\varphi)^N &\coloneq \Box\varphi^N, &
    (\Diamond\varphi)^N &\coloneq \neg \Box \neg \varphi^N.
  \end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.664083+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f70c928b376b6f60597a43fae1e743d3682e0d69eac9b55e32d06b808cd26188","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let $k,d\in\mathbb{N}$ with $d\ge 2$, and let $a,b>0$. Set
\[
\beta_1:=\frac{1}{2k(d-1)+1}
\quad\text{and}\quad
s:=\frac{d(2k-1)}{4k(d-1)}.
\]
Then, for every pair of mappings $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k)$ with
$f_j,g_j\in \mathcal{P}_d(\gamma)$,
\[
\int_E \Delta_f\,d\gamma\ge a,
\quad
\int_E \Delta_g\,d\gamma\ge a,
\]
and
\[
\max_{1\le j\le k}\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(f_j)\le b,
\quad
\max_{1\le j\le k}\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(g_j)\le b,
\]
one has, for every $\beta\in(0,\beta_1)$,
\begin{equation}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
C_1k^{3/2}d\,(\beta_1-\beta)^{-s}
\bigl(1+a^{-\frac{1}{2k(d-1)}}b^{\frac{2k-1}{4k(d-1)}}\bigr)\,
d_{\mathrm{KR}}(f,g)^\beta,
\end{equation}
where $C_1>0$ is an absolute constant. In particular, if $d_{\mathrm{KR}}(f,g)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
C_2k^{3/2}d
\bigl(1+a^{-\frac{1}{2k(d-1)}}b^{\frac{2k-1}{4k(d-1)}}\bigr)
\bigl(1+\ln\tfrac{2}{d_{\mathrm{KR}}(f,g)}\bigr)^s
d_{\mathrm{KR}}(f,g)^{\beta_1},
\end{equation}
where $C_2>0$ is an absolute constant.

More generally, for every $r\in\mathbb{N}$, setting
\[
\beta_r:=\frac{1}{2rk(d-1)+1},
\]
one has, for every $\beta\in(0,\beta_r)$,
\begin{equation}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
C_1(r,k)\,d\,(\beta_r-\beta)^{-s}
\bigl(1+a^{-\frac{1}{2k(d-1)}}b^{\frac{2k-1}{4k(d-1)}}\bigr)\,
d_r(f,g)^\beta,
\end{equation}
where $C_1(r,k)>0$ depends only on $r$ and $k$. Moreover, if $d_r(f,g)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
C_2(r,k)\,d
\bigl(1+a^{-\frac{1}{2k(d-1)}}b^{\frac{2k-1}{4k(d-1)}}\bigr)
\bigl(1+\ln\tfrac{2}{d_r(f,g)}\bigr)^s
d_r(f,g)^{\beta_r},
\end{equation}
where $C_2(r,k)>0$ depends only on $r$ and $k$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.315653+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f719255e06f6f9de992a413b02946463e46b5faae29dffcbf889cd8607f70ba9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \((N,R_{+},R_{-},\gamma)\) be a sutured manifold and \(S\) be a properly embedded surface in \(N\).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.648450+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f721a0fc3932ce77e99e32722ed09256cb9bcf14c3dc9fea1afe7a28652e1337","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 9 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] [See \cite[Definitions~3.8, 3.9 and 3.11]{Ya}.]
A pre-log Dieudonn\'e algebra
\[
\sA^*=(A^*,d,F,\alpha:L\to A^0,\delta:L\to A^1)
\]
over $\sR$ is \emph{saturated} if its underlying Dieudonn\'e algebra is
saturated in the sense of \cite[Definition~3.4.1]{BLM}. Let
\[
i_A\colon A^*\longrightarrow\Sat(A^*)
\]
be the saturation map of the underlying Dieudonn\'e algebra. We equip
$\Sat(A^*)$ with the same monoid $L$ and with maps
\[
\alpha_{\rm sat}:=i_A^0\circ\alpha,
\qquad
\delta_{\rm sat}:=i_A^1\circ\delta.
\]
The resulting pre-log Dieudonn\'e algebra is denoted by $\Sat(\sA^*)$.

A saturated pre-log Dieudonn\'e algebra is \emph{strict} if its
underlying saturated Dieudonn\'e algebra is strict in the sense of
\cite[Definition~3.5.6]{BLM}. If
\[
\rho_A\colon A^*\longrightarrow W(A^*)
=
\varprojlim_r A^*/\mathrm{Fil}^rA^*
\]
is the strictification map of the underlying Dieudonn\'e algebra, we
equip $W(A^*)$ with the same monoid $L$ and with maps
\[
\alpha_W:=\rho_A^0\circ\alpha,
\qquad
\delta_W:=\rho_A^1\circ\delta.
\]
We write $W(\sA^*)$ for the resulting strict pre-log Dieudonn\'e
algebra and set
\[
\WSat(\sA^*):=W(\Sat(\sA^*)).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.579901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f72476ea5c1f80b99b0a20816b02be7cd0cadac4de38b1a46bfc46c40a0d11d9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop u11 of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] Assume that the existence condition~(equation intro:existence of the paper) is satisfied and that the drift $\mu$ is non-zero.
Denote by $\mu_1^{-}$ and $\mu_2^{-}$ the negative parts of the drift components (defined by $\mu_i^-=\max(-\mu_i,0)$). 
The process $Z$ is transient if and only if
\begin{equation}
\mu_1 + r_{2}\mu_2^{-} > 0 
\quad \text{or} \quad 
\mu_2 + r_{1}\mu_1^{-} > 0,

\end{equation}
and recurrent if and only if
\begin{equation}
\mu_1 + r_{2}\mu_2^{-} \le 0 
\quad \text{and} \quad 
\mu_2 + r_{1}\mu_1^{-} \le 0.

\end{equation}
In the latter case, the process is positive recurrent and admits a unique stationary
distribution if and only if
\begin{equation}
\mu_1 + r_{2}\mu_2^{-} < 0 
\quad \text{and} \quad 
\mu_2 + r_{1}\mu_1^{-} < 0,

\end{equation}
and is null recurrent if and only if
\[
\mu_1 + r_{2}\mu_2^{-} = 0 
\quad \text{or} \quad 
\mu_2 + r_{1}\mu_1^{-} = 0.
\]
In this case, the invariant measure is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure and we denote by $\pi$ its density. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:06:55.296364+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f74645ce7f612705654b2c889792a5e0b49273dd3ca9515050c8c9fec90fe96d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:cross-sign of arXiv:2602.19192, 'Bakry--\'Emery Curvature of the Fractional Laplacian\\ via Fractional Brownian Covariance'] For $n,m > 0$:
\begin{equation}
  \Psi_\gamma(n,-m) = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(n^\gamma + m^\gamma
  - (n+m)^\gamma\bigr).
\end{equation}
This vanishes identically if and only if $\gamma = 1$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item At $\gamma = 1$: $\Psi_1(n,-m)
  = \tfrac{1}{2}(n + m - (n+m)) = 0$ for all $n,m > 0$.
\item For $\gamma < 1$: $\Psi_\gamma(n,-m) > 0$
  (subadditivity of $|\cdot|^\gamma$).
\item For $\gamma > 1$: $\Psi_\gamma(n,-m) < 0$
  (superadditivity of $|\cdot|^\gamma$).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

        Let $L$ be the generator of $F_t$, and let $D \subset \operatorname{dom} L$ be another Banach space with $\|\cdot\|_D \geq \|\cdot\|_B$ such that
        \[
        \|Lf\|_B \leq l \|f\|_D \, \forall f \in D.
        \]
        Assume also that $F_t$ is bounded in $D$:
        \[
        \max_{s \in [0,t]} \|F_s\|_{D \to D} \leq e^{m t},
        \]
        for some $m \geq 0$.
        
        
        Let $U_h$ be a family of linear bounded operators in $B$ with 
        \[
          \| U_h \|_{B \to B} \leq e^{q h},
          \qquad q\ge0,
        \]
        and let
        \begin{align} 
        \left\| \left( \frac{U_h - 1}{h} - L \right) f \right\|_B &\leq \epsilon_h \|f\|_D, \\
        
        \left\| \left( \frac{F_h - 1}{h} - L \right) f \right\|_B &\leq \chi_h \|f\|_D, 
        \end{align}
        where $\epsilon_h,\chi_h>0$ are monotone and tend to zero as $h\to0$.
        
        Then
        \begin{equation} 
        \begin{aligned}
            \sup_{s \leq t} \left\| (U_h)^{\lfloor s/h\rfloor} f - F_s f \right\|_B
            &\leq
            (\chi_h + \epsilon_h) \|f\|_D
            \int_0^t e^{ms + q (t-s)} \, ds  \\
            &\quad
            + e^{\bar m t} h (l + \epsilon_h) \|f\|_D .
        \end{aligned}
        \end{equation}

        For the killed semigroups with rate $c>0$,
        \begin{equation} 
        \begin{aligned}
            \sup_{s \leq t}
            \left\| e^{-c\lfloor s/h\rfloor h } (U_h)^{\lfloor s/h\rfloor} f
            - e^{-cs} F_s f \right\|_B
            &\leq
            (\chi_h + \epsilon_h) \|f\|_D
            \int_0^t e^{(m-c)s + (q-c) (t-s)} \, ds  \\
            &\quad
            + e^{(\bar m - c) t} h (l + \epsilon_h + c) \|f\|_D .
        \end{aligned}
        \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d>=1,N>=2d+1,n>=0,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=ell<=r integers","Paired A/S VC class; uniform contexts then uniform truths; independent uniform r-subsets in A, all truths in S","Actual iid factual samples without tags; independent uniform ell-subset verifier in every variable context including S","Unresolved sibling pairs have equal distinct observed-plus-certified counts h<=r; identified pairs are logically certified by an S context with >r known truths; each identified A count j is >= maximum unresolved h (vacuous if none)","All generators; robust exact-level source calibration across every compatible orientation and residual support"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:39.295480+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; partial truth verification","id":"claim_f75b182c10094807f8f65295a7c116ffcea2d51b7b906b0cc0c6c75d7a006c10","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent review pending. # Pair-balanced factual identities under partial verification

T379-C015 v2, proof (unaudited). Both exact verification suites PASS;
independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending.
Targets 1 and 2. This is a conditional data-regime result, not a global
expected minimax claim. The unresolved unequal-sibling-count regime is
the hardest missing piece; C010 shows why its ordering cannot be assumed.

## Model and data region

Use the paired VC-d experiment: d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K integers;
one A and one S per pair, all remaining contexts known S. S has K true
candidates, A has an independent uniform r-subset. The source p chooses
contexts uniformly, then true candidates uniformly. Observe n>=0 iid
factual context/candidate samples without orientation tags. Independently
a perfect verifier supplies a uniform ell-subset of truths in each
variable context, including S, 0<=ell<=r. Let C_x be the union of
distinct observed and verified candidate identities in context x.

Condition on any positive-probability data outcome for which every pair
has |C_left|=|C_right|=h_j<=r. The actual identities may differ. Thus no
orientation is logically excluded, and every one of 2^d orientations
is compatible. Counts and likelihoods of repeated observations can be
unequal: uniform orientation weights below are an ARTIFICIAL proof
distribution, not the actual Bayesian posterior. Under a chosen
orientation, the A support ranges uniformly over r-subsets containing
C_A. Put D_h=#{j:h_j=h}, ell<=h<=r.

Define

 b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N),
 tau_h=(K-r)/(2(K-h)),
 M_h=(D_h/N)*(2-h/r-h/K),
 T_h=sum_{t=h}^r M_t.

Over ALL generators, with source Mis_infinity<=c required in every
compatible world (including every compatible A support), the proposed
exact conditional worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V_D(c)=tau_ell*(T_ell-c)_+
        +sum_{h=ell+1}^r (tau_h-tau_{h-1})*(T_h-c)_+.       (1)

All formulas allow missing D_h and c in [0,1]. Exact score bins define
source Mis_infinity=TV(g,p_Pi), with p uniformly coarsened in each bin.

## Lower bound across arbitrary mixed bins

Average orientations fairly and A supports uniformly conditional on
containing their known identities. Let mu be the resulting mean law.
Every known true atom in a variable context has density

 a=(1/r+1/K)/(2N).

The uncertified atoms of a pair at count h have density b_h and false
probability tau_h under this artificial prior. Their total mu mass is
M_h across the D_h pairs. Known S atoms have density 1/(NK).

As h increases, tau_h increases and b_h decreases: directly,
b_h-b_{h+1}=(K-r)/(2Nr(K-h)(K-h-1)) when h<r. All safe densities
are >=1/(NK)>=b_h. Thus E_h, the union of uncertified atoms in pairs
with count at least h, consists of lower-density atoms than its entire
complement. For ANY partition Pi, uniform coarsening increases its mass:

 mu_Pi(E_h)>=mu(E_h)=T_h.

Indeed in each cell the mean density over E_h is at most the mean over
its complement, so replacing both means by the cell mean transfers
mass into E_h. This proves the assertion per bin, not merely globally.

Robust feasibility and linearity/TV convexity give TV(mu_Pi(g),g)<=c.
Hence g(E_h)>=(T_h-c)_+. Layer-cake decomposition of the artificial
average false risk gives

 max_world H(g)>=tau_ell*g(E_ell)
                   +sum_{h>ell}(tau_h-tau_{h-1})*g(E_h)
                >=V_D(c).

No joint-probability multiplication or actual-posterior identity is used.

## Matching construction

Start from mu. Remove mass min(c,T_ell) from uncertified groups in
decreasing h order, uniformly within each h group, and add it uniformly
to the fixed known S reservoir. All remaining g(E_h)=(T_h-c)_+.
Each pair's known-true group has h atoms from each sibling and invariant
source mass h*(1/r+1/K)/N. Its uncertified group has K-h atoms from
each sibling and invariant source mass (2-h/r-h/K)/N, regardless of
orientation or which residual truths occupy A. The constructed g is
constant on every such group. Exact score bins only merge invariant
groups, so p_Pi=mu_Pi in every compatible world. Since g_Pi=g,
Mis_infinity<=TV(mu,g)<=c. The uncertified false-atom fraction in each
h group equals tau_h in every world. Thus actual H equals V_D(c)
worldwise, proving conditional sharpness of (1).

## Same-data oracle and exact estimation penalty

If the true partition is additionally supplied, let

 A_h=D_h*(r-h)/(Nr), Q_h=sum_{t=h}^r A_t,
 alpha_h=(K-r)/(K-h)=2tau_h.

The same-data known-partition frontier, by the ordered known-A groups,
is

 O_D(c)=alpha_ell*(Q_ell-c)_+
        +sum_{h>ell}(alpha_h-alpha_{h-1})*(Q_h-c)_+.       (2)

Here A_h is the posterior mass of unknown true candidates of the actual
A contexts, and their densities decrease while their false risks rise.
The same mixed-bin tail proof and transfer-to-S construction apply.
Thus V_D(c)=O_D(c)+[V_D(c)-O_D(c)] is an exact matching decomposition,
with nonnegative difference because giving the partition enlarges
feasibility. At c=0 it simplifies to the explicit positive penalty

 V_D(0)-O_D(0)
   =sum_{h=ell}^r D_h*h*(K-r)^2/(2NrK(K-h)).             (3)

The penalty is zero at h=0, and at h=r contributes kappa/(2N) per pair,
recovering C013's unresolved full-verifier value. In general it depends
on the factual-support histogram, not merely VC dimension or a single
unweighted classification-error scalar. A fair completion among the
2^d support-consistent ERM orientations has conditional expected
classification error 1/N per pair; (3) weights that error by
h*(K-r)^2/[2rK(K-h)]. This is a specified ERM, not an optimal posterior
classification claim. The conditional minimax lower bound is not
silently averaged into a global expected lower bound; C014 forbids
that shortcut at positive budgets.

## Scope

This removes supplied tags and retains actual factual identities for
every balanced outcome, all n,K,r,ell and all calibration budgets. It
allows different h across pairs, but does not cover unequal sibling
counts, already identified pairs, or an unconditional exact expected
frontier. Equal h in every pair reduces the conditional formula to the
corresponding earlier C008 experiment with that many known truths;
the histogram, actual untagged-data applicability and explicit oracle
penalty are the proposed extension, not a claim that C008 was unknown.
Primary basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9;
own earlier C008/C009 are unaudited drafts. No novelty or target score
is certified until independent mathematical and priority review.

## Extension: include identified pairs under a coverage ordering

The same theorem extends as follows. Partition the d pairs into resolved
and unresolved pairs. A resolved pair has a context with >r distinct
known truths, logically forcing S and identifying its sibling as A.
Let E_j count these known A contexts with j distinct known truths,
ell<=j<=r. Each unresolved pair still has balanced count h<=r; D_h
now counts just these unresolved pairs. Require

 j>=h_max for every resolved A, where
 h_max=max{h:D_h>0}.                                    (4)

If no unresolved pairs exist, condition (4) is vacuous. Known facts
in identified S and fixed S contexts are all safe and have density
1/(NK), irrespective of their observed identities or counts.

There are two positive-risk group types under the artificial compatible
prior (independent fair unresolved orientations and uniform compatible
A supports):

* Unresolved count h: mass M_h as before, risk tau_h, density b_h.
* Resolved A count j: mass L_j=E_j*(r-j)/(Nr), risk
  alpha_j=(K-r)/(K-j), density a_j=(r-j)/(Nr(K-j)).

Groups at j=r can have zero factual mass and risk one; retain them
without dividing by their mass. All safe groups have density >=1/(NK).
For resolved groups, j increasing makes risk increase and density
decrease. Across the two types condition (4) implies

 alpha_j>=alpha_hmax=2tau_hmax>=tau_h,
 a_j<=a_hmax<=b_hmax<=b_h.

Thus ALL groups are ordered in opposite directions by density and risk.
Let 0<xi_1<...<xi_s<=1 be their distinct risk values; aggregate masses
at equal risk into m_i, and let R_i=sum_{k=i}^s m_k, xi_0=0. The exact
combined conditional robust frontier is

 V(c)=sum_{i=1}^s (xi_i-xi_{i-1})*(R_i-c)_+.             (5)

The same arbitrary-bin tail argument proves the lower bound. Remove
mass in decreasing risk order, uniformly inside each group, and transfer
to fixed S for the upper bound. Resolved A certified and uncertified
groups have world-invariant p masses because all residual supports
have the same size and contain the known truths. Unresolved balanced
groups have the invariance proved earlier. Consequently exact score
mergers remain valid for every compatible support and orientation.
False fractions equal the specified risks in EACH actual world, so
the construction attains (5) worldwise, not just on artificial average.

The same-data partition oracle is formula (2) with A_h replaced by

 (D_h+E_h)*(r-h)/(Nr).

At c=0 its exact difference from (5) is still formula (3), now summed
over unresolved pairs only. The identified-pair terms cancel. At any
c, both explicit formulas match their respective conditional minima.
When ell=r, every resolved A has j=r and condition (4) always holds;
this reduces (5) to C013's conditional frontier for arbitrary mixtures
of resolved and unresolved pairs. For ell<r this is a larger untagged
partial-verifier data regime than the all-unresolved case.

Unequal sibling counts or failure of (4) are NOT covered. No exact
global expected minimax value follows by averaging (5). This extension
has a separate route check, logs/route_014_extension_check.txt, and its
finite exact verification is kept separate from the general derivation.

## Zero-budget pointwise scope and an explicit control

If all pairs are unresolved and share ONE count h, every atom of the
artificial mean law has density at least b_h. Robust zero calibration
implies g=mu_Pi, hence g(atom)>=b_h. Each actual world has exactly
d(K-r) false atoms. Consequently every such generator obeys the
POINTWISE bound H>=d(K-r)b_h=V_D(0), and the construction attains it.
This separate observation applies regardless of actual orientation
likelihoods. It does not extend to varying h by the same argument.

In fact varying h can destroy even a zero-budget pointwise version of
the conditional bound. Take N=5,d=2,K=3,r=2,ell=0 and counts h_0=0,
h_1=1; use C_2=C_3={0}. These are possible actual untagged data, e.g.
the two observations (2,0),(3,0). Form a bin B containing all three
atoms of context 0 and the four uncertified atoms of contexts 2 and 3.
Its source mass is 1/5+7/30=13/30, independent of orientations and
residual A supports; set g=13/210 on its seven atoms. Other bins are
all of context 1 (g=1/15), both certified atoms of contexts 2 and 3
(g=1/12), and all fixed-S context 4 (g=1/15). Merging the equal 1/15
scores preserves invariance. This g is robustly source-calibrated at
zero in every compatible world.

If context 0 is A its actual false mass is 13/105, strictly below
V_D(0)=1/8 by 1/840. If context 1 is A, its false mass is 9/70,
strictly above 1/8. This is a real compatible-world control, not a
violation of (1) or (5): the theorem is conditional WORST-WORLD, and
the latter world meets that lower bound. It forbids silently replacing
the conditional maximum by a per-world bound even at zero budget in
the varying-count family. No claim about the global sampling minimax
value follows from this single outcome.

Verification logs: pair_balanced_partial_check.json records 5212
arbitrary-bin tail checks, 1806 mixed-bin generator bounds, 2356
world/budget attainer checks and 622 oracle checks. The mixed extension
log pair_balanced_mixed_check.json adds 2400 tail checks, 2125 attainer
checks, 850 oracle checks and 11 exact oracle-gap identities. Controls
show actual failure of score-bin invariance without pair balance,
density ordering without sufficient identified-A coverage, and the
zero-budget pointwise extension under varying pair counts. Finite
verification supports, and does not replace, the general proof above.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.223559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f764e9af75369a9134ec5839aa3b6763404fc9db4737dd3f521f97756a4ba387","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:deterministiclimit of arXiv:2608.21931, 'Interacting Urn Schemes on Finite Ancestral Directed Acyclic Graphs'] Suppose that Assumption~(asm:deterministiclimit of the paper) holds. Then the entire
system $\{\U{n}{v}:n\ge0,\ v\in V\}$ converges almost surely to a
deterministic limit $\{\us{}{v}:v\in V\}$; that is,
\[
\U{n}{v}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\us{}{v},
\qquad
\text{as }n\to\infty,\ \forall v\in V.
\]

For the sum-reinforcement scheme, the limiting proportions are
characterized as follows. For each generator $g\in G$, the limit
$\us{}{g}$ is the normalized Perron--Frobenius eigenvector of
$R^{(g,g)}$. For $v\in V\setminus G$,
\begin{equation}
\us{}{v}:=
\begin{cases}
\U{0}{v}, & \text{if }v\in S,\\[0.25cm]
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{b_v}
\sum_{p:p\rightsquigarrow v}
\us{}{p}R^{(p,v)},
& \text{if }v\in V\setminus(G\cup S),
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where
\[
b_v:=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\sum_{p:p\rightsquigarrow v}r\big((p,v)\big),
& \text{if }v\in V\setminus S,\\[0.25cm]
1, & \text{if }v\in S,
\end{cases}
\]
is referred to as the \emph{total balance} of the vertex $v$.

For the average-reinforcement scheme, the limiting proportions are
obtained from (equation 11 of the paper) by replacing each reinforcement matrix
$R^{(p,v)}$ with $R^{(p,v)}/d_v^{\mathrm{in}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:19:06.723182+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f77389720c250b74364c48fca65841504eff16da8c3a8c96aa76f450fdb23087","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm SD-closure of arXiv:2606.02056, 'Special Dirichlet Processes: Structure, Uniqueness and Stability'] Let \(X\) be a Special--Dirichlet process on \([0,t]\), with canonical
decomposition
\[
        X=M+\Gamma,
        \qquad M_0=0,
\]
where \(M\) is a local martingale and \(\Gamma\) is an adapted càdlàg
process such that
$
        [\Gamma]^c_t=0,
$
and whose jumps are carried by a thin predictable set and satisfy
$
        \Delta\Gamma_s\in\mathcal F_{s-}.
$
Let \(f\) be the primitive of a locally bounded function \(f'\) with an
at most countable set of discontinuities. Assume that
\[
        \int_0^t
        \mathbf 1_{\{X_s\notin\operatorname{diff}(f)\}}\,d[X]^c_s=0.
\]
Then \(f(X)\) is again a Special--Dirichlet process.

More precisely, 

\[
        f(X)=M^f+\Gamma^f,
\]
where
\[
        M^f_t
        :=
        \int_0^t f'(X_{s-}+\Delta\Gamma_s)\,dM^c_s
        +
        \int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R}
        \left(f(X_{s-}+\Delta\Gamma_s+x)-f(X_{s-}+\Delta\Gamma_s)\right)(\mu^M-\nu^M)(ds,dx)
\]
is a local martingale, and \(\Gamma^f:=f(X)-M^f\) satisfies
$
        [\Gamma^f]^c_t=0.
$

Moreover,
\[
        \Delta\Gamma^f_s
        =
        f(X_{s-}+\Delta\Gamma_s)-f(X_{s-})
        +
        \int_{\mathbb R}
        \left(f(X_{s-}+\Delta\Gamma_s+x)-f(X_{s-}+\Delta\Gamma_s)\right)\nu^M(\{s\},dx).
\]

In particular, the jumps of \(\Gamma^f\) are carried by a thin predictable
set and satisfy
\[
        \Delta\Gamma^f_s\in\mathcal F_{s-}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent with values in [0,1]","mu = E[X] (or an upper bound for the upper tail, a lower bound for the lower tail)","delta > 0 for the upper tail, delta in (0,1) for the lower tail"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627655+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f775c5fa2e540b2589eacffb12479d8bef99ff8b2cb5632909466593daef0e77","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be INDEPENDENT random variables with values in [0,1], let X = sum_i X_i and mu = E[X]. with state space $E$ and

$\mathbb{S}=(S_t)_{t\geqslant 0}$ as in Theorem (thm4.1 of the paper). 
Let $m$ be a positive $\sigma$-finite measure on $E$ which is
{\it subinvariant} for both $\mathbb{S}$ and  $\mathbb{T}$ and let $p\in (1, \infty)$. 

Consider  the generators $(L_p, {\mathcal D}(L_p))$,  $(D_p, {\mathcal D}(D_p))$, and $({L}_p^\Phi, {\mathcal D}({L}_p^\Phi))$
of  $\mathbb{T}$, $\mathbb{S}$,  and respectively   ${\mathbb{T}}^\Phi$as $C_0$-semigroups on $L^p(E, m)$,
where $\mathbb{T}^\Phi=(T^\Phi_t)_{t\geqslant 0}$ is defined as 
\begin{equation*}
    T^\Phi_t:= S_t T_t \mbox{ for all } t\geqslant 0.
\end{equation*}
Let further   ${\mathcal D}_o:= U_\alpha V_\beta(L^p(E, m)),$    $\alpha, \beta >0$, where ${\mathcal U}$  and ${\mathcal V}$ are the resolvents
 of $\mathbb{T}$ and $\mathbb{S}$ on $L^p(E, m)$.
Then  the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}

    $$
    \item[(ii)] Let $X^\phi_t:= \Phi_t(X_t)$, $t\geqslant 0$, $g_0\in L_+^{p'}(E,\mu)$ (where $\frac 1p + \frac{1}{p'}=1$) be such that $\int_E g_0 \, \mathrm{d} m =1$, and put $\nu=g_0\! \cdot \! m$. 
    Then $(X_t^\Phi)_{t\geqslant 0}$ solves the martingale problem for $\bigl(L^\Phi_p,{\mathcal D}(L^\Phi_p)\bigr)$ under  $\mathbb{P}^\nu=\int_E \; \mathbb{P}^x\nu(\, \mathrm{d} x)$, that is, for every $u\in {\mathcal D}(L^\Phi_p)$

distinct elements of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.768974+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f7dbf836a05f41a00bd1299185f3ee24cfb36b5feef295ea2da4368efb74c035","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.31168, 'The anisotropic Michael-Simon inequality for surfaces in every codimension'] Let $J$ be a normal $1$-current in $\bR^2$.
Then, there exist non-negative measures $\lambda, \mu$; a family of injective arcs $\{ \gamma_{\sigma} \}_{\sigma \in \Sigma}$ of finite length; and a family of integral $1$-cycles $\{ \Gamma_{\xi} \}_{\xi \in \Xi}$, each of which is a countable union of finite-length loops, such that
\[
J = \int_{\Sigma} [\![ \gamma_{\sigma} ]\!] \, d \lambda(\sigma) + \int_{\Xi} \Gamma_{\xi} \, d \mu(\xi)
\]
with no cancellation of mass.

Moreover, the arc part has no boundary cancellation: for every open set $\Omega \subset \bR^2$, it holds that
\[
\mathbf{M}( \partial J ; \Omega) = \int \mathbf{M} ( \partial [\![ \gamma_{\sigma} ]\!] ; \Omega) \, d \lambda(\sigma)
\]
Consequently, if $\Sigma_{\Omega}$ denotes the collection of arcs having at least one endpoint in $\Omega$, we have
\[
\Sigma_{\Omega} := \{ \sigma : \gamma_{\sigma} \; \text{has an endpoint in } \Omega \}, \qquad \lambda(\Sigma_{\Omega}) \leq \mathbf{M} ( \partial J; \Omega).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:49.204465+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f7eb8993ced6a5a30eaf669e1d59bbb453f63aab5960c3325dfbe770e82ab095","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 (Matrix Freedman) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] Consider a finite matrix martingale sequence $(\mtx{S}_0, \dots, \mtx{S}_n)$
consisting of $d_1 \times d_2$ matrices, real or complex.

Suppose that the elements of the difference sequence 
$(\mtx{X}_1, \dots, \mtx{X}_n)$ are uniformly bounded:
$\norm{ \mtx{X}_k } \leq B$.

Introduce the \term{conditional quadratic variation} sequence:
\[
V_k \coloneqq
	\lnorm{ \sum_{j=1}^k \Expect\big[ \mtx{X}_j \mtx{X}_j^* \condbar \coll{F}_{j-1} \big] }
	\vee \lnorm{ \sum_{j=1}^k \Expect\big[ \mtx{X}_j^* \mtx{X}_j \condbar \coll{F}_{j-1} \big] }
	\quad\text{for $k = 1, \dots, n$.}
\]
For parameters $v, t \geq 0$, we have the probability inequalities
\begin{align}

\Prob{ \exists k : \norm{\mtx{S}_k - \mtx{S}_0 } \geq \sqrt{2 v t} + Bt/3 \ \text{and} \
	V_k \leq v } &\leq (d_1+d_2) \, \econst^{-t}; \\

\Prob{ \exists k : \norm{\mtx{S}_k - \mtx{S}_0 } \geq t \ \text{and} \
	V_k \leq v } &\leq (d_1+d_2) \exp\left( \frac{-t^2/2}{v + Bt/3} \right).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:48:35.820831+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f8133eb2abaaa0d099df45667c7e5cd34a5973f80e5f7bb261d591ebb82917af","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Analogue of lemma 3.9 of arXiv:2411.09614, 'Moment estimates for the stochastic heat equation on Cartan-Hadamard manifolds'] Suppose $u_0\in L^\infty(M)\cap L^r(M)$, $1\leq r\leq +\infty$.
    Let $b=b(r)=\frac{(n-1)^2}{2\max(2,r)}K_1$ (it is 0 if $r=+\infty$). There exist three functions $F_1,F_2,F_3:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}_+$ such that for every $t>0$, $x\in M$, the following holds for $\alpha>\frac{n-2}{4}$ and $\rho >0$,
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
        \item If $\frac{n-2}{4}<\alpha<\frac{n}{4}$, $$\norm{f_k(\cdot,t,x)}_{\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}}^2\leq C^k e^{-2bt}\frac{\beta^{2k}}{k!}\norm{u_0}_{\infty}^2e^{\rho t}F_1(\rho)^k.$$

    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]

{"assumptions":["Rate-independent random recursive tree attachment.","The cited recursive-tree height estimate and standard root-subtree size limit."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364062+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f8302037ad42a1dd803c8611710c6292f630e9af8a604deb9e7eedb3628d95f2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the combinatorial identities (layer = second-largest branch height, maximum layer = floor(diam/2) <= height) were verified by brute-force leaf stripping on 40 random recursive trees of sizes 6 to 120 (480 vertices), with the 5-vertex path as a control] This is the layer part of the campaign answer to Conjecture 2 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. For each integer n>=3, let T_n be a random recursive tree on vertices 1,...,n, in which each vertex j>=2 chooses its parent independently and uniformly from 1,...,j-1. Repeatedly remove all vertices of degree at most one, assigning layer zero to the first removed set and successively increasing the layer. Let L_n be the maximum layer. As n tends to infinity, L_n=e log n-(3/2)log log n+O_P(1), where logarithms are natural and O_P(1) means that the centered sequence is bounded in probability. Under this removal rule, L_n=floor(diameter(T_n)/2); other conventions for the last vertex left standing change the maximum by at most one. The proof uses the recursive-tree height estimate of Addario-Berry and Ford (Corollary 1.3) and the fact that the root's normalized subtree sizes have a stick-breaking limit whose second-largest term is positive almost surely. The maximum-rank part of Conjecture 2 is not addressed. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:09:49.787578+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f868a77842da1f89ed5470d6eedcdc78ced28a7408a4582cd07ae131a43f5be4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 8 of arXiv:2609.03061, '2609.03061'] Let $K :U(n) \subset Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$ be the inclusion $X+ i \ Y \mapsto
\left( \begin{array}{cc} X & -Y \\ Y & X \end{array} \right)$. Here $X^t Y = Y^tX$ and  $X^tX+Y^tY=Id[n], \ i \mapsto -J_n$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] For $M \in Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$ as above; the $n \times n$ \textbf{complex matrix}
$$
G[M] = ( a + i \ c) \cdot D[M]^{-1/2}
$$
is unitary.

Note that for $(X+i \ Y) \in U(n)$, $G[ K(X+i \ Y)]=(X + i \ Y)$. Hence, $M \mapsto G[M]$ is a retraction of
$Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$ onto $U(n)$.

\item[2.] Let $L_0 = \mathbb{R}^n \oplus 0$ be the reference Lagrangian and
$M \cdot L_0$ be the result of the action of $M$ on $L_0$. That is,
$M \cdot L_0$ is the real span of the first $n$ columns of $M$.
Then
$$
M \cdot L_0 = K(G[M]) \cdot L_0.
$$
That is, the span of the first $n$ columns of $M$, $=\left( \begin{array}{c|c} a  & b \\ c &d \end{array} \right)$,
 equals the span of the first $n$ columns of $K(G[M])$,
$ =\left( \begin{array}{c|c} a \cdot D[M]^{-1/2} & - c \cdot D[M]^{-1/2}\\ c \cdot D[M]^{-1/2} &  a \cdot D[M]^{-1/2} \end{array} \right)$.

For example, for any continuous path $M: [a,b] \rightarrow Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$
there is the equality
$$
\{M(t) \cdot L_0 = K(G[M(t)]) \cdot L_0, \ a \le t \le b\}:
$$
a reduction from symplectic to unitary geometry.

\item[3.] The symplectic matrix $M $ equals a product of
of symplectic matrices
$$
M = K(G[M]) \cdot \left( \begin{array}{cc} D[M]^{+1/2} & 0 \\ 0 & D[M]^{-1/2} \end{array} \right)
\cdot \left( \begin{array}{cc} Id[n] & \alpha \\ 0 & Id[n] \end{array} \right)
$$
with $\alpha = D[M]^{-1} \cdot (a^t b + c^td)$. Moreover, $\alpha$ is symmetric; i.e.,
$$
 D[M]^{-1} \cdot (a^t b + c^td)  =( b^ta +d^t c) \cdot D[M]^{-1}.
 $$

 \item[4.] There is a natural deformation retraction of $Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$ onto $U(n)$
 defined for $M \in Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$ and $0 \le u \le 1$ by :
 $$
 H(M,u) =K(G[M]) \cdot \left( \begin{array}{cc} D[M]^{+1/2} & 0 \\ 0 & D[M]^{-1/2} \end{array} \right)^{(1-u)}
\cdot \left( \begin{array}{cc} Id[n] & \alpha \\ 0 & Id[n] \end{array} \right)^{(1-u)}
 $$

\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.424290+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f86e5b7499bf5ed8ed32178485677a83cf9456d8c6f90d356413d0a742862c1a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition lem:discrete_antitrap_from_CT of arXiv:2605.17725, 'Limit theorems for random walks with spatio-temporal drift'] Let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a filtration, and let $(G_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an
$\mathbb R^d$-valued adapted process satisfying
$$
G_{n+1}-G_n=\upsilon_{n+1}F_n+c_{n+1}(\varepsilon_{n+1}+r_{n+1}),
\quad n\ge0,
$$
where $(\upsilon_n)_{n\ge1}$ and $(c_n)_{n\ge1}$ are deterministic nonnegative
sequences such that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n^2<\infty$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\upsilon_n=\infty$; for each $n\ge 0$, $F_n$, $\varepsilon_{n+1}$ and $r_{n+1}$ are $\mathcal F_n$-measurable, and
$$
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=0, \quad \mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon_n\|^2<\infty.
$$

Let $\Gamma\in\mathcal F_\infty$ be an event, where
$\mathcal F_\infty:=\sigma\bigl(\bigcup_{n\ge0}\mathcal F_n\bigr)$.
Assume that there exist a deterministic constant $\rho>0$, a finite random
integer $T_0$, a deterministic nonincreasing sequence $(b_n)_{n\ge0}$, and an
event $\Omega_*\in\mathcal F_\infty$ with $\mathbb P(\Omega_*)=1$ such that the
following hold.

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] On $\Gamma\cap\Omega_*$, for all $n\ge T_0$,
$$
\langle G_n, F_n\rangle\ge0
\text{ whenever }\|G_n\|<2\rho; \quad \text{and}\quad
\upsilon_{n+1}\|F_n\|<\rho.
$$

\item[(b)] There exist deterministic constants $a_0,a_1>0$ such that on $\Gamma$,
$$
0<a_0\le \liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\|\varepsilon_{n+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_n]
\le
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\|\varepsilon_{n+1}\|^2\mid\mathcal F_n]
\le a_1<\infty.
$$

\item[(c)] On $\Omega_*$, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$
c_{n+1}\|\varepsilon_{n+1}\|\le b_n.
$

\item[(d)] $
b_n^2=O(\alpha_n^2).
$ with 
$
\alpha_n:=\left(\sum_{k\ge n+1}c_k^2\right)^{1/2}.
$

\item[(e)] On $\Gamma$,
$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|r_n\|^2<\infty.
$
\end{itemize}

Then
$
\mathbb P\bigl(\Gamma\cap\{G_n\to0\}\bigr)=0.
$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:37:08.311265+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f89142b3ce3207a5f8a77e9d9fadf6b6d2e60a06c33b0f009a7d0dd0e6b49e25","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:quagmire of arXiv:2608.28505, 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests'] Given an uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ and a set $S \subseteq \mathrm{Lim}(\kappa)$, a\linebreak \emph{$(\kappa, S)$-quagmire} is a quadruple $(T, {<}, {\lhd}, Q)$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label={(Q\arabic*)},  start=0]
\item 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $(T, <)$ is a $\kappa$-Kurepa tree,
\item $\lhd$ is a binary relation on $T$ whose restriction to each level of $T$ is a strict linear order; nodes of distinct heights are $\lhd$-incomparable,
\item the function $Q$ is a partial function from $T^2$ to $T$ whose domain consists of the pairs $(x, y) \in T^2$ such that $\mathrm{ht}(x) < \mathrm{ht}(y)$ and $x \lhd \pi_{\mathrm{ht}(x)}(y)$,
\end{enumerate}

\item if $(x, y) \in \mathrm{dom}(Q)$, then $x < Q(x, y) \lhd y$,
\item if $(x, y) \in \mathrm{dom}(Q)$ and $y < z$, then $Q(Q(x, y), z) = Q(x,z)$,
\item if $(y, z) \in \mathrm{dom}(Q)$ and $x \lhd y$, then $Q(x, Q(y, z)) = Q(x, z)$,
\item if $x \lhd y$ and $\mathrm{ht}(x) \in S \cup \{\kappa\}$, then there exists $\alpha < \mathrm{ht}(x)$ such that $\pi_\alpha(x) \lhd \pi_\alpha(y)$ and $x = Q(\pi_\alpha(x), y)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Ordinary nearest-neighbour hard-core model on Z^2","Uniform lambda>0; n>m>=1","Occupied even exterior outside U_n and m-odd input as defined","R, W and gamma are the published completed-contour construction, not arbitrary regions or uncompleted odd occupations"],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:05:12.238545+00:00","domain":"probability; Gibbs measures; hard-core Peierls repair; contour fibres","id":"claim_f8b5445b41601b80d49258c2783f442a0df9ed15e98684d17a12bcc94ca6055f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let lambda>0 and integers n>m>=1. Let R be the connected component containing U_m in the completed odd vertices together with their neighbours, and fill its finite complementary components to get W. Let gamma be the edge boundary of W and Gamma its midpoint contour constructed in Section 3.1. Each edge of gamma has an unoccupied even interior endpoint and an odd exterior endpoint outside I-prime. For a unit coordinate shift s, put I_s=(I outside W) union ((I intersect W)+s) and F_s={v in W: v-s outside W}. I_s and I_s union F_s are independent, the shift preserves the occupied count within U_n, and F_s is disjoint from I_s. Some s has |F_s|>=|gamma|/4. For every S subset F_s, J=I_s union S is independent. For fixed gamma and s, J determines S=J intersect F_s, then I_s=J minus S and finally the original I by inverse shift. Thus there is at most one input per gamma and s. The normalized repair flow f(I,J)=lambda^|S|/(1+lambda)^|F_s| has each row summing to one and each weighted incoming term lambda^(|I intersect U_n|-|J intersect U_n|) f(I,J)=(1+lambda)^(-|F_s|). $\sigma:=\liminf_{A\to\infty}\Psi_A$. Then,
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $v$ is relaxation enhancing (or $\dot{\mathcal{I}}(v)=\emptyset$)
if and only if $\sigma=\infty$, and also if and only if $\lim_{A\to\infty}m_A=\infty$.

\item  If $\sigma<\infty$, then $\dot{\mathcal{I}}(v)$
is nonempty and 
\begin{gather}
\sigma=\lim_{A\to\infty}m_A=r(v).
\end{gather}
\end{enumerate}

\[
\mathcal{H}(\rho(t)| \pi)=\int q \log q \pi dx \le C\int |h|^2\pi \,dx \le C_1\exp(-(\sigma-\delta) t),
\]
where $C_1$ depends only on the two constants in Assumption (ass:warmstart of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:38:04.491046+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f8d05297e5d3764a5b489eb2619e5696dc6c1f881f025b71d7e76a8b89469178","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma improved-one-step of arXiv:2607.05054, 'Root Dynamics of Differentiated Polynomials with Rotationally Invariant Structure'] Let $(r_j)_{1 \le j \le n}$ be an increasing sequence of positive real numbers, and let  
\[
\alpha \ge \max_{1 \le j \le n-1} \frac{r_j}{r_{j+1}} .
\]  
Suppose the $j$-th smallest root of $Q$ is exactly $r_j$ for $1 \le j \le n$. Define  
\begin{align}
y = \frac{2 + \log_{-}(\log(\alpha^{-1}))}{\log(\alpha^{-1})}, \qquad \log_{-}(x) = \max(0, -\log x).
\end{align}

Then, for integers $m \ge 1$ and $1 \le q \le m-1$, the $j$-th smallest root $z_j$ of  
\[
S(z) = q Q(z) + m z Q'(z), \qquad 2 \le j \le n,
\]  
satisfies  

\[
\left(1 - \frac{1}{\max(1,\, j-1 - y)}\right) r_j \;\le\; z_j \;\le\; \left(1 - \frac{\alpha}{j+1+2y}\right) r_j .
\]

For $q = 0$ and $3 \le j \le n$, the $(j-1)$-th smallest root of $Q'$ satisfies the same upper bound, and for $2 \le j \le n$ the same lower bound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:52:51.757105+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f8d6783728d74b3758ce08483a909446659b5f98b8ad6ef7da5a5eda5be0e804","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfs df0 of arXiv:2604.24061, 'A characterization of ruin-inducing probability measures in a renewal risk model'] \normalfont
		Let $Q$ be a probability measure on $(\varOmega,\varSigma)$.   \smallskip
		
		\noindent\textbf{(a)} If $\mathcal G{\,\subseteq\,}\varSigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra of subsets of $\varOmega$, then  $Q$ is \textit{absolutely continuous}  with respect to $P$ on $\mathcal G$ (in symbols $Q{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G{\,\ll\,}P{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G$) if
		\[
		\forall\; A\in\mathcal G\quad  \Big( P(A)=0\Rightarrow Q(A)=0 \Big).
		\] 
		In addition, if $P{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G{\,\ll\,} Q{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G$, then $Q$ and $P$ are \textit{equivalent} on $\mathcal G$ (in symbols $Q{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G{\,\sim\,}P{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G$). For $\mathcal G{\,=\,}\varSigma$ simply write $Q{\,\ll\,} P$ and $Q{\sim}P$.  
		\smallskip
		
		\noindent  	\textbf{(b)} If $\{\mathcal G_t\}_{t\in\mathbb R_+}$ is a filtration for $\varSigma$, then $Q$ and $P$ are \textit{progressively equivalent} on $\{\mathcal G_t\}_{t\in\mathbb R_+}$, if $Q$ and $P$   are equivalent on each  $\mathcal G_t$ (i.e., $Q{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G_t{\,\sim\,} P{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G_t$). If $P$ and $Q$  are progressively equivalent with respect to $\{\mathcal G_t\}_{t\in\mathbb R_+}$, we write
		\[
		\frac{dQ}{dP}{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G_t:=\frac{d(Q{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G_t)}{d(P{\upharpoonright}\mathcal G_t)} \,\,\text{ for all }  t\in\mathbb R_+
		\]
		for simplicity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.777843+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f8f52a7e05acc89b83e8617baed86520f71863de4a0ee9b6906540e8539892b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 11 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Let $\chi$ be a Navier--Stokes potential on an open fiber domain  \(\mathscr F\subset\mathscr E\) (containing its zero section) of a relaxation bundle \(\mathscr E\subseteq\Sym^2T^*\Mcal\). Then, a \textbf{relaxation rate map} consists of a smooth fiberwise map $\mathscr B=\mathscr B(\beta,\zeta)\in\mathscr E^*$ defined for all future timelike $\beta$ and all $\zeta \in \mathscr F$, satisfying the following conditions.

\bei 

\item \emph{Stable equilibrium property:}
\bel{eq:pot-relax-map}
\mathscr B(\beta,0)=0,
\qquad
\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}(\beta,\zeta)\geq0,
\qquad
\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}(\beta,\zeta)=0
\Longleftrightarrow
\zeta=0.
\ee

\item \emph{Positivity property:}  Its linearization along the equilibrium manifold $\mathbb M$ given by 
\bel{eq:pot-relax-linearization}
\mathbb M^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}(\beta)
\coloneqq
\frac{\del\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}}{\del\zeta_{\gamma\delta}}(\beta,0)
\ee
must be symmetric under interchange of the two index pairs and positive definite on~$\mathscr E$, namely
\be
\eta_{\alpha\beta}\mathbb M^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}(\beta)\eta_{\gamma\delta}>0
\qquad
\text{for every nonzero }\eta\in\mathscr E.
\ee
\eei
Furthermore, the associated \textbf{production term} is
\bel{production-term-value}
\mathfrak d_{\mathscr B}
\coloneqq
\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}
\geq0.
\ee","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:22:46.469883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f91ae9995f56c7ca6971bd9b28ef171924136e10dae560f12186b13da0d67f02","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 82 (The Levi-Civita connection $\nullangD$ of $\gnulltori$ and related differential operators) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill

\begin{enumerate}
\item We denote the Levi-Civita connection of $\gnulltori$ by $\nullangD$.
	In particular,
	for $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$-tangent tensorfields $\upxi$, 
	we have $\nullangD \upxi = \nulltorusproject \Dfour \upxi$.
\item If $\Xi$ is an $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$-tangent one-form, 
	then we define its $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$-divergence 
	to be the scalar function
	$\nullangDiv \Xi \eqdef \gnulltori^{-1} \cdot \nullangD \Xi$. 
	Similarly, if $V$ is an $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$-tangent vectorfield, 
	then we define its $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$-divergence to be the scalar function

 &&\downarrow h&&\downarrow u&&\Vert\\

{"assumptions":["(a_n)_{n >= 0} is a real sequence","the second differences a_n - 2a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} are nonnegative for every n >= 0 (convexity)","a_n -> 0 as n -> infinity","consequences used and derived from these: a_n >= 0, a_n nonincreasing, n(a_n - a_{n+1}) -> 0, sum (n+1)(a_n - 2a_{n+1} + a_{n+2}) = a_0","integrability is with respect to Lebesgue measure on the circle"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815245+00:00","domain":"Fourier analysis, trigonometric series","id":"claim_f95cf78453cad9016df951c8497b0e8bcbb54049fe66f88a10ab868d7db99aa2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (a_n)_{n >= 0} be real numbers which are CONVEX, meaning the second differences D2 a_n := a_n - 2 a_{n+1} + a_{n+2} are >= 0 for every n >= 0, and which tend to 0. (These two hypotheses already force a_n >= 0 and a_n nonincreasing: the first differences a_{n+1} - a_n are nondecreasing, so if one of them were positive the sequence would tend to +infinity. They also force n(a_n - a_{n+1}) -> 0, since the differences are monotone.) THEOREM (Young; Zygmund, Trigonometric Series, Ch. V). Put S(x) = a_0/2 + sum_{n >= 1} a_n cos(nx). Then: (1) the series converges for every x not in 2 pi Z, uniformly on every compact subset of (0, 2 pi); (2) S(x) >= 0 for all such x; (3) S is Lebesgue integrable on (-pi, pi), with (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of S over (-pi,pi) equal to a_0/2; (4) the series IS the Fourier series of S, that is a_n = (1/pi) times the integral over (-pi,pi) of S(x) cos(nx) dx for every n >= 0. The whole theorem rests on one identity: with K_n(x) = (1/(n+1)) (sin((n+1)x/2) / sin(x/2))^2 >= 0 the Fejer kernel, normalised so that (1/(2 pi)) times the integral of K_n over (-pi,pi) is 1, double summation by parts gives S(x) = sum_{n >= 0} (n+1) (D2 a_n) (1/2) K_n(x), with sum_{n >= 0} (n+1) D2 a_n = a_0 < infinity. Nonnegativity is then read off from D2 a_n >= 0 and K_n >= 0, and integrability from the normalisation. SHARP EDGES. (a) It is CONVEXITY, not monotone decrease, that does the work: monotone decrease to zero gives convergence off the origin by Dirichlet's test, but it does not produce the Fejer representation and therefore gives neither nonnegativity nor integrability of the sum. (b) The SINE analogue is false in this form. If (b_n) is convex and decreases to 0, then sum b_n sin(nx) still converges pointwise off 2 pi Z, but its sum is Lebesgue integrable if and only if sum b_n / n converges. The classical counterexample is b_n = 1/log n for n >= 2, which is convex and decreases to 0 while sum 1/(n log n) diverges: the resulting series converges everywhere but is not the Fourier series of any Lebesgue integrable function. Never transport the cosine statement to the sine case. (c) 'Integrable' cannot be improved to 'bounded': for a_n of order 1/n the sum behaves like log(1/|x|) near 0, which is integrable and unbounded. (d) The conclusion S >= 0 is on (0, 2 pi); nothing is claimed at x in 2 pi Z, where the series may diverge (it diverges precisely when sum a_n = infinity). (e) Convexity is only assumed for n >= 0 on the given sequence; a sequence that is eventually convex gives the same conclusions after subtracting a trigonometric polynomial, but then nonnegativity of the sum is lost.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:18.035605+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f961166414767107453b8fca4b1b9fd18f01fce78d89f0c59ac2429d58dbc9af","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:VEB-volume of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] There exists a real number $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/2)$ such that the following holds. Consider any $\lambda \in (0,\lambda_0)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ such $p_0=1$ and, for all $i \ge 1$, $W_i \le (4/\lambda)^i$. Suppose that $\overline{p}$ has finitely many bins which are strongly exposed. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with
birth rate~$2 \lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set~$\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
Let $j_0\geq 5$ be a sufficiently large positive integer
where  all strongly-exposed bins are in $[j_0-1]$.
Let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$ be any event determined by 
$\{n^{X^B}(t') : t'\in [T^{\overline{p},j_0}]\}$
which entails that each 
$n^{X^B}(t')$ in this set is at least~$1$.
We will condition on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$.

Let
$\tau_0 =  T^{\overline{p},j_0}$. 
Let
$\Psi_0$ be the  initialising high-level state   
with $\tau^{\Psi_0} = \tau_0$ and $j^{\Psi_0} = j_0$. 
 
Let $\mathrm{hls}$ be   the $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule from Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-rule of the paper) and let $\ensuremath{\Psi^{\mathrm{BB}}(\Psi_0)}$  (Definition~(def:backoff-bounding-state-space of the paper)) be the  $\Psi_0$-closure (Definition~(def:hls-closed of the paper)) of~$\mathrm{hls}$.  
The $\Psi_0$-backoff bounding rule~$\mathrm{hls}$ is a transition rule (Definition~(def:transition-rule of the paper)) by Observation~(obs:BB-bounding-is-transrule of the paper) and 
it is $\ensuremath{\Psi^{\mathrm{BB}}(\Psi_0)}$-valid (Definition~(def:valid of the paper)) by
Lemma~(lem:backoff-bounding-valid of the paper).

Conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{init}}$, the VEB-coupling (Definition~(def:VEB-couple of the paper))   couples $X$ with a volume process $V$ from $\Psi(\tau_0)=\Psi_0$ with  transition rule $\mathrm{hls}$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$
and with a sequence $E_1, E_2,\ldots $ of escape processes with send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$. 
With probability at least~$99/100$,  
both of the following hold.

  
 
  
\begin{itemize}
\item for all $t \ge \tau_0$, $\textup{type}^{\Psi(t)} \ne \textup{failure}$. 
\item for all $j \ge j_0$, there is
a positive integer $t \le \tau_0 + 1+ {(8j)}^{\phi+1}(W_{j_0}+\dots + W_{j-1})$ such that 
$\Psi(t)$ is $j$-filling or $j$-advancing.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.545854+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f986deb0243b0fdeb46824059e927a217b9dd4adfc062cb50b1c5255b34023da","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 56 (Villain model) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix $d\in\Z_{\geq 1}$ and $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
    For any domain $\Lambda$ and $\zeta:\Z^d\to\S^1$,
    the \emph{Villain model} on $\Lambda$ with boundary condition $\zeta$
    at inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure  on $\sigma\in(\S^1)^\Lambda$ given by
    \[
        \diff\mu_{\Villain,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta(\sigma) = \frac1{Z_{\Villain,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta} e^{-H_{\Villain,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta(\sigma)} \diff\sigma,
    \]
    where $Z_{\Villain,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta$ is the normalising constant,
    $\diff\sigma$ the Haar measure, and
    \begin{multline}
         e^{-H_{\Villain,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta(\sigma)}
         =
         \Big(\prod_{\substack{\{x,y\}\subset\Lambda\\x\sim y}}p_\beta(\sigma_x,\sigma_y)\Big)
            \Big(\prod_{\substack{x\in\Lambda,\,y\in\Lambda^c\\x\sim y}}p_\beta(\sigma_x,\zeta_y)\Big);
            \\
         p_\beta(z,z'):=\sum_{m\in\Z} e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}\big(\arg(z)-\arg(z')+2\pi m\big)^2}.
    \end{multline}
    Notice that the Hamiltonian is defined somewhat atypically and incorporates
    the dependency on $\beta$; more on this later.
    The \emph{critical inverse temperature} is defined as the largest $\beta_c^{\Villain}=\beta_c^{\Villain}(d)\in(0,\infty)$
    such that $\mu_{\Villain,\Lambda_n,\beta}^{+1}[\sigma_0]$ decays exponentially fast in $n$
    for any fixed $\beta\in[0,\beta_c^{\Villain})$.
    Classical arguments based on correlations inequalities imply the existence of an infinite-volume Gibbs measure with $+1$ boundary conditions at inverse temperature $\beta\geq 0$, that we refer to as $\mu^{+1}_{\Villain, \beta}$.
    The label $\Villain$ is omitted from notations when it is clear from the context.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:47:22.239270+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f99b599f90227991931d47eb6c0310a834e7f837ff4205f54718d241e3d55c9c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2605.25206, 'An extension of Stein's method incorporating dependence'] Let $M, Y$ be random variables on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, with respective laws $\mu_M$ and $\mu_Y$, and with the dependence of $M$ on $Y$ given by the family $(\nu_y)_{\mathring{Y}(\Omega)}$ of probability laws, where
$\mathring{Y}(\Omega)$ is the essential range of $Y$, and where
\[
    \mu_M(A) = \int_\R \nu_y(A) \mu_Y(\mathrm{d}y), \quad (\forall A \in \mathcal{B}_\R).
\]
We assume given a Stein operator $\mathcal{N}_y$ for the law $\nu_y$ for
all $y \in \mathring{Y}(\Omega)$, as well as a suitable common class $\mathcal{C}$ of functions for the family of operators $(\mathcal{N}_y)_{y \in \mathring{Y}(\Omega)}$. Let $X$ be a given random variable.
With $d_{\textrm{TV}}$ denoting the total variation distance, and
$d_{\textrm{W}}$ the Wasserstein distance between laws, we have:
\begin{equation*} 
    d_{\textrm{TV}} (\mathbb{P}_{X,Y}, \mathbb{P}_{M,Y}) \leq
    \sup_{f \in \tilde{\mathcal{E}}_{TV}} \E{\mathcal{N}_Y \! f(X,Y)}
\end{equation*} 
and
\begin{equation*}
    d_{\textrm{W}} (\mathbb{P}_{X,Y}, \mathbb{P}_{M,Y}) \leq
    \sup_{f \in \tilde{\mathcal{E}}_{W}} \E{\mathcal{N}_Y \! f(X,Y)}.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.742275+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f99f13972b0f2210ac324d0b64dbb26246970424a68182403f08bf02de00314f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 121 (Complexified momentum-fiber disintegration) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let
\[
 \mathcal G_a^{\mathbb R}
 :=\{F\in L^2([0,T]\times\R^3;\mathbb C):
 F(s,-\eta)=\overline{F(s,\eta)}\}
\]
with the real inner product from
\eqref{eq:hermitian-gaussian-hilbert-space}, and let
$\mathcal G_a^{\mathbb C}$ be its Hilbert-space complexification.  The map
from $\mathcal G_a^{\mathbb C}$ to the full complex space
$L^2([0,T]\times\R^3;\mathbb C)$ is unitary.  Consequently the changes of
variables
\[
 (\eta,\zeta)\mapsto(m=\eta+\zeta,\eta),
 \qquad
 (\eta,\zeta,r)\mapsto(\xi=\eta+\zeta+r,\eta,\zeta)
\]
induce the complex Hilbert direct-integral identifications
\begin{align}
 \mathcal G_a^{\mathbb C}\otimes_2\mathcal G_b^{\mathbb C}
 &\simeq\int_{\R^3}^{\oplus}
 L^2([0,T]^2\times\R^3_\eta)\dd m,
 \\
 \mathcal G_a^{\mathbb C}\otimes_2\mathcal G_b^{\mathbb C}
 \otimes_2\mathcal G_a^{\mathbb C}
 &\simeq\int_{\R^3}^{\oplus}
 L^2([0,T]^3\times\R^6_{\eta,\zeta})\dd\xi.
 
\end{align}
At finite cutoff, normalize the deterministic Wiener kernels so that the
first-Picard field and the linear field have measurable momentum fibers
$m\mapsto F_m^{\Lambda,\epsilon_{\mathrm P}}(t)$ and
$r\mapsto g_r^\Lambda(t)$.  With
\begin{equation}
 q_{a^\perp,0,\Lambda}^{[\epsilon_{\mathrm P}]}(t,m)
 :=|m_\Lambda(m)|^{2\epsilon_{\mathrm P}}
 q_{a^\perp,0,\Lambda}(t,m),
\end{equation}
their fiber norms satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \|F_m^{\Lambda,\epsilon_{\mathrm P}}(t)\|^2
 =q_{a^\perp,0,\Lambda}^{[\epsilon_{\mathrm P}]}(t,m),
 \qquad
 \|g_r^\Lambda(t)\|^2
 =p_{a,\Lambda}(t,r)
\end{equation}
for almost every $m,r$.  Since the admissible multipliers are uniformly
bounded, the flagged density in
\eqref{eq:cubic-flagged-first-picard-density} is uniformly dominated by a
fixed multiple of the unflagged density.  Swapping the two color-$a$
slots preserves the total momentum $\xi$ and is unitary on every fiber of
\eqref{eq:three-noise-direct-integral}.  Hence
$\Sym_a=(I+\tau_{13})/2$ is a fiberwise orthogonal projection.

All these statements are made in the complexification of the same real
isonormal process.  The reality relation appears as conjugacy between the

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.978158+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f9cb263f6e1d40ff7157a22d038c301b82fd7832a9bde9c1c7dbf9ca104b4248","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 57 (Orthogonal block saturation) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let \(H=\bigoplus_{j\geq1}E_j\), where
\(d_j:=\dim E_j\uparrow\infty\).  Let \(W^Q\) be a \(Q\)-Wiener process
with
\[
 Q=\bigoplus_{j\geq1}q_jI_{E_j},
 \qquad q_j>0,\qquad\sum_jq_jd_j<\infty.
\]
If \(A\) is its area on \([0,1]\), then the compressions are independent
and
\begin{equation}
 P_{E_j}AP_{E_j}\stackrel{\mathrm d}=q_j\mathcal L^{(d_j)}.
 
\end{equation}
This distributional statement holds for every choice of the blocks and
weights above.

Conversely, given any prescribed \(m_j\uparrow\infty\), the even
dimensions \(d_j\) can be chosen recursively so that the failure
probabilities in \eqref{cc:eq-critical-Brownian-bulk} and
\eqref{cc:eq-critical-Brownian-edge} are summable.  For that choice of
dimensions, and for any positive weights satisfying
\(\sum_jq_jd_j<\infty\), the resulting almost-sure event has, eventually,
\begin{align}
 s_n(A)&\geq aq_j,\qquad
 1\leq n\leq\lfloor\eta d_j\rfloor,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.207321+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f9d0739d9e23ab53e239f28ab875855eaf9b4d07e87c68393341a2de9cc9aac1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:Bary-Subdiv-Weighted of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] \ \vskip 0.1cm
 For a weighted simplicial complex $(K,\mu)$, define the weight of the barycenter $b_{\sigma}$ of any simplex $\sigma$ in $K$ to be $\mu(\sigma)$. Then define a weight  $Sd(\mu)$ on $Sd(K)$ by:
    \begin{equation} 
     Sd(\mu)\big([ b_{\sigma_0},\cdots, b_{\sigma_l}]\big)=\mu(\sigma_l),\ \sigma_0\subsetneq \cdots\subsetneq \sigma_l \in K.
     \end{equation}
   
   Note that we have either
   $\mu(\sigma_0)\, | \, \cdots \, | \,\mu(\sigma_l)$ or 
    $\mu(\sigma_l) \, |\, \cdots\, |\, \mu(\sigma_0)$ depending on whether $\mu$ is ascending or descending. Then it is easy to 
    check that $Sd(\mu)$ is a divisible weight on $Sd(K)$ which is ascending (or descending) if so is $\mu$.  
     We call $(Sd(K),Sd(\mu))$ the \emph{barycentric subdivision} of $(K,\mu)$. For any integer $m\geqslant 1$, let $(Sd^m(K),Sd^m(\mu))$ 
 denote the $m$ iterated barycentric subdivisions of $(K,\mu)$.","status":"unverified"}

 \partial_tv_t=-\Delta_{g(t)}v_t+R_{g(t)}v_t,

{"assumptions":["an i.i.d., or ergodic and suitably mixing, random environment","a directional transience condition, typically Sznitman's (T) or (T'), or an equivalent ballisticity condition, in some direction l","uniform ellipticity of the transition probabilities, standard though sometimes relaxed in specific results","existence of well-defined regeneration times with positive probability of never backtracking, verified from the environment's independence or mixing structure"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988973+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f9f2aaae6b2438ff5a64f4f66dc265aa11c167d9a714a9526edfe927fb576ab3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For random walk in a random environment on Z^d satisfying a directional transience condition, such as Sznitman's condition (T) or the stronger (T') in a direction l, or a simpler ballisticity/non-nestling condition, one constructs regeneration times tau_1 < tau_2 < ... at which the walk achieves a new running maximum in direction l and never backtracks below that level afterward. Under condition (T'), or the weaker (T), the increments (X_{tau_{k+1}} - X_{tau_k}, tau_{k+1} - tau_k), for k >= 1, form an i.i.d. sequence, reducing the walk, which is not itself Markovian once the environment is averaged out, to a genuine i.i.d.-increment structure from which a law of large numbers (a deterministic limiting velocity) follows directly, and, with additional finite-moment control on the regeneration increments, a central limit theorem follows via classical tools for sums of i.i.d. variables. This does not establish the directional transience condition itself, verifying (T) or (T') for a given environment law is typically the hard remaining step; it does not directly give a central limit theorem without separately checking finite second moments of the regeneration increments, which can genuinely fail in slow or near-critical regimes; and it is specific to the static, fixed-in-time environment model. Typical failure: Assuming the regeneration increments automatically have finite variance, and hence a central limit theorem follows, once ballisticity or condition (T') has been established; ballisticity under (T') only guarantees a finite mean regeneration time, and a genuine central limit theorem requires an additional, often delicate, verification of finite second moments, a point on which the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer branching-with-migration machinery exists precisely because these moments can fail. Canonical reference: Sznitman and Zerner, 1999, Annals of Probability; Sznitman, 2002, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.676581+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f9f69ff4e16be248ed2489e90a72a3f133f2b54399d82438053d6e943930c925","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 10 (Operational state-selection theorem) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $\mathfrak R$ be a declared response program on
$(\mathsf U_0,\mathbb I)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item Every compatible primitive response factors uniquely through the
information quotient.  All algebraic, causal, restart, and uniformly continuous
postcomposition identities descend with it.
\item Let $\mathbf R^{\mathbb I}$ be the descended joint profile and put
\[
 u\sim_{\mathfrak R}v
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathbf R^{\mathbb I}(u)=\mathbf R^{\mathbb I}(v).
\]
The quotient by this response congruence carries the Hausdorff initial
uniformity generated by the responses.  The closure of its joint response image
in the product target is the completed response state, and every uniformly
continuous descended constructor extends uniquely to it.  If the program is
causally calibrated in the sense of
\Cref{def:causally-calibrated-response-program}, then the quotient and its
completion inherit the induced truncations, and every equivariant uniformly
continuous constructor extends as a stable-causal map.
\item If a required response fails information descent, no pointwise
realization on the full raw carrier that factors through $q_{\mathbb I}$ can
realize the program.  A probabilistic implementation relative to $\cP$ may
instead impose descent on the realized support; that is a support-relative
program rather than a realization of the full raw one.
\item The calibrated completion is unique in the following precise sense.  Every
complete faithful realization of the descended response presentation whose
uniformity is the initial uniformity generated by the extended responses is
uniquely uniformly isomorphic to the response completion; equivalently, no
second complete geometry can realize the same calibrated profile faithfully.
This is the deterministic uniqueness theorem
\Cref{thm:canonical-response-completion}.
\item Suppose in addition that a probabilistic implementation carries a
$\cP$-causal state $Z$ with stable-causal joint encoder
$\Phi:\mathsf Z\to\mathsf R$ whose value $\Phi(Z)$ is the declared joint
response under every $P\in\cP$, and a global stable-causal decoder
$D_{\mathfrak R}:\mathsf R\to\mathsf Z$ satisfying
$D_{\mathfrak R}\Phi=I_{\mathsf Z}$.  Then, for every $\cP$-causal state $S$,
joint realization of the completed package is equivalent to $Z\preceqsc S$,
and a joint readout $\Psi$ has the factor
\[
 R_S=D_{\mathfrak R}\Psi.
\]
If the decoder factors through one distinguished response,
$D_{\mathfrak R}=D_\star\Pi_\star$, and that response is
$\Pi_\star\Phi(Z)$, then a separate realization $\Psi_\star$ of it already
yields the factor $D_\star\Psi_\star$.
Thus $Z$ is the unique least sufficient realized state up to stable-causal
equivalence; the factor is unique on the realized source state.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.543019+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fa18f25af7b7b7bf663f7e66579a87c2a4d4c15e3c11603a7ee5fb076d7082d4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 19 (The models are EFIIDs) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] All three models alluded to above are EFIIDs.
    More precisely, we obtain the following results.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[\emph{\textbf{XY}}] Consider the XY model in dimension $d\in\Z_{\geq 2}$
        at inverse temperature $\beta\in[0,\beta_c(d))$.
        Then the infinite-volume Gibbs measure $\mu_{\XY,\beta}^{+1}$
        is an EFIID.
        \item[\emph{\textbf{SWM}}] Consider the SWM in dimension $d\in\Z_{\geq 2}$
        at inverse temperature $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
        Then the infinite-volume Gibbs measure $\mu_{\SWM,\beta}^0$
        is an EFIID.
        \item[\emph{\textbf{Coulomb}}] Consider the two-dimensional Coulomb gas at $\beta\in[0,\beta_{\BKT}(\Villain))$.
        Then the sequence $(\mu_{\Coulomb,\Lambda_n,\beta}^\free)_n$
        tends to some infinite-volume measure $\mu_{\Coulomb,\beta}^\free$ on $\Z^{F(\Z^2)}$ as $n\to\infty$ in the local convergence topology,
        and this limit is an EFIID.
    \end{itemize}
    In the case of the Coulomb gas, we are careful not to call this measure a Gibbs measure, as the Hamiltonian of the model is non-local and therefore it is not so clear what it means exactly to be a Gibbs measure.

    In particular, these results imply that for any of the three models,
    correlations between bounded observables decay exponentially fast in the distance at which they are measured. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Add an artificial parent of the root, returning deterministically to the root from it. Let beta(T) be the probability, starting at the root, of never hitting that artificial parent. For child subtrees T_i, beta(T)=sum_i beta(T_i)/(lambda+sum_i beta(T_i)); the harmonic exit ray chooses child i with probability beta(T_i)/sum_j beta(T_j). Equip the boundary with distance exp(-|xi wedge eta|), where |xi wedge eta| is the common-prefix length. Let T-prime be an independent tree with the same Galton-Watson law, and S-prime=sum_{i=1}^{N-prime}beta(T-prime_i). For u in the range of beta define kappa(u)=E[u S-prime/(lambda-1+u+S-prime)], and let C_0=E[kappa(beta(T))]. Then 0<C_0<infinity. The probability measure mu with density kappa(beta(T))/C_0 relative to the Galton-Watson law is invariant for the tree viewed from the harmonic ray, whose transition from T is to T_i with the displayed harmonic child probabilities. Harmonic measure is almost surely exact-dimensional with deterministic dimension d_lambda=log(lambda)-E_mu[log(1-beta(T))]. Equivalently d_lambda=log(lambda)-C_0^(-1)E[log(1-beta(T)) beta(T) S-prime/(lambda-1+beta(T)+S-prime)]. When lambda<1, beta(T)>1-lambda almost surely, making the denominator positive. All logarithms are natural. Source: Invariant Measures, Hausdorff Dimension and Dimension Drop of some Harmonic Measures on Galton-Watson Trees, Theorem 4.1 and proof, pp.15-17; equations (9)-(12), pp.15-16; standing assumptions Section 2.4, p.8.","status":"unverified"}

At rate $1$, on each bond $(x,x+1)$, the total  number of particles $\\xi(x)+\\xi(x+1)$ is redistributed according to a random variable  $R \\sim  \\mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n, \\alpha, \\alpha)$ random variable with  $n=\\xi(x)+\\xi(x+1)$, such that at every Poisson time $T$,  $(\\xi(T^-,x), \\xi(T^-,x+1))$ becomes\n    $$ (R, \\xi(T^-,x)+ \\xi(T^-,x+1)-R)\\,. $$\n    We recall that a random variable $R\\sim \\text{BetaBinomial}(n,\\alpha,\\beta)$, if it has density given by $$ \\mathbb{P}(R=k)=\\binom{n}{k}\\int_{0}^{1}p^{\\alpha+k-1}(1-p)^{\\beta+n-k-1}dp\\,.$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.190930+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_fa474a8a4624814fe97709dafbef801fb0755ea4276210b20d5a5f868b3d8f3d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 109 (regularity for spatially smoothed coefficients) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} are continuously differentiable in the space coordinate, and satisfy the bounds
	\[
	\Big(
	\|\sB^N\|_\infty
    +
    \|\partial_y\sB^N\|_\infty\Big)^2
	+ \max\bigg\{
    \|\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    +\|\partial_y\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    : \tilde{A}\in\{ \sV,\sU,\srrr,\swww\}^N
    \bigg\}
	\le 
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
with $\MAX_N$ as in \eqref{e:MAX.N} and Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. To simplify notation, we mostly suppress the dependence on $N$ inside the proof. Consider
	\[
	\sB(t,y)
	=\frac{\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)}
	\equiv \frac{\Num(t,y)}{\Den(t,y)}\,.
	\]
We first aim to lower bound the denominator $\Den$.
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} that $\sphi$ has support $[-\sep,\sep]^3$, and is $\ge \Omega(1)/\sep^3$ on $[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3$. 
From the construction of $\vX^\frozen$ and $\vY^\frozen$
(Definitions \ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:rerand.Ising}), we see that $\varrho_t$ gives measure at least $\Omega( \sep^3 /\trK^{O(1)} )$ to any box of side length $\sep$ contained in $[-2\trK,2\trK]^3$. It follows that, for all $\vy\in[-2\trK+1,2\trK-1]^3$,
	\[
	\varrho_t*\sphi(\vy)
	\ge \int_{[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3}
		\sphi(\vy-\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}\,.
	\]
Integrating over $\vy\in H(y)$ (as defined by \eqref{e:hspace.y}) gives
	\beq
	\Den(t,y)
	= \overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}
	\eeq
for all $y\in[-5\trK,5\trK]$. Next note that since particles outside $[-\trK,\trK]^3$ are frozen (see Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the numerator $\Num(t,y)$ must be zero for $y\notin[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$. For $y\in[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$, we bound
	\begin{align*}
	|\Num(t,y)|
	&=\Big|\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\Big|
	=\bigg| \int_{H(y)}
	\int_{\R^3} \sphi(\vy-\vx)B(t,\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx) \,d\vy\bigg|\\
	&=\bigg| \int_{\R^3}
	B(t,\vx) \overline{\sphi}(y-(\underline{1},\vx))\,\varrho_t(d\vx)\bigg|
	\le \|\overline{\sphi}\|_\infty \cdot \int_{\R^3}
	|B(t,\vx)|\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le  \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last step uses the quenched moment bound on $\bbb$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.I.second.quenched}, together with the bound $(p^N)' \le  L^2$ from \eqref{e:sdelimits.pprime}. Combining with \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} gives
	\[\|\sB\|_\infty 
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}
		{\sep}
		\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,.
	\]
We can also apply \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} to obtain
	\beq
	\Big|\partial_y \tilde{B}(t,y)\Big|
	\le \trK^{O(1)}
	\bigg|
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)
	- \tilde{B}(t,y)
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Den(t,y)
	\bigg|\,.\eeq
The first term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be bounded by
	\begin{align*}
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)\bigg|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	=\bigg| 
	\int_{\R^3} B(t,\vx)
	\overline{\sphi}' (y-(\vec{1},\vx))
	\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\bigg|\\
	&\le
	\|\overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty
	\int_{\R^3} | B(t,\vx) | \,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \MAX_N\,.
	\end{align*}
The second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be controlled using the preceding bound on $\tilde{B}$, together with a similar  calculation as above:
	\[
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
		\Den(t,y) \bigg|
	=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	\le  \| \overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty \cdot
	\int_{\R^3} \varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \frac{1}{\sep^{O(1)} }\,.
	\]
Combining the above gives the claimed bound on $\partial_y \sB$.
The bounds on $\sV$, $\sU$, $\srrr$, and $\swww$ follow by the same argument, using the quenched moment bounds from Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched}.
